Multi-language — Unit names and permission display names are all in the database. Whether they need translation columns is unanswered.

docs.title: H-0 ✅ Closed — the medical record was cited everywhere and defined nowhere, and it turns out there was nothing to define
docs.text:
Found while starting the health-records module, and it changes what that module is. Sentences across five files discuss who may read the medical record as though it were a table:

Where What it says §H, this file, Health records row "a view guardian already sees them" E-7 "a guardian either sees everything about the child or nothing" permission-catalog §9 a view guardian "reaches the fee history and the health record" data-model/08 §7 "the medical file, which no event permission reaches" data-model/04 §2 the case the old codes existed for is "access to medical information"

No document defines one. There is no health or medical entity in any data-model file and no box in the ERD. The only thing that ever had a medical shape in this model was a medical_form requirement code, and D-044 deleted that table. So the referent is a habit of speech inherited from the old dependent.medical.* permission codes, which named a sub-resource of a table that was itself removed with D-074.

What this does to the arguments built on it — most of them survive, one does not.

  • E-7 stands, and is sharper than it looked. "One right level cannot separate the medical record from the profile" is still true about a record that does not exist: it says the guardian model has no granularity to offer whenever something sensitive is later attached to a person. That is a real finding about the model, not about a table.
  • "No event permission reaches the medical record" is true but empty. Nothing reaches it, because nothing is there. The paragraph in 08-events that leans on this to reassure is right about permissions and wrong about the risk: the only health data the system actually holds today is in event_answer.value — free text typed into a form, read by whoever runs the event, with no retention policy (EV-2). The sensitive data is in the weakest place, not the strongest.
  • "A view guardian already sees them" is simply false, and was written as a reason not to design the module early. It is replaced by the question below.

The question, before any field is designed. What is a health record in this system? Not "which fields" — the shape. Three coherent answers, and they imply different systems:

  1. Structured entries (allergy, medication, condition, instruction) — queryable, so "who in this unit has a nut allergy" is answerable, and the price is that the organization is now a custodian of diagnosable data with everything that implies.
  2. Documents only — a scanned form filed against the person, using the document scope that already exists in the catalog. Cheap, legally simple, and useless in an emergency, because nobody reads a PDF at 23:00 in a tent.
  3. Hybrid — a small set of structured, actionable entries plus documents behind them for anything a form can hold. This is what organizations actually do on paper, and the option the rest of the corpus seems to assume.

Why this is H-0 and not a row in the table. Every other open question about health — who may read it, whether the guardian default changes, what event organizers get, how long answers survive, whether E-7 needs its exception — takes a different answer depending on this one. It is also the only module whose absence is already load-bearing: two documents cite the medical record's protections in order to argue that something else is safe.

Answered (round 7), by rejecting the framing. You answered the three-way question with a fourth answer: "I consider everything apart from name, gender and age a 'medical record'. It is fields in the database, not files." So the referent was not missing — the category was missing, and the phrase in those five files was groping at a distinction nobody makes: there is no medical record inside the person record, because the person record is the thing, and it is fields. Recorded as D-083, with the shape of the layer in D-084 and the boundary in D-085. The three options above are recorded nowhere else, which is right: they were the shape of the question, not the shape of the answer.

See: section Ga, data-model/09-attributes.md.

docs.title: MSG-1 ✅ Closed — a direct message to a minor is mirrored to their guardians
docs.text:
Raised by D-077, which declined the restriction rather than forgetting it.

The situation. Messaging has two sender tiers — direct, which everyone may do, and broadcast, which is a permission. Neither tier mentions age. So any person with an account may send a private message to any child with an account, and nothing in the model prevents it, records it as unusual, or tells anyone. This is not a gap created by oversight: the question asked whether staff may address a child or only their guardians, and the answer replaced it with a model in which age is not a sender concept at all. The rule the communication section had promised — "a rule against contacting minors directly" — is therefore not implemented, and it is worth being blunt that this is the most consequential unanswered question in the file.

Why restricting senders is the wrong fix here. An age branch in the resolver is what D-070 refused for events, on the grounds that a condition evaluated at check time which the capability model does not know about becomes the first rule in a rule engine nobody wants. It would also be the kind of restriction that gets loosened the first time it inconveniences a leader, and a permission that is routinely bypassed on a messaging system is worse than none, because it makes the bypass normal.

Recommendation — restrict visibility, not permission. Mirror direct messages reaching a minor to that minor's guardians, and make the mirroring visible to the sender. Then:

  • nothing is blocked, so the resolver still has no age branch;
  • nothing is secretly unread, which is the actual safeguarding property;
  • it is built on the guardianship rows the organization already maintains, so it needs no new authority concept;
  • and it degrades honestly — a child with no guardian on record gets no mirroring, which is the same safeguarding gap check 4 in data-model/04 §6 already alerts on, arriving through a second channel.

The variant to reject. "Only guardians and unit leaders may message a child." That is the restriction wearing the visibility recommendation's clothes: it is a sender rule, it needs the age branch, and it silently tells a child that the adult messaging them has been vetted — which the model does not establish, and the organization records no background checks (D-043).

Answered (round 6): the recommendation is adopted, as D-082 — mirror to guardians, tell the sender, block nothing. Three details were settled with it, because "mirror it to the guardians" does not by itself say who the guardians are to this message:

  • Which guardians. Those whose right level is view or write. A guardian at none receives nothing: none is the organization having already decided that this party sees nothing about the child, and a safeguarding rule is not a licence to undo a recorded decision by side effect. A minor whose guardians are all none is therefore reported with the minors who have no guardian at all — otherwise the exclusion would be a way to make a child silently unwatched.
  • Which set, as of when. The guardianships open at the moment the message is sent, frozen into the delivery. A guardianship closed afterwards does not lose its mirror, and a guardian added later does not acquire old threads — same discipline as 06-audit §2, which keeps the trail answering "what was true then".
  • Broadcast is not mirrored. A scoped broadcast is already addressed to a set, recorded, and attributable; mirroring exists for the private case, which is the one that can be invisible.

What mirroring is not. Not approval, not a gate, and not evidence anyone read it. It buys the one property the safeguarding argument actually needs — no private conversation about a child is secretly unread — without putting an age into the resolver.

See: D-082, permission-catalog's message row, glossary — Mirroring.

docs.title: R. Resolved — moved to the decision log
docs.text:
Kept here so a reader of this file knows the question was asked and where the answer lives, rather than finding it silently deleted.

Was Question Settled by In one line A-1 The organizational structure D-035 One root; all sub-units nest arbitrarily beneath it. A-1 The unit type vocabulary D-054 Not seeded — org_unit_type is runtime data; only the root type ships. B-1 How much legacy data, in what shape? D-056 Large, with legacy member numbers — exact matches, so review is a work queue. D-9 Is household load-bearing at all? D-057 No — removed entirely. Addresses are temporal person_contact rows. F-1 Which permissions and roles does the organization need? D-055 The catalog stays large and granular; it is a menu, not a checklist. — Eligibility for an event — a separate rule engine? D-060 No — eligibility is capability. event.register_self at contribute, via audiences. — Is unanswered a stored attendance value? D-059 No — absence of a row. Two stored values: attending, not_attending. — Is a weekly meeting an event? D-058 No — it is unit_participation. No recurrence, no series table. — One owning unit per event, or several? D-058 Exactly one. A joint camp is one unit's event another unit participates in. — Are organizers a grant or a roster? D-062 A roster on the event — labelled and ordered. Grants stay separate. — Do unit roles reach the unit's own events? D-063 Yes — an event is an artifact of its unit, not a child. Not inheritance (D-031 stands). — Does an event have a status (draft, published)? D-064 No status column. Visibility is the permission model; cancellation is a fact. — What happens when a full event gets another registration? D-065 Waitlisted for self-service; admitted for organizers; the overrun reported. — Does paying confirm a place? D-066 Yes when the event has a fee; most events are free and confirm immediately. — Do organizers record who actually came? D-067 Yes — was_present, three-valued. It is the "who was in our care" record. — May an event form collect medical detail? D-061 Effectively yes: answers are read by that event's organizers, and no event permission reaches the health record, so the form is the only route for a camp leader to learn an allergy at all. A recorded widening, restated after D-074 removed the namespace the original wording relied on. A-2 Permissions conditioned on membership status D-039 Yes, enforced by the resolver, with guardianship and ownership carved out. A-3 Activate on payment or on approval? D-040 On payment; the fee expires yearly and a dated renewal window replaces a grace status. A-4 Background checks D-043 None are recorded in this system. A-4 The expiry date D-047 1 January; the organizational year runs with the calendar. A-4 The renewal window length D-048 60 days, stored as a parameter rather than compiled in. C-1 May the root read into its sub-units? D-049 No. scope_exposure is the only crossing; no reporting channel is built. D-6 How may the membership gate be waived? D-051 A person-level system.gate_exempt permission, in addition to the role flag. D-7 The root participation row at renewal D-050 Extended across the renewed period; one row, no gap. B-3 (part) Erasure: what shape? your answer, round 5 Redact the person, keep the financial and membership skeleton. (The retention policy is still open — see B-3.) C-1 (largely) Organization-wide operational roles without downward inheritance D-035 The problem dissolves: the root owns the registry and the fees. What remains is a reporting question — see C-1. C-2 May units be reparented retroactively? D-036 Not at all — a unit that moves is a new unit. D-1 Fee per person or per household? D-037 Per person, flat, yearly. D-2 One open membership, or several of different types? D-037, D-041 One type, so one open membership, enforced person-wide. D-3 Age-out timing D-038 Retired — there is no age-out. D-4 Child → adult transition D-038 Retired — there are no membership categories to transition between. D-5 Membership type vocabulary D-037 One type, member; counselor is a position, not a type. E-1 Default rights when a guardianship is created D-046 write for a self-registered child's guardian; view for staff-created and imported rows; chosen at creation when recorded manually. D-074 turned the answer from a code bundle into one level, which is why the decision still stands on its original wording. F-2 Polymorphic scope_id vs a grantable_item supertable your answer, round 6 Polymorphic — scope_type plus scope_id, as currently designed. — The bulk scope-exposure tool D-045 Removed once audiences existed to cover the case it was for. — What a membership request must contain D-044 Identity and the fee. The whole requirement mechanism is gone. — Whether grants may target groups D-042 Yes — built-in rule-evaluated audiences plus admin-managed named groups. E-2 What happens to guardianship at majority? D-069 Nothing — no job, no queue, no computed date. A person ends the row. (Reverses D-024.) F-3 Must a high-authority role assignment have an end date? D-071 No. The membership gate plus a human review report; the earlier "yes" recommendation is withdrawn. F-4 Should person.admin subsume merge and redact? D-068 Moot — there are no per-resource admin permissions. The choice moved into reviewable role contents. (Reverses D-007.) — Should every resource expose an admin permission? D-068 No. Sixteen codes and the resolver's prefix match are gone; roles are the bundle. EV-1 Does an event need an age ceiling? D-070 No. The grant is the rule; a future ceiling would be a built-in audience, not a column. EV-5 Should event.manage_participants split? this round Yes — event.presence.mark at contribute, one level below the roster.

docs.title: How to answer
docs.text:
The blocking set is now empty. Four rounds have cleared every question that was holding the schema still, so nothing here has to be answered before implementation could start.

What remains is genuinely deferrable, and the most useful next ones are:

  1. F-5 — which built-in audiences are needed, and whether parameterised ones are seeded per instance or created on demand
  2. F-3 — should high-authority role assignments require a valid_to?
  3. E-2 / E-4 — guardianship at majority, and confirming the gate's guardianship carve-out is intended
  4. B-2 / B-3 — merge chains, and the retention policy (the latter needs legal input, not design)

Everything else can be answered as we go. The schema is built so that most answers change data rather than structure — which is why the four above are worth a moment and the rest are not.

Answered in round 4: the unit type vocabulary (A-1 — not seeded, D-054); the permission catalog (F-1 — comprehensive and granular on purpose, D-055); the legacy corpus (B-1 — large, with member numbers, D-056); and household (D-9 — removed entirely, D-057). All four are in § R with links to the decisions that settled them.

Answered in round 3, for reference: the organizational calendar (A-4 — 1 January, 60 days); the root's read access into sub-units (C-1 — scope_exposure only); the membership gate's waiver (D-6 — a person-level permission, in addition to the role flag); and the root participation row at renewal (D-7 — extended).

docs.title: Appendix — Entity Relationship Diagrams
docs.text:
This appendix describes relationships — what points at what, how many, and whether the link is temporal. Field-level definitions live in the data-model documents, each in the one that owns the entity, and are deliberately not repeated here.

Diagrams of the schema in ../data-model/00-conventions.md. Split by subject area so each stays readable; the areas connect through person, which appears in all of them.

Notation: → is a foreign key pointing at the referenced table. ⇒ is a polymorphic reference (no database-level foreign key). Temporal tables are marked [T].

docs.title: 1a. Personal attributes — everything that is not a name, a gender or an age
docs.text:
┌────────────────────────────────────┐
        │        attribute_definition        │
        │  code, label, description          │
        │  value_type ← rendering, not law   │      ┌────────────────────────────┐
        │  value_unit, sort_order            │◄─────│      attribute_option      │
        │  allow_multiple                    │      │  definition_id             │
        │  status: proposed | live | retired │      │  code, label, sort_order   │
        │  category  ← grouping ONLY         │      │  status                    │
        │  proposed_by, proposed_at          │      └───────────┬────────────────┘
        │  retired_at, retired_reason        │
        └───────┬────────────────────────────┘
                │                                               │
                │                    ┌──────────────────────────┘
                │                    │
                ▼                    ▼
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │               person_attribute               │
    │  person_id → person                          │
    │  attribute_definition_id                     │
    │  value_option_id      (a `one_of` choice)    │
    │  value  ← always TEXT                        │
    │  recorded_note, source                       │
    │  created_at/_by = recorded at/by             │
    │  NO valid_from / valid_to   ← (D-085)        │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key point: these three tables are the whole of what the system knows about a person beyond name, gender and age. There is no health table beside them and no privileged corner inside them: D-083 removed the category and D-084 put an organization-maintained vocabulary in its place. Reading is person.view, writing is person.edit, and only the vocabulary needs a code of its own (attribute.define). Fields and rules: ../data-model/09-attributes.md.

None of the three is [T], and the no beside them in §7 is a decision, not an omission. A person_attribute row is the current belief, overwritten in place, and audit_log holds the sequence of beliefs, values included — which is why the trail is guarded as person data is (the permission catalog §8). This corpus gives periods to things that are true over an interval — a membership, an address, a position, a guardian's authority — and a descriptive value is not one of those: it is a statement made now about whatever it is about, with a timestamp on the assertion. A valid_from here would ask a volunteer when an allergy began, which is a question the organization is not competent to record and has no rule that could use (D-085). The cost is named rather than left out: the history of a value lives in the one control D-081 calls the corpus's weakest, and §7 lists it as the accepted risk. It is also a deliberate departure from guardianship two sections below, which keeps its current value and its history in business tables — because authority is asked "what was it on that date?" as a routine part of answering whether an act was permitted, and an allergy list is not.

The two vocabulary tables are non-temporal for a smaller reason of their own: a code leaves service by status, not by a period, so a value recorded against a retired option keeps meaning what it meant on the day it was chosen. Retiring therefore never touches a fact — only redacting a person erases one (../domain/08-person-data.md).

  ┌──────────────────────────┐

Three points that matter:

  • membership_request has two person references: person_id (the child, who would become a member) and submitted_by_person_id (the parent, who applied). Collapsing them makes the audit trail false.
  • unit_participation.person_id points at person, not membership. This is the deliberate trade-off that makes the 1990s import possible — an imported roster records who took part, and frequently no membership row exists to point at: ../data-model/03-membership.md.
  • membership_type exists with exactly one row, and category, min_age, max_age and requires_background_check are all gone. Membership is ageless (D-038); age is read from person.birth_date where it matters, which is guardianship and position eligibility, not membership.

Authority is per guardianship row, and since D-074 that row carries one value — none, view or write — so a parent may write one child's records and only read another's. See ../data-model/04-relationships.md.

                                      grant)          grant)          grant)

                                                                              membership → the
                                                                              role grants nothing,
                                                                              unless the role
                                                                              opts out.

Key points:

  • role_assignment and access_grant are the same idea at two granularities: authority held for a period, in a scope, granted by someone. They share scope_type, the level model, and the resolver.
  • There is no wildcard permission. A check for X.y needs an exact grant of X.y, or system.admin. The old <resource>.admin prefix match was removed with its sixteen codes (D-068, reversing D-007); "can do everything about events" is a role listing all thirteen event.* codes. Note access_level.admin (rank 40) is a grant level and survives — same word, different mechanism.
  • Deny is absolute. An explicit revoked at any scope is checked first and beats everything — including the admin level, ownership, and guardianship. "Most specific scope wins" applies only to allows (step 3).
  • The guardianship channel is entered by shape, not by permission name (D-079): the check is about someone other than the actor, and the channel answers with allows only. A sufficient right_level returns true; no row, none, or too low a level returns nothing at all and the actor's own grants are tried. A prohibition is therefore a revoked grant, never a low level.
  • Authority never inherits downward. A role assigned over a parent unit does not cover its sub-units. unit_ancestors() is not called by the resolver at all. A sub-unit's authority reaches outward only through a scope_exposure row, and the row is written by the sub-unit granting coverage over itself — the crossing is offered from below, never imposed from above. The sole exception is system_admin. But note what the root owns: the person registry, the memberships and the fees live at the root unit, so an organization-scoped role acting on them is working at its own scope, not reaching down (D-035).
  • The membership gate sits on the role tier and nowhere else (D-039). Ownership and guardianship return before it, which is what keeps a lapsed person able to reach their own renewal screen and a lapsed parent able to act for their child. Tiers a–c are not gated: a grant is an explicit act, not an inherited one.
  • A grantee may be an audience. access_grant.person_id and audience_id are mutually exclusive. Built-in audiences (everyone, all_members, the participants of a unit) are rules evaluated at check time; named groups are stored lists and carry the stale-group problem knowingly (D-042).
  • scope_exposure points at a specific role_assignment, not at a role, so coverage is per-person and expires with the assignment. There is no bulk tool and no bulk: marker (D-045). The role tier is the table's only consumer: an exposure extends an assignment, and a direct access_grant carries no assignment for one to attach to, so the unit-grant tier matches exactly and stops (D-078).
  • scope_id is polymorphic (no FK) so a new grantable item type is a config row, not a migration. Accepted cost, with mandatory mitigations.

See ../data-model/05-authorization.md and ../domain/06-authorization-model.md.

docs.title: 6. Temporal pattern, illustrated
docs.text:
Every [T] table above uses the same shape. The returning-member case shows why:

person 100 — Jan Novák
│
├─ membership #1   member   1990-09-01 ──────────────► 2010-06-30   terminated
│    unit_participation  Pack 12  1990-09-01 ──────► 1998-06-30
│    unit_participation  Pack 31  1998-09-01 ──────────────► 2010-06-30
│
│      ← 14-year gap, no rows. Visible as data, not inferred. →
│
├─ membership #2   member   2024-10-01 ──────────────► NULL (open, current)
│    unit_participation  [ROOT]    2024-10-01 ──────► NULL   ← created with the
│    unit_participation  Pack 5    2024-10-01 ──────► NULL     membership, so the
│    position_assignment  scoutmaster, Pack 5  2025-01-01 ──► NULL   roster is uniform
│    role_assignment  unit_leader @ Pack 5     2025-01-01 ──► 2025-12-31
│                      (requires_membership = false → survives a lapse, D-039;
│                       the person-level alternative is system.gate_exempt, D-051)
│
├─ guardianship → child A    2015-03-01 ──────────► NULL
│    guardianship_permission  right_level = write      (source='self' → write)
└─ guardianship → child B    2018-07-01 ──────────► NULL
     guardianship_permission  right_level = view       (court-restricted)

Note the two membership rows have the same type. They differ only in period and end reason — this person was a member twice, and was a child and then an adult throughout. The old diagram called them child and adult; that was the framing the ageless decision replaced (D-038).

Questions this shape supports, all of which fail against a design with person.is_member:

  • Was this person a member on 1998-06-01?
  • How many years of membership, excluding the gap?
  • Which unit were they in during 2003?
  • How old were they when they joined the second time? — answered from person.birth_date, which the membership rows never copy.
  • Who are the returning members — more than one membership with a gap between?

Every one of them is answered as of a date, and an as-of date must be applied to every join in the answer, not only to the root row — a period joined without it leaks the present into the past. That is what the [T] marking on the tables above exists to make visible.

docs.title: 7. Table inventory
docs.text:
One entry per entity: what it is, what it references, how many may exist, and whether it is temporal. ⇒ marks a polymorphic reference with no foreign key. Entries that exist only to join two other entities say so.

Read the [T] column as a decision, not a default. A no is normally a lookup table, a definition, or an append-only trail — the kinds of thing that have no period to carry. Exactly one no in this inventory is a choice about a person's data rather than a lack of one: person_attribute, and the reason is written out under its own block below and in §1a.

Identity

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] person The human being. Holds identity only — no status, no role, no membership Nothing, except itself: merged_into_person_id ⇒ self One per human, effectively; a merged row survives as a tombstone and is never deleted no person_name One name a person has had, and when person Many per person; one current row per name_type yes account The ability to log in. Optional, and independent of membership person Zero or many per person over a lifetime; at most one live row no account_credential One authentication method's secret or external handle account — deliberately not person Many per account; one current row per external issuer and reference pair yes person_contact An email, phone or postal address, as a dated row rather than a column person Many per person; one current primary per type and purpose yes person_identifier An identifier issued outside the system person; identifier_scheme for its scheme Many per person; (scheme, value) unique among current rows yes identifier_scheme The vocabulary of identifier schemes Nothing Lookup table, one row per scheme no identity_hypothesis A proposal that two person rows are the same human person twice; the reviewer is a person At most one live hypothesis per pair; a rejected pair may be re-proposed no person_merge The record that one row was absorbed into another, and how to undo it person twice; identity_hypothesis, optional One per merge performed; a reversal is recorded on the same row no field_conflict One value a merge could not decide between two candidates — raised for either half of the record, an identity field or a descriptive value (§1a) person_merge; ⇒ (entity_table, entity_id) — polymorphic by nature Many per merge no

Personal attributes — everything known about a person other than name, gender and age (§1a)

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] attribute_definition One thing the organization collects about people: the code, its label, its type, and whether several values may be current at once Nothing One code per normalized spelling — Allergy and allergy are one row; statuses proposed, live, retired, and retiring keeps the row and its values no attribute_option One allowed value of a one_of definition attribute_definition One row per code per definition; a retired option is never re-meaning, because values stored against it are historical facts no person_attribute The value one person currently has for one code person, attribute_definition, and attribute_option when the type is one_of One current row per person and code; more only where the definition sets allow_multiple, which no constraint can check (it reads another table) no — deliberately

That last no is the decision, and it is the reason this row spells it out. Values are overwritten in place and audit_log — carrying the values themselves — is the only history: this is the one place in the schema where "what did we believe in 2019?" is answered from the trail rather than from business data, and D-081 records the trail as discipline rather than guarantee. The trade was made with that in view and is reversible in one entry (D-085, ../data-model/09-attributes.md §3). The two vocabulary tables carry status instead of periods, which is what lets a code be retired without touching a fact; only redacting a person erases values, and a redacted person still holding attribute rows, or still having their values readable in the trail, means the redaction did not happen (../data-model/09-attributes.md §8).

Organization

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] org_unit_type The organization's own vocabulary of kinds of unit Nothing One current row per code; retired rows keep theirs yes org_unit_type_rule Join entity: one permitted parent-type / child-type pairing, and nothing else org_unit_type at both ends At most one live rule per pair yes org_unit A unit — the root, or anything nested beneath it to any depth org_unit_type; org_unit as parent, which is immutable once set Exactly one unit at the root, over all rows; children unlimited yes org_unit_name One name or code a unit has carried org_unit Many per unit; exactly one current, and org_unit.name copies it yes org_unit_relationship A typed lineage between two units — split_from, merged_into, successor_of, renamed_to org_unit twice As many as the truth requires; the same pair, and the same kind, may repeat no position A defined slot in a kind of unit, filled or not org_unit_type One live code per unit type yes position_assignment A person filling a position in a unit for a period position, org_unit, person Many per position — several holders is the default; never overlapping for the same person and position, over all rows yes

Membership

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] membership_type The fee and renewal parameters. One row, member, kept as a table so the vocabulary can grow Nothing Exactly one row today (D-037) yes membership One period of membership, with its own ending person, membership_type; itself via renewed_from_membership_id Many per person over a lifetime; one open at a time, ever yes membership_request An application. Two person references on purpose: the subject and the submitter person twice, membership_type, org_unit, and membership twice (what it produced, what it renews) At most one open request per person no unit_participation Belonging to one unit — the root's mirror of a membership, or a sub-unit's roster person (not membership — the import case), org_unit Many per person at once; one at a time per unit, over all rows yes

Relationships

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] guardianship One adult's responsibility for one dependent, carrying one right_level person twice — never the same person twice One current row per pair; unlimited past rows; a dependent may have any number of guardians at once yes guardianship_permission The temporal history of that row's right level — not a capability list since D-074 guardianship Exactly one open row per guardianship; its value is what guardianship.right_level copies yes

Authorization

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] permission One coded capability — the only thing a check looks at Nothing One row per code; the code never changes no role A named bundle of permissions. A definition, valid always — the period lives on the assignment Nothing One row per code; a role ever assigned cannot be deleted no role_permission Join entity: this role carries this permission, and nothing else role, permission One row per pair no role_assignment Authority held for a period over a scope — system-wide authority person, role; org_unit when unit-scoped; itself when it is a delegation At most one open assignment per person, role and scope yes scope_exposure A unit granting one named assignment coverage over itself — the only downward crossing org_unit (the grantor), role_assignment (never a role); the people who exposed and withdrew it At most one live exposure per unit and assignment yes access_grant Authority over one item, for a person or for a set of them person or audience, never both; grant_scope_type and ⇒ scope_id; access_level; person when delegated As many as needed; a delegation must carry an end date yes access_level The ordered ladder — revoked, view, contribute, manage, admin Nothing Lookup table, five rows, compared by rank and never by string no grant_scope_type The registry of things a grant may point at, and the table its id lives in Nothing One row per scope kind; every grant's scope_type names one no permission_level Join entity: this permission needs this level on this kind of scope permission, grant_scope_type, access_level One row per permission and scope kind no audience A set of people a grant may name: a built-in rule, or a stored group Nothing directly; resolver_key names the rule a built-in evaluates One row per code among built-ins; named groups carry no code yes audience_member Join entity: a person in a named group, for a period audience, person No overlapping periods per audience and person, over all rows; built-ins have none, being rules yes access_log The audit trail — who did what, by what authority, with what result person as actor and as subject; ⇒ authorization_ref_id across role_assignment, access_grant and guardianship_permission; ⇒ entity_id Append-only; nothing is ever updated or deleted no permission_cache A computed answer kept briefly so checks are cheap person, plus the code and scope it answers for One row per person, code, scope type and scope id, each with an expiry. Derived and disposable — never a source of truth no

Audit and import

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] audit_log The row-level trail of changes to business tables, before and after values included ⇒ (table_name, record_id) — polymorphic; person as actor, and on whose behalf One row per change; append-only no redaction_log That a redaction happened to a person, by whom, and to what person; the person who requested and the person who performed it One per redaction performed no import_batch One arrival of historical data, and where it stands person as creator, applier and reverting party One per batch; staging rows may be truncated once applied no staging_import A raw source row, verbatim, with its file and line import_batch One per source row per batch no staging_import_row That row parsed, plus what the parse could not decide, and what it eventually created staging_import; person as resolver, and the membership and unit_participation rows it produced One per staged row no

Finance (provisional)

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] fee_schedule What may be charged, for what kind of period membership_type and org_unit, both optional — absent means it applies broadly As the organization defines yes fee_obligation What one person owes for exactly one thing person (who it is for), fee_schedule, and exactly one of membership, membership_request, event_registration Many per person; the target is never two and never none no payment Money that arrived person as payer — deliberately not the person the fee is for One per recorded receipt no payment_allocation Join entity: this payment counted towards this obligation, by how much payment, fee_obligation A given payment is allocated to a given obligation at most once no payment_request The ask, carrying the variable symbol that ties a bank transfer back to it fee_obligation — the amount is copied, never recomputed Several per obligation over time; at most one live; the symbol is unique over every symbol ever issued no bank_transaction One incoming transfer as the bank reported it payment_request when matched — absent means it is in the queue; import_batch Unique per bank reference within an account; immutable once imported no

Events

Entity What it is Points at How many [T] event A dated occasion people register for, owned by exactly one unit org_unit — required, exactly one owner (D-049); fee_schedule when it costs money One row per occasion; no recurrence, no series no event_organizer Who is running an event, with a label and an order — an appointment, not a grant event, person Many per event; the list is the domain answer to "who runs this" no event_registration One person's answer about one event, plus whether they turned up event, person One per person per event; unanswered is the absence of a row (D-059) no event_question One thing this event asks, of attendees, organizers or both event As many as the event asks yes event_answer What one person said to one question, stored as a row and not as JSON event_question, event_registration One row per question per person no

Reference vocabularies — reason_code, access_level, grant_scope_type, identifier_scheme, permission, org_unit_type. Each is named by a value held elsewhere rather than pointing at anything, and each exists so that a vocabulary is data the organization can see rather than a list inside the application. attribute_definition is the same kind of thing in spirit and a different shape in fact — it has a curation lifecycle, a child table, and rows pointing back at it — so it is inventoried above rather than here.

event carries no [T] — it has no valid_from / valid_to, because an event is a dated occasion rather than a period-tracked record. Its lifecycle is starts_at / ends_at / cancelled_at, and it has no status column at all (D-064). event_registration likewise stores no period: a person is attending, or they are not, and "unanswered" is the absence of a row (D-059).

Removed since the first draft, listed so the inventory stays honest: requirement_code and membership_request_requirement (nothing gates a request — D-044); unit_membership (renamed unit_participation — D-041); and every background-check structure (D-043).

[T] = temporal, carries valid_from / valid_to. A no says it does not; where the reason for not is a decision about someone's data rather than the nature of the table, the row says so — which in this inventory is person_attribute, and nowhere else.

docs.title: 8. Foreign key summary
docs.text:
Tables with no FK on a column, and why:

Column Why no FK access_grant.scope_id Polymorphic by design. Validated by grant_scope_type + orphan checks. access_log.scope_id Same. access_log.authorization_ref_id Points at one of three grant tables depending on authorization_channel. access_log.entity_id Polymorphic target of the audited action. field_conflict.entity_id Polymorphic; recorded alongside entity_table. audit_log.record_id Polymorphic; recorded alongside table_name.

access_grant.grantee is the one mutual-exclusion rather than missing-FK case: exactly one of person_id / audience_id is set — never both, never neither. The two columns are nullable, so nothing but that rule says which one a grant means; a grant naming neither is meaningless and a grant naming both is ambiguous about whom in the audience it speaks for.

Every other column ending in _id has a real foreign key with ON DELETE RESTRICT. No table anywhere uses ON DELETE CASCADE — see ../data-model/00-conventions.md.

docs.title: Appendix — Permission Catalog
docs.text:
Every permission code, its namespace, and the channel that resolves it.

This is the proposed catalog, seeded in ../data-model/05-authorization.md.

Deliberately comprehensive and granular, and staying that way (D-055). This is a menu, not a checklist. Administrators assign people only the permissions they actually need; that is only possible if the capabilities exist as separate rows to assign. Further permissions arrive with the modules not yet specified — events, documents, communication, reporting (§10).

This is the opposite disposition from roles, and the asymmetry is deliberate. Roles are runtime data the organization invents (D-052); permissions are capabilities the code implements. You cannot assign a power the data model cannot express, so a comprehensive permission catalog costs only rows — while a comprehensive role list would be a specification pretending to be data.

Codes are still stable identifiers: adding one is free, renaming one is a migration (§1). What is not yet settled is the exact contents — tracked in §12.

docs.title: Code shape
docs.text:
<resource>.<action>              e.g.  membership.request.approve
<resource>.<subresource>.<action> e.g.  unit_participation.view

resource is always the first segment and matches permission.resource. Codes are stable identifiers — the display_name may change, the code may not. Renaming a code is a breaking change requiring a migration that rewrites role_permission rows.

docs.title: There is no wildcard, except system.admin
docs.text:
Every capability in this catalog is narrow and explicit. A check for X.y is satisfied by an exact grant of X.y — or by system.admin, which is checked outright and is the only permission in the system that means everything.

A check for 'X.y' is satisfied by: an exact grant of 'X.y', OR 'system.admin'.

There are no per-resource admin permissions. The earlier convention that every resource should expose an <resource>.admin subsuming its narrower codes — a prefix match computed in the resolver — was reversed by D-068, which also deleted the resolver branch that implemented it.

"Someone who can do everything about events" is a role, not a permission — the organization composes it from the thirteen event.* codes. That is the division D-052 already drew: the code implements capabilities, the organization groups them. A per-resource admin was the code guessing at a bundle on the organization's behalf.

The cost, because it is real. A new narrow permission is not automatically covered by roles that should imply it; someone must add it. Integrity check 18 is the safety net the wildcard used to be — it lists permissions no role grants, which is what a missed bundle looks like. It fails closed: a capability goes unheld and somebody says so, rather than a capability going unmeant and nobody saying so.

docs.title: Two things named "admin", which are not the same thing
docs.text:
The word used to be ambiguous three ways. Two rounds of deletion left two, and the third is recorded as deleted rather than quietly dropped:

Shape What it is Status access_level.admin (rank 40) A grant level — how much authority a grant carries, in view < contribute < manage < admin. Used by permission_level to decide whether a given grant satisfies a given permission. Real, untouched system.admin The one wildcard permission: everything, held through a role, never through an item grant Real, untouched <resource>.admin A wildcard permission code implying every sibling on that resource Deleted — all sixteen, by D-068 dependent.medical.admin, dependent.admin An action meaning "edit", paired against .view inside a sub-resource; plus a shorthand for the whole set Deleted — by D-074, which reduced a guardian's rights to none / view / write

D-068 exempted dependent.admin on purpose, and D-074 withdrew the exemption. The reason D-068 kept it was sound at the time: it was not a prefix match inferred by code but a value a person deliberately stored on one row about one child. What changed is not the reasoning about wildcards but the thing it was a value of — there is no longer a set of guardian capabilities for a shorthand to stand for. Read the two decisions together before reinstating anything that spells admin.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Namespace Resolved against Channel NULL role_assignment, access_grant, ownership 1, 3, 4 system role_assignment only — never item grants 4

There is no dependent namespace (D-074); §9 explains what replaced it, and what was lost with it.

That leaves the guardianship channel with no prefix to dispatch on, which has to be answered rather than left implied. It used to route on dependent., and the reason for routing by prefix was that no caller should decide which channel applies — otherwise the same authorization rule gets implemented twice, once correctly. It now routes on a fact about the request instead of a fact about the name: the channel is consulted whenever the person the action is about differs from the person performing it. That is stronger than the prefix rule, not weaker — under the old rule a guardian asking to change their child's address with a person.contact.edit code would not have routed through guardianship at all, because the code did not carry the right prefix. Nobody chooses a channel; the shape of the request selects it.

The guardianship.* codes are additionally satisfiable by being a party to the row, and not only by a grant (D-073).

system permissions remain non-grantable by item grant: system.admin must never be delegable to a single event or to a parent.

docs.title: Sensitivity marker
docs.text:
The Sens. column flags permissions that need extra care:

Mark Meaning ⚠ Granting it exposes personal data ⚠⚠ Granting it exposes children's personal data — or the same about an adult, where the code reads a whole person record rather than one field of it. Since D-083 there is no separate health data class to name: the mark grades what a grant exposes, not which field the code points at 🔒 Granting it confers authority over the permission system itself ⛔ Granting it can end someone's membership or standing

These marks should drive UI warnings and the alerting in ../data-model/05-authorization.md.

docs.title: 2. People and identity
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants person.view — ⚠⚠ See person records — all of them, including every descriptive value person.create — Add a person record person.edit — ⚠ Change person details, including descriptive values person.contact.view — ⚠ See contact points person.contact.edit — ⚠ Change contact points person.merge — 🔒 Confirm identity matches and merge people person.unmerge — 🔒 Reverse a merge person.redact — 🔒 Perform a GDPR-style erasure attribute.define — Curate the vocabulary of descriptive data — create, rename, merge or retire a code

person.merge and person.redact are separated from person.edit deliberately. Both are irreversible in practice and both have privacy consequences far beyond editing a record.

Before D-068, the way to keep them apart was to carve them out of person.admin's prefix match — a special case in the resolver that was invisible in every role editor. Now there is no wildcard to carve out of, and the question moves somewhere reviewable: a role bundling all of person.* reaches them, and you can see it in role_permission. The guidance that replaces the special case is in §11 — no seeded role mixes person.merge or person.redact with routine person.edit, and one that does should be named for what it is. This is now a report a person can read, not a caveat about a resolver rule.

person.background_check.* is gone (D-043). The organization has no background checks handled by this system, so there is nothing to view and nothing to record. If that changes, the permission pair and a dated record with an expires_at are the natural shape — and it would belong here, next to person.*, because a clearance is a fact about a person and not about their membership.

docs.title: Descriptive data: two old codes and one new one
docs.text:
Everything the system knows about a person other than their name, their gender and their age is one class of data, in fields the organization defines while it runs (../domain/08-person-data.md, ../data-model/09-attributes.md, D-083, D-084). The catalog's whole involvement in that is one row added and none removed:

  • Read: person.view. Write: person.edit. That is the entire access story. No read or write code was added for descriptive data, because there is nothing left for one to gate — a code that separated, say, the allergy list from the rest of the record would reinstate the privileged subset D-083 refused on the merits. There is therefore no health.* or medical.* namespace and no per-field access rule, deliberately: category on a definition groups a form and grants nothing. If a narrower tier is ever genuinely needed, the route is a decision entry about a second grant scope over a defined set of data, not a code with a suggestive name.
  • attribute.define is the new one, and it is the narrow one (D-084): it creates, renames, merges and retires a code — deciding what the organization collects, which is what makes the data queryable. Recording a value against a code that does not exist needs no such permission: it saves as a proposed definition and waits in the curation queue. The mark column stays empty for it because it reads nobody's data — the vocabulary is rows about codes, and the values underneath it are reached through person.view like anything else.
  • person.view moved from ⚠ to ⚠⚠, and the reason is the same decision: the marker grades what a grant exposes, and this one now exposes everything known about a child — an allergy list, an insurance number, a note about who the child actually lives with — through a single code that used to be graded as ordinary personal data from when the record was smaller than the person.

person.redact reaches the layer too, and in the opposite direction from retiring a code: retiring one keeps the values, redacting a person erases theirs — in the audit trail as well as in the row, since a trail that still reads out an erased value has preserved it rather than missed it (../data-model/09-attributes.md §6).

docs.title: 3. Accounts
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants account.view — ⚠ See account records account.create — Create an account for someone account.suspend — ⚠ Suspend an account account.close — ⚠ Close an account account.credential.reset — 🔒 Issue a credential reset

account.suspend is not membership.suspend. Suspending a login does not remove someone from the organization; the two are separate lifecycles and separate permissions.

docs.title: 4. Membership
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants membership.view — ⚠ See membership records membership.request.create — Submit an application membership.request.review — ⚠ Read and work an application membership.request.approve — ⛔ Approve or reject an application membership.activate — Activate a membership membership.lapse — ⛔ Lapse a membership (administrative, non-payment) membership.suspend — ⛔ Temporarily suspend a membership membership.terminate — ⛔ End a membership for cause / expel membership.backdate — ⚠ Enter or correct historical membership periods unit_participation.view — ⚠ See who takes part in a sub-unit unit_participation.manage — ⚠ Add, move or end participation

membership.terminate is the most consequential non-system permission in the catalog. A lapse is administrative; a termination is a decision about a person's standing in a youth organization, frequently with safeguarding and reputational consequences. It should be held by very few people, and it must not be implied by membership.lapse. Grant it explicitly, per person.

membership.transfer is gone. "Transfer a member between units" was an artefact of units holding memberships. With participation (D-041), moving between sub-units is unit_participation.manage — close one row, open another — and it does not touch the person's membership at all. There is nothing to transfer.

These permissions are gated by membership when held through a role that requires one (D-039). The gate is a property of the role, not of the permission, so it is not visible in this table — see ../data-model/05-authorization.md §3. The single exception is system.gate_exempt (§7), which is the gate's waiver and is therefore exempt from the gate itself (D-051).

docs.title: 5. Organization and positions
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants org_unit.view — See units org_unit.create — Create a unit org_unit.edit — Edit a unit's details org_unit.rename — Rename or renumber a unit org_unit.restructure — ⚠ Split or merge units org_unit.close — ⚠ Close a unit position.view — See positions position.assign — ⚠ Appoint someone to a position

org_unit.restructure is separated because a split rewrites the answer to historical questions. It is not routine editing. Reparenting is no longer among the things it grants — a unit cannot change parent at all (D-036), so the permission covers splits and mergers and the closing of a unit that "moved".

docs.title: 5a. Scope exposure and audiences
docs.text:
Two mechanisms that had been missing from this catalog while sitting in the seed data and carrying some of the design's weight. Both are now listed, and the first is arguably the most consequential permission in the authorization model.

Code Namespace Sens. Grants scope.expose — 🔒 Expose this unit's scope to a parent unit's role assignment scope.exposure.review — ⚠ See and revoke the exposures made over this unit audience.view — See built-in audiences and named groups audience.manage — ⚠ Create and populate named groups

scope.expose is the only door between unit levels. Authority never inherits downward (D-031), and this permission is the single mechanism that crosses the boundary — so it is graded 🔒 despite being an obscure-sounding code, and it is higher-stakes than several codes with more obvious names.

What makes it safe is who can write it. Every scope_exposure row is written by the unit it covers: a parent unit's officer cannot satisfy it for a child unit, which is what makes the no-inheritance rule enforceable rather than aspirational (D-049). There is no bulk variant (D-045) — every row is a deliberate, individual, attributable decision about one assignment.

audience.manage is the permission that creates a grant target. Whoever holds it can assemble a named list of people which a later access_grant may then address (D-042) — so it is authority over who could be granted, one step removed from granting. Whether it belongs to a dedicated audience_admin or to unit leaders is open (§12).

docs.title: 6. Guardianship
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants guardianship.view — ⚠⚠ See guardianship relationships guardianship.create — ⚠⚠ Record a guardianship guardianship.end — ⚠⚠ End a guardianship guardianship.assign — ⚠⚠ Add another guardian over the same dependent guardianship.change_right — 🔒 Change a guardianship's right_level

These four are the only codes in the catalog that a private individual holds over their own household, without being granted them. D-073 makes the parties to a guardianship principals on the row: a guardian may end it, add another guardian, and change its level; the adult subject may end it over themselves. Staff hold the same codes and are an route, never the route.

guardianship.permission.grant is deleted — it granted individual codes from the dependent.* namespace, and there is no such namespace to grant from (D-074). guardianship.change_right replaces it, and does less: one value, three choices.

docs.title: 7. Permissions administration
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants role.view system See roles and their permissions role.create system 🔒🔒 Create a role role.edit system 🔒🔒 Change what a role grants — takes effect immediately for every holder role.delete system 🔒🔒 Delete a role. Only possible if it was never assigned and is not a system role role.assign system 🔒🔒 Assign a role to a person role.unassign system 🔒 End a role assignment permission.view system See the permission catalog permission.edit system 🔒🔒 Change the permission catalog access_grant.create — ⚠ Create an item grant access_grant.revoke — ⚠ Revoke an item grant system.admin system 🔒🔒 Everything. Single top-level capability. system.gate_exempt system 🔒 Waive the membership gate for this person. Every gated role they hold keeps granting while their fee is unpaid (D-051).

role.assign is the permission to escalate privilege. Whoever holds it can grant themselves system.admin. It must be held by very few people and every assignment must be logged and alerted on. Note that system.admin is deliberately a single top-level permission rather than a per-resource one — concentrating the most dangerous capability and alarming on its holders is safer than scattering equivalents of it.

Roles are runtime data, and these four permissions are how the organization administers them. role.create composes a new permission group; role.edit changes what an existing one grants; role.delete removes one that was created by mistake. The seed roles in §11 are therefore a starting point to be edited, not a fixed vocabulary — which is why §11 no longer claims to answer "which roles carry system.gate_exempt". That is a configuration decision the organization makes at runtime, not one the specification can make for it.

There is no role.retire, and a role cannot be switched off (D-053). A role is a definition and is valid always; the period lives on the assignment. Ending a role's use means ending its assignments, which is role.unassign — one person at a time, or a loop over the holders. This is the right shape: what ends is someone's authority, and that is a fact about a person, not about a definition.

role.edit is a bulk privilege change wearing the clothes of a settings screen. Editing a role's permissions takes effect immediately for every holder, with no assignment touched and no notification. It is marked 🔒🔒 alongside role.assign for that reason. The two are different powers — role.assign escalates one person, role.edit escalates everyone holding the role — and neither is implied by the other.

role.delete only works on a role that has never been assigned and is not is_system. No delete may leave a role_assignment pointing at a role that is gone: ../data-model/05-authorization.md §3 states the guard and the order it refuses in. The two halves are not equally strong, and the difference is the reason this permission is not self-policing. The first is referential integrity — role_assignment.role_id references role.id, which is a migration-level constraint, so it refuses a delete that arrives from an import, from a manual fix, or from a second client as surely as from the screens. The second, is_system, is a property of the row being deleted and no index can see it: it is a check inside the transaction that deletes, and a model-layer guard there is a friendlier message, not the refusal. A role that has been held is left in place, so the answer to "what authority did this person have in 2019?" survives — which is precisely when someone asks it.

access_grant.create is scoped by permission_level: holding it lets you grant others access to items you have admin on, and only at a level at or below your own. Without that restriction, any item-grant holder becomes a universal grantor.

docs.title: 8. Audit and system
docs.text:
Code Namespace Sens. Grants audit.view — ⚠⚠ Read the audit log — including the before/after values it carries, which are person data like any other audit.export — ⚠⚠ Export audit records import.view — ⚠ See import batches import.stage — Stage an import import.apply — 🔒 Apply a staged import import.revert — 🔒 Revert an applied import report.view — ⚠ Run standard reports report.export — ⚠⚠ Export report data

audit.view is graded ⚠⚠, and the reason is a property of the trail rather than of any field it touches. audit_log carries the before and after images of what changed, which makes it a second copy of the person record — descriptive values included, on the same terms as a person_contact or a note change. There is no exclusion list doing that work, and there must not be one: a rule naming the person fields whose values may not be logged is a privileged subset of the record, which is precisely what D-083 refused — and it would hollow out D-085, whose entire justification for overwriting a value in place is that the trail holds the sequence. So reading the trail over a scope is reading person data over that scope, and reading more than person.view shows: the current row is the organization's present belief, the trail is every belief it has held. What protects the trail is therefore the guard on it — scope, this mark, and who is granted it — exactly as the guard on person.view protects the record. The grading rule this applies — the mark follows what a grant exposes, not the table a code names — is D-086, taken during propagation rather than from an answer, and reversible on one line.

The excluded-keys list survives, with a smaller and honest job. Values that must never be logged at all belong on it: credential secrets, tokens, session material. Personal data does not, because personal data is protected by who may read the table, not by a list of its names.

Erasure reaches the payload. A redaction that rewrote the business tables while the erased values stayed readable in the trail is a failed redaction, not a partial one (../data-model/06-audit-and-import.md §2, ../data-model/09-attributes.md §6).

audit.export sits at ⚠⚠ for a reason unrelated to what it reads. An export carries the payload outside every mechanism this catalog governs: scope stops at the file, revoking the grant does not recall the copy, and a later redaction cannot reach it. It is graded by where the data goes, not by what the code is allowed to see.

Whether one permission is enough of a guard for all that is itself open — tracked as AT-4 (../open-questions.md). The grading above is what is settled: the trail is read with the guard of person data, whichever permission or combination of permissions that guard turns out to be.

docs.title: 8a. Events
docs.text:
The per-item grant scope the whole authorization model was built toward. Registration is eligibility — event.register_self at contribute is the rule for who may sign up, and there is no separate eligibility mechanism (D-060).

Code Namespace Sens. Grants event.view — See an event event.create — Create an event event.edit — Change an event's details, dates, capacity event.cancel — ⚠ Cancel an event — keeps registrations, notifies nobody by itself event.organizer.manage — ⚠ Add or remove organizers event.register_self — Register yourself — this is the eligibility rule event.register_other — ⚠ Register someone else (a minor, a walk-in) event.manage_participants — ⚠ Manage the roster — add or remove registrations, work the waitlist, promote event.presence.mark — ⚠ Mark who turned up — nothing else event.answer.view — ⚠⚠ Read registrant answers (tent, dietary, …) — see the note in §8a event.question.manage — ⚠ Define what the event asks event.grant_access — 🔒 Grant access to an event. Requires level admin event.delete — 🔒 Delete an event — only possible with no registrations Permission scope_type required_level event.view event view event.register_self event contribute event.presence.mark event contribute event.edit, event.manage_participants, event.cancel event manage event.grant_access, event.delete event admin

event.presence.mark is split off event.manage_participants on purpose, and it sits a level lower. Marking presence is a task handed to whoever is at the door with a clipboard; managing the roster is a task for the event's leadership. One permission covering both forces the organization to hand the clipboard-holder the ability to delete a child from the camp roster. Splitting it costs two rows and makes the ordinary delegation ordinary — and note the level: presence is contribute, so the volunteer taking the register is somebody with contribute on the event, which is the same bar as being able to register. That is the right bar for the job, and it is not the bar for altering who is coming.

It follows the shape of membership.lapse versus membership.terminate (D-022) — one routine, one consequential — and it is free to add because the catalog is a menu, not a fixed set (D-055). It was previously an open question (EV-5); it is resolved here as a split.

event.register_self at contribute is the whole of D-060. Granting a whole audience contribute on an event is how an open camp is opened, and it is one row: an access_grant scoped to that event, addressed to the all_members audience, at level contribute. One row is the point — nobody is enumerated, so nobody is left out when the roster changes, and nothing has to be re-run when someone joins.

An age-restricted camp is a unit:<id>:participants audience instead. There is no age rule on the event and there will not be one — an open event with an age ceiling is accepted as a risk, on the grounds that a registration-time condition the capability model does not know about is the first rule-engine rule (D-070). If it ever needs closing, the shape is a new built-in audience, not a column.

event.cancel is separated from event.edit deliberately. Cancelling is the most consequential thing anyone does to an event: it affects every registrant, it usually involves money, and it is a decision rather than an edit. It does not notify anyone — that is the communication module's job, and conflating the two makes "who cancelled this, and when?" harder to answer than it should be.

event.delete is on this list and org_unit has no equivalent, because events are the one thing in this data model that can be deleted. A draft event with no registrations is a mistake to be cleaned up; anything else is cancelled, not deleted (D-064). No event with even one registration row may be deleted — Guard 2 in ../data-model/08-events.md §8 is the rule, and cancelling is what to do instead. The obligation is not the permission's to carry: event.delete decides who may ask, and only a migration-level constraint — event_registration.event_id referencing event.id with no cascade — refuses the same delete when it arrives from an import or a hand-written fix instead of a screen. Enforcing this in the model layer alone would leave the record of who was coming deletable by everything except the intended route.

event.answer.view is where D-061 lives. Answers to an event's questions are readable by that event's organizers with no additional gate, because a unit leader holds no guardianship over the children in their unit — guardianship authority belongs to the guardians (§9). That is a deliberate widening and it is recorded as one.

Its premise has since been narrowed, and not by reversing it (D-085). D-061 was written when an event form was the only route by which a camp leader learned a child has a nut allergy, because nothing else was readable. Descriptive data now exists (../domain/08-person-data.md) and a leader holding person.view over that unit reads a recorded allergy there, so the form is the fallback for a fact the organization has not recorded, not the ceiling on what an organizer may know. What survives unchanged is the decision itself, and the discipline below it.

This code is graded ⚠⚠, and it is the second time in this round that the marker followed the content rather than the category. It sat at ⚠ beside a paragraph conceding that the answers under it can be clinical, which is the same mismatch audit.view had one section above: a payload that is children's personal data, graded as though it were logistics. D-083 refuses a class of data more delicate than the rest, so either an adrenaline-pen answer is person data — it is — or the grading on the audit trail was wrong. The raise narrows nothing: D-061 stands, an event's organizers read that event's answers with no additional gate, and all that changed is what a reviewer should notice before ticking the box for a role handed to thirty volunteers.

Which leaves the discipline exactly where it was, and says so plainly: the rule that only preference-level detail belongs on a form is guidance on the form's label and nothing more. No layer enforces it and no layer can: nothing distinguishes "vegetarian" from "carries an adrenaline pen" to a database (../data-model/08-events.md §7). It rests entirely on whoever writes the form — a convention, not a guard, and D-072's own sentence is the right way to read that.

docs.title: 9. There is no dependent.* namespace
docs.text:
Eighteen codes deleted by D-074. A guardian's rights are none, view, or write — one value on the guardianship row, not a capability list. Nothing in this namespace may be reinstated by pattern-matching the old names; there is no set of codes left for a name to stand for.

Old code Became dependent.profile.view, dependent.contact.view, dependent.membership.view, dependent.event.view, dependent.fee.view, dependent.medical.view, dependent.achievement.view, dependent.document.view view — all of them, together. They can no longer be separated dependent.profile.admin, dependent.contact.manage, dependent.medical.admin, dependent.consent.admin write dependent.membership.request, dependent.event.register, dependent.event.answer, dependent.fee.pay, dependent.consent.give write — an act is not a narrower category than an edit dependent.admin Nothing. There is no set left to be a shorthand for

What is lost, stated as plainly as it should be. A court order restricting one parent's access to a child's medical record while leaving everything else in place cannot be expressed. "Read-only, but not the medical file" cannot be expressed. A grandmother granted roster visibility and nothing else is now a view guardian, which reaches the fee history and everything else the system holds about that child. The old namespace existed for exactly these cases, and D-074 traded them for a vocabulary a volunteer treasurer can hold in their head.

The separation was then declined, not merely left unimplemented — and the difference matters to anyone reading this table as a to-do list. D-083 put the court-order story to the organization directly and it was refused on the merits ("medical data is not different in any way"), and the same answer removed the referent: there is no medical record inside the person record to be shut out of, because everything other than name, gender and age is one class of data reached by person.view and governed by the guardian's right level whole (../domain/08-person-data.md). So "read everything except the diagnoses" is not a sentence waiting on a mechanism somebody has yet to build; it is a sentence the organization declined to want, which is why E-7 closed as a dissolved question rather than an answered one. Read the inexpressibility above as settled, not as pending work.

What still holds:

  • write ranks at contribute (20), not manage. A guardian cannot do organization-wide things, and cannot reach a different dependent's records — authority is per guardianship row.
  • The organization-wide deny channel is untouched. A deny still beats any grant, at any scope (D-032), so "this guardian, nothing" remains expressible. What was lost is a narrow deny, not the ability to refuse.
  • A guardianship at none grants literally nothing, so being a guardian still grants nothing by itself — the safeguarding property that motivated the eighteen codes survives without them.
  • Answers to an event's questions are still read through event.answer.view, which is a role-side permission and never was a guardian one (D-061).

If the split turns out to matter in operation it is still a new decision — one grant scope over a defined set of data, argued from the current documents — and not a restoration from this table. E-7 is closed, so reopening it means producing the case that was declined, not finding the code that was deleted.

See ../data-model/04-relationships.md §2 for the value, its defaults by source, and the ladder it is a range of.

docs.title: 10. Deferred namespaces
docs.text:
Placeholders for features you have not specified. Listed so the naming convention is established before anyone invents an inconsistent one.

Resource Permission Notes document document.view, document.create, document.edit, document.delete, document.grant_access fee fee.view, fee.create, fee.waive, fee.refund ⛔ fee.waive and fee.refund are sensitive — hardship waivers must not be visible to unit leaders. payment payment.view, payment.record, payment.reverse report report.finance.view, report.membership.view, report.safeguarding.view ⚠⚠ report.safeguarding.view consent consent.template.edit, consent.record.view message message.send_direct, message.broadcast Decided in shape, undesigned in detail (D-077). Everyone may send direct; broadcast is an ordinary scoped permission, so granted on a unit it reaches that unit and granted organization-wide it reaches everyone. The older send_to_unit / send_to_org pair is replaced by one code at two scopes. Recipient chooses the channel, which is not a permission at all. A direct message to a minor is mirrored to that minor's guardians and the sender is told it will be — no permission, no age branch in the resolver (D-082) partner (namespace) For external organizations, if the model expands.

Generate each resource's permission_level rows at the same time — see ../data-model/05-authorization.md.

docs.title: 11. Roles — proposed seed set
docs.text:
A starting point, not a specification. Roles are runtime data: the organization creates them, composes them from permissions, assigns them, edits what they grant, and deletes the unused ones (§7). This section exists to show the shape of a plausible set, so that the model can be reviewed against something concrete. Do not read a row here as a requirement, and do not expect the list to survive contact with the organization.

Role Scope required Req. Waives gate Key permissions Term system_admin organization — yes system.admin, system.gate_exempt 12 mo registrar organization yes no membership.request.*, membership.activate, person.* (except merge/redact), unit_participation.view (root rows only — see note), import.* 12 mo membership_approver organization yes no membership.request.review, membership.request.approve 12 mo treasurer organization or unit yes no fee.*, payment.*, report.finance.view 12 mo safeguarding_officer organization yes no report.safeguarding.view, membership.terminate 12 mo unit_admin org_unit yes no org_unit.view, unit_participation.view, position.view, org_unit.edit (own unit only) 12 mo unit_leader org_unit no no org_unit.view, unit_participation.view, position.view, event.* (own unit), report.membership.view (own unit) 12 mo assistant_leader org_unit no no Subset of unit_leader 12 mo audience_admin organization or unit yes no audience.view, audience.manage 12 mo identity_reviewer organization yes no person.merge, import.view, import.apply 12 mo auditor organization no no audit.view, audit.export, report.view — read-only, no writes 12 mo

Read the * shorthand as a bundle to be written out, not a wildcard to be relied on. Since D-068 there is no resolver rule that makes person.* mean anything; the notation here is an abbreviation for "every person. code listed in §2", and a real role holds an explicit role_permission row for each. Two consequences for whoever seeds this:

  1. registrar is written as person.* except person.merge and person.redact, and that exclusion is now literal. It used to be a caveat about a wildcard's prefix match. It is now just the rows you do not insert — and it is visible in role_permission, dated, and alarmable. identity_reviewer is the role that does hold person.merge, listed beside it so the difference between the two is legible. A role that bundles a resource including its irreversible codes should be named for that, since nothing else records the choice any more.
  2. unit_leader holding event.* means thirteen explicit rows (§8a), and a fourteenth added later is not in the role until someone adds it. Integrity check 18 surfaces an orphaned permission — one no role grants at all. It does not surface "this role arguably should have had it." That is the cost D-068 accepts, and it lands here, in the seed table, rather than being absorbed silently by the resolver.
  3. auditor is a role that reads the whole person record, and does it without person.view. audit.view is graded ⚠⚠ in §8 precisely because the payload is a second copy of the record, so this row grants a ⚠⚠ read over everything the system has ever believed about a child, dated backwards. Nothing here forbids that — it is a plausible role — but the row must not be described to anyone as "just the logs", and it is scoped and term-limited for the same reason the ⚠⚠ rows above it are.

Req. is role.requires_membership: whether the role stops granting anything when the holder's fee lapses (D-039). The proposals follow one rule — staff-like roles working on the organization's own records require a membership; volunteer-facing roles do not.

Waives gate is the separate, person-level permission system.gate_exempt (D-051). The two columns answer different questions and are not alternatives: Req. = no exempts everyone who holds the role, everywhere; system.gate_exempt exempts a named person across every role they hold. system_admin carries it because on 1 January the sweep lapses every membership including the administrator's — without the exemption, the person who would repair the system loses the ability to use it on the day it breaks.

This table is a starting set, not a specification — and the Waives gate column is the clearest case of why. Roles are runtime data: the organization creates, edits and deletes them (§7). Whether a treasurer or a safeguarding officer should also survive their own lapse is a configuration decision the organization makes in the admin UI, not one this document can settle for it. Only system_admin is marked certain, because the lockout case above is a property of the system rather than a policy preference.

registrar holding unit_participation.view at organization scope is not a bug, and it will be read as one (D-049). Scope is an exact match: the registrar's scope is the root unit, so the role reads the root participation rows — which is what "who is in the organization?" needs (D-041). It does not reach into any pack's roster; that requires the pack to write a scope_exposure. Someone who assumes a parent can see its children will "fix" this by widening the role, and that fix would silently reverse D-049.

Four properties worth noting:
