  1. membership_approver is separate from registrar. Deciding who becomes a member is a different act from processing records. If your organization wants one person to do both, grant both roles — but keep them separately attributable.
  2. safeguarding_officer holds membership.terminate. The permission to end someone's membership sits with the person responsible for safeguarding, not with whoever chases fees. This is deliberate. Note that the role lost person.background_check.* and gained nothing in its place, because the organization records no background checks (D-043).
  3. No role is a guardian. There used to be a rule that no role bundles dependent.*, and the namespace it named no longer exists (D-074). The safeguarding property it protected is the one that survives, restated against the mechanism that now provides it: the guardianship channel is only consulted when the subject of the act is someone else, and it only finds a guardianship row. Leadership is not guardianship, so no role hands anyone a guardian's right over a child — not the right to act for that child, and not the row that decides what the family may see. What a role can now do, and does openly, is read the child's record. That sentence used to be false, and D-083 is why it is not: with no privileged subset inside the person record, a leader granted person.view over their own unit reads the whole of a member's descriptive data, allergy list included (../domain/08-person-data.md). Nothing about leading a unit grants it — no channel opens on its own, and the row that would is explicit, scoped, dated and readable in role_permission. That is also why §2 now grades that code ⚠⚠: the safeguarding review moved from "is there a code we kept out of roles?" to "which roles were given this one?", which is a question the catalog can actually answer. Do not re-derive the old rule as a list of codes to keep out of roles — the rule is about the channel, and there is no code left to quarantine.
  4. unit_leader and assistant_leader are Req. = no. They are held by volunteers, and the failure this prevents is specific: the volunteer whose own fee is unpaid still runs the Thursday meeting, and must not lose their roster the night it lapses. The corresponding position.requires_membership stays true, so the unpaid volunteer shows up on a chase-up report — the report is how the organization notices, the resolver is not how it punishes. See ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §4.

docs.title: 12. Open issues
docs.text:
• The catalog's disposition is settled; its contents are not. It stays comprehensive and granular (D-055), so there is no longer a "prune this down" review to do. What remains is additive: each unbuilt module brings its own permissions as it is specified, and unused rows cost nothing.
  • Req. and Waives gate are configuration, not specification. Both columns are attributes of roles, and roles are runtime data the organization administers (§7). The values shown are reasoned defaults to start from (D-039, D-051); the organization changes them in the admin UI. The one value that is not a preference is system_admin carrying system.gate_exempt — the 1 January lockout is a property of the system, not a policy choice.
  • Whether report.* should be per-report permissions or one report.view with row-level filtering.
  • Whether the organization has roles this catalog does not anticipate (a chaplain, a quartermaster, a camp chief). This is now answerable by the organization itself rather than by a change to the data model and a migration — which is the point of roles being runtime data.
  • Which built-in audiences the organization needs, and who may create named groups — audience_admin is proposed, but it may belong to unit leaders instead (D-042).
  • attribute.define is in the catalog and in no seed role, and that gap is the open half of the design. The permission and its rules are settled (§2); who holds it, and how long a proposed code may sit before it is an embarrassment rather than a queue, are not — tracked as AT-2 in ../open-questions.md. The risk of leaving it unheld is specific and slow: proposals keep arriving through ordinary data entry, and a vocabulary nobody curates stops answering questions while still storing everything (../data-model/09-attributes.md §8).

Resolved and no longer open, kept visible so the reasoning survives: whether person.admin should subsume person.merge and person.redact (moot — there are no per-resource admin permissions at all, and the question moved into reviewable role contents, D-068); whether event.manage_participants should split off presence (it did, into event.presence.mark at contribute — EV-5); the event resource's real permission set (§8a, thirteen codes); whether any permission should require current membership status (yes, via the role — D-039); person.background_check.* (removed — D-043); membership.transfer (obsolete once participation replaced unit membership — D-041); and whether org_unit.restructure includes reparenting (it cannot — D-036).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model Conventions
docs.text:
Read this before reading any other document in this folder. Every entity in this system is described using the patterns here, and the patterns are load-bearing — deviating from them in one table creates bugs that only appear across decades of history.

What this file is, since D-072. It used to be the preamble to a set of CREATE TABLE statements. Those statements are gone — the schema is the ORM's job — and what remains is the part that was never about SQL: the rules about time, identity, deletion and rank that a generated schema will happily violate without noticing. Nothing here is a suggestion. A convention in this folder is a bug that has already happened somewhere, written down.

docs.title: 1. Target platform
docs.text:
Assumption: PostgreSQL 14+, reached through an ORM.

The design relies on four things from the platform, and it is worth being exact about which four, because an ORM hides the list:

  • Range types with an overlap operator (daterange, tstzrange, &&) — for the "no overlapping periods" invariants that the whole temporal model depends on.
  • Exclusion constraints (EXCLUDE USING gist, with btree_gist) — the only way to state "no two open rows may overlap" that survives every possible writer.
  • A structured column type (jsonb) — for match signals, audit diffs, event answers and other semi-structured payloads whose shape is per-row by design.
  • Recursive queries — for the unit hierarchy. Note that this one is only for structure: no authorization path may walk the hierarchy (../domain/06-authorization-model.md).

Native enum types are avoided — see §5.

What the ORM changes, and what it must not be allowed to change: see §6a. Read it before generating the first migration. The short version is that most ORMs cannot emit an exclusion constraint, and the fallback they offer — validation in the model layer — is precisely the mechanism this document has always warned against. Hand-written migrations for those tables are not a deviation from "use the ORM", they are the condition on which it is safe.

If the target turns out not to be PostgreSQL, exclusion constraints become triggers plus periodic consistency reports. That is a materially weaker guarantee and it must be recorded as an accepted decision, not discovered as an outage. Tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: 2. Naming
docs.text:
Object Convention Example Table snake_case, singular person, membership_request Column snake_case valid_from, person_id Primary key id always the same name, so joins read uniformly Foreign key <referenced_table_singular>_id person_id → person.id Boolean is_ / has_ / requires_ prefix is_primary, requires_membership Timestamp <verb>_at created_at, verified_at Date/period valid_from / valid_to never start_date/end_date Junction table <a>_<b> in alphabetical order role_permission, not permission_role Lookup table singular of the vocabulary it is access_level, reason_code Index names the table and what it answers "the open rows for one person", not idx_3

Singular table names are not aesthetic. membership reads correctly in a sentence about one row, which is how most of this system's rules are written; plural table names produce code that says memberships[0].membership_id and reviewers stop reading it.

There is no deleted_at column. Deletion is handled by temporal closure and tombstones, never by a soft-delete flag — see §4.

Naming survives the move to an ORM; it is the one section of this file that the ORM will follow without being told, provided someone wrote these rules into the ORM's own conventions.

docs.title: 3. Primary keys
docs.text:
Every table has a surrogate id. No natural keys as primary keys, ever.

Rationale specific to this project: natural keys here are things like names, old member numbers, and email addresses — all of which change, repeat, and get corrected. A name is not unique (and was less so in 1994). An email address is reused by providers and reassigned between people. A legacy member number may be absent, or duplicated across two source systems. A natural key that turns out to be wrong is a key that must be rewritten, and a rewritten primary key rewrites every historical reference beside it.

The surrogate key is a 64-bit integer, not 32-bit, because this system accumulates rows for decades and because access_grant.scope_id must never run out of room or recycle.

Exception, and it is a security requirement: person.public_id — a separate UUID column, used for every external exposure.

Rationale: access_grant.scope_id is a bare bigint with no foreign key, and ids appear in URLs and exports. Sequential ids leak record counts and — more seriously — let someone enumerate /person/1001, /person/1002 and discover members. Expose public_id in all external interfaces; keep id internal. An ORM that marshals entities by primary key has, by default, published the internal counter.

docs.title: 4. Deletion policy
docs.text:
Nothing is hard-deleted. There is no deleted_at and no delete for business data. Two exceptions are named below — a staging truncate, and one delete that erasure has to make — and both are narrow enough to prove the rule rather than erode it.

Situation Mechanism A period ended Set valid_to A person left the organization Close their membership; the person row remains A grant revoked Set access_grant.valid_to; keep the row Two people merged Tombstone: set merged_into_person_id; row remains A unit closed Set org_unit.valid_to and status = 'closed' GDPR-style erasure requested Redact field values; do not delete rows — see §8. One table is deleted rather than redacted; the exception below names it and why

This is not nostalgia. Historical foreign keys — "who attended this camp in 2003" — must resolve forever. A hard delete breaks the audit trail and, in a youth organization, the safeguarding record.

The first exception: staging tables (staging_import*) may be truncated after a batch is applied, subject to the project's retention policy.

The second exception is not convenience and it should be read as a decision, not an oversight. Redacting a person deletes their person_attribute rows (§8 item 2). Everywhere else in this file, erasure means overwriting a value and keeping the row, because the row is what old references point at. A descriptive value is the one thing that has no row worth keeping: the row is the value — there is no period that closed, no assignment that ended, no id another table cites. Blanking the value instead would leave the shape of a person's erased life behind as a permanent record of it: which codes they had, how many of each, and the dates they were first recorded. Retiring the code is not the answer either, and D-084 is explicit that retirement must never destroy values — retirement is an act about the vocabulary, erasure is an act about the person, and the two point in opposite directions on purpose (09-attributes.md §6). This exception is safe only while nothing references an attribute row, and nothing does today. Should a future table ever point at one — an event question bound to a stored value is the obvious candidate, and it is open as AT-1 — that table must be designed around this rule rather than discovering it, because at that point the delete stops being invisible and becomes the referential integrity problem §9 exists to prevent.

This rule is now carried entirely by discipline, and that is worth saying out loud. A ON DELETE RESTRICT default, a revoke of DELETE from the application role, an ORM whose delete method nobody has ever called — those were enforcement. What remains is an instruction to whoever configures the ORM: deleting business rows is not a feature this system has. Do not wire a "remove" button to an ORM delete call. The audit log will not save you, because it records changes to rows that still exist.

docs.title: 5. Enumerations
docs.text:
Status vocabularies are text with an allowed-value list, not the database's native enum type.

Why, given that native enums are more compact:

  • Adding a value to a native enum is easy; removing or reordering one is painful, and over a 40-year lifespan a status vocabulary will be revised.
  • Native enum ordering is baked in, and the order of states here is meaningful — and it is not the order the type would infer (see below).
  • An allowed-value list is visible in schema introspection and in every migration tool, which makes review and diffing straightforward.

This section used to carry the CREATE TABLE and CHECK syntax that expressed it. D-072 deleted it, and the rule it expressed is unchanged: the vocabulary lives with the entity, the values are closed, and the vocabulary is reviewable without reading application code.

docs.title: Critical rule: status strings are ordered, and the order is not alphabetical
docs.text:
Several status columns have a meaningful progression, and code must compare by rank, never by string. Wherever rank matters there is a lookup table carrying an integer rank, and the one that matters most is this one:

Level Rank Meaning revoked 0 Explicitly denied; overrides all grants view 10 Read only contribute 20 Read and add manage 30 Full control of the item admin 40 Full control including granting access

Gaps of ten are deliberate: insertions between levels (an approve tier between view and contribute) must not require renumbering a stored vocabulary.

Never compare level strings lexicographically. 'admin' < 'contribute' alphabetically. A system that sorts grants by string therefore ranks full control including granting access below read and add — a security bug that produces no error, no failed test, and no log line. This is the single most dangerous sentence in this file, and it is the reason the ladder is data rather than a language feature.

One ladder, every ladder. A guardian's right over a child is none, view, or write, and those map onto this same ladder at 0, 10 and 20 rather than getting a second scale (D-074). Two scales would have to be kept in step and would eventually not be, which is how a guardian ends up able to do more than a manager. When adding any new ordered vocabulary, ask whether it is this ladder wearing a name.

docs.title: 6. The temporal pattern
docs.text:
The pattern behind every period in this system.

entity
  id
  the thing the period is about        e.g. person_id
  valid_from    DATE        NOT NULL
  valid_to      DATE        NULL       -- NULL = still true
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL

docs.title: The four rules
docs.text:
1. valid_to IS NULL means "still true". Not a far-future sentinel date. A sentinel like '9999-12-31' looks convenient and breaks every "is open" check, every range query, and every index on open rows. Do not use one.
  2. Periods are half-open [valid_from, valid_to). A membership ending 2010-06-30 and another starting 2010-06-30 do not overlap. Closed intervals make adjacent periods collide, and you will spend a day debugging it. This rule is invisible in a schema and cannot be inferred from column names; it must be written in whatever the ORM uses to express such a thing, and tested.
  3. Overlap is prevented below the application, not inside it. An import script, a manual data fix, a future API, and a bulk edit all bypass model-layer validation. The invariant must hold for writers that were never written. → §6a.
  4. created_at is audit time, not world time. It is distinct from valid_from — a membership backdated to 1990 during a 2026 import has valid_from = 1990-09-01 and created_at = 2026-…. Never conflate them, and never derive one from the other. A system that sets valid_from from the clock cannot import its own history.

docs.title: Why days, not timestamps
docs.text:
DATE granularity is correct for most periods here: memberships, guardianships, unit assignments, fees and exposures start and end on days. Timestamps invite timezone-dependent boundary bugs on questions like "was this person a member on 1 June?".

Where sub-day precision genuinely matters — session validity, a delegation in force during one meeting — the same pattern uses timestamps. Both patterns exist in this system; each entity states which one it uses, because a comparison between the two is where the boundary bugs live.

docs.title: Indexing the pattern
docs.text:
Two access paths carry the load and both must exist when the schema is generated:

  • One entity's periods, newest first — the history view.
  • The open periods for one entity — restricted to rows with no valid_to. This is the index that matters. "Currently active" is the overwhelmingly common question, it stays small because open rows are a small fraction of history, and it is the one an ORM will not create on its own, because it is not an index on a column combination the model declares — it is an index with a condition. If your migrations do not contain a filtered index, nobody thought about this.

docs.title: 6a. Who enforces an invariant now
docs.text:
This section did not exist before D-072. It exists because deleting the constraints moved responsibility, and a moved responsibility that nobody names is a responsibility nobody holds.

Every data-model document in this folder states its rules as prose: "no two open rows may overlap", "at most one primary contact", "a revoked grant must name who revoked it". Prose does not reject a row. Three layers could do it, and they are not equivalent:

Layer Survives an import? Survives a manual fix? Survives a second client? Model-layer validation in the ORM No No No Migration-level database constraint Yes Yes Yes Nightly consistency report Yes, eventually Yes, eventually Yes, eventually

The rule for this system, stated once and applied everywhere: an invariant that is a correctness property of the data belongs in the database, emitted by a migration, even when the ORM cannot generate it and the migration must be written by hand. Model-layer validation is a usability feature — it produces a good error message before a round trip — and it is not an invariant. The nightly report is a safety net for the invariants that were never expressible as a constraint at all, and each document's "Invariants to verify" section is exactly that list.

Three consequences that are easy to get wrong:

  1. The overlap invariants need hand-written migrations on PostgreSQL. Most ORMs cannot emit an exclusion constraint over a range built from two columns. Writing those twenty-odd lines once, per temporal table, is cheaper than the alternative — which is duplicate open rows discovered in 2031 by someone who cannot tell which one was ever real.
  2. Uniqueness that depends on a condition needs a partial unique index. "One open request per person and type", "one primary contact per child among open rows", "one live exposure per unit and assignment" are all this shape. A unique constraint over the unconditioned columns is not the same rule and is usually wrong in the direction of too strict — it forbids the second closed row, which history requires.
  3. Uniqueness decided by data cannot live in an index at all. identifier_scheme.is_unique says per scheme whether a value may repeat (01-identity.md §7); no index can consult a row of a different table. This one is genuinely application-level plus a report, and it is documented as such rather than being pretended away. The earlier version of that document had the opposite bug — an index that applied to every scheme, ignoring the flag and making school_id unrepeatable in fact.

And the honest cost, stated in D-072's own terms: some rules now have no enforcement anywhere automatic can reach. They are written as invariants to verify and they will catch drift only if someone runs them. A prohibition nobody runs is a convention, not a guard.

docs.title: 7. Standard columns
docs.text:
Every business table carries:

Column Kind Purpose id 64-bit surrogate key Set by the database, never by the caller created_at timestamp, required Audit time of insert created_by person, optional Who inserted. Absent for system and import jobs. updated_at timestamp, optional Audit time of last change updated_by person, optional Who last changed it import_batch_id import batch, optional Set on imported rows — the only way to undo a bad import

Temporal entities additionally carry valid_from / valid_to.

Entities that record a decision about a person (terminations, rejections, rejections of identity hypotheses) additionally carry a reason:

Column Kind <verb>_reason_code reference to reason_code <verb>_reason_note free text, for the human explanation

Reason codes are a lookup table, not free text. "Why was this membership terminated?" must be reportable and comparable across years. Free text is not. The note exists so the code does not have to carry the nuance, and a decision with a code and no note is fine while the reverse is not.

updated_at and updated_by were maintained by a database trigger. With the schema generated, nothing maintains them unless someone says so — and an ORM that sets them only on the paths the application happens to take gives you an audit trail that is silently incomplete. Either maintain them at the database level or accept that updated_at means "last changed through the app". Do not leave it undecided; an audit column nobody thinks about is worse than no audit column, because people rely on it.

docs.title: 8. Personal data and erasure
docs.text:
This system holds data about children, which raises the stakes on every decision here.

Requirements the design must satisfy:

  1. A deletion request must not destroy the audit trail. Implement as redaction: set person.redacted_at, overwrite names and contact points with a redaction marker, and keep the row and its ids so historical references still resolve. The person is no longer identifiable; the record that someone was in Troop 12 in 2003 survives.
  2. Redaction must cascade. It reaches contact points, identifiers, and free-text notes that may contain personal data — and it deletes every person_attribute row belonging to the person (09-attributes.md §6). That is the one place in this system where erasure deletes rather than overwrites, and §4 says why it is the only row that can be handled that way. A redacted person with attribute values attached is a redaction that did not happen. A redaction_log records what was redacted and when.
  3. Some data must not be redacted — membership periods, unit memberships, and position assignments are organizational history rather than personal data, and removing them would falsify records that the organization is often obliged to keep.
  4. Whatever keeps its own retention policy must be able to see person.redacted_at, and erasure reaching it is a rule that store has to implement. This item used to read "health and safeguarding records have separate retention rules and are out of scope for this document", which pointed at a body of data that D-083 has since dissolved: a diagnosis is an attribute value now, with the same access, protection and retention as a shoe size (09-attributes.md), so there is no health store left for the sentence to have pointed at. What survives is the other half, and it is worth keeping precisely because it is easy to wave through: audit_log is the store this system has, its retention is an open legal question (06-audit-and-import.md §6), and a redaction that stops at the business tables while the trail keeps the erased values is a redaction that failed in the one place a regulator looks. This section describing erasure does not make a store honour it; the check in that document's §5 is what notices.
  5. Sensitive attributes should not be over-collected. person.gender is included because Scouting-type organizations typically must report it; if yours does not, remove the field rather than keeping it "just in case". The same test now applies per code, since most of what is collected is decided at runtime: a code nobody can justify is retired (09-attributes.md §2), and retirement — which stops the collecting without destroying what was already recorded — is the mechanism. Erasing what was recorded is item 2, and only item 2.
  6. Redaction is invisible in listings and visible in the database. A redacted person must not appear where people are listed, and must still resolve wherever an old record points at them (01-identity.md §9). These two requirements are one rule with two halves and the first version of that document had only one of them.
  7. The trail is a second copy of the person record and has to be guarded like one. For a person's descriptive data the trail holds the value — the before and after image, exactly as it does for a contact point or a note — because D-085 chose overwrite-in-place on the strength of the trail being the history there is, and a trail that records a value existed without recording which one answers neither of the two questions an audit entry is built for (who said this and what did they say). The consequence is therefore about the log rather than about the shape of a row: an audit entry about a person is as sensitive as the person data it carries, which is a requirement on a permission's sensitivity mark and not on anything the schema can express — see 05-authorization.md §9, which argues against copying data into a less-guarded place and describes this table better than it knows: the trail is such a copy, holding the whole person record in its payloads while historically being graded below it. Nothing here makes that guard true; the catalog does, or does not (../appendix/permission-catalog.md §8). The mechanism that implements erasure against this table is in 06-audit-and-import.md §2.2 and its §4, and 09-attributes.md §6 is where the trade is stated next to the values.

Legal review is required before implementing §8. This section describes the technical mechanism, not the compliance policy. Tracked in ../open-questions.md.

The key-name list is not how personal data is protected in the trail, and it helps to say so out loud. The redactor used to be described as the thing that kept personal data out of the audit trail, and it worked by holding a list of sensitive key names — notes, custody_arrangement, and the rest — and stripping any image that carried one. That design presupposed a sensitive subset of the person record, because a list of names is a way of pointing at some fields and not others. D-083 removed the subset, and a list that was standing in for a rule about a category is now a list of arbitrary fields. It fails on the first value stored under a name nobody predicted, and an attribute layer whose whole purpose is that nobody can enumerate its names guarantees one such name every time the organization invents a code — so the list is not the thing keeping personal data out of the trail, and item 7 is. What is left for it is one job, narrow enough that a list can genuinely do it: the values that must never enter the trail at all — credentials, tokens, the secret half of an integration — the only values where being in a log is itself the harm. Personal data is not on that list and does not belong on it: the answer to who may read a child's address was never a list of field names, it is the guard on the table that holds it, and item 7 exists to make that answer cover the table that quotes it. So notes, the reason fields and an attribute value are all logged, in the clear, protected by who may read the log. Read the list as a credential filter and it is a working mechanism; read it as the personal-data filter, notice that allergy is not in it, and conclude the payload is covered — which is wrong in exactly the way described two sentences ago. 09-attributes.md §6 carries the same warning next to the values themselves.

Two mechanisms that used to help here are gone, and they failed in different directions. Redaction of the audit payload was automatic: a trigger stripped listed keys out of the before/after images on their way into the log. There is no trigger now, so what is left of that job — the credential stripping, and the scrub item 2 and item 7 require when a person is erased — is application behaviour, and forgetting the first writes a secret into a table designed to be read later by auditors, while forgetting the second leaves an erased person's values sitting in the trail with a redaction_log row next to them saying they are gone. (Worth recording: inside that trigger was a list of keys to scrub unconditionally, and nothing ever read it. A dead list of forbidden fields is not a protection — and a live one is a mechanism with a far smaller job than the sentences describing it used to imply, which is what the paragraph above is about.) The other half is the listing view that excluded redacted rows, which is §6a's problem in general. Neither failure is loud. Both are written down because a compliance property resting on a code review is the kind of thing an organization discovers from a regulator.

docs.title: 9. Referential integrity rules
docs.text:
Rule Rationale References restrict; none cascade a delete Nothing cascades. A person cannot be removed while memberships reference them. No cascading deletes anywhere Cascade delete is the enemy of a 40-year audit trail, and ORM relation configs default to it. Check every one. Optional references document why they are optional An optional reference is usually a design decision worth recording, and it is invisible in the schema. access_grant.scope_id is the one reference-less key It is polymorphic by design; see ../domain/06-authorization-model.md. Nothing else may be. Circular references are broken with an optional column, not a deferred constraint membership_request ↔ membership is the one instance; the two-step insert is documented where it lives.

The polymorphic access_grant.scope_id deserves its warning again now that the schema is generated: an ORM will want to make this a real relation, and making it one is a design change. It points at a person, a unit, an event or an organization depending on a sibling column. No foreign key can express that, and every query that joins it must filter on scope_type first. If the ORM maps it as a relation to one table, the others become silent wrong answers rather than errors.

docs.title: 10. Migration discipline
docs.text:
• Every migration is reversible, or explicitly marked irreversible with a rationale. A migration that drops a column holding historical data is irreversible by definition.
  • Never rewrite a historical row's meaning. Adding a column is fine; changing what an existing value means is a data migration that needs its own review, and it is the kind of change that makes old audit entries lie.
  • Backfills are separate from schema changes, in their own migration, so a failed backfill does not roll back a schema change and vice versa.
  • Seed data for vocabularies (access_level, permission, org_unit_type, reason_code) lives in migrations, not in application startup code, so the vocabulary is versioned with the data it describes. Application-startup seeding produces environments that disagree about what contribute means.
  • Two documents are the source of truth for what a migration must achieve: each data-model file's Rules block for the constraints, and its Invariants to verify block for the reports. A migration that implements neither set completely has generated a schema, not a design.

docs.title: 11. Where each subject is described
docs.text:
Not "where the DDL lives" — that question stopped meaning anything at D-072. Each document below states the fields, rules, invariants and open issues for its part of the model.

Document Entities 01-identity.md person, person_name, account, account_credential, person_contact, person_identifier, identity_hypothesis, person_merge 02-organization.md org_unit, org_unit_type, org_unit_type_rule, org_unit_name, org_unit_relationship, position, position_assignment 03-membership.md membership, membership_type, membership_request, unit_participation 04-relationships.md guardianship (carrying the guardian's current right_level), guardianship_permission (the history of that value) 05-authorization.md permission, role, role_permission, role_assignment, scope_exposure, access_grant, permission_level, audience, audience_member, access_log 06-audit-and-import.md audit_log, field_conflict, redaction_log, import_batch, staging_import* 07-finance.md fee_schedule, fee_obligation, payment_request, payment, bank_transaction — provisional on policy 08-events.md event, event_organizer, event_registration, event_question, event_answer 09-attributes.md attribute_definition, attribute_option, person_attribute — everything the system knows about a person other than their name, their gender and their age (D-083, D-084). It is last in this table because it is last in every other document's account of a person: it references person and nothing references it

Each document presents its entities in dependency order: one appears only after everything it references. That ordering was needed to make a schema file execute; it is kept because it is also the order in which the model is understandable.

Messaging is not in this table. message and message_recipient are decided at D-077 and not yet designed; they will need their own document. The absence is tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Identity
docs.text:
person, account, contact points, identifiers, identity hypotheses, and merges.

Every pattern referenced here is defined in 00-conventions.md.

docs.title: 1. The central claim
docs.text:
person   ── what the organization knows about a human. No status. No role. No type.
account  ── how that human logs in. Optional. Zero or more over a lifetime.

There is no is_member, member_type, is_child, is_adult, unit_id, or role on person. Each of those is either a period in another table or a derived fact. This is the single most important property of the schema and the one most likely to be undone by a well-meaning future change.

docs.title: 2. person
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only public_id external identifier, required Unique. Generated when the row is created. This is what URLs and exports carry given_name text, required Names are also stored as temporal rows in person_name (§3). These two columns are the current, canonical form, denormalised for display and search; history and legal-name variants live in person_name family_name text, required As above birth_date date, optional Nullable because legacy records frequently lack it. Never required — a 1994 roster with no birth date must still import birth_date_precision text, optional One of: exact, month, year, unknown. Because an imported birth date of 1990-01-01 often means "year 1990, month and day unknown". Storing the precision prevents false matches on a guessed day and prevents "happy 1 January birthday" emails gender text, optional One of: male, female, other, unknown. Included because youth organizations typically must report it. Remove if yours does not need it — do not collect what you cannot justify preferred_name text, optional What the person is actually called. Distinct from given_name so that the organization's records stay legally correct while the person is addressed correctly — "Alexandra" recorded, "Lex" displayed record_origin text, required One of: self_registered, staff_created, legacy_import. Default self_registered data_confidence text, required One of: high, medium, low. Default high. low for imported rows: it drives whether a merge may absorb this row, and whether the UI warns before displaying it as fact merged_into_person_id reference to person, optional Tombstone. When set, this row is absorbed and queries must follow the pointer. Never deleted (§8) merged_at timestamp, audit time, optional redacted_at timestamp, audit time, optional Set when a GDPR-style erasure was performed. Names and contacts are overwritten and the person's person_attribute rows are deleted; the row and its id survive so historical references still resolve (00-conventions §8) notes text, optional Free text about a person, and the only such text that lives outside the attribute vocabulary — see What is deliberately not on this table below. May contain anything, including a diagnosis sitting under a column nobody would call medical. It is logged with its contents, like every other field on this row, and it is deliberately not on the redactor's list — a column named as an exception is the field-name rule D-083 removed, and the protection is the guard on the trail (00-conventions §8 item 7). Whether the column should exist at all is argued below created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional Set on imported rows. Its link to import_batch can only be made once that table exists

Rules

  • There is deliberately no deceased flag. The organization does not record whether a person has died. A membership simply ends; the reason for the ending lives in the generic reason-code fields (membership.termination_reason_code, membership.ended_note) like any other ending, and the organization's own vocabulary for such reasons is theirs to define. Do not add is_deceased or deceased_at back: it is not data the organization keeps.
  • public_id is unique.
  • A person may not be merged into themselves — merged_into_person_id may never name this same row.
  • merged_into_person_id and merged_at are set together or both left null. A pointer with no date, or a date with no pointer, cannot be explained to anyone.
  • A birth_date_precision may be recorded without a birth_date only when it says unknown. Every other precision claims something about a date that is not there.

Indexes

  • Person search by name, with both names compared case-insensitively.
  • Persons by birth_date, restricted to rows that have one.
  • Persons that have not been merged — a partial index, because every ordinary listing must exclude merged rows and it has to stay cheap.
  • Persons that have not been redacted — same reason.
  • Lookup by public_id.

docs.title: Notes on specific choices
docs.text:
birth_date_precision. Without it, a legacy import that only knows the year produces 1990-01-01, which then matches every other year-only record born in 1990 on the same invented day, and sends birthday greetings on 1 January. Cheap column, prevents a whole class of matching noise.

public_id alongside id. External references use public_id. Sequential internal ids appear in access_grant.scope_id and in URLs; exposing them would let anyone enumerate member records. See 00-conventions.md.

merged_into_person_id and redacted_at are both on person rather than in side tables. They are read on every query (every listing must exclude merged and redacted rows from ordinary views), so they need to be cheap. They are also the reason the two partial indexes above exist.

docs.title: What is deliberately not on this table
docs.text:
Everything the system knows about a person other than their name, their gender and their age is a descriptive value in person_attribute, and this table carries no column for any of it — no allergy, no medication, no insurance number, no shoe size, no preferred contact language, no diagnosis (09-attributes.md, D-083). That is not a gap waiting for the next module. An earlier design did put the medical facts on a shelf of their own, behind codes of their own, and the answer that produced D-083 refused the shelf: a drug dosage and a clothing size are the same kind of object — recorded by the organization, wrong in three years, unenumerable in advance — and a permission that reads a person reads the whole record whatever the shelf is called (domain/08-person-data.md).

given_name/family_name/preferred_name, gender and birth_date are the only descriptive facts that are columns here, and they are the last the model will accept. The test for keeping one is not sensitivity — notes sits in the field table above and is a worse exposure than most of what moved out. The test is whether a rule exists that an open layer physically cannot hold. "One current name per person", "exactly one primary postal contact among the open rows", "a school id may repeat, a birth number may not" — each is a constraint over a known set of columns, and a key/value layer has no known set of columns, which is the whole of what it is for. Folding person_name, person_contact or person_identifier into the attribute layer would have relocated four working constraints into application code and been called uniformity (F-10 shape 3). Identity is closed because it was enumerated years ago and has not changed; description is open because nobody can enumerate it (D-085).

The rule cuts both ways, and review is where it is applied. A fact with no such rule behind it does not earn a column here, however reasonable it looks — that is the sentence that keeps is_deceased's cousins out. And a table already in this document does not lose its columns because the new layer looks tidier — that is the sentence that keeps a well-meaning unification of "everything about a person" from quietly turning four enforced rules into four hopes.

One consequence names itself. person.notes is the last free text about a person kept outside the vocabulary, and it is the column a reviewer should ask about: a sentence typed there is invisible to the curation queue, to any report on a code, and to the screen a first aider reads at 23:00, while the same sentence recorded as a value against a proposed code is visible to all three (09-attributes.md §2). Whether the column should exist at all is open and already argued (06-audit-and-import.md §6); what is settled is that it carries no protection the attribute layer does not carry, and less readability.

docs.title: The answer to "who is a member?" is never on this table
docs.text:
To be unambiguous, the two facts:

  • Currently a member — the person has a membership whose valid_to is absent and whose status is active.
  • Was a member on 1998-06-01 — the person has a membership whose period contains that date: valid_from on or before it, and valid_to either absent or after it. Its status is one of active, completed, lapsed, terminated.

Note the second fact includes closed statuses — "was a member in 1998" is true regardless of how the membership later ended. Getting this wrong is why "years of membership" reports are usually wrong.

docs.title: 3. person_name — name history
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required name_type text, required One of: legal, preferred, maiden, former, alias, imported given_name text, required family_name text, required middle_name text, optional valid_from date, optional Optional because an imported name often arrives with no start date at all valid_to date, optional NULL = current for this name_type source text, optional self, staff, legacy_import import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional

Rules

  • valid_to is either absent, or valid_from is absent, or valid_to is later than valid_from.

Indexes

  • A person's names.
  • Fuzzy search across all historical names — both names lowercased, family name first, and usable for prefix matching. This is what legacy matching reads.

Why name history is a table. Three concrete cases:

  1. A member married and changed their family name. The 1998 roster has the maiden name; the 2026 registration has the married name. Legacy matching must find the link, and the historical record must keep the name it actually had.
  2. An imported name has a typo (Novak for Novák). Correcting it must not destroy the imported form, because that is what the paper says and someone will ask.
  3. A person goes by a different name than their legal one. Both must be storable, and which is used where must be deterministic.

person.given_name/family_name are the denormalised current values and are what the UI displays. person_name is the source of truth for matching and for historical queries. This is a deliberate denormalization — the alternative is joining on every list view — and it must be updated in the same transaction whenever the canonical name changes.

Assumption: display should use person.preferred_name ?? person.given_name. If the organization requires legal names on official documents, that rule lives in the document layer, not here.

docs.title: 4. account
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required Not unique. Uniqueness applies only to live accounts, under Rules username text, optional status text, required One of: pending_verification, active, suspended, closed. Default pending_verification verified_at timestamp, audit time, optional guardian_consent_at timestamp, audit time, optional Set when a guardian confirmed a minor's account. NULL for adults (domain/02-actors.md §2) created_by_staff boolean, required Default false last_login_at timestamp, audit time, optional failed_login_count integer, required Default 0 locked_until timestamp, audit time, optional status_reason_code text, optional Why suspended or closed status_note text, optional The human explanation created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person, optional

Rules

  • At most one live account per person: unique over person_id across the rows whose status is pending_verification, active or suspended. Closed rows are not covered, so a person may accumulate as many closed accounts as their history contains.
  • username is unique compared case-insensitively, over the rows that have one and are not closed. A closed account releases its username for someone else to take. It covers live rows only, not all rows.
  • An account may not reach active while verified_at is absent.

Indexes

  • A person's accounts.

Why person_id is not unique. The partial unique index expresses the real rule: one live account per person, while permitting closed historical accounts. A plain UNIQUE (person_id) would make it impossible to close an old account and open a new one — which is exactly the returning-member case at the account level.

Why guardian_consent_at is on account, not person. Consent is about the act of creating login credentials, not about the human. A person who was registered as a child and later reaches majority keeps the same person row; the consent record stays attached to the account it was given for.

A suspended account does not suspend a membership. They are independent lifecycles. The schema enforces this by simply not linking them.

docs.title: 5. account_credential
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id account_id reference to account, required credential_type text, required One of: password, passkey, totp, oauth, staff_link. Multiple methods per account. oauth supports a national Scout identity provider; staff_link supports a one-time link issued to a member who cannot self-serve secret_hash text, optional Password/OTP hash. Absent for passkey and oauth external_ref text, optional OAuth subject id, or WebAuthn credential id external_issuer text, optional OAuth issuer valid_from timestamp, audit time, required Default: now valid_to timestamp, audit time, optional NULL = current last_used_at timestamp, audit time, optional revoked_reason text, optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • A password, totp or staff_link credential must carry a secret_hash. A passkey or oauth credential must carry both external_ref and external_issuer. A credential with nothing to check against cannot exist.
  • valid_to is either absent or later than valid_from.
  • One current credential per (external_issuer, external_ref) pair among oauth rows that are still current. It covers open rows only — an expired credential does not hold its external identity back.

Indexes

  • An account's current credentials — the open half of the period only.
  • The oauth uniqueness above, which is itself a lookup: given an issuer and a subject id, which account is this.

Why credentials are not columns on account. Adding passkeys, an organizational SSO, or a one-time-link flow later must not require restructuring account and migrating every existing password. Keeping secret_hash off the account table also means the common "show me the user" query never touches credential material.

valid_to on a credential is how password history and revocation are expressed. A revoked credential stays as a row, so "was this account ever accessed with a credential that has since been revoked?" is answerable.

docs.title: 6. person_contact
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required contact_type text, required One of: email, phone, postal, website, messaging purpose text, required One of: login, membership, emergency, billing, guardian, general value text, required Normalised per type: emails lowercased, phones E.164, postal as structured JSON value_detail free-form jsonb, optional For postal addresses: {street, city, postal_code, country}. Avoids six optional fields that only apply to one contact_type label text, optional home, work, school — display only is_primary boolean, required Default false verified_at timestamp, audit time, optional verified_by text, optional One of: self, staff, bounce_check, import valid_from date, required Default: today valid_to date, optional NULL = current. Addresses change; history is required source text, optional self, staff, legacy_import import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional

Rules

  • valid_to is either absent or later than valid_from.
  • At most one current primary per (person, contact_type, purpose). It covers open rows only: a superseded primary does not block the new one.

Indexes

  • A person's contact points.
  • A person's current contact points by type and purpose — open rows only.
  • Email lookup on value lowercased, over current email rows only.
  • Phone lookup on value as stored, over current phone rows only.

purpose is the column that makes this operationally useful. It lets the permission system distinguish "a unit leader may see emergency contacts for camp" from "only billing staff may see payment email addresses". Without purpose, every contact is equally sensitive and the only safe choice is to hide all of them.

The partial unique index on the primary contact enforces "one primary email per person per purpose" without preventing a person from having four non-primary addresses. Note this index is what makes the merge conflict in §8 possible — resolving two is_primary rows is a review step, not a rule.

The email index is functional — it indexes value lowercased because email matching in the legacy importer must be case-insensitive, and a plain index cannot serve that.

docs.title: 7. person_identifier
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required scheme text, required national_scout_id, legacy_member_no, legacy_member_no_oldsystem, government_id, school_id, insurance_no. Validated against identifier_scheme below value text, required issued_at date, optional valid_to date, optional IDs expire or are superseded verified_at timestamp, audit time, optional source text, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional created_at timestamp, audit time

identifier_scheme — the vocabulary of schemes.

Fields

Field Kind Notes code text, required The value person_identifier.scheme holds name text, required is_unique boolean, required Default true. True: a value may appear on only one person (national id, member number). False: values legitimately repeat (school id across schools) description text, optional

Rules

  • Uniqueness is per scheme, and identifier_scheme.is_unique decides it. For a scheme flagged unique, (scheme, value) is unique over the identifiers that are still current — those with no valid_to. A superseded number may be reused; a current one may not be shared. The rule covers open rows only.
  • For a scheme flagged not-unique there is no such rule, and that is the point of the flag. school_id repeats by design: the same school issues the same number to many children, and each of them is a different person who genuinely carries it. is_unique = false means one value may appear on any number of people, and means it at enforcement time, not as a note in a description column.
  • Corrected here, and worth reading as a lesson. The rule as first written applied to every scheme and never read the flag; the flag and the rule were the same idea stated twice, once enforced and once decorative. The effect was that school_id could not in fact repeat — the second child at that school with the same number would have been rejected as a duplicate identifier, at import time, by a constraint whose own table said it should not exist. A column that no rule reads is not documentation, it is a promise. This is the same failure D-072 warns about from the other side: a rule nobody runs is a convention, and a flag nothing consults is decoration. Both read correctly on the page.

Indexes

  • A person's identifiers.
  • The uniqueness lookup above.

This table is the highest-value asset in the legacy import. If the old system issued member numbers, an exact (scheme='legacy_member_no', value=…) match is the strongest identity signal available — strong enough to short-circuit a fuzzy name comparison. See ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md.

Why not put these on person as columns. A person may have zero identifiers (most self-registered children), one, or several; schemes appear and disappear over decades; and national_scout_id must be unique while school_id must not. Columns would mean a schema change per scheme and a nullable-unique mess.

docs.title: 8. identity_hypothesis and person_merge
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_a_id reference to person, required The lower of the two ids — canonical ordering, so that (a,b) and (b,a) cannot both exist person_b_id reference to person, required confidence number between 0 and 1, required Inclusive of both ends match_signals jsonb, required A list of signals, each with a name, a weight and whether it matched — [{signal: 'birth_date_exact', weight: 0.4, matched: true}, {signal: 'name_normalised', weight: 0.3, matched: true}, …]. Stored so a human reviewer can see WHY the matcher proposed this status text, required One of: proposed, needs_review, confirmed, rejected, superseded. Default proposed proposed_by text, required One of: import_job, match_job, person, staff. match_job is the nightly batch matcher, as opposed to a person suggesting a match by hand. (Named background_match before background checks were removed from the design; renamed so the two never get confused.) proposed_by_person_id reference to person, optional Set when a person proposed it proposed_at timestamp, audit time Default: now reviewed_by reference to person, optional reviewed_at timestamp, audit time, optional review_note text, optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • person_a_id names a lower person id than person_b_id, and the two are never the same person.
  • A hypothesis cannot be confirmed or rejected without a reviewed_at.
  • One live hypothesis per pair: unique over (person_a_id, person_b_id) while the status is proposed, needs_review or confirmed. A rejected or superseded hypothesis does not block a new one, so the pair can be re-proposed later.

Indexes

  • The review queue: status, then confidence highest first, restricted to the rows still waiting — proposed and needs_review.

person_merge — the record that one person row was absorbed into another.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id surviving_person_id reference to person, required merged_person_id reference to person, required The absorbed row. It keeps its id; person.merged_into_person_id points here hypothesis_id reference to identity hypothesis, optional The hypothesis this merge came from, when one did merged_at timestamp, audit time Default: now merged_by reference to person, required reason text, optional reversed_at timestamp, audit time, optional reversed_by reference to person, optional reversal_note text, optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • A person may not be merged into themselves: surviving_person_id and merged_person_id are never the same person.

Indexes

  • Merges by surviving person, and merges by merged person — both directions get asked.
  • Merges by merged person that have not been reversed — the "who is this person now" query.

The canonical ordering (person_a_id before person_b_id) is not cosmetic. Without it the matcher can create both (100, 847) and (847, 100), and a reviewer will confirm one while the other sits in the queue forever — or worse, confirm both. The ordering rule plus the partial unique index makes the pair identity unambiguous.

match_signals as JSONB rather than columns, because the signal set will evolve as the matcher improves, and because these are write-once-read-for-review, never queried analytically.

person_merge is append-only — reversed_at is set, rows are never deleted. An unmerge does not remove the merge record; it records that it was undone, so the history of the mistake is visible. See ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md.

docs.title: Merge conflicts
docs.text:
field_conflict — one field the merge could not decide.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id merge_id reference to person merge, required entity_table text, required person, person_contact, membership, … entity_id surrogate id, required The row in entity_table. No reference — with the table named per row it would point at any table in the schema field_name text, required surviving_value text, optional merged_value text, optional resolution text, optional One of: kept_surviving, took_merged, manual, unresolved resolved_value text, optional resolved_by reference to person, optional resolved_at timestamp, audit time, optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Indexes

  • A merge's conflicts by resolution.
  • A merge's conflicts that are still unresolved — the reportable set.

Every field the merge could not resolve automatically lands here as unresolved. A merge with unresolved conflicts must be visible in an operational report — otherwise these rows accumulate silently and the data is quietly wrong.

Conflict cases worth naming, because each needs a human decision and none has a safe rule:

Case Why it cannot be automatic Two is_primary emails of the same purpose Which one does the person actually use? Two different birth_date values One is a typo; guessing produces a wrong legal record. Two overlapping memberships May be legitimate, or may mean the merge is wrong. Two different current names One may be a maiden name, or they may be different people. Two accounts, both active Which one is in use?

docs.title: 9. Views
docs.text:
Convenience views that encode the "always exclude merged and redacted" and "point in time" rules, so that application code cannot forget them.

v_person — the person rows most queries actually want: a person who is neither merged away nor redacted. Both exclusions, not one. They are different reasons and they must not be collapsed: a merged row is a duplicate that points at the real answer, while a redacted row is a person who was erased, whose names and contacts no longer exist. Neither belongs in a list of people, and a listing that shows one and hides the other is worse than either, because it teaches the reader that the redacted child is a data-entry error.

This is a correction, not a restatement. The view as this document first carried it excluded merged rows only, while §1 and §2 both said every listing must exclude redacted ones too, and §9's own opening sentence claimed the views encoded both. Three statements, one of them the code. The code lost. It is fixed here rather than noted as a discrepancy, because with the SQL gone (§1 of D-072) there is nothing left to disagree with the prose — the prose is now the only place the rule lives, so it has to be right.

What is deliberately not excluded anywhere: the row itself. A redacted person is still a row with a still-working id, so historical references keep resolving (§2's redacted_at). Anything that must reach a merged or redacted row — audit, as-of reconstruction, resolve_person — queries person directly and says so. v_person is the view for "people", and people is not what an audit trail is asking for.

resolve_person(id) — turns a possibly-merged id into the survivor. These steps run in this order, and the order is the rule:

  1. Begin at the person row carrying the given id.
  2. If that row has no merged_into_person_id, stop; this id is the answer.
  3. Otherwise move to the row its merged_into_person_id names and repeat from step 2.

v_person_display — one row per person v_person admits, carrying id, public_id, a display given name (preferred_name where present, given_name otherwise), family_name, a display name formed by putting the two together with a space, birth_date, birth_date_precision and redacted_at.

What v_person_display does not carry, and why that is a rule rather than an omission. It is a display row — the columns needed to name a person in a list — and it carries no descriptive values. It cannot: a view is a fixed list of columns and the attribute layer is the part of a person with no fixed list, which is §2's test arriving from the other side. Naming the boundary matters because the failure mode is silent. Anything asked about a person, rather than about what they are called, reads person and person_attribute together under the one person.view that reaches both (09-attributes.md §4) — the allergy list a first aider asks for, the record a guardian opens, the form a leader fills in. A screen built on v_person_display alone answers those questions with a name and a birth date, shows no empty field where an allergy should be, and looks entirely healthy while doing it (domain/08-person-data.md §3). The view stays narrow for the reason it exists — every picker and roster in the system reads it and none of them needs the record — and the obligation sits on the caller: do not answer a question about a person out of a view that only knows how to print one.

resolve_person follows every hop because merges chain: A absorbed into B, later B absorbed into C. A single-level pointer lookup would return B, whose row is itself tombstoned. Every place that accepts a person id from outside must call this. Getting it wrong means a historical record links to a tombstone and the UI shows a blank name — or the wrong one.

Assumption: merge chains are allowed rather than flattened at merge time. Flattening (silently repointing every existing pointer to the new survivor) is faster to query but rewrites history and makes unmerge nearly impossible. Tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: 10. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Checks that should run nightly and alert. These encode invariants that no per-column rule above can express.

Invariants to verify

  • A person with more than one live account. Count account rows per person whose status is pending_verification, active or suspended; anything above one is a breach of the rule in §4, and the point of the check is to confirm that rule really does exclude the pending-plus-active combination.
  • A tombstoned person with no merge record. Count persons whose merge pointer is set but who do not appear as the merged person of any un-reversed person_merge row; non-zero means merge chains longer than expected, which signals repeated bad merges.
  • A tombstoned row still referenced as a survivor. Count person_merge rows whose surviving_person_id has its own merge pointer set; non-zero means a merge names as its survivor a person who has themselves been absorbed.
  • Unresolved merge conflicts older than 30 days. Count field_conflict rows resolved to unresolved and created more than 30 days ago; non-zero means the review queue is being ignored and the data is quietly wrong.
  • Redacted people still referenced by a live account. Count account rows that are not closed and belong to a person with redacted_at set; non-zero means an erasure left a working login behind.
  • Imported people with no membership. Count people whose record_origin is legacy_import and who have no membership row at all; non-zero probably means a partially applied batch.
  • A redacted person with descriptive values still attached. Stated where the rows are, as check 6 of 09-attributes.md §8 — attribute rows belonging to a redacted person, and attribute values still present in audit_log. It is named here because the redaction checks above are the same erasure guarantee read from the identity side, and a half-finished erasure does not announce which table it stopped in. Of everything on either list, that is the one that should alert rather than log.

docs.title: 11. Open issues
docs.text:
• Whether merge chains are allowed or flattened at merge time (§9).
  • Whether a person may hold two live accounts simultaneously — recommend no, enforced by the partial index in §4.
  • Erasure policy specifics: what must be redacted vs. retained, and the retention period. Requires legal input. See 00-conventions.md.
  • Whether person.gender is needed at all; if so, what value set.
  • Whether the organization has (or will have) a national SSO identity provider — this determines how much of account_credential is actually used.

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Organization Structure
docs.text:
org_unit, unit types, name history, restructuring, positions, and assignments.

Domain rationale: ../domain/04-organization-structure.md.

docs.title: 1. org_unit_type
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes code text, required 'organization', then whatever the organization defines. name text, required description text, optional allows_minors boolean, required, defaults to true Safeguarding, not a membership rule. Membership is ageless (D-038); this flag lets the system refuse to place a minor in a unit that does not supervise them, without hardcoding which type codes those are. There is no allows_adults sibling: no unit in this organization excludes adults, and the units that must contain adults (anything with a leadership position) say so through position eligibility instead. See §7. is_leaf boolean, required, defaults to false A leaf may contain participants but not sub-units. A weekly meeting group is usually a leaf, but not necessarily — nesting is arbitrary (D-035). max_depth integer, optional Maximum nesting depth for this type, relative to the root. Unset = unconstrained. sort_order integer rank, required, defaults to 0 valid_from, valid_to period (from/to, open-ended allowed); both ends optional Types are retired, not deleted: a 1995 six unit type must still resolve in historical queries. created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • code is unique over all rows, retired ones included — a type that has been withdrawn still holds its name against a newcomer.
  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from. Either end may be absent, and no comparison is attempted when one is.
  • One row per code is the current one; the current row for a code is found among the rows with no valid_to.

Types are rows, not an enum, so the vocabulary can change across decades without a deployment. See ../domain/04-organization-structure.md.

allows_minors is the replacement for hardcoded type checks. The validation "a minor may not take part in the organization's legal-and-filing unit" reads this flag rather than listing type codes in code. Note it constrains participation and position assignment, not membership: a person of any age may be a member of the organization, because membership is ageless and lives at the root (D-038).

docs.title: 2. org_unit_type_rule
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes parent_type_id reference to org_unit_type, optional A parent_type_id that is absent means "at the root" — this type may be a top-level unit. child_type_id reference to org_unit_type, required is_required boolean, required, defaults to false True: a unit of child_type must have a parent of parent_type. False: permissive. max_children integer, optional Optional cap on how many children of this type a parent may have. valid_from, valid_to period (from/to, open-ended allowed); both ends optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • A rule may not name the same type as both its parent and its child. A rule with no parent type is exempt, because it has no parent to collide with.
  • At most one live rule per (parent_type_id, child_type_id) pair — live rows only, so a superseded rule does not block its replacement. An absent parent_type_id counts as a value in that comparison; compared as plain nulls, duplicate root rules would slip through.

Why a table rather than CHECK constraints or code. Nesting rules in this organization will change (a new level added, a type retired). A rule expressed in code is invisible to the people configuring the organization and requires a deployment to change. A rule in a table can be reviewed, exported, and audited.

Enforcement note. A CHECK cannot express "the parent's type must be permitted by a rule", because it requires a lookup into another table — and nothing else declarative expresses it either. The enforcement is therefore one ordered check, run once per row inside the transaction that writes the unit, on insert and on any update that touches parent_unit_id or unit_type_id. Inside the transaction is the part worth holding onto: a nesting validated only in the model layer is walked straight past by the legacy import, by a row someone corrects by hand, and by a second client, and all three exist here by design (00-conventions.md §6a). Validating the same steps in the application is still worth writing, because it produces the good error message; it is not the enforcement. The steps and their order are the rule:

  1. If the unit has no parent, look for a rule with no parent type whose child type is this unit's type and whose valid_to is absent or still in the future. (This branch reads valid_to only; valid_from is not part of it.)
  2. If none was found and any rule at all names this type as its child — disregarding whether that rule is still live — refuse: this unit type may not exist at the root.
  3. If none was found and no rule names this type as its child at all, accept. This is the permissive default.
  4. If the unit does have a parent, read that parent unit's type.
  5. Look for a rule pairing that parent type with this unit's type whose valid_from is absent or already reached and whose valid_to is absent or still in the future.
  6. If none was found and the parent type has any rule at all — again disregarding validity — refuse: this unit type may not be nested under that one.
  7. Otherwise accept.

The two refusals are each conditional on rules existing for the relevant side, and that condition is evaluated unconditionally, against retired rules as well as live ones. A type therefore has exactly two states: governed by rules, or untouched by them.

Note the permissive fallback: a type with no rules defined at all is unconstrained. This matters during initial setup — the check must refuse nothing while the rule table is still empty, or the first units could never be created. It also means the rules are opt-in, and §9 verifies them.

docs.title: 3. org_unit
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only; never exposed. public_id uuid, required, generated The identifier used outside the system, and unique. unit_type_id reference to org_unit_type, required parent_unit_id self-reference to org_unit (the parent), optional Nullable only for the single root unit — the organization itself. See uq_org_unit_single_root below, and D-035. Immutable once set — see A unit never changes parent, and D-036. code text, optional Short human code, e.g. T12. Not unique globally — two sub-units may both have a T1. name text, required Current display name. Denormalised convenience. The history is in org_unit_name (§4). Queries about the past must read org_unit_name, never this column. status text, required, defaults to active One of proposed, active, merged, closed. valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = still exists. closed_reason_code text, optional closed_note text, optional path text, required Denormalised for fast ancestor queries. Maintained on write, see §6. depth integer, required Number of segments in path; §6. data_confidence text, required, defaults to high One of high, medium, low. created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person The standard audit columns. created_by is NULL for system and import jobs. import_batch_id reference to the import batch, optional Set on imported rows.

Rules

  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from.
  • A unit may not be its own parent.
  • code is unique within a parent, compared case-insensitively, among live units only — a closed unit's code is free again. Units with no code are outside the rule, and units at the root are compared with one another rather than exempted: an absent parent counts as a value.
  • Exactly one unit may exist at the root. The organization itself. uq_org_unit_single_root is the name this rule carries here, and the layer that must carry it is a migration: it is uniqueness over the rows that have no parent, which is the conditional shape 00-conventions.md §6a says an ORM will not emit and a migration must.

Indexes

  • On path, for prefix matching — this is what makes the set-based subtree question in §6.1 cheap.
  • On parent_unit_id, for walking one level of the tree.
  • On unit_type_id, restricted to live units, and on live units generally: "what exists right now" is the question the partial indexes are for.

The one-root rule is the whole of "there is one organization", and it is the load-bearing kind: a constraint, not a convention. At most one row with parent_unit_id IS NULL may exist, and the rule deliberately ignores valid_to — even a closed root is still the root. A second root is not an untidy state but a second organization, and only something running at the database can refuse the insert that creates one. It is shape 2 of open question F-10 — unique, but only among rows satisfying a condition — so the migration emits a partial unique index and not the plain one, which would be a different rule: a plain unique constraint over parent_unit_id would reject every sub-unit, since they all share a parent. See D-035.

A unit cannot be closed without an end date (ck_org_unit_closed is this rule's name). Two columns of one row, so a migration can state it directly as a check on the row — the easy shape, and worth stating as a requirement precisely because no object in this repository carries it any more. Without it you get closed units with valid_to IS NULL, which then appear in "currently active units" queries forever.

Why code is not globally unique. Unit numbering restarts and has been reused across decades, and with arbitrary nesting two sub-units under different parents will legitimately both be "1". A global unique constraint would reject real historical data during import. Uniqueness is scoped to the parent and to live rows.

docs.title: A unit never changes parent
docs.text:
parent_unit_id is immutable. This is not a convention — it is enforced inside the transaction that writes the row, once per row, on any update that touches parent_unit_id, in this order:

  1. If parent_unit_id differs from its previous value in any way — including being set from nothing, or cleared to nothing — refuse, naming the unit, and say what to do instead: a unit that moves is a new unit; close this one and create its successor under the new parent, recording the lineage in org_unit_relationship.
  2. Otherwise allow the write.

Why a guard inside the database rather than a rule in the application. Reparenting is the one edit that would silently rewrite history: it changes what every historical report means, moves a unit in and out of every ancestor's scope, and invalidates the materialized path for the whole subtree. None of those failures are visible at the moment of the edit — which is exactly why checking them in the application does not qualify, since the legacy import, the hand-corrected row and a second client all change parents without ever passing the screen that would refuse them. The comparison still costs something, and the migration must be able to pay it: this is shape 4 of open question F-10 — a column that may not change once it is set — and no declarative constraint in any database states it, so this guard is one the migration writes by hand rather than one an ORM generates. See D-036.

The consequence is a simplification, not a loss. Because the parent never changes, the path/depth denormalisation never needs a subtree cascade rewrite, and "who was in this unit in 2001?" keeps answering the same thing forever.

A genuine move is recorded as a succession, and the people are moved across explicitly — see org_unit_relationship in §5.

docs.title: 4. org_unit_name — rename and renumber history
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes org_unit_id reference to org_unit, required name text, required The name the unit went by in this period. code text, optional The code that went with it. valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = the current name. change_reason text, required One of established, rename, renumber, reorganisation, correction, import. change_note text, optional source text, optional staff or legacy_import. import_batch_id reference to the import batch, optional Set on imported rows. created_at, created_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person

Rules

  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from.

One unit, one current name. uq_org_unit_name_open is this rule's name; it is conditional uniqueness over the open rows, the shape 00-conventions.md §6a says a migration must emit by hand, and a uniqueness constraint over all rows would be a different and wrong rule. The denormalised org_unit.name must always equal that row, and nothing maintains the copy by itself any more: no write may change the current name row without setting org_unit.name in the same transaction.
