The failure mode is the one invariant 4 in §9 counts — a system that displays one name and reports under another — and it is reachable from any path that writes org_unit_name, the legacy import included, so the pairing is a requirement on the write rather than something a form handler remembers. Invariants 3 and 4 are the net beneath it, not the guard.

Renumbering is a rename, not a new unit. "4th Pack" becoming "Pack 12" with the same participants is one org_unit row and two org_unit_name rows. Creating a new unit would orphan all historical unit_participation rows and make "who was in Pack 12 in 1998?" unanswerable.

change_reason distinguishes a correction from a rename. A correction means the record was wrong (a typo fixed in 2026 about a 1998 name); a rename means the world changed. Only the latter is real history. Conflating them corrupts historical reporting.

docs.title: 5. org_unit_relationship — splits, mergers, succession
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes source_unit_id reference to org_unit, required target_unit_id reference to org_unit, required relationship text, required One of split_from, merged_into, successor_of, renamed_to. Direction is source → target. split_from: the target was created from the source. merged_into: the source was absorbed into the target. effective_date date, required note text, optional source text, optional import_batch_id reference to the import batch, optional Set on imported rows. created_at, created_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person

Rules

  • A unit may not have a relationship to itself.
  • Nothing else is unique: the same pair of units may carry several relationships, and the same kind of relationship more than once.

Indexes

  • On source_unit_id and, separately, on target_unit_id. Lineage is asked in both directions — "what did this unit become?" and "what did this one come from?" — and neither question may have to scan the table.

This table exists so that historical lineage is answerable. When Troop 12 splits into Troop 12 and Troop 31, the question "was this 2003 member in the unit that is now Troop 31?" requires following the relationship. Without it, the answer is only guessable from overlapping member sets.

Note it is not a tree. A unit may have been split from one parent and merged into another; the same pair may even have multiple relationships over time (split in 1998, merged back in 2005). Hence effective_date and no uniqueness constraint beyond the pair.

Do not rewrite history on a split. Participants who moved to the new unit get a new unit_participation row starting at the split date; their old row closes at the same date. Rewriting the old row destroys "where was this child in 2003?" — see §8.

docs.title: 6. Hierarchy traversal
docs.text: Two mechanisms. One is stored and is only as correct as whatever wrote it; the other is computed when it is asked and is correct by construction.

docs.title: 6.1 Materialized path (fast ancestor/descendant queries)
docs.text:
org_unit.path holds a slash-delimited id path: /1/7/42/103/. depth is the number of segments. It is derived, never supplied: the rule runs inside the transaction that writes the row, once per row, on insert and on any update that touches parent_unit_id, in this order. A caller that wrote path itself would be writing a number nobody verified.

  1. A unit with no parent gets a path of its own id between two slashes, and depth 0.
  2. A unit with a parent reads that parent unit's path and depth.
  3. If there is no such unit, refuse the write — a unit cannot be placed under a parent that does not exist.
  4. Its path is the parent's path with its own id appended, and its depth is the parent's depth plus one.

The order is the rule: the parent's own path must already be correct, which is why a unit can only be created after its parent.

No subtree cascade is needed, ever. Because parent_unit_id is immutable (§3), a unit's path is computed once at insert and never rewritten. The repeat of this rule on an update to parent_unit_id is therefore defensive only — the no-reparenting check rejects the change before it.

This is the payoff of D-036: the materialized path is a pure insert-time denormalisation, which is the only kind that stays trustworthy without versioning.

docs.title: 6.2 Recursive CTE (correct regardless of path integrity)
docs.text:
Two questions, each answered by following parent_unit_id one hop at a time from a starting unit until there is nowhere further to go:

  • unit_ancestors(unit) — which units are above this one? Every ancestor, nearest first, and the unit itself excluded. Distance from the starting unit is part of the answer, so "this unit's district" and "this unit's region" are the same question at different distances.
  • unit_descendants(unit) — which units are below this one? Every descendant, the unit itself again excluded.

Both read nothing but parent_unit_id, so both stay correct whatever path currently says.

unit_ancestors() must NOT be used by the permission resolver. Authority does not flow down the hierarchy. The resolver matches scopes exactly, plus explicit scope_exposure rows — see ../domain/06-authorization-model.md. unit_ancestors() is used for reporting ("everyone in this district"), for the path-consistency check below, and for the exposure-direction integrity check — never in a permission path. Integrity check 13 in 05-authorization.md asserts this in CI.

Both mechanisms are kept. The path is for set-based queries — one prefix test over the stored path rather than a walk — which is dramatically faster for "everyone in this district". The recursive CTE is the authority when the path might be stale, and is used by the nightly consistency check:

Nightly, for every unit that has a parent: take its ancestors with unit_ancestors(), rebuild the path that chain implies — every ancestor's id nearest-first, then the unit's own id last, each delimited by slashes — and report the units whose stored path is not that string. Root units are excluded; their path is their own id by definition, and there is no chain to check it against. This is invariant 1 in §9.

docs.title: 7. position and position_assignment
docs.text:
Fields — position

Field Kind Notes unit_type_id reference to org_unit_type, required A position is defined per unit type, not per unit: every troop has a scoutmaster slot. The slot is instantiated implicitly by the unit existing. code text, required title text, required description text, optional max_holders integer, optional How many people may occupy this position in one unit at the same time. Unset = unlimited. 1 = a single holder (a scoutmaster). The default is unset, i.e. unlimited, because multiple occupancy is the normal case in this organization: a troop may have several assistant leaders, several quartermasters, several instructors. Single occupancy is the exception and must be declared by the position itself. Note this is a limit a position declares about itself. It is never imposed from outside the unit. See domain/06-authorization-model.md §2 for why authority over a unit's structure originates at the unit. is_leadership boolean, required, defaults to false Flags positions that carry organizational authority. Used to drive the convenience workflow that also creates a role_assignment. requires_membership boolean, required, defaults to true What it says here is reported, not enforced. The flag drives the "leaders whose membership has lapsed" worklist below. Whether holding the corresponding role survives a lapse is a separate switch, role.requires_membership, and that one is enforced by the permission resolver (D-039). The two are deliberately not the same column: an adult volunteer commonly holds a position for years while their membership lapses and is renewed, and the organization wants to see that on a report without losing the volunteer's access. min_age integer, optional Position eligibility, a real constraint: a scoutmaster must be an adult. This is about the position, not about membership — membership is ageless (D-038). sort_order integer rank, required, defaults to 0 valid_from, valid_to period (from/to, open-ended allowed); both ends optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules — position

  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from. Either end may be absent, and no comparison is attempted when one is.
  • max_holders is either unset or at least 1. There is no position that admits nobody.
  • A position code is unique within its unit type, compared case-insensitively, among live positions only.

Fields — position_assignment

Field Kind Notes position_id reference to position, required org_unit_id reference to org_unit, required The concrete unit. position.unit_type_id must match that unit's org_unit.unit_type_id; a reference between two rows cannot express this, so it is verified on write, and invariant 6 in §9 reports what slips through. person_id reference to person, required valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = still in post. is_primary boolean, required, defaults to true Some people hold several positions; one is primary for display and contact. appointment_reference text, optional ended_reason_code text, optional ended_note text, optional created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person import_batch_id reference to the import batch, optional Set on imported rows.

Rules — position_assignment

  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from.
  • A person may not hold the same position in the same unit over overlapping periods. The rule covers every row, open and closed alike — there is no status to scope it by.

Indexes — position_assignment

  • On person_id with valid_from descending, for "what does this person hold, most recent first".
  • On org_unit_id, and on position_id, each restricted to open assignments: "who runs this unit now" and "who holds this slot now" are the questions that run constantly, and both look only at rows that are still in post.

The holder limit. Where a position declares one, no write may leave the unit holding more open assignments of it than the limit allows. It is enforced inside the transaction that writes the assignment, once per row, on insert and on any update that touches position_id, org_unit_id or valid_to — and the count is read inside that transaction, not before it, because two inserts that each counted before either had landed are how a single-scoutmaster unit ends up with two scoutmasters. The order is the rule:

  1. Read the position's max_holders.
  2. If it is unset, or the row being written is itself a closed assignment, allow it — there is no limit, or nothing is being opened.
  3. Count the open assignments of this position in this unit, excluding the row being written from its own count.
  4. If that count has reached max_holders, refuse, naming the position, the unit, the current holder count and the limit.
  5. Otherwise allow it.

Why no unique index does this, whatever emits it. The limit is position.max_holders, which lives in another table, so an index predicate cannot express it — and a partial index predicate may not contain a subquery in any case. Nothing declarative handles max_holders > 1 either: an index can say at most one, never at most n, where n is a column of another table's row. None of that argument was about the mechanism that D-072 deleted; it stands, and it now reads as a statement about what the migration must be able to express and cannot. This is the weakest-enforced rule in this document. It is shape 3 of open question F-10, the class whose answer comes from another table, and F-10's remedy for that class has two parts: a check inside the writing transaction, plus a report. The first is required above; the second does not exist — §9 lists no over-limit report — so if the migration omits its guard, the limit holds only for as long as every caller chooses to obey it.

Note the absence of a uniqueness rule on the assignment triple. There is deliberately no uniqueness over the triple of person, position and unit: a person may hold the same position in the same unit across separate periods (left in 2020, returned in 2024), which is historical fact and must remain representable. Overlap is still prevented, directly on the row:

One person, one position, one unit: no two assignments of the same person to the same position in the same unit may cover the same date. Periods are half-open, so a row ending on a day and a row beginning on that same day do not collide.

Without this, the same person could be double-counted as holder of the same position in the same unit over overlapping dates — which would defeat the holder limit itself by consuming two of the slots.

What no database constraint can enforce, and must be handled elsewhere:

7.1 requires_membership and min_age. Both depend on temporal state in other tables, so no FK or check constraint can express them. They are application-level validations plus a periodic report:

  • Holders who are not currently paid-up members. Every assignment still in post, of a position that asks for membership, whose holder is_current_member() says is not a member. Needs attention, but is not an access problem — see the note below.
  • Holders below the position's minimum age. Every assignment still in post, of a position that sets min_age, whose holder has not yet reached that age today. A holder with no recorded birth date is reported as well: eligibility cannot be established for them either.

An unpaid volunteer holding a position is a bookkeeping problem, not a safeguarding one. The important consequences:

  • Note that requires_membership here is a report, while role.requires_membership is enforced by the resolver (D-039). The holder may lose their system access the moment the fee lapses, while still legitimately holding the position. That asymmetry is intentional — see 03-membership.md §6 — but any role that exists to make a position work should almost certainly be defined with requires_membership = false, or the volunteer loses access to the tools their position needs.
  • No background checks are recorded in this system at all (D-043). If the organization ever introduces them, the natural home is a dated record with an expires_at, plus a person_identifier scheme — and it would warrant a daily alerting report, because a lapsed clearance is a safeguarding matter rather than a data-quality one.

7.2 Holder limits are a per-position declaration, not a structural rule. See the holder limit above and max_holders. The important consequences:

  • Multiple occupancy is the default. max_holders IS NULL means unlimited, so a new position kind accepts several holders without anyone having to state it.
  • Single occupancy never arises from the hierarchy. A parent unit cannot declare that a nested unit has one scoutmaster. The limit is a property the position carries, and the positions in a unit are that unit's own business.
  • An over-limit condition is a business error, not a crash. Two people legitimately sharing a position during a handover is a normal transient state; resolution is either closing one assignment or raising the limit.

Positions are not permissions. Holding scoutmaster grants no system capability. The association between a position and authority is made explicitly through role_assignment, and position.is_leadership exists only so a workflow can offer to create both at once. See ../domain/04-organization-structure.md.

docs.title: 8. unit_participation lives in 03-membership.md
docs.text:
Taking part in a sub-unit is a separate table from membership of the organization, because they have different lifetimes — a person may hold a membership while taking part in no sub-unit at all, or take part in several at once.

The name matters: this is participation, not a second kind of membership (D-041). Everyone registers and pays at the root; the sub-units hold rosters, not memberships.

See 03-membership.md.

docs.title: 9. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify

  1. A stored path that disagrees with the actual tree (§6.2). Counts units whose stored path is not the one their parent chain implies; any non-zero count means the insert-time denormalisation has drifted.
  2. A unit whose parent is closed but which is itself open. Counts live units hanging off a unit that has ended; non-zero means the tree currently claims to contain something inside a unit that no longer exists.
  3. A live unit with no current name row. Counts live units with no open org_unit_name row at all; non-zero violates the denormalisation invariant directly — there is no current name to copy into org_unit.name.
  4. org_unit.name disagreeing with the unit's current org_unit_name row. Counts live units whose denormalised display name differs from the open name row; non-zero means the system displays one name and reports another.
  5. A live unit type with no nesting rules at all — neither as a parent nor as a child. Usually fine: nesting is permissive by default and a new type starts unconstrained. But a type that has been in use for years with no rules is probably an oversight worth reviewing.
  6. A position assignment whose position's unit type is not the unit's type. Counts assignments pairing a position defined for one type with a unit of another; non-zero means the check on write was bypassed.
  7. A unit with exactly one live child. Non-zero is often a data-entry error and sometimes real; it is a list to read, not a failure.
  8. A position holding more people than its own limit allows. Counts, for each position with max_holders set, its open assignments, and reports the positions where the count exceeds it. Unlike event capacity (08-events.md §10 check 5) an overrun here is not permitted: §7 calls it a business error rather than a choice an adult may make deliberately, and a non-zero result therefore means the check on write was bypassed — an import, a bulk reorganisation, a hand-fixed row. This check exists because the guard alone is not enough to notice. The holder limit cannot be stated as a constraint at all (F-10 shape 3), so if the migration omits it the only evidence that anything was expected is §7's prose, which a database cannot read. A limit nobody checks and nothing reports is a limit that holds until the first import.
  9. The single-root rule still exists. A second root is impossible while uq_org_unit_single_root is carried by a migration, so what is verified here is that the migration really emitted it — the rule's existence rather than the data: should it ever be dropped, this fails even though nothing in the table has gone wrong, and the build must fail with it. The same pattern as the unit_ancestors() assertion in 05-authorization.md.

Checks 9 and 10 are not data-quality reports and should not be read like one. They fail on a missing guarantee rather than on bad rows, so both belong in CI: check 9 is the only thing that would notice an unenforced holder limit, and check 10 asserts that a migration emitted a constraint. Check 10 is the structural one — with reparenting prohibited (§3), the single-root rule and the recursive ancestor walk are the two things everything else in the authorization model assumes, and both are worth asserting rather than trusting.

Checks 3 and 4 are the ones to read every morning. They detect the denormalisation drifting, which otherwise produces a system that displays one name and reports under another.

docs.title: 10. Seed data
docs.text:
The vocabulary is data, so it belongs in a migration. Two parts: the single root, and whatever sub-unit types the organization actually uses.

Concretely, the organization begins with two rows of data and nothing else: one unit type for itself — organization, not a leaf — and the single root unit that carries it. The root unit has no parent (§3), and a period that opens early enough to precede anything the organization will later import and never closes. No sub-unit type is seeded at all: the organization defines its own (D-054).

The sub-unit vocabulary is not seeded, and this is the decision rather than a gap. The seed contains the root and nothing else; org_unit_type is runtime data, exactly like role (D-052). The organization creates the types it actually uses, renames them, and adds new ones as its structure changes (D-054).

Previous revisions seeded a guess — pack/group/team, and before that a national/region/district ladder. Both were invented words that read as a specification. Not guessing is the better answer, because a wrong vocabulary in seed data is harder to dislodge than an absent one.

The words still appear throughout these docs as illustration. "A pack has its own roster" explains a self-governing sub-unit; it is not a type the system ships with. Read them as "some sub-unit type the organization has defined".

Nesting is therefore entirely permissive — org_unit_type_nesting is seeded with nothing, so any type may sit under any other, including directly under the root, until the organization states a rule. A new type is usable the moment it is created.

The root type is the one exception and must stay seeded. Exactly one unit has parent_unit_id IS NULL (D-035) and it needs a type; note allows_minors = false on it, since no minor belongs to "The Organization" as a unit — minors hold memberships and sub-unit participation.

Position definitions, by contrast, are a real starting set and worth filling in — they are what position_assignment hangs off, and min_age / requires_membership on them are the eligibility rules §7.1 reports on — reports, because nothing rejects those two at the write.

docs.title: 11. Open issues
docs.text:
• The real sub-unit type vocabulary (§10). One root and arbitrary nesting are settled; the words are not.
  • May the root read what happens in its sub-units, or must each sub-unit expose its scope first? The root owns the registry and the fees, so this is narrower than it was — it is about the sub-units' own events and rosters. See ../open-questions.md.
  • Whether a person may hold positions in units of different types simultaneously.
  • Whether is_leadership should automatically create a role_assignment, or only suggest it.
  • Whether allows_minors should also constrain position_assignment, or only unit_participation — currently it is specified for participation and the position side relies on position.min_age instead (a minor could in principle hold a position defined with min_age IS NULL in a unit that excludes minors).

Resolved and no longer open, kept visible so the reasoning survives: the organizational structure itself (one root, arbitrary nesting — D-035); retroactive reparenting (prohibited outright, and enforced inside the database rather than in the application — D-036); organization-wide operational roles (largely dissolved by D-035, since the root owns the registry and the fees); and background checks (none are recorded — D-043).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Membership
docs.text:
membership_type, membership, membership_request, and unit_participation.

Domain rationale: ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md.

docs.title: 1. membership_type — one row, kept as a table
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes code text, required 'member' — and nothing else, for now. name text, required description text, optional duration_months integer, required, defaults to 12 12: the fee is yearly. Kept as a column rather than a constant so a type with a different term could be added as a row, with no migration. expiry_month, expiry_day integers, required, both defaulting to 1 When the fee expires (D-047): 1 January. The organizational year runs with the calendar, so "a member this year" means what a reader expects, and the sweep, the campaign and the reports all land on a boundary nobody has to look up. These are columns, not a constant in a scheduled job, for the reason the user gave for the window below: the date is a parameter the organization may move, and moving it must not require a code change. Every lapse date, the yearly sweep and the renewal worklist derive from these two values. renewal_grace_days integer, required, defaults to 60 The renewal window after valid_to, during which a payment restores the membership without re-applying and backdates the new period to the expiry date. Dates, not a status: the person is expired throughout (D-040). 60 days (D-048). Read it from here; never hardcode 60 in a job or a front end (D-048). The requirement attached to that answer was precisely that the value stays tunable. is_self_registerable boolean, required, defaults to true requires_approval boolean, required, defaults to true sort_order integer rank, required, defaults to 0 valid_from, valid_to period (from/to, open-ended allowed); both ends optional created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • code is unique over all rows.
  • expiry_month is between 1 and 12; expiry_day is between 1 and 31.
  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from. Either end may be absent, and no comparison is attempted when one is.

docs.title: Why this table still exists with one row
docs.text:
There is exactly one membership (D-037). Everyone who is a member holds membership_type = 'member', the fee is flat and per person, and being a counselor or a leader is a position, never a type.

The table survives rather than collapsing into a constant for two reasons:

  1. Consistency with the design's own principle. Vocabularies are rows, not enums — the same argument that keeps org_unit_type and position as tables. A second kind of membership (a supporting or honorary one) would then be a data change.
  2. A place for the organizational calendar to live. The term, the expiry date and the renewal window are genuinely type-dependent parameters even when there is one type — and they are the parameters most likely to be tuned. Putting them in a row rather than in code is what makes "it should not be hard to modify" (D-048) true by construction rather than by discipline.

The cost is honest and small: an FK that currently always holds one value. Recorded here rather than hidden.

docs.title: What was removed, and why
docs.text:
Removed Reason category (child/adult/special) Membership is ageless (D-038). Age is a fact about the person. min_age, max_age No age floor, ceiling, or automatic age-out. requires_background_check The system records no background checks (D-043). requires_references, requires_guardian_consent Nothing gates a request but identity and payment (D-044). allows_concurrent With one type and a person-scoped overlap constraint, this cannot arise. grace_period_days (as a status) Replaced by renewal_grace_days — a window, not a state (D-040). fee_schedule_id The fee is flat and per person (D-037), so there is nothing type-specific to schedule. The schedule attaches to the obligation instead — 07-finance.md §2.

The age checks that used to sit on the type go with them (ck_membership_type_ages was their name). With no ages on the row there is nothing for a migration to express and nothing left for a report to verify, so the removal is complete rather than a rule left hanging.

docs.title: 2. membership_request
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only. public_id uuid, required, generated The identifier used outside the system; unique. person_id reference to person, required The subject: the person who would become a member. For a minor's application this is the child, not the parent. submitted_by_person_id reference to person, optional Who actually submitted it. Equals person_id for self-application; differs when a guardian (or staff) applies on behalf. This is the act-on-behalf record. requested_membership_type_id reference to membership_type, required requested_unit_id reference to org_unit, optional The applicant may express a preference, or the organization may assign the unit at approval. status text, required, defaults to draft One of draft, submitted, under_review, approved, rejected, withdrawn, expired. submitted_at timestamp, optional decided_at timestamp, optional decided_by reference to person, optional rejection_reason_code text, optional rejection_note text, optional membership_id reference to membership, optional Set on approval. The reference is added only once membership exists (§3): this is the design's circular pair, resolved with a deferred reference. previous_membership_id reference to membership, optional Links a renewal or re-application to the prior membership. This is how a returning member's chain is expressed. expires_at timestamp, optional An unreviewed request eventually goes stale. Needed so the review queue does not accumulate abandoned drafts forever. notes text, optional source text, optional self, guardian, staff or import. created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person The standard audit columns.

Rules

  • A request in approved or rejected has both decided_at and decided_by. There is no decision without a decider and a time.
  • Any request that is not draft has a submitted_at.
  • An approved request points at a membership. The one allowance is a request decided at a time still in the future, which is how the request and the membership are inserted in two steps inside one transaction; the link is not optional once that transaction is over.
  • At most one open request per person per membership type. Open means draft, submitted or under_review. Decided requests — approved, rejected, withdrawn, expired — are outside the rule, which is what lets a person apply again after being turned down.

Indexes

  • On person_id with submitted_at descending: one person's applications, newest first.
  • A partial index over the review queue only — rows in submitted or under_review, which is the whole queue and nothing else.
  • On submitted_by_person_id and on requested_unit_id, each covering only the rows where those optional columns are actually set.

person_id vs submitted_by_person_id is the most important pair in this table. The subject is the child; the submitter is the parent. Collapsing them into one column — which is what most systems do — makes it impossible to answer "who applied for this child?" and falsely attributes the parent's action to the child. See ../domain/02-actors.md.

Why requests are a separate table from memberships. A rejected request produces no membership and must not pollute member listings; a person may submit several over time; and review data (who decided, why) has no meaning on a membership. See ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md.

A rejection requires a reason code (ck_request_rejection_reason is the rule's name): no rejected request may be written without one. Two columns of the same row, so a migration can state it directly as a check on the row — and it belongs there rather than only in the model layer, because the two paths that most need catching, an import and a hand-corrected row, never reach a model-layer guard. "Why was this application turned down?" is asked months later, sometimes by the family. A rejection with no recorded reason is an answerable question made unanswerable.

previous_membership_id is what makes the returning-member chain explicit rather than inferred from date arithmetic.

docs.title: 3. membership
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only. public_id uuid, required, generated The identifier used outside the system; unique. person_id reference to person, required membership_type_id reference to membership_type, required status text, required One of pending_payment, active, suspended, lapsed, terminated, completed. No default — the state is always chosen deliberately. valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = open / current. joined_via_request_id reference to membership_request, optional renewed_from_membership_id self-reference to membership (the previous one), optional Forms the renewal chain. See domain/05 §6. outstanding_balance money amount, optional Denormalised from fee_obligation/payment. 07-finance.md §3 recommends dropping this column in favour of v_fee_obligation_balance — a wrong balance suspends the wrong child. Kept here only until that decision is taken. NULL for imported historical memberships with no payment data. termination_reason_code text, optional termination_note text, optional ended_by reference to person, optional ended_at timestamp, optional data_confidence text, required, defaults to high One of high, medium, low. import_batch_id reference to the import batch, optional Set on imported rows. notes text, optional created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person The standard audit columns.

Rules

  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from.
  • A terminated membership has both a termination_reason_code and an ended_at.
  • A membership may not be renewed from itself: renewed_from_membership_id never points at its own row.
  • THE critical rule — one person, one membership, full stop. Two rows for the same person may not cover the same date while either of them is pending_payment, active or suspended. Periods are half-open, so one ending on a day and another beginning on that day do not collide. Statuses outside those three are outside the rule entirely, and the rule reaches every person regardless of membership type — the type is not part of it, and that omission is deliberate, as the next section explains.

Indexes

  • ix_membership_current — per person, over rows that are open and active. The membership gate reads through this, and it is the index a far-future sentinel date would defeat — see Why valid_to IS NULL and not a sentinel below.
  • On valid_to over active rows that have one. This drives the renewal worklist: who expires soon, who is in their renewal window.
  • On (status, valid_to) over active and pending_payment rows — the states anyone is actually queried in.
  • On person_id with valid_from descending, and a period index per person: one person's membership history, and the range scan the overlap rule and every point-in-time question use.

docs.title: The constraint dropped membership_type_id — that is the point
docs.text:
The old constraint was scoped to the type, to permit an honorary member who is also an active member. With one membership type (D-037) that case cannot arise, so the type is gone from the constraint and "one person, one open membership" becomes an enforceable invariant rather than a convention. It is conditional uniqueness — one open row per person — which is the shape 00-conventions.md §6a says a migration must emit by hand: a unique constraint over all rows is a different rule and the wrong one, because it forbids the second closed membership that the person's history requires.

This is what makes the membership gate (D-039) implementable: is_current_member() is a question about one row, one status, one date, not a question that has to reconcile three concurrent memberships.

docs.title: renewed_from_membership_id and the renewal window
docs.text:
When a person pays inside the renewal window (D-040), the new membership's valid_from is set to the previous row's valid_to, not to the payment date. Two consequences worth stating:

  • The history shows continuous coverage — no gap, no spurious "returning member".
  • The person is nevertheless expired during the window (D-040). The two facts are compatible because the window is a date range, not a status: they were not a member while it was open, and the record of that period is filled in retrospectively once they pay. Nothing needs backdating in the audit sense, because the new row's as-of start is the expiry date and its audit time is the payment date — the two-times distinction in 00-conventions.md.

A payment after the window opens the new membership at the payment date, and the gap is real.

docs.title: The exclusion constraint and status transitions
docs.text:
The overlap rule covers only pending_payment, active, suspended. A terminated/lapsed/completed row is excluded, so a new membership can be created with a valid_from inside an old one's period without violating the constraint. This is deliberate — a returning member's new membership may legitimately overlap the tail of a lapsed one if the dates were entered imprecisely. Historical imports rely on this.

Consequence: the constraint does not prevent two active memberships with overlapping periods if one was inserted while in another status and then transitioned. A status update re-evaluates the constraint (PostgreSQL does check exclusion constraints on UPDATE), so this is safe — but the transition from lapsed back to active can therefore fail with a constraint violation. That is correct behaviour: it means the person has two overlapping claims to membership and someone must resolve it. Handle it as a business error, not a crash.

Which layer carries all of that: the migration. A status transition that re-checks the overlap is only a violation if the constraint is in the database, and no ORM emits an exclusion over a period assembled from valid_from and valid_to scoped to three statuses — the migration writes it, as 00-conventions.md §6a requires. The same check performed in the model layer returns a friendlier message a moment earlier and guarantees nothing: the legacy import writes memberships by the thousand and a hand-corrected row never passes through the model layer either. Both still meet the constraint; neither would ever meet a model-layer check.

docs.title: Why valid_to IS NULL and not a sentinel
docs.text: Repeated from the conventions because it is the mistake most likely to be made here. A '9999-12-31' sentinel breaks IS NULL checks, makes daterange spans enormous, and defeats the ix_membership_current partial index. Use NULL.

docs.title: renewed_from_membership_id
docs.text:
Renewal opens a new row (Shape A in ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md). The self-reference makes the chain explicit:

membership 501  member  1990-09-01 → 1991-06-30   completed
     ↑ renewed_from
membership 502  member  1991-09-01 → 1992-06-30   completed
     ↑ renewed_from
membership 503  member  1992-09-01 → 1993-06-30   completed
(The type is member on every row — there is only one type, and the person's age is not part of it: §1, D-037, D-038.)

"Why does this person have 15 membership rows?" is then answerable by following the chain rather than by reasoning about dates. And a gap — a missing link — is visible as data.

docs.title: Current-membership queries
docs.text:
Five questions the membership table has to answer, each with the exact rule that decides it. The wording of each is load-bearing; the differences between them are the design.

  • Is this person a member right now? is_current_member(person) — true when they have a membership whose status is active and whose period covers today: valid_from on or before today, valid_to absent or after today. No grace coalescing: a lapsed membership is lapsed, and the renewal window (§6) is a date range for rejoining, not a state in which the person is a member.
  • Was this person a member on a given past date? was_member_on(person, date) — true when a membership of theirs covers that date, on the same half-open terms, and its status is anything except pending_payment. Note the asymmetry with the question above: now demands active, then admits every terminal status, because how a membership ended does not change that it existed.
  • When does the organizational year containing a date expire? membership_expiry_date(as_of) — expiry_month and expiry_day read off the member row, applied to the year of as_of. Always derived from those two columns and never from a constant (D-047).
  • May this person renew without re-applying? in_renewal_window(person, as_of) — true when they have a membership of theirs that has ended (valid_to set) with valid_to on or before as_of, and valid_to plus that type's renewal_grace_days still after as_of; in other words the window is [expiry, expiry + grace), half-open like every other period here. No status is consulted — this is arithmetic on dates alone. D-040: expired, but inside the window. This is the distinction a grace_period_days membership status would have blurred: they are not a member, and they may rejoin cheaply. 60 days, read from the row (D-048). Not a member during the window: this answers "may they rejoin cheaply?", never "do they have access?".
  • How long has this person been a member? membership_years(person) — the sum of the lengths of their memberships, with today standing in for an open valid_to and any pending_payment row left out, expressed in years of 365.25 days.

membership_years sums the periods rather than subtracting the first join date from today. The difference is the 14-year gap in the returning-member case, and getting it wrong mislabels a returning member as having 36 years of service.

current_member_category() is gone. It existed to answer "is this person currently a child or an adult?", which is no longer a question the membership table can answer, because membership is ageless (D-038). Age is a fact about the person:

Is this person a minor? is_minor(person, as_of) — true when person.birth_date is recorded and as_of falls before their eighteenth birthday. A person with no recorded birth date is not a minor by this test; nothing guesses one. A fact about the person, never about their membership.

This matters for guardianship and safeguarding, which are where age legitimately bears — not for whether someone may be a member.

docs.title: 4. No request requirements — removed entirely
docs.text:
requirement_code and membership_request_requirement do not exist (D-044).

Why. Your answer, asked what a membership request must contain in order to be accepted: "Just identity and the fee — nothing to verify." The option of keeping the mechanism as empty infrastructure was offered and not taken, so it is gone rather than left dangling.

What a request therefore is: a person, a submitted timestamp, a reviewer, a decision, and a payment. The membership_request table in §2 is complete as it stands — it never referenced requirements except through this table.

Guardian consent is unaffected. It was never a membership requirement; it belongs to the guardianship layer, where it is a relationship fact rather than a checklist item. See 04-relationships.md.

If a requirement ever appears — a form, an interview, a document — the honest starting point is to add the table back deliberately, with the requirement that made it necessary recorded as a decision. The removed design was general enough to carry one; it is recorded in the decision log rather than deleted from history.

docs.title: 5. unit_participation
docs.text:
Renamed from unit_membership. Belonging to a sub-unit is participation, not a species of membership (D-041). The old name asserted something untrue, and the rename is the fix.

Fields

Field Kind Notes person_id reference to person, required Deliberately person_id, not membership_id. Participation history must survive independently of how organization membership is recorded: imported 1998 rosters often have a unit and a year but no formal membership row, and linking to membership would make those unrepresentable — which would break the whole historical dataset. The trade-off is that nothing here can enforce "participation implies membership": it is application-level validation plus invariant 1 in §7, named as such rather than pretended away, in the register of 00-conventions.md §6a. org_unit_id reference to org_unit, required May be the root unit. A participation row on the root is created alongside each membership, so that "everyone in unit X" is one uniform question whether X is the organization or a Thursday-evening pack. See §5.1. role_in_unit text, optional One of member, leader, assistant, guest. A denormalised convenience for display and historical import. Not an authorization fact — authority is in role_assignment. valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = current. join_reason_code text, optional initial, transfer, promotion or reorganisation. leave_reason_code text, optional transfer_out, unit_closed or stopped_attending. is_primary boolean, required, defaults to true Which group to show first, for a person in several. data_confidence text, required, defaults to high One of high, medium, low. import_batch_id reference to the import batch, optional Set on imported rows. source text, optional self, staff or legacy_import. created_at, created_by, updated_at, updated_by timestamp, audit time; reference to person The standard audit columns.

Rules

  • Where both ends of the period are set, valid_to is later than valid_from.
  • A person takes part in a given unit only once at a time. No two participation rows for the same person and the same unit may cover the same date. The rule covers every row, open and closed alike; taking part again later is a separate, later period and is fine.

Indexes

  • On person_id, and on org_unit_id, both with valid_from descending: a person's roster history, and a unit's, newest first.
  • On (org_unit_id, person_id) restricted to open rows — the current roster of a unit, which stays small while the history does not.
  • A period index per unit, which is what the no-overlap rule and "was this row open on that date" both scan.

docs.title: 5.1 A participation row on the root unit
docs.text:
When a membership is created, a matching unit_participation row for the root unit is created over the same period, and similarly closed when the membership ends.

This buys one thing: "everyone in unit X" is one query, with one shape, at every level.

The question is who is in unit X on date D, and unit_participation answers it on its own: the rows of that unit whose valid_from is on or before D and whose valid_to is absent or after D, read with the person, ordered by family name and then given name. It works whether X is the organization (depth 0) or a Thursday group (depth 4). The date has to be applied to the participation rows themselves; filtering the unit, or a membership above it, by that date and leaving these rows unfiltered answers a different question.

Without it, "who is in the organization?" would be a query against membership and "who is in a pack?" a query against unit_participation — two shapes for one question, and every report would have to know which case it was in.

The redundancy is deliberate and bounded. The root row and the membership always have the same period, so the root row is derivable — and it is derived by nothing. No write may change a membership's period, or open or close one, without making the matching change to that person's root-unit participation row in the same transaction. The two rows are one fact written twice, so the obligation falls on every path that writes a membership, the legacy import above all: it creates memberships by the thousand and must create their root rows beside them. Integrity check 1b in §7 is the net under that, not the guard — it finds the drift afterwards, on a report somebody has to run. The alternative, a UNION in every roster query, is worse.

The root row is the only participation row that is extended rather than closed and reopened (D-050). A transfer between sub-units is still close-and-open (§5.2); the root row is different because it mirrors a period that is itself backdated:

  1. The yearly expiry sweep gives the membership a valid_to of the expiry date and moves its status to lapsed.
  2. The root participation row is not closed with it — it is moved forward to the same date, so it is neither open-ended nor a second row (D-050). Only that person's still-open row on the root unit is touched; a participation row carries no membership reference, so person and unit are how it is found.
  3. A renewal inside the window opens a new membership row starting at the expiry date ([D-016], D-040).
  4. The root row is then stretched to the new period's end, which is exactly "extend the existing row": one row spanning both periods, no gap, no overlap.

Steps 2 and 4 are the same edit — moving the open end of the root row — performed at two different moments.

The match in step 4 is the whole of D-050, and it is easy to get wrong. The root row is matched to the new membership by person and date, not through renewed_from_membership_id — the participation row carries no membership FK, deliberately (D-008, §5). So the condition is new_m.valid_from = up.valid_to: the renewal begins exactly where the root row was swept to. Anything looser would stretch a single row across a genuine post-window rejoin, where the gap is real and must stay.

This erases the visual evidence of the lapse, and that is the accepted trade (D-050). A person who lapsed and renewed looks, in unit_participation, exactly like a person who never lapsed. The lapse is still fully visible in membership, which is the authority on payment. The participation table answers "who was in this unit when" — a roster question — and for that question a child who was in the pack across the period has exactly one answer.

"Who was in the 4th Pack on 1 June 1998?" is then exactly the query above.

docs.title: 5.2 Transfers between sub-units are cheap
docs.text:
Because participation is not membership (D-041), moving a person between groups is one row edit — close one, open another. Nothing about their membership, their fee, or their status as a member changes.

Moving person 100 from pack 12 to pack 31 effective 1998-09-01 is two writes, in this order:

  1. Close the row that is open for person 100 in pack 12: valid_to becomes 1998-09-01, leave_reason_code becomes transfer_out, and updated_at/updated_by record who did it.
  2. Open a row for pack 31 with valid_from 1998-09-01, join_reason_code transfer, a source of staff, and the actor recorded as created_by.

Rewriting the old row would destroy the answer to "where was this child in 2003?" — the question the whole temporal design exists to answer. Close and open; never update org_unit_id in place.

Under the old model this was much more expensive: a "unit membership" was a membership, so moving a child between groups raised questions about which membership was which and whether a fee was owed twice. Participation removes the question.

docs.title: Unit reorganizations
docs.text: When a unit is split or merged, members are transferred by the same close-and-open pattern, with join_reason_code = 'reorganisation' and the org_unit_relationship row recording the lineage. A bulk operation should be a single named procedure with a dry-run mode — it will be run on hundreds of rows during an import and must be testable before it commits.

docs.title: 6. Membership and the authorization system
docs.text:
The resolver evaluates membership state. This is settled (D-039) and it is the single largest coupling in the design, so it is worth stating in full rather than in a footnote.

A role grants access ONLY IF the holder has a current membership,
    unless  role.requires_membership = false    (appointed counselors, local leaders)
    or      the channel is guardianship         (a legal relationship, not a membership)
    or      the channel is ownership            (your own record — see below)

The carve-outs, and why each exists:

Carve-out Why Guardianship A parent's authority over their child comes from a legal relationship. An unpaid fee must not make a parent unable to act for their child. Appointed counselors and local leaders The organization needs them present regardless of their own fee status. Marked per-role with requires_membership = false. Ownership Otherwise a lapse locks a person out of the very screen they renew on.

The cost, named plainly:

  • The permission cache must be invalidated on every membership transition — including the yearly expiry sweep, which is a bulk event touching every member at once. The cache design has to be built for this from the start; retrofitting it is where the bugs will be.
  • A lapse silently removes access. That is the intent, but "why can't I see this?" now has an answer that is a date rather than a decision.
  • role.requires_membership changed meaning — from a flag that drove a report to a value the resolver enforces.

The "leaver with access" report remains valuable, but its purpose changes. It no longer prevents access — the resolver already does that — so what it now detects is a role that should have been closed and was not. That is still worth a worklist, because a stale assignment silently springs back to life the moment the person renews:

Concretely: every role_assignment still open whose holder is_current_member() says is not a member, shown with the role's own requires_membership and with the enforced ones first — those are the assignments the resolver is holding back today, and the ones that will matter on renewal.

Dormant authority is a real hazard. A membership that lapses and is renewed a year later would otherwise resurrect every role the person held in the interim, including ones a human had quietly decided not to reinstate. Closing the assignment at the same time as the membership is the honest fix; this report finds the ones that were missed.

A role assignment should not outlive the membership that justified it.

docs.title: 7. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify

  • 1. Participation rows without a corresponding organization membership at that time. Counts participation rows for which the same person has no membership that is not pending_payment and whose period overlaps the participation's — one beginning on or before the participation ends (or begins, if it is still open) and ending after the participation begins. Non-zero is the case no constraint here can express, deliberately: someone taking part who was never a member.
  • 1b. The root participation row disagreeing with the membership it mirrors (§5.1). Counts memberships whose root-unit participation row has either end of its period different from the membership's own. Nothing maintains the root row on its own behalf — §5.1 makes the pairing an obligation on whoever writes the membership — so a non-zero count names the path that wrote one row and forgot the other.
  • 2. Participants in units that do not allow minors. Counts open participation rows in a unit whose type says allows_minors = false, where the person has a recorded birth date that makes them under 18 today. A unit that does not supervise minors may not have any placed in it — safeguarding, not membership: membership itself is ageless (D-038).
  • 3. Non-members holding a role that requires membership. Counts open role assignments on a role with requires_membership true whose holder is not a current member. The resolver blocks these (D-039), so this is not an access breach — it is a stale assignment that will spring back to life when the person renews (§6).
  • 4. Approved requests that never produced a membership. Counts requests that are approved, carry no membership_id, and were decided more than seven days ago. Non-zero is an approval that went nowhere.
  • 5. Memberships expiring soon. Counts active memberships ending within the next 90 days — the renewal campaign worklist (§6 of domain/05), not a fault.
  • 6. Renewal chains with a broken link. Counts memberships whose renewed_from_membership_id names a row that does not exist. Non-zero means the chain is followed into nothing.
  • 7. Renewals inside the window whose new period does not start at the previous expiry date. Counts renewals whose valid_from differs from the previous membership's valid_to and begins less than 91 days after it. The renewal rule (D-040) backdates the new period, so a mismatch means either a genuine post-window rejoin or a bug.

Check 3 is the one that matters most now. Under D-039 the resolver already blocks a non-member's roles, so this is no longer an access breach — but it detects dormant authority, which is the failure mode the membership gate introduces: a role nobody closed that silently reactivates on renewal.

Check 5 is operational (a worklist for the renewal campaign), and check 1b guards the one deliberate redundancy in the model (§5.1). The rest are data-quality checks for cases no constraint rejects at the write.

docs.title: 8. Seed data
docs.text:
The organization starts with a single membership type — member, named and described in plain words, open for a person to register themselves for, and left to requires_approval at its default of true. The term and the calendar parameters on that row are §1's, not constants anywhere else.

One row, and that is the whole vocabulary (D-037). The fee is flat and per person, so there is nothing to vary by type; being a counselor or leader is a position, not a type; and membership is ageless, so there are no age limits to seed (D-038).

The calendar is now settled — 1 January, 60 days (D-047, D-048). The term (12 months) remains a placeholder that nothing currently depends on. All four are columns rather than constants, so tuning any of them is an UPDATE, not a release.

The one rule about these four values: read them from the row. A scheduled job, a front end or a report that contains the literal 60 or 1 has quietly reverted a parameter to a constant, and the organization will discover it the first time it changes its mind.

No requirement_code seed. That table does not exist (D-044). The formerly seeded rows — guardian_consent, background_check, medical_form, references, previous_unit_transfer, photo_consent — are all gone: consent moved to the guardianship layer where it belongs, background checks are not recorded at all (D-043), and the rest were never required.

docs.title: 9. Open issues
docs.text:
• The real membership term and renewal-window length (§1, §8) — the two remaining type-level parameters.
  • Whether outstanding_balance should exist as a denormalised column or be computed (§3) — depends on the finance design in 07-finance.md.
  • Whether unit_participation should reference membership_id in addition to person_id, to get referential integrity without losing the import case. Possible as a nullable column, but it would be unenforced for imports.
  • What the root-unit participation row does when a membership is renewed inside the window — it must extend across the (retrospectively filled) period without creating an overlapping row (§5.1).

Resolved and no longer open, kept visible so the reasoning survives: whether a person may hold several open memberships (no — one type, person-scoped constraint, §3); whether membership activates on payment (yes, §3); whether permissions depend on membership state (yes, with carve-outs — D-039, §6); the age limits and age-out (§8); the grace period as a status (§6); and the whole requirement mechanism (§4).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Relationships
docs.text:
guardianship, and the single right level that travels with it.

Domain rationale: ../domain/02-actors.md.

This document describes requirements. It contains no DDL (D-072); the ORM decides how each rule is enforced.

docs.title: 1. guardianship
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id internal identifier Never appears in a URL or an external reference guardian_person_id reference to person, required One side of the relationship dependent_person_id reference to person, required The other side. Must not equal the guardian relationship enum: parent / legal_guardian / foster_parent / step_parent / grandparent / sibling / other, required sibling and other exist because the organization will meet cases that do not fit, and forcing them into parent corrupts the data. A 19-year-old legal guardian of a 12-year-old sibling is real right_level enum: none / view / write The whole of the guardian's authority (D-074). Current value, denormalised for the read that happens on every authorization check; history in guardianship_permission (§2) valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = current. Set by a person — a party to the row (§1 "Guardianship ends"), or a staff member asked to record it. Never by a job: the system takes no position on majority (D-069) is_primary_contact boolean, required, default false Who the organization calls in an emergency. Independent of right_level — a grandparent with no system access at all can still be the emergency contact. See ../domain/02-actors.md §6 is_legal_decision_maker boolean, required, default false Distinguishes who may make legal decisions — consent for medical treatment, travel — from who provides day-to-day care. Often different people lives_with boolean, optional Deliberately optional: false means guardianship without cohabitation (shared custody, a guardian in another city), which is a different fact from unknown. Relevant to contact routing, never to authority custody_arrangement free text A description, not a computable fact, and kept that way on purpose (§7) source enum: self / staff / import / court_order Decides the starting right_level (§2 defaults, D-046) verified_at timestamp, optional verified_by reference to person, optional evidence_reference free text Where the proof of guardianship is filed. For legal guardianship this matters: the organization must be able to show that it checked ended_reason_code free text / reason code ended_note free text created_at, updated_at timestamps created_by, updated_by reference to person import_batch_id reference to import batch Legacy rows only

Rules

  • A person may not be a guardian of themselves: the two person references must differ.
  • valid_to, when present, must be after valid_from.
  • At most one current guardianship per (guardian, dependent) pair. Their periods may not overlap. Past ones are unlimited and expected: a court order lapses and is renewed.
  • A dependent may have any number of simultaneous guardians, each with its own row and its own right_level.
  • is_primary_contact is not unique per dependent. A child can have two primary contacts.

Indexes

  • Lookups in both directions by person and valid_to — "who is this person's guardian" and "who does this person guard" are equally common.
  • A partial index on current rows only, and a second on current rows that are primary contacts: the emergency-contact lookup must not scan history.

docs.title: The relation is a general graph, not a two-level hierarchy
docs.text:
The requirements permit:

  • One guardian → many dependents. Multiple rows with the same guardian. This is "one parent can manage multiple children".
  • Many guardians → one dependent. Both parents, brothers' grandparents, a legal guardian plus a step-parent. Nothing assumes a child has exactly two guardians.
  • A person being both. Person A is guardian of B and dependent of C. Costs nothing to allow, and avoids a rewrite when a member reaches majority and becomes guardian to a younger sibling.

You specified the first two explicitly. The third is free.

docs.title: Per-dependent authority
docs.text:
Authority is per guardianship row, never per person. A parent can hold write for one child and view for another — a realistic shared-custody arrangement, and one the model must represent without inventing a second parent identity.

What changed with D-074 is the grain, not the location. Per row it used to be a set of capability codes; per row it is now one of three values. See §2 for what that costs.

docs.title: Guardianship ends — and who is allowed to end it
docs.text:
valid_to is set when:

  • a party to the row ends it. The guardian, or the adult who is the subject of it (D-073);
  • a court order changes the arrangement, which staff record;
  • the guardian dies — and note the organization does not record death (D-034), so this too arrives as a person ending a row, with whatever reason the organization uses.

Staff may always do it when asked. Staff may never be the only way it happens.

The parties are principals, not third parties with a grant. A guardianship row is not the guardian's record, and it is not the subject's record. It is a record of a relationship between them, and both hold it. This is scope authority — the rule that authority over a nested thing originates at that thing (D-031) — applied to a household instead of a unit.

It is not the ownership channel, and the distinction is worth keeping. Ownership is your own record. Ending a guardianship over yourself is not editing your own record; it is dissolving a relationship you are one half of. Mechanically this is the guardianship channel gaining a direction: it already asks "may guardian G act on D's records?", and it now also answers "may a party act on the guardianship row itself?", for exactly three acts — ending it, adding another guardian, and changing the right level. The resolver still has four channels (D-010, and the channels' dispatch changed in D-079).

The three acts a party may take, and no others:

Act Guardian Subject (adult) Staff End the row ✅ ✅ ✅ Add another guardian over the same dependent ✅ ❌ ✅ Change right_level downward ✅ ✅ ✅ Change right_level upward ✅ ❌ ✅ Edit the dependent's records per right_level own record per role

Read the last row against the first four, because an implementation will get this backwards. The four acts above are not gated by right_level: a guardian whose right is view, or even none, may still end the guardianship, and a person who has never been a guardian at all may not. The level ranks what you may do to the child's records, which is the fifth row and nothing else — it is not a general competence over the relationship, and reading it as one would mean that lowering someone's access to a medical file also locked them out of leaving the arrangement. The party direction follows the same rule as the record direction: it can only say yes (D-079). Being a party grants the act; not being one leaves the actor's own guardianship.* role permissions to be tried, which is how staff in the table above get their ✅s. An explicit deny still runs first and beats both.

The asymmetry, stated plainly. A guardian may appoint a guardian: anyone with authority over a child can give a second person that same authority with no approval from the organization. The ordinary case is a mother adding the father. The design does not prevent the non-ordinary case; it attributes it instead — who added whom, when, from which account, is audited, and the other party is notified. That is a deterrent and an evidence trail, not a wall. See E-6.

The system does not notice birthdays in this connection. No job, no review queue, no computed candidate date (D-069, reversing D-024 and closing E-2).

Why not, including why the gentler version was also refused. The legal reasoning is unchanged and still correct: in many jurisdictions a parent's authority over health and school records does not end at 18, and in some it ends at a different age, so any computed date is a claim the system cannot support. What D-069 adds is that a review queue makes the same claim more quietly. A queue asserts this arrangement is now suspect, in every case, for every family, including the ones where the adult child actively wants their parent to keep handling the paperwork. Deferring a decision is not declining to make one, and the queue was a decision.

D-069 refused, D-073 supplies. Read as one decision in two halves: a legal relationship between two people ends when one of those people says so, and the organization's job is to be told rather than to permit it. Without D-073, D-069 was a refusal with no alternative; the exit it assumed had no door.

What is lost, precisely: a prompt, not a record. valid_from/valid_to mean "who is listed as my guardian, and since when?" is a query with a complete answer including the date each ended. What replaces the prompt is the report in §6, run by a person on purpose.

docs.title: is_primary_contact vs is_legal_decision_maker
docs.text:
Two distinct questions that a single "is primary parent" flag conflates:

Question Column Who do we phone at 2am when the child is injured at camp? is_primary_contact Who may sign the consent form for that treatment? is_legal_decision_maker

They are often different people, and conflating them means either the wrong person is called or an invalid consent is accepted. Both are separate flags rather than one is_primary, because a child can have two primary contacts and one decision maker.

docs.title: 2. The guardian's right: none, view, or write
docs.text:
A guardian either cannot see the child's records, can see them, or can change them. That is the entire vocabulary (D-074).

guardianship_permission survives as the history of that value, not as a capability list. One row per change, exactly one row open at a time, so "what was this guardian allowed to see in March 2024?" stays answerable — the same current-value-plus-temporal-history shape that person uses for names.

Field Kind Notes guardianship_id reference to guardianship, required Scoped to the row, never to the (guardian, dependent) pair right_level enum: none / view / write, required The value being recorded valid_from date, required valid_to date, optional NULL = current. Ending this row without ending the guardianship changes the right; a new row starts it again changed_reason free text e.g. default for self-registered guardianship, court order 2026-03-14, guardian request changed_by reference to person, optional NULL when the default was applied by the application at creation

Rules

  • Exactly one row per guardianship may be open at a time.
  • Every change is a row; the value on guardianship.right_level is always the open row's value. If the two disagree, the row is authoritative and the copy is wrong.
  • Scoping to the guardianship row and not to the person pair is deliberate (D-020): when a guardianship ends and a new one begins — a renewed court order, a lapse and re-establishment — the rights must not silently carry over. A new relationship is a new row and a new, deliberate level.

docs.title: It is the same ladder, not a new one
docs.text:
The system already ranks authority as revoked(0) < view(10) < contribute(20) < manage(30) < admin(40) and compares by integer rank, never by string. The three guardian rights map onto it: none → 0, view → 10, write → 20.

This is not a convenience. A parallel enum would have meant a second authorization model with its own comparison rules, and the resolver would have needed a special case to know which ladder it was on. Guardian authority is a range of the existing ladder, and write landing on contribute rather than on manage or admin is what keeps a guardian from being able to do organization-wide things.

docs.title: What the collapse gives up, written down rather than discovered later
docs.text:
Before D-074, a guardianship carried a set of capability codes — dependent.profile.view, dependent.medical.view, dependent.consent.give, dependent.fee.pay, and thirteen others, with dependent.admin as a shorthand for all of them. Every dependent.* code is deleted.

The consequence is specific and should not be softened: it is no longer expressible that this guardian may register the child for events but may not read the medical record. The case the old model existed for — a court order restricting one parent's access to medical information while their other access continues — cannot be represented. A grandmother who was granted roster visibility and nothing else is now a view guardian, which means she can see the fee history and the medical file too.

What still holds:

  • write is contribute, not manage. A guardian cannot do organization-wide things.
  • Authority is per row, so a guardian of one child sees nothing of another's.
  • The organization-wide deny channel is untouched: a guardianship row granting write can still be refused by a deny, because deny is absolute and scope-independent (D-032). What was lost is a narrow deny — "not medical" — not the ability to say no.

If the split turns out to matter in operation it is a new decision, not a permission to be re-added quietly (E-7).

docs.title: Defaults still depend on how the guardianship arose
docs.text:
D-046 survives, with one value where it used to have a set:

source Starting right_level Why self — a parent registering their own child write They created the record and are asserting the relationship. There is nobody better placed to hold authority over it staff, import — recorded by someone else view, chosen at creation and raisable A person who did not assert the relationship is not handed authority by a default court_order view, and raised only by the person who filed the order The document says what the authority is; the system should not guess above it

Applied by the code that creates the row, at creation — and this is the correct layer, not a compromise. A default depends on why the row is being created, which is a fact about the user's intent that no database rule can inspect. What must not happen is the default being applied only by a form: an import that omits it produces a view guardian where the person meant full rights, and nothing objects. And nothing in §6 catches this either, which is worth being plain about: a default that was never applied leaves no inconsistent row behind — only a quiet view where a write was intended, indistinguishable from a deliberate restriction. That gap is a consequence of §2's collapse. Before D-074 an omitted bundle of grants was visible as an empty set, and an empty set is reportable where view is not. What closes it is not a report but the shape of the write path: one place creates guardianships, it reads source, and it does not accept a right_level from a caller who is not entitled to choose one. The staff and court_order paths need a human choosing a value, and a default that fires before anybody is asked is not a default, it is a decision made on someone's behalf — the same refusal D-069 and D-076 make elsewhere.

Why source and changed_reason are both kept. The same word — "guardian" — now means two different starting scopes depending on paperwork, and the record has to say which was chosen and why. A guardian with read-only access and a guardian with full access are indistinguishable in the domain language and must not be in the data.

docs.title: 3. There is no household table
docs.text: Removed (D-057). An address is a person_contact row of type postal (01-identity.md §6), which already exists, already keeps history (valid_from / valid_to), and already carries a purpose — 'billing' for the address an invoice goes to. A separate household table was duplicating it under a different key, and the duplication had gone stale: its postal_address column was documented as denormalised from the billing contact's postal contact, with nothing keeping the copy true.

docs.title: Shared address still grants no access
docs.text:
Living at the same address does not grant any permission over another person at that address. A stepparent with no guardianship row has no access to the children's records. A grandparent at the address has no access. This is deliberate and it is a safeguarding property, not an oversight.

This was true when household existed (D-019) and it is true now, for a simple reason worth stating so nobody re-derives it: the access never came from the household tables. All authority over a child's records comes from guardianship (§1–2). Removing a table that granted nothing cannot grant anything.

docs.title: What replaced it
docs.text:
Household feature Now Billing address person_contact of type postal with purpose billing "Which children lived at this address in 2003?" A query over the temporal person_contact history (domain/03 §4) One invoice for three siblings The fee is flat and per person (D-037); there is no family price to invoice fee_obligation.household_id Column and its index removed (07-finance.md §2)

What was genuinely lost, recorded rather than glossed: a household was a group with a name and its own lifetime. Two people at one address are now related by a query, not by a row, so there is nowhere to hang "the Novák family" as a first-class thing and no valid_from for the grouping itself. Accepted, because nothing was using it — no code set fee_obligation.household_id, and household.name had no consumer. If family-level communication or a family discount is ever wanted, this is the decision to revisit, and the shape to bring back is a group with a period, not a fake person.

docs.title: Why not a family person row
docs.text: Some systems model a household as a fake person so that memberships and payments can attach to it. Do not. It creates rows in person that are not people, which breaks identity matching, produces nonsense in name searches, and — because it is a person — can receive a membership, an account, and eventually permissions.

docs.title: 4. How the resolver uses these tables
docs.text:
The guardianship channel is step 4 of the resolver (../domain/06-authorization-model.md).

How the channel is selected — a change D-074 forces, and it is an improvement. It used to be selected by the permission code's namespace: a code beginning dependent. routed here, and the point of routing by prefix was that no caller gets to choose which channel applies, which is what stops one authorization rule being implemented twice, once wrong. With no dependent.* codes there is no prefix, so the channel is now selected by a fact about the request: the person the action is about is not the person performing it. Nobody picks a channel; the shape of the call picks it. And it catches what the prefix missed — a parent editing their child's address under a person.* code previously did not route through guardianship at all, because the code's name said otherwise.

Asked about another person, it resolves in this fixed order, and it produces one of two outcomes: an allow, or no answer at all. It never answers "no".

  1. Is there a current guardianship row between this actor and this subject, at the date being asked about? If not, this step is not the channel's business and says nothing — the resolver continues to the actor's own roles and grants. Silence, not refusal (D-079).
  2. Is there an explicit deny covering this check? Deny wins here as everywhere else, and independently of how broad the underlying grant is (D-032) — but note that this deny is found by channel 0 of the resolver, before this step runs, so nothing in this list can override it. It is listed second only because it is the other reason a guardian with a sufficient right_level still gets nothing.
  3. Read the row's right_level and rank it: none 0, view 10, write 20.
  4. Compare against what the action needs. Reading a profile needs 10; editing a contact needs
  5. At or above the requirement → allow. Below it, or none → no answer, and the actor's own roles are tried.

Why step 1 and step 4 fall through instead of refusing, when refusing is what this channel used to do. It used to be entered only by codes no role could hold, so its refusal was the whole answer. Now it is entered by ordinary codes that a role may also carry, and finality produces an absurd result the moment one person wears two hats: the parent who is also the event registrar, holding view over their own child, refused the right to mark attendance. The relationship should not be able to revoke a job. What is not given up: none still grants nothing (that is what D-074 promised, not a power to block other bases), and an organization that genuinely must stop a specific person touching a specific child's records uses an explicit deny, which runs first, everywhere, at any scope.
