The requirement is that no part of the permission path — resolver, grant lookup, guardianship lookup, or any view an authorization check reads — may walk the unit hierarchy. A unit's ancestors are not in scope for a check, full stop; unit_ancestors() exists for the structural questions (nesting rules, paths, reports) and must never be reachable from an authorization decision. Anything that reaches it means authority is flowing downward through a permission path, which the design forbids. What was lost here is the mechanism, not the rule: this used to be a build-time assertion that grepped the stored definitions of the three resolver functions, so an inheriting view added by a later migration failed the build rather than passing review. D-072 removed the SQL and with it the only form of this check that could fail automatically. It is now a code review instruction, and the ORM makes it harder, not easier, to write the bad thing conspicuously — an implicit join through a parent relation looks like ordinary fetching. Whoever builds this should restore an automatic version, in whatever the ORM's test layer is.
  • 15. TIME-BOMB for the membership gate (D-039). Same shape, same loss: the role channel had to contain both the gate (is_current_member) and the role-level opt-out (requires_membership), so that neither could be dropped quietly — deleting the gate revives the problem D-039 closed, and deleting the opt-out makes a role that is supposed to survive a lapse unable to. The requirement stands as written in step 6 of §10; only the grep that enforced it is gone.
  • 16. Role deletions. A role_assignment pointing at a role that is no longer there. The delete guard on role enforces this; the check exists because a restored dump or a manually disabled guard bypasses it, and the loss is unrecoverable — the assignments go with the role. Zero expected.
  • 17. Unused roles. A non-system role with no assignment that is open or still in the future. A role nobody holds is not an error: it is either one about to be used or one stopped using and not deleted, and there is no third possibility, because a role has no period (D-053) and cannot be switched off, only held or not held. Expected: unused, non-system roles. Delete the mistakes, keep the ones on the roadmap.
  • 18. Orphaned permissions. An assignable permission that no role grants. This check exists because of D-068: with no .admin wildcard, a permission that ought to be inside some role and was never added to it is silently unusable, and no resolver rule covers it by accident any more. This is the net the wildcard used to be. Expected: empty after a seeding pass. A row means either a permission nobody has bundled yet — fine on a roadmap, wrong in production — or a module was added and its roles were not. Note what it cannot see: a permission granted to a role but not to the role that arguably should have it. That residual is the accepted cost of D-068 and nothing closes it; it is a human reading the starter list in §12 against the catalog.
  • 19. TIME-BOMB for D-068: the .admin prefix match must stay deleted. Two parts, both written as CI assertions when this document still carried SQL; both are prose now, which D-072 records as a real weakening. First, no step of the resolver may build a permission code by concatenating a resource with .admin. This is a rule about the code, not about a particular query, and it survives the move to an ORM untouched — it is the one invariant here that is about program text rather than about data, and it is the one an ORM migration will never violate on its own. A reintroduced wildcard re-creates implied capabilities for every resource, including resources added after the day it was added back. Second, no permission may have admin as its action except exactly one: system.admin. D-068 exempted four others on purpose, and D-074 withdrew all four exemptions along with the namespace they lived in, so the allow-list is a single code and the check is now an equality, not a set membership. system.admin is explained in the catalog's §1 as one of the two things still named "admin"; anything else carrying admin as an action is a re-created wildcard. Zero rows expected. The whole point of this entry is that the first version of the second half accepted five exceptions and the second version accepts one: an allow-list is where a wildcard comes back to life.

Checks 3, 7, 7b, 14 and 15 are the ones to wire to alerts.

  • Check 7b is the new one worth wiring to an alert. Check 7 answers "who can rewrite the system?"; 7b answers "who keeps authority while lapsed?" — a shorter list with a different failure mode, and the one the membership gate introduces. Neither should ever grow quietly.
  • Check 7 should email someone every time its result changes — a new system_admin is either a planned change or an incident, and either way someone should know within the hour.
  • Checks 14 and 15 are CI assertions, not reports. They are the automated guards on the two rules most likely to be "simplified" away when someone optimizes the resolver: the no-inheritance rule and the membership gate. Both fail the build rather than silently changing who can do what.
  • Check 9 catches the direction being broken in the way the resolver cannot see. A row that reaches sideways to a sibling unit, or down to a descendant, would be honoured happily by can() — nothing else in this list would notice it, and it is precisely the shape that lets authority be claimed from outside.
  • Checks 12 and 13 guard the audience model. Built-ins must not accumulate member rows (they are rules), and an empty named group is usually an abandoned one.

docs.title: 12. What the organization starts with
docs.text:
Starting catalog. Expect to edit this heavily; it is a proposal, not a specification.

This section and ../appendix/permission-catalog.md are the same list written twice, and they drift. When this was reconciled, 22 documented permissions had no INSERT row — among them unit_participation.view, which five of the catalog's own seed roles assign, and person.redact, which is one of the two codes D-068 exists to protect. A further 12 were the event.* set, added to the catalog when events were designed and never carried here. Under the old wildcard much of this was harmless: a role holding unit_participation.admin reached the code whether or not the row existed, so the catalog could advertise a capability the database could not name and nothing noticed. The permission editor was the only place the gap showed. D-068 removed that cushion. Now a role that lists a code with no row either fails to insert or grants nothing, and integrity check 18 reads the table, so it cannot see that the catalog promised something the seed never contained.

There is no SQL check for this — one side is a Markdown file. The discipline is the check: when adding a permission, add it in both places in the same edit, and treat a catalog row with no INSERT row as a bug of the same class as a missing migration. The reconciliation is mechanical enough to script if this file ever grows again:

a diff of the codes the catalog lists against the codes that exist. Anything in the catalog and not in the database is a permission that cannot be granted; anything in the database and not in the catalog is an undocumented capability. Both were present at the same time.

Roles are data, and the organization administers them at runtime. This section seeds the permissions — the vocabulary of things anyone might do. The role names used throughout the docs are worked examples of composing those permissions into groups, not a fixed list. Creating a role, changing what it grants, assigning it and deleting an unused one are all supported operations (role.create, role.edit, role.assign, role.unassign, role.delete).

The consequence for this document: it does not need to know which roles exist, and where it names a role it is illustrating, not specifying. In particular, which roles carry system.gate_exempt is a configuration decision that belongs to the organization, not to the specification.

What §12 must fix, and does, is the shape. system.gate_exempt is a system- namespace permission: it can only arrive through a role, never through an item grant. That is not a configuration choice — it is the structural guarantee that an access_grant can never lift the membership gate. Whether the organization puts it in one role or five is its own business.

What the organization starts with. The platform ships a vocabulary — the permissions, each marked as a system row so it cannot be deleted or renamed — and that is the whole of what these documents fix. Roles, assignments and grants are runtime data (D-052): the organization composes them, edits what they grant, and deletes the ones nobody held. The starter roles the catalog sketches are proposals to edit, and the permissions themselves are starter material too.

Those permissions span the namespaces this document and its neighbours describe: people — viewing, creating, editing, merging, contacts, and the two irreversible codes; the vocabulary of personal attributes, where recording a value needs no new code and naming a thing needs attribute.define; accounts, including suspension, closure and credential reset; membership, including requests, activation, lapse, suspension, termination and backdating; participation in sub-units; units, their renaming, restructuring and closing; scope exposure and its review; audiences; positions; guardianship and the granting of guardian permissions; the administration of roles and permissions themselves; item grants; audit; legacy import; reporting; the thirteen event.* codes; and the messaging codes. **What is not on that list is the set that used to follow it: the eighteen dependent.* codes are deleted, because a guardian's authority is now a level on the guardianship row rather than a bundle of permissions (D-074), and the guardian-facing acts that survive are ordinary guardianship.* codes in the catalog. The one remaining list is ../appendix/permission-catalog.md. It is the catalog; this document deliberately no longer keeps a second copy of it, because the two copies disagreed for exactly the reason the note above describes.

A few of those codes carry a decision in their shape, and those are worth naming:

  • person.merge, person.unmerge and person.redact are separate codes, not flavours of person.edit. They are irreversible, and with no person.admin to imply them (D-068) a role that reaches them does so by listing them, visibly. identity_reviewer holds person.merge; no starter role holds person.redact.
  • person.view reaches the whole record, and that is a change of reach rather than a new capability. Since D-083 there is no privileged corner of the record for it to stop outside: whoever holds it over a person reads their descriptive values — the allergy list, the insurance number, the note about who the child actually lives with — on the same grant that reads their name (09-attributes.md §4). It is therefore the widest read permission in the system, and the catalog's sensitivity mark is where that has to be visible: a mark set when "read a person" meant name and birth date now understates the code, and the honest mark is the catalog's top tier — which is worded around whose data a grant exposes rather than around a category of fields, because a category is what D-083 deleted. Read a bundling role with that in front of you — person.view inside a role now means this role reads medical facts, because that is what reading a person means. Any future narrowing is a decision entry about a second grant scope over a defined set of data, and not a code with a suggestive name; the case for it ("everything except the diagnoses") was put and declined (domain/08-person-data.md §4).
  • audit.view is graded against what the trail quotes, not against what a log is usually for. audit_log carries before and after images, and since D-085 those images are the only place a child's past descriptive values exist; an entry is therefore as sensitive as the person data it quotes, and reading history has to sit in the same tier as reading a person. The alternative — keeping the values out of the payload — was taken once during this round and withdrawn (D-083), because it graded descriptive fields above a change of address and left the history empty; what is left is this bullet, which is a mark on a line of a table and nothing else, and is the reason 09-attributes.md §6 calls the guard the weakest link rather than the last line of defence.
  • attribute.define is the narrow half of a deliberate pair: values are open to anyone who may already edit the person, so that the fact gets recorded, and codes are held by few people, because the codes are what make the data queryable (09-attributes.md §2). It is an ordinary permission — no namespace, no resolver branch, no structural consequence — and it is the only code this area adds.
  • scope.expose is scoped to the unit being covered. A parent unit's officer cannot satisfy it for a child unit, which is what makes the no-inheritance rule enforceable, and there is no bulk variant (D-045): every exposure row is written by the unit it covers.
  • role.unassign is the only thing that ends authority, because a role has no period (D-053) and nothing forces an assignment to end (D-071).
  • system.gate_exempt sits in the system namespace on purpose (D-051), so it can only arrive through a role assignment and never through an item grant. It is scope-independent by design: the gate is a property of the person, so the waiver has to be. Holding it means every gated role you hold keeps granting whether or not your own fee is current.
  • membership.terminate expels, and is restricted as such; membership.lapse is an administrative end for non-payment.
  • org_unit.restructure is split, merge and successor units — it is not reparenting (D-036).
  • unit_participation.view held at organization scope reads the root's own participation rows, not a pack roster, because scope is matched exactly. That looks like a bug and is not (D-049).
  • event.presence.mark sits one level below event.manage_participants on purpose, and event.register_self is the eligibility rule (D-060) rather than an expression of one. No wildcard sits among the thirteen, so a role that runs events holds all thirteen explicitly; the rationale is in catalog §8a.
  • There is no wildcard left at all, and that is worth noticing. dependent.admin was the last deliberate one — one stored fact granting everything for one child — and D-074 replaced it with right_level = write, which does the same job without being a permission: it is a property of the relationship, so it cannot be listed in a role, granted to a unit, or discovered by prefix matching. The catalog's §1 now lists two things named "admin" where it once listed three. The residue is the opposite problem: with no wildcard, nothing implies anything, so a role that should have a new permission must be told (invariant 18 is the net).
  • audit has no audit.admin — per-resource admin codes were removed (D-068).

Reporting is seeded coarse, and left open on purpose. Only report.view and report.export are starters. Whether reporting is per-report (report.finance.view, report.membership.view, report.safeguarding.view) or one report.view with row-level filtering is still open (catalog §12), and the starter roles in catalog §11 name the granular ones only to illustrate that unresolved choice. Do not ship both shapes; pick one when reporting is designed.

Levels and scope types are vocabulary, not configuration. The five levels — revoked at rank 0, then view, contribute, manage, admin — arrive with the schema, because a rank ordering that can be edited at runtime is a security control with no owner; their meanings are in §6 and in 00-conventions.md. The grantable scope types start as organization, which is not item-scoped, then org_unit, membership, event (designed in 08-events.md) and document (a document layer still to be designed).

Built-in audiences come in two shapes. everyone and all_members exist once for the whole system, marked as system rows. The parameterised ones are created where they are needed rather than seeded everywhere: unit_participants and unit_leaders one row per unit that needs one, with scope_parameter naming that unit — the case that replaced the bulk exposure tool, and named by convention along the lines of unit:42:participants and unit:42:leaders — and guardians_of one per dependent whose guardians need a shared target. None of them ever has member rows (integrity check 12, §11).

system.admin is deliberately a single top-level permission, not a per-resource one. Holding it satisfies everything, and check 7 in §11 alerts on its holders. Keeping the most dangerous capability concentrated and alarmed is safer than spreading equivalents of it across every resource.

docs.title: 13. Open issues
docs.text:
• The complete permission catalog and real role definitions (§12) — needs your input. Specifically: which roles are marked requires_membership = false. That flag is now the line between "a lapse silently removes this" and "it does not", and it needs a deliberate answer per role rather than a default.
  • Whether valid_to should be mandatory for high-authority assignments (§4).
  • Polymorphic scope_id vs a grantable_item supertable (§6) — a real fork.
  • Which built-in audiences are needed beyond everyone and all_members, and whether the parameterised ones are seeded per instance or created on demand (§8).
  • How long a permission_cache entry may live given the membership gate (§10) — the shorter the TTL, the smaller the window in which a lapse has not yet taken effect.
  • Cache vs materialized effective-permission table (§10).
  • Retention policy for access_log — legal input required.
  • Whether access_log needs human annotation (recommend a separate table if so).

Resolved and no longer open, kept visible so the reasoning survives: the bulk exposure tool (removed — D-045); whether permissions depend on membership status (yes, with three carve-outs — D-039); background-check permissions (removed — D-043); and the organization-wide-roles tension (§4), which is much reduced now that membership and the registry live at the single root unit (D-035).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Audit and Import
docs.text:
audit_log, import_batch, staging tables, and the redaction log.

access_log (the authorization audit trail) is in 05-authorization.md. This document covers the data-change audit trail, the legacy import pipeline, and erasure.

docs.title: 1. Two audit trails, and why both
docs.text:
access_log audit_log Records Who did what, and by what authority Which fields of a row changed, and their values before and after — except a person's descriptive values, which are never in the entry (§2.2) Answers "Who accessed this child's record, and were they allowed to?" "When did this person's address change, and who changed it?" Volume Very high High Raised by Application code, on every permission check and action Every write to an audited table, on every path — §2.1 names who owes that write now that no trigger is defined anywhere

Keeping them separate is deliberate. They have different retention needs, different query patterns, and different access permissions. Merging them produces a table that is too large to query and too sensitive to expose to anyone who needs one half of it.

One wording change, because this table used to ask about a thing that no longer exists. The first cell read "who accessed this child's medical record", a phrase this corpus cited in five places and defined in none. D-083 resolved it by removing the referent rather than by building it: there is one record about a person, and everything in it other than name, gender and age lives in person_attribute (09-attributes.md). The question this trail answers is unchanged and is now sharper — it is asked about the whole record, which is the thing person.view really reaches.

docs.title: 2. audit_log
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id occurred_at timestamp, audit time Default: now transaction_id integer, required Default: the id of the enclosing transaction. Groups all changes made in one transaction, so a multi-table operation (approve a request → create a membership → open a unit participation) reads as one event rather than three unrelated ones actor_person_id reference to person, optional Taken from the request context, not from the row. NULL for migrations, imports, and batch jobs actor_label text, optional system, migration:0042, import_batch:17 — for changes with no person actor. Otherwise a forensic gap operation text, required One of: insert, update, delete table_name text, required record_id surrogate id, required The row that changed. No reference: the table is named per row, so it points at any table in the database changed_fields list of text Which columns changed. Enables targeted history queries without parsing JSON old_values free-form jsonb, optional Redacted before insert. See §2.2 new_values free-form jsonb, optional Redacted before insert. See §2.2 on_behalf_of reference to person, optional Set when the actor was acting for another person. Mirrors access_log.on_behalf (04-relationships.md §5) session_id text, optional ip_address network address, optional request_id text, optional

Indexes

  • One row's history: table name and record_id, newest occurred_at first.
  • One actor's actions, newest first.
  • Everything in one transaction, by transaction_id.
  • By time alone, newest first.
  • Rows by a member of changed_fields. The targeted history queries ask "which rows changed this column", so the list has to be searchable element-wise rather than as a whole value.

docs.title: 2.1 The trigger
docs.text:
The heading is kept because the obligation under it is unchanged; what changed is that nothing in this repository defines a trigger any more. A trigger used to be how this section guaranteed its own rule, and D-072 removed it without removing the rule, so the rule is now stated as what it is: every insert and every update to an audited table writes exactly one audit_log row, and the change and its audit row stand or fail together. "The audit trail usually has it" is not a version of this rule — the trail is how the organization answers "who changed this child's address, and when?", and an answer that depends on which code path made the change is not an answer. The layer that owes it is the write itself, on every path: the screens, the legacy import, the yearly expiry sweep, a bulk reorganisation, and a row somebody corrects by hand. Model-layer validation logs the intended path, which is the only path that was never at risk; check 5 in §5 is the net under the rest, and it is a report, not a guard.

The steps below are what is owed, in the order that makes it safe. The order is a rule, not a detail: the redaction step has to run before the write, and the "nothing changed" test has to run before anything is spent on a row that would log noise.

  1. Read the acting person and the on-behalf-of person from the request context (app.current_person_id, app.on_behalf_of); an unset or empty value means no actor, not an error.
  2. On an insert, take the new row as the after-image.
  3. On an update, take both the old and the new row, and work out the changed fields: the keys present in both images whose values differ, named in key order.
  4. If that comparison found nothing, stop and write nothing — a no-op update must not log noise.
  5. On a delete, take the old row as the before-image; there is no after-image.
  6. Redact both images (§2.2): the credential values that must never be logged at all, and — where the row belongs to a redacted person — the personal data erasure has already removed from the business tables. Everything else is stored as it stands, including a person's descriptive values, which are guarded by §8 item 7 rather than stripped here.
  7. Write one audit row carrying: the actor and the on-behalf-of persons, the operation as lower-cased insert, update or delete, the table name, the record id taken from the new row and falling back to the old one, the changed fields, both redacted images, and the session id, ip address and request id from the request context.
  8. Change nothing about the row being written. The audit row describes the change and never amends it — and it commits in the same transaction as the change. That togetherness is the property a trigger used to supply for nothing, and the one a logging step written beside the write has to supply deliberately.

The obligation covers inserts and updates on person, membership, guardianship, role_assignment and access_grant; on role and role_permission — the role tables, not just the assignments, because a role is runtime data the organization edits (D-052) and editing one changes effective permissions for every holder at once with no assignment written, so without these two tables the single largest privilege change available in the system leaves no trace on any other audited row; and on every remaining business table — the exact set is still open in §6, and the recommendation there is all of them. There is nothing left to attach this to, which changes what the sentence is and not what it covers. It is the list of tables for which a write path owes an audit row; a business table created next year is inside it from the day it exists; and check 5 in §5 is what notices when the list and the write paths drift apart.

person_attribute is inside that obligation on exactly the same terms as any other business table, and the sentence is worth writing down because this document asked for an exception here and was refused. A write to a descriptive value owes its audit row like any write, and it carries its before and after images like any write (00-conventions §8 item 7). The reason no exception survives is that both halves of the design collapse without one: D-085 chose overwrite-in-place on the strength of this trail being the only history a value has, so a trail recording a value changed without recording which one would be a history of nothing; and D-083 says a diagnosis is not a different kind of fact from a shoe size, so excluding attribute values from the payload while person_contact changes are logged with their values would be a sensitive subset of the person record re-enacted inside the logging rules — the privileged corner arriving as a list of table names after it was deleted as a list of permission names.

Therefore this table holds a child's allergy list in the clear, in a table designed to be read by auditors and kept longer than the record it describes. That is the design, not an accident of it, and what it means is that the guard on audit_log is now load-bearing in a way it was not: an audit entry about a person is as sensitive as the person data it quotes, which is stated as a requirement on audit.view's sensitivity mark in ../appendix/permission-catalog.md §8 and argued in 05-authorization.md §9 — where the case against copying data into a less-guarded place applies to this table directly, since this table is the copy. The failure mode inverts, and it is worth naming because the shape is unfamiliar: everywhere else the worry is a table nobody audits, and here it is a table whose payloads outrank its own permission. No check in §5 can see that — a sensitivity mark is a line in a document, not a row in the database — so it is a review item with exactly one place it is written down, and that is the fragility.

role and role_permission are audited for a reason the other tables do not share. Everywhere else, the audit log answers "who changed this record?". Here it answers the harder question the next incident will ask: "what did role X grant on the date this decision was made?" Because a role edit rewrites the meaning of every assignment that points at it, in place, there is no way to answer that from the assignments — the assignments did not change. The log is the only record of what the role said at the time.

DELETE is intentionally outside the audited operations on business tables, because nothing in this data model is hard-deleted (see 00-conventions.md). Staging tables do get deleted; they are not audited. The absence is a consequence of the deletion policy rather than a gap in the obligation above. It is, however, true of ordinary operation and false of exactly two moments, and saying so is the honest version of the paragraph.

The first is §3's import revert, which does hard-delete business rows — the person, membership and unit_participation rows a batch created — and those rows were live, referenced and visible to real users before they went. So a revert writes audit entries for its deletes, naming the batch and the row it removed.

The second is §4's erasure, which deletes the person_attribute rows of the person being anonymised (00-conventions §4 records why that one table is erased by deletion rather than by overwriting, and the condition on which that stays safe — nothing may reference an attribute row). It is recorded once, in redaction_log, naming person_attribute in redacted_tables — and not as one audit_log row per erased value. That is a consequence of §2.2 rather than an exception to the revert rule, and the difference is worth seeing: revert deletes rows whose contents are safe to quote and whose existence is what someone will ask about, while erasure deletes rows whose contents must not be quotable afterwards and whose existence is the only fact that may survive. Note what this argument is, because §2.1's argument is the opposite one and both have to be true at once: per-value audit entries here would either write the erased value into a row that outlives the erasure — which is a redaction that failed, and precisely the copy §2.2 exists to destroy — or accumulate hundreds of identical rows whose entire content is "something was erased", which is exactly what §4's log is for. So values are quoted in the trail as a rule, and the rule stops at the moment the person they describe asks not to be described any more.

DELETE is outside the audited operations everywhere else only because there is no third path that reaches a business row with a delete. That makes revert the one place the list in §5 check 5 cannot be derived from table names alone: an audited operation rather than an audited table, which is why check 5's replacement assertion enumerates the paths that may delete, not just the tables that may be written. Erasure is the second such path and belongs on that enumerated list too; it audits nothing per row, so the assertion has to know it exists rather than infer it.

docs.title: 2.2 Redaction before logging
docs.text:
Two mechanisms operate here. An earlier draft of this section described three, and the third has been withdrawn below rather than quietly deleted, because the mistake is the useful part.

An audit log that stores the data it audits is a second copy of that data, with weaker access controls and a longer retention period. This sentence is still true, and it still describes audit_log, which holds the whole person record in its payloads. What changed is which half of it is treated as the defect. The first response was to empty the payload; the answer here is the other half — the log's access controls and retention are what is wrong about the copy, and emptying the payload fixes neither while destroying the reason the table exists. See 00-conventions.md §8 item 7 and 05-authorization.md §9, which argues against copying data into a less-guarded place and, read against this table, names the copy in question.

Mechanism one is a small set of values that must never enter the trail at all. Credentials, tokens, the secret half of an integration: for these, being in a log is the harm, and no guard is wide enough to make them safe there. This is the only job the key-name list below has.

Mechanism two is erasure reaching payloads that were written lawfully at the time. Redacting a person removes their values from images already in the trail (§4, and check 6 in §5); nothing here prevents those values from having been written, and the erasure is what unmakes them.

The redactor takes one table name and one row image and does this:

  1. If there is no image at all, there is nothing to redact — return no value.
  2. For each key in the credential list — secret_hash and the integration secrets beside it — if the image carries that key, replace its value with the marker «redacted». Keys the image does not have are left alone. The list is applied wherever a listed key turns up, in any table.
  3. Return the image.

That is the whole mechanism, and the list is short on purpose. It is keyed on field names, which is the right shape for it: a name-based rule is the only kind that reaches a credential hidden in an unexpected column, and a credential is safe behind no guard, so the rule has to fire on sight.

The rule that used to sit above these steps, and why it is gone. An earlier draft reduced a person_attribute image to its two references — person_id and attribute_definition_id, saying whose fact and which fact and nothing of its content, with no «redacted» marker either — on the grounds that a log read by more people than the record should not hold what the record holds. It is withdrawn, for two reasons that came from the decisions this section already reflects:

  • It re-created, inside the logging rules, the sensitive subset D-083 deleted (../decisions/decision-log.md#d-083--there-is-no-medical-record-personal-data-is-one-class-of-data). A rule that strips attribute values while person_contact changes are logged with their values is a list of more-sensitive-than fields wearing a table name instead of a permission name.
  • It left D-085's history empty. Overwrite-in-place was chosen because the trail is the history; an entry that records a value changed without recording which one is a history of nothing, and the question this table's history is actually asked for — what did we believe about this child in March? — would have been unanswerable by design rather than by accident.

What the draft got right survives as the guard instead: the copy is as sensitive as what it quotes, so the permission that reads it belongs at the top of the catalog (../appendix/permission-catalog.md §8), and that is a line in a document rather than a mechanism, which is the honest weakness.

What the credential list is not, stated where a reviewer will read it. It is not the thing protecting personal data, and it cannot become that, because a list of names is only as good as somebody having predicted the name of every field that would ever matter — and this system generates those names at runtime, one per code the organization invents. allergy is not on the list and never will be, which is now the correct state of affairs rather than a hole: an allergy is a value in person_attribute, it is logged, and it is protected by who may read the table it was logged into.

Which half of that sentence is the requirement, and which was a mechanism. "In the trigger" used to appear here, and D-072 deleted the trigger. What survives is the ordering, which is the part with the teeth and which now applies to mechanism one alone: credential stripping runs on the way in, never in a cleanup job that might not run. The trigger was one way to guarantee that; a code path that redacts, then writes, is another; a code path that writes and repairs afterwards is not that, because for one transaction the secret is in the log and readable, and because the repair is the cleanup job this sentence forbids. With no trigger there is nothing stopping the third option except whoever writes it, which is why the sentence is stated as a rule about ordering rather than about a database feature. Mechanism two runs in the opposite direction — it reaches rows already written, which is the only way an erasure can affect a trail that must not be rewritten — and the two are not in tension because one is about a value that should never have been written and the other is about a value that was. See 00-conventions.md §8 for what else the move to generated schema took out of this section's defence in depth.

The personal-data entries in the old redaction list are gone, and they were removed rather than renamed. It used to read secret_hash, notes, custody_arrangement, termination_note, rejection_note, status_note, on the theory that free text is where a diagnosis hides; a second, shorter always-redacted set repeated notes and custody_arrangement for emphasis, which already told you the mechanism was running on intuition about which fields looked sensitive. All of them are logged now, for the same two reasons as above: the fields are person data and D-083 refuses to grade person data, and a scrubbed history is a history that did not happen. The residual risk is stated plainly rather than left implicit — an audit table holding a child's descriptive values is a wider surface than any single screen, and the thing standing between it and a volunteer with an interest is one sensitivity mark plus whoever implements it.

What still argues against person.notes, and it is not this. Consider whether person.notes should exist at all: it is the last free text about a person outside the attribute vocabulary, the vocabulary is where such a sentence is visible to a report and to a curator rather than only to whoever next opens the record, and the open question is argued there in 01-identity.md §2 as well as here.

docs.title: 2.3 History query
docs.text:
The full change history of one row is found by taking the audit_log rows for its table name and record id, newest occurred_at first, and reading out when it happened, the operation, which fields changed, the old and new values, and who did it — the actor's person name where there is an actor, and actor_label where there is not.

For a person_attribute row this query is the history, not a shadow of it. Values are overwritten in place (D-085), so every value a child's allergy list ever held sits under one record_id, and this is where the question "what did we believe about this child in March, and who wrote it down?" gets answered. The consequence is the one §2.2 spends its length on, restated where it bites: a history screen over this table is a person-data surface. It is reached through audit.view, and it deserves to be reached through person.view too — a reader who may see that an allergy was recorded in 2019 but may not see the allergy is holding the second question and will ask it out loud. The guard on the trail is what is relied on; a per-entry "could this reader see this field" check inside the history view was considered and left unimplemented, because it would mean running the resolver per audit row against a value that no longer exists anywhere as a row to resolve against. It is a registered question rather than an omission now: AT-4.

docs.title: 3. Import pipeline
docs.text:
Six stages, from ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md. The guiding requirements: idempotent, reversible per batch, never overwrites self-registered data, preserves provenance.

import_batch — one run of the pipeline, and the unit revert works on.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id name text, required description text, optional source_type text, required One of: csv, xlsx, json, sql_dump, manual_entry, other source_reference text, optional Where the file lives, or what it is. Enough to find the original again source_hash text, optional SHA-256 of the source file. Detects re-importing the same file under a new name row_count integer, optional status text, required One of: staging, parsed, matching, review, applying, applied, reverted, failed. Default staging dry_run boolean, required Default false. A dry run parses and matches but writes nothing to business tables created_by reference to person, required created_at timestamp, audit time applied_at timestamp, audit time, optional applied_by reference to person, optional reverted_at timestamp, audit time, optional reverted_by reference to person, optional revert_note text, optional field_mapping free-form jsonb, optional This batch's raw-column → attribute-code map: one entry per raw column in the source, each naming one code or discard with a reason. Fixed for the batch, reviewed as a unit, editable only as a new decision — see The legacy field→code mapping below, which explains why the grain is a column and not a row error_summary text, optional notes text, optional

Indexes

  • Batches by status — the queue of runs that are not finished.

staging_import — one source row, kept exactly as it arrived.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id batch_id reference to import batch, required source_row_number integer, optional raw_data free-form jsonb, required The row VERBATIM. Never modified. This is the evidence source_row_hash text, required Deterministic hash of the meaningful fields. The idempotency key: re-importing a file matches on this and skips already-applied rows

Rules

  • (batch_id, source_row_hash) is unique — one staged row per batch per source row. It covers all rows, not only unapplied ones.

Indexes

  • The staged rows of one batch.

staging_import_row — what the parser made of that source row, and what became of it.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id staging_id reference to staging row, required parsed_given_name text, optional parsed_family_name text, optional parsed_name_normalised text, optional Diacritics stripped, casefolded parsed_birth_date date, optional parsed_birth_precision text, optional Reuses the person.birth_date_precision values parsed_unit_code text, optional parsed_unit_name text, optional parsed_period_from date, optional parsed_period_to date, optional Often NULL; see the inference rules below parse_status text, required One of: ok, warning, error. Default ok parse_warnings list of text For example birth_date_year_only, unit_not_found, ambiguous_name. Warnings do not block; errors do resolution text, optional One of: link_existing, create_new, discard, deferred resolved_person_id reference to person, optional resolved_by reference to person, optional resolved_at timestamp, audit time, optional resolution_note text, optional applied boolean, required Default false applied_person_id reference to person, optional What this row created applied_membership_id reference to membership, optional What this row created applied_participation_id reference to unit participation, optional What this row created created_at timestamp, audit time

Indexes

  • The staged rows of one parsed row.
  • The review queue: parse status and resolution, restricted to rows with no resolution or a deferred one. Decided rows are not in it.
  • Applied rows only.

docs.title: The legacy field→code mapping
docs.text:
Any legacy column that is not identity machinery becomes an attribute code, and this is where the vocabulary comes from: most of the first two hundred definitions arrive here rather than from a deliberate act of design (09-attributes.md §7 owns the rule, and states why; what follows is only what the pipeline has to obey).

  • Every raw field name in a batch maps to a code, or is mapped to discard with a reason, or the batch stops. An unmapped column maps to a proposed code named from the raw column — never to an existing code picked by similarity, because an import-time merge is invisible and unreviewable and a human makes that judgement afterwards, with both codes in front of them.
  • The mapping is recorded on the batch, in import_batch.field_mapping, so a mapping later found wrong can be re-run rather than reverse-engineered from the damage it did. The mapping is not the schema: changing it is an act of curation with an audit entry, not a migration.
  • Which table it is not on, because the wrong one is plausible. An earlier draft of this subsection said the mapping sat "on staging_import_row alongside the raw value", and that is the wrong grain twice over: staging_import_row is one row per person and holds a fixed set of parsed_* columns, so a per-column fact has nowhere to sit there, and anything per-row would be a mapping that can differ between two people in the same batch — which is precisely how one legacy column ends up as two codes, quietly, with nothing to review. The raw values themselves stay where they always were, verbatim in staging_import.raw_data; the map is one table up.

What this costs is a stage that is allowed to fail loudly. A batch with unmapped columns does not apply, and somebody has to say what those columns were — friction at the worst possible moment, since imports are always late. It is the cheaper failure. The alternative is a silent drop, which is the same loss as deleting the column and the same one §3's guiding requirements were written against: in 2031 someone asks what the old system's POZNAMKA column held, and the answer is that a script nobody still works with decided it was not interesting.

docs.title: Reversibility
docs.text:
staging_import_row holding the three created ids is what makes per-batch revert possible. Revert removes only what this batch created, and it runs in this order:

  1. Take every staged row of the batch being reverted.
  2. Undo what they created, dependents first: the unit_participation rows, then the membership rows, then the person rows — and a row the batch created outright is removed rather than merely amended.
  3. Finally mark the staged rows themselves unapplied.

Revert is only safe before live data references the imported rows. Once a real person has been linked, or an event attendance recorded against an imported membership, deleting the row breaks it. Therefore:

  • Revert is allowed only while import_batch.status = 'applied' and no row created by the batch has been referenced by a later live record.
  • Detecting that requires checking for references — implement as a pre-flight check that reports which rows cannot be reverted, and refuse rather than partially applying.
  • After that window, corrections are made by editing the data, not by reverting. This is the honest behaviour; a "revert" that silently orphans references is worse than refusing.
  • Step 2's removals are audited like any other write, one entry per row deleted, each naming the batch. This is the only hard delete a business row can meet, and it is precisely the case where someone will later ask "this person existed in March and is gone now — what happened?" An undo that erases the rows and leaves no trace of having erased them is not a rollback but a cover-up, and it is the same undo a reviewer is trusting when they agree to revert at all. 00-conventions.md §4 is why no other path is allowed to do this.

Bias toward import in small batches and review before applying. Reversibility is a safety net, not a workflow.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
The (batch_id, source_row_hash) uniqueness above makes re-staging cheap. Idempotency across batches needs the hash to be computed from the row's semantic content, not its position:

source_row_hash = sha256(
    normalise(given_name) || '|' ||
    normalise(family_name) || '|' ||
    coalesce(birth_date::text,'') || '|' ||
    coalesce(unit_code,'') || '|' ||
    coalesce(period_from::text,'')
)

Then a re-import of an overlapping roster produces rows that match already-applied ones, and the pipeline can skip them. The hash function must be stable — changing it invalidates every previously staged row. Version it if it must change.

docs.title: End-date inference
docs.text:
Imported rosters rarely state when a period ended. Three defensible options:

Rule Effect Risk Leave valid_to NULL Person appears to be current Wrong and dangerous — inflates the member count, and an open membership also passes the permission gate (§3.1) End at the end of the organizational year of the last roster the person appears in Defensible, documented May truncate a period that continued End at the last date the person appears in any roster Best fidelity, needs all rosters Requires the complete dataset

Recommended default: end at the end of the organizational year of the last roster in which the person appears, marked data_confidence = 'low' and with a parse warning. Never NULL.

docs.title: 3.1 What a roster actually evidences
docs.text:
A roster proves that someone took part in a unit in a period. It does not prove they paid a fee, and under D-041 sub-unit belonging is a unit_participation, not a membership at all — which is the row the import should create by default, and the row for which "the last date they appear" is a genuinely good answer.

The dangerous case is the inferred membership. If the import also generates a membership row for each historical participant — plausibly, because the fee was paid — then an open-ended one from 1998 does something a participation row never does: it satisfies is_current_member(), so a 2003 roster member would hold current member authority today through every role that is gated. The end-date rule above is what prevents that, and check 1 in §5 is what catches it when the rule is not applied.

Where the money is unknown, prefer participation. Import a participation row with a period, and leave the membership to be inferred only where there is evidence of payment — a receipt, a ledger, a dues column. Erring toward participation loses a little fidelity in "were they a member in 1998?" and removes an entire class of false-current-member.

docs.title: 4. Redaction log
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required The row is NOT deleted. The id survives so historical references resolve requested_at timestamp, audit time Default: now requested_by reference to person, optional legal_basis text, optional gdpr_art17, court_order, internal_policy — required for accountability performed_at timestamp, audit time, optional performed_by reference to person, optional redacted_tables list of text Which tables had values overwritten — and which had rows deleted. person_attribute is erased by deletion rather than by overwriting (00-conventions §4), so naming it here is what records that the erasure reached the person's descriptive data, and omitting it is indistinguishable from not having reached it retained_reason text, optional Why some data was kept. Membership periods and unit participation periods are organizational history, not personal data, and removing them would falsify records the organization may be obliged to keep. This field records that judgement per case note text, optional

Rules

  • A redaction cannot record when it was performed without recording who performed it: performed_at without performed_by is illegal.

Indexes

  • A person's redaction history.

This log is the answer to "prove you honoured the erasure request". It records what was removed, when, on what legal basis, and — importantly — what was deliberately retained and why. A redaction performed without a record is indistinguishable from a data loss incident.

For the descriptive part of a person's record this log is the only surviving record, by design. The attribute rows are deleted; the audit entries that quoted their values are scrubbed by the same act (§2.2's mechanism two, which is the only direction in which a trail that must not be rewritten can still be erased); and the codes they pointed at stay live because a code belongs to the organization and not to the erased person (09-attributes.md §6 draws the two directions: retiring a code is an act about the vocabulary and keeps values, erasing a person is an act about the person and removes them). So redacted_tables naming person_attribute is the whole of what the system can honestly say — this person had descriptive data and it is gone — and it is enough, because the sentence the organization is entitled to keep is that it held a record and removed it, not what the record said.

docs.title: 5. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify

  • Imported memberships with no end date. Count membership rows that carry an import_batch_id and have no valid_to. Zero is the only acceptable answer: these are the rows that silently satisfy the permission gate, so this is a security check as much as a data-quality one (§3).
  • Imported people who were later merged away. Count people whose record_origin is legacy_import and whose merge pointer is set. Non-zero is probably fine and worth an eye.
  • Batches left in a non-terminal state for a long time. Count import_batch rows whose status is none of applied, reverted, failed and which were created more than 30 days ago; non-zero means a run somebody stopped steering.
  • Audit rows with no actor at all. Count audit_log rows with neither an actor_person_id nor an actor_label; any non-zero count is a forensic gap.
  • Tables whose write path does not audit. Compare the business tables this system has — staging tables excluded — against the maintained list of audited ones. Non-zero means a table is writing history that is never recorded. Read this one carefully, because its meaning got worse rather than weaker. While a trigger existed, a table was audited by being named in a trigger definition, and forgetting one was a decision somebody made in a migration and could see. Now a table is audited because the code that writes it calls the audit entry point, so the list and the code are two artifacts that must agree and nothing forces them to — which makes this report the entire control over the completeness of the audit trail, and the one check here that should alert rather than log. If it ever reports a table, the finding is not "some history is missing"; it is "every change to that table since it was added is unrecorded, and that period cannot be reconstructed later."
  • Redacted people with surviving personal data. Count redacted people whose names are not the redaction marker and who still have a current contact point whose value is not redacted; non-zero means an erasure was left half done. The count now reaches two more places. First, person_attribute: a redacted person with any attribute row is an erasure that did not happen, since those rows are deleted rather than overwritten (00-conventions §4). That is check 6 of 09-attributes.md §8 read from this side — the same assertion, not a second one. Second, and a different assertion, which only exists because values are logged on purpose: for a redacted person, no audit_log row about one of their person_attribute changes may still carry content. Content means value, value_option_id or recorded_note inside old_values or new_values; person_id, attribute_definition_id and source are not content and survive the scrub deliberately, because they are the only way this check can still find the rows after the erasure deleted the business ones — an audit row keeps its table_name and record_id when the row they named is gone, and its person_id is what ties it back to the person who asked to be forgotten. Read this check correctly and it has exactly one meaning: the scrub did not run. Before an erasure, a payload full of descriptive values is the design working (§2.2); afterwards it is the thing the person asked for the system to stop having. Note what the check structurally cannot see — a copy that is present, readable, and perfectly legal, held by somebody whose permission is graded below its contents — because that failure leaves no rows to count; it is the guard, and the guard is reviewed by a person. This check and check 5 are the two here that should alert rather than log. A redaction property that is reported once a month is a redaction property that fails between the reports, and unlike a missing audit row, a value that outlives its erasure is not something anyone notices until a regulator asks what the table holds.

Check 5 is worth automating as a test, not just a nightly query — a test that reads the table list in these documents and asserts every business table on it appears on the audited list, since that is the nearest thing left to what asking the database used to answer. A new table added without being put on that list is a silent, permanent hole in the audit trail — and it will be discovered only when someone needs the history that was never recorded.

docs.title: 6. Open issues
docs.text:
• Which tables must be audited. Recommend: all business tables. The cost is storage; the cost of a gap is unbounded.
  • Retention period for audit_log before archival to cold storage. Legal input required.
  • Whether audit_log should be partitioned by month from the start (recommend yes, given the write volume and the multi-decade horizon).
  • The definitive end-date inference rule for imported rosters (§3.1) — needs your input on the organizational year boundary (tracked as ../open-questions.md A-4).
  • Whether the import should create a membership at all for a historical roster, or only a unit_participation (§3.1). The safe default is participation-only; the alternative needs payment evidence per row.
  • Exact redaction scope: which fields are personal data vs. organizational history (§4). Requires legal review.
  • Whether person.notes should exist at all, given the redaction burden it creates.

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: ⚠ PROVISIONAL ON POLICY, SETTLED ON ARCHITECTURE
docs.text:
How money moves is now decided. Money arrives from a bank API and is requested by a variable symbol and a QR code (D-075); money that cannot be matched waits for a person (D-076). There is no card gateway, no checkout and no dispute handling, and §2a is the consequence.

What the money is for is still open. Amount, proration, discounts, whether the fee buys insurance, and who may waive it are all unanswered — §5. Those are policy questions this document cannot answer, and several need somebody in the organization to be asked.

This document exists because membership activation depends on payment (../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md), and because the yearly expiry and renewal window (D-040) need somewhere to read a due date from.

docs.title: 1. What the domain requires (from what you have said)
docs.text:
Settled:

  • There is a yearly fee, flat, per person — it does not vary by age, by household, or by membership type, because there is one membership type (D-037).
  • Becoming a member requires paying it; the membership activates on payment (D-040).
  • The fee expires on a fixed organizational date, typically January. At that date the membership lapses — the person is not a member — and a renewal window follows during which they may renew without re-applying. A payment inside the window opens the new period at the expiry date, so the record shows no gap.
  • There is no grace status. The window is tracked as dates, and the resolver does not know it exists.

Unspecified — the fee amount, proration, family discounts, who may authorize a waiver, whether the fee buys insurance, and currency.

Settled in round 6, and it was the big one — the organization collects, but not through a card gateway: money is requested by variable symbol + QR code and arrives from the bank API already tagged (§2a, D-075).

docs.title: 2. Minimal provisional shape
docs.text:
Four tables, deliberately small and easy to replace.

fee_schedule — a price, together with the period during which that price was the price.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id code text, required name text, required description text, optional membership_type_id reference to membership type, optional NULL = applies to any type, e.g. an organization-wide surcharge org_unit_id reference to org unit, optional NULL = organization-wide. Set for a unit-level supplementary fee period_months integer, required Default 12 amount money, required Zero or more currency three-letter currency code, required Default EUR. Explicit even though the organization is single-currency — multi-currency later is far easier with the column already present valid_from date, required Fee amounts change yearly, so a price is stored against a validity period rather than overwritten valid_to date, optional NULL = still the current price. Storing the amount this way means a historical obligation can be recomputed correctly — critical for "what did we charge in 1998?" and for correcting a mis-applied fee is_active boolean, required Default true created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional

Rules

  • code is unique. It covers all rows, not only active ones.
  • valid_to is either absent or later than valid_from.
  • amount is zero or more.

Indexes

  • The one lookup that matters is "the schedules for one membership type, valid_from newest first, restricted to active ones".

fee_obligation — one thing someone owes.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required The person the fee is for. Not the payer — see paid_by_person_id on payment membership_id reference to membership, optional One of the three target columns; exactly one is set membership_request_id reference to membership request, optional One of the three target columns event_registration_id reference to event registration, optional One of the three target columns. The event arm is real, not a hedge: an event with a fee_schedule creates one obligation per registration (D-066), and payment confirms the place. It replaced the dormant household_id arm that D-057 removed — same shape, but with data behind it this time fee_schedule_id reference to fee schedule, required Snapshotted so the amount is reproducible even if the schedule is edited description text, required period_from date, required period_to date, required amount_due money, required amount_discount money, required Default 0 amount_paid money, required Default 0 currency three-letter currency code, required status text, required Default unpaid. One of: unpaid, partially_paid, paid, waived, refunded, written_off, overdue due_date date, required The yearly fee expires on a fixed organizational date (D-040); this obligation's due_date is what the lapse sweep compares against (§4). The renewal window that follows is carried as dates, not as a status (§1) waived_by reference to person, optional waived_reason text, optional created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional updated_at timestamp, audit time updated_by reference to person, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional Set on imported rows

Rules

  • period_to is later than period_from.
  • amount_due, amount_discount and amount_paid are each zero or more.
  • Exactly one of membership_id, membership_request_id and event_registration_id is set — one, not zero and not two. Every obligation is for exactly one thing: a membership period, a membership request, or one person's place at one event. The per-person choice for events is deliberate: the fee is flat and per person (D-037), and a per-family price would need the household grouping designed again first (D-057).
  • A status of waived requires both waived_by and waived_reason. There is no waived obligation whose waiver is unattributed or unexplained.

Indexes

  • One person's obligations, by status.
  • Obligations ordered by due_date, restricted to the rows still open — status unpaid, partially_paid or overdue. Closed rows are not in it.
  • Obligations carrying the event arm, and obligations carrying the membership arm — each restricted to the rows where that column is set.
  • Obligations within a period_from / period_to range.

The household arm is gone, and an event arm took its place — a real one. D-037 settled the fee as flat and per person; D-057 then removed the household table itself, so household_id, its CHECK arm and ix_obligation_household went with it. Events then supplied a third target that is genuinely used: one obligation per registration, created by the code that places the registration, paid to confirm the place. Nothing creates it if that code is not written — the obligation used to be created by a database trigger, and a trigger could not be forgotten; see 00-conventions §6a. An event with a fee and no obligation is invisible until someone reconciles money against the roster. (D-066).

Exactly one, never zero and never two — and unlike most rules in these documents this one can still be stated declaratively, so a migration should state it. Three columns, exactly one set: count how many are present and require that count to be one, which is a condition on the row and nothing else. No subquery, no other table, and therefore emittable by any migration that can put a condition on a row at all — the case where the ORM argument simply does not apply. It is worth naming explicitly, because it is the counterexample to the general worry — most of what D-072 deleted genuinely cannot be restated declaratively (open question F-10), and this is not one of them.

What is worth keeping from this rule's history is its shape: the previous version admitted at most two of the three, because one of the arms was a dormant household_id kept against a hypothetical. At most two with a hedge is not the same domain as exactly one over three real targets, and the difference only shows up when someone adds a fourth: if a new target appears, ask whether it is used before widening this, and expect the answer to be no.

If a family discount is ever wanted, the row is still the right shape — one obligation covering several people — but it now needs the grouping to be re-introduced first, as a group with a period rather than a fake person (04 §3).

payment — money that moved, as one recorded act.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id public_id external identifier, required Unique. Appears in URLs and exports; id stays internal (00-conventions §3) amount money, required Never zero. A negative amount represents a reversal currency three-letter currency code, required paid_at timestamp, required When the payment occurred, which may differ from when it was recorded — a bank transfer recorded a week later. Both matter recorded_at timestamp, audit time Default: now method text, required One of: bank_transfer, cash, voucher, credit_note, other. card and direct_debit removed — there is no card gateway and no mandate system (D-075) variable_symbol text, optional The symbol the money arrived under, copied verbatim from the bank statement. Set on every row the import created; the join back to payment_request. Never typed by hand reference text, optional Bank reference, transaction id, receipt number paid_by_person_id reference to person, optional Who actually paid. May differ from the person the fee is for — a parent paying for a child, a grandparent paying for a grandchild, a sponsor. This is the act-on-behalf record for money on_behalf_of reference to person, optional status text, required Default confirmed. confirmed or reversed, and nothing else. A bank transfer the bank has reported does not later fail, expire, or get reversed by a card network; the two remaining values describe whether we still stand behind the row. pending and failed were deleted with the card gateway (D-075) confirmed_by reference to person, optional notes text, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional Set on imported rows created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional

Rules

  • amount is never zero; zero is meaningless. Negative amounts are reversals.
  • public_id is unique.

Indexes

  • A payer's payments, newest paid_at first.
  • Payments by date, newest first.
  • Lookup by reference, restricted to rows that have one.

payment_allocation — which payments satisfy which obligations. It is many-to-many in both directions: one payment may cover several obligations, and one obligation may be paid in instalments.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id payment_id reference to payment, required fee_obligation_id reference to fee obligation, required amount money, required Never zero allocated_at timestamp, audit time Default: now allocated_by reference to person, optional note text, optional

Rules

  • A given payment is allocated to a given obligation at most once — one row per pair, over all rows.
  • amount is never zero.

Indexes

  • Allocations of one payment, and allocations of one obligation — both directions are asked.

The allocation table is the part most likely to be right. A payment and an obligation are genuinely many-to-many, and any design that puts payment_id on the obligation (or vice versa) breaks the first time a parent pays for three children in one transfer. That is the common case in this organization, not an edge case.

docs.title: 2a. How money actually arrives
docs.text:
D-075. The system requests a payment and then reads one. It never touches the money.

The flow, in order:

  1. A liability exists — a membership period, a membership request, a place at an event.
  2. The system issues a payment_request carrying a variable symbol and an amount.
  3. The payer is shown the symbol, the amount, and a QR code that encodes all three.
  4. The payer's own bank moves the money. The system is not involved and learns nothing yet.
  5. A bank import reads the account statement and produces a bank_transaction for each incoming transfer, with the variable symbol still attached.
  6. The symbol resolves to a live request. The import creates a payment, links it, and the obligation's balance falls.
  7. If the symbol resolves to nothing live, the row goes to the queue (§2b).

payment_request — the liability rendered payable.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id variable_symbol text, required Unique across all rows, forever, including cancelled and long-settled ones. Eleven digits from a sequence fee_obligation_id reference to fee obligation, required What is owed. The request never invents an amount of its own amount money, required Copied from the obligation at issue time, so a later price change cannot rewrite what someone was asked for currency three-letter currency code, required recipient_account text, required The account the QR code tells people to pay into issued_at timestamp, audit time expires_at date, optional When the request stops being payable — the close of a renewal window, or the day before an event voided_at timestamp, optional Set by a person, or by cancelling the event the request was for (§2b) voided_reason text, optional

Rules

  • variable_symbol is unique over every row that ever existed, not over live rows. A symbol issued in 2019 must never resolve to a 2026 obligation, because bank statements get re-imported and late payments are the entire reason the renewal window exists.
  • The symbol comes from a sequence. It is never derived from a birth date, a membership id, a member number, or anything else a person can guess or work out. Anyone can type eleven digits into a payment form at their bank; a guessable symbol means a stranger's money lands in a child's record, and the damage is not cosmetic — it reads as a paid fee, an active membership, and possibly insurance cover that does not exist.
  • amount is a copy, not a live reference. What a person was asked to pay is a historical fact about the ask, and recomputing it from the current schedule would make every price change rewrite history.
  • One obligation may have several requests over time — a first request expires, or the amount is corrected — but at most one live request per obligation.
  • A request is not an invoice. Nothing is delivered, nothing is numbered for a tax authority, and whether the organization also owes people invoices is still an open question (§5).

bank_transaction — one incoming transfer as the bank reported it.

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id bank_account text, required bank_reference text, required Unique per bank account. This is the idempotency key: the same statement imported twice must create nothing the second time arrived_at date, required The bank's date, not the import's — this is the date D-040's renewal window is measured against amount money, required variable_symbol text, optional As reported. Can be absent, wrong, or a stranger's payer_description text, optional Whatever the bank gives: a name, sometimes an address matched_payment_request_id reference to payment request, optional NULL means unmatched, which is the queue imported_at timestamp, audit time import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional

Rules

  • bank_reference is unique within a bank account. Re-importing a statement is safe and must be.
  • A transaction is immutable once imported. Corrections are new rows or a re-import, never an edit — this is the organization's copy of somebody else's ledger, and the only version of it that will ever agree with the bank.

The renewal window stops being a promise. D-040 backdates a renewal to the expiry date when payment lands inside the window, and its own note said that rule was only as good as the reliability of payment dates. Until now they arrived when somebody noticed a transfer. They now arrive from the bank, dated by the bank. The sweep in §4 can run unattended because the thing it depends on is no longer a person remembering in February.

What this deletes from the design. No checkout, no card tokens, no PCI surface, no webhook endpoint to authenticate, no dispute or chargeback state, no reconciliation report against a processor's payout. payment.status loses pending and failed: a bank transfer the bank has reported is confirmed on arrival, and there is no in-between state to model. What remains in status is whether we still stand behind the row — confirmed or reversed.

docs.title: 2b. Money that cannot be matched
docs.text:
D-076.

An unmatched transaction is a fact with no subject, so the absence gets stored rather than guessed at — the same discipline as "unanswered is the absence of a row" (D-059). matched_payment_request_id IS NULL is the queue; there is no separate worklist table to fall out of sync with the rows it describes.

How a transaction ends up there: the symbol matches no request. The symbol matches a request that has been voided. The request is already settled. The amount is less than asked, or more. There is no symbol at all — cash-basis donors and people who type their own name in the wrong field.

What the system does with any of those: nothing. It records the money and waits.

A person decides, and there are exactly four outcomes:

Outcome When Attach it to a different request The symbol was mistyped; the real obligation is obvious from the payer Split it across requests One transfer, three siblings — the ordinary shape of family payment here Record as a donation Money with no obligation behind it, which is not the same as money that is missing one Refund it, by hand Nothing was meant to be owed. A second payment in the opposite direction (D-075)

Why the tempting shortcut is refused. Falling back to the payer's identity when the symbol fails looks like it removes most of the queue. It removes most of the queue's accuracy instead: a parent with two children pays one amount against one symbol is the normal case, not the edge case, and an identity fallback resolves it to whichever child the query reaches first. A fee recorded against the wrong child is a finance error, a membership that appears paid when it is not, and — if the fee buys insurance — a coverage record that is untrue, all at once. A fallback is not allowed to be wrong on the common path.

Auto-refunding is refused for two reasons: it needs the bank integration to work outbound as well as inbound, which is a second integration with its own authorization; and it returns the grandparent's attempt at a camp contribution.

Cancellation is where most of the volume comes from, and it is decided now rather than later. D-064 made cancellation a recorded fact rather than a state, so the event survives, the registrations survive — and so would an outstanding request against an occasion that is not going to happen. So:

  • Cancelling an event voids its outstanding payment requests, recording why.
  • Money already received for a cancelled event becomes a queue item, for a person to refund or to carry forward to a later event. It is not auto-refunded, for the reasons above.

This is EV-3's answer, which is why it is closed here rather than left parked in the events module.

The queue is not allowed to be silently ignored. It is a count on a dashboard, not a page nobody navigates to, and its oldest item is a number someone sees monthly. Unmatched money is the one finance backlog that gets worse by itself: the payer believes they have paid, and the organization believes they have not.

docs.title: 3. Keeping membership.outstanding_balance honest
docs.text:
03-membership.md has a denormalised outstanding_balance. If it stays, it must be maintained in the same transaction as any allocation change, or it will drift. Two options:

Option Pros Cons Maintain it inside the transaction that writes payment_allocation Always current, no recompute Every path that writes an allocation has to do it — the trigger that used to do it for all of them at once is gone — and the arithmetic is easy to get subtly wrong Drop the column, compute on demand Cannot drift Slower worklist queries Keep as a materialized view Cannot drift, fast Refresh lag

Recommendation: drop the column and use a view. The "approved but unpaid" worklist is not a hot path, and a wrong balance produces either a wrongly-suspended member or a wrongly-chased family. A wrong number here has a human consequence.

The definition, stated once, wherever it is implemented:

balance = amount_due − amount_discount − the sum of allocations whose payment is confirmed

Only confirmed payments count. An obligation is not settled by money that has been promised, intended, described in an email, or reported by a payer who believes they sent it. Under D-075 this rule got sharper rather than weaker: pending is gone from payment.status, so there is no longer a state for a transfer that is on its way — either the bank has reported it and it is confirmed, or the system has not heard of it. A member is activated by the first, never by the second.

docs.title: 4. How this connects to membership
docs.text: The activation gate. A membership's fee is settled when no obligation attached to it has a positive balance after discounts — where obligations carrying waived, written_off or refunded are excluded from the question entirely, because a waived fee that nobody is going to collect must not read as an unpaid one. "Settled" is the only thing money says about membership; it does not grant permissions by itself (D-039).

docs.title: The yearly expiry sweep
docs.text:
Run on 1 January (D-047). This is the one automatic membership transition in the system, and the only thing in this document that changes a person's status.

For every membership that is active, has an obligation with a positive balance, and whose due date has passed:

  1. Mark it lapsed, ending it at the expiry date — not at today. The period ended on that date whether or not anyone noticed.
  2. Do not close the root unit_participation row. Move its valid_to forward instead, so a renewal inside the window extends one continuous row rather than starting a second one (D-050, 03-membership.md §5.1).
  3. Invalidate the permission cache per person, for every person returned — not per scope (domain/06 §8). A lapsed member whose gated roles still resolve is a member who keeps leading.
  4. Open the renewal window as a date, never as a status. The resolver does not know windows exist.
