Note the personnel consequence, which is easy to miss and fatal to get wrong. This runs for everyone at once, including the person who runs it. Without system.gate_exempt (D-051) the administrator locks themselves out on this date, with no permission left with which to undo it.

This reverses an earlier recommendation, and the reversal is worth recording. This document previously said "do not auto-lapse — produce the worklist and let a human act." The reasoning was sound: automatically removing membership from a child because a bank transfer was recorded late is a real harm.

D-040 resolves it differently, and the resolution is that the expiry is a date, not a decision. The fee covers a fixed period and the period ends. Nobody decides anything, and the renewal window exists to absorb exactly the late-transfer case: a payment inside it backdates the new period to the expiry date, so the record shows no gap and the person was never misclassified.

Where the old caution still applies is the case the window cannot absorb — a payment that arrived before the expiry but was recorded after it. That is a data-entry lag, not a non-payment, and it should be corrected with membership.backdate rather than left as a real gap. Worth a report: members who lapsed and then paid within a few days.

docs.title: 5. Open issues — the whole of this document, essentially
docs.text:
1. Is the fee prorated for mid-year joins? Note this is a sharper question than it was: with the expiry on a fixed date (D-040), someone joining in October pays for three months of a twelve-month fee unless the organization prorates — and the renewal twelve months later is a full year. Whether that is fair is a policy question; whether the data model supports it is amount_due vs amount_expected.
  2. Are there family/sibling discounts? amount_discount exists but the rules are unspecified. With a flat per-person fee (D-037), this is the only remaining fee variation, so it is worth a deliberate yes or no. Note that D-057 has now removed the household grouping, so a per-family discount is no longer a constraint change — it needs that grouping designed again first. A per-person discount is unaffected and is just amount_discount.
  3. ~~Refunds: policy, and who may authorize them. Affects the payment.status values.~~ Mostly answered by D-075: a refund is a second payment in the opposite direction, not a status, so it cannot corrupt the original record and there is no reversal state to authorize. Still open: who may authorize initiating one, which is the part the question was actually about and which fee.refund already flags 🔒.
  4. ~~Payment methods: which does the organization actually accept? The enum is a guess.~~ Closed — bank_transfer arrives by import, cash is recorded by hand, and card plus direct_debit are deleted (§2). voucher and credit_note stay until someone says otherwise.
  5. Invoicing: does the organization issue invoices (legal requirement in some jurisdictions)? If so, an invoice entity and a numbering sequence are needed. Sharper now: a payment_request looks like an invoice, prints like one, and is not one — it has no tax identity, no sequence required by law, and no delivery record. If invoices are legally required, the honest answer is a second document over the same obligation, not a renaming of this one.
  6. ~~Is the organization collecting payments or only recording them?~~ Closed — it collects, by bank API with a variable symbol and a QR code, and there is no card gateway (D-075, §2a). The renewal window's dependence on reliable payment dates is what made this urgent, and the bank import is what resolved it.
  7. Accounting integration: does anything need to be exported to an accounting system?
  8. Currency and jurisdiction — currently assumed EUR.
  9. Does the fee cover insurance? If so, "member on the date of the incident" becomes a legal record with its own retention needs. This one interacts directly with the new lapse rule (D-040): if the fee buys insurance, then the date the membership lapses is the date cover ends, and the renewal window does not extend it. That is worth confirming with whoever handles the policy, because the softer "still covered during grace" reading was the alternative D-040 explicitly rejected.
  10. Scholarships/hardship waivers — a waived status exists but the process is unspecified, and in a youth organization this is often a sensitive, need-to-know process that must not be visible to unit leaders.

  11. What gets a variable symbol, and one per what? — new, and raised by D-075 rather than left over. That decision fixed how money arrives and named the payment_request that carries it, but not the two choices the module is actually built from.

    • Scope. Do event fees get a symbol, or only membership fees? A camp fee is the same mechanism, and a symbol is what lets a family pay for it at their own bank without staff involvement. Recommendation: every payable, because the alternative is a second, hand-recorded money path sitting beside an automatic one — and hand-recorded is what D-040's renewal window just escaped.
    • Granularity. One live request per liability, matching the fee_obligation row exactly — which is what §2a already assumes. Not per person, because a parent paying for two children in one transfer is the ordinary case and per-person symbols make that impossible to match. Not per person-year either: a camp is a separate liability from a fee and must never share a symbol with one.
    • The amount mismatch, which D-076 defers and this question cannot. 500 sent against a 550 request goes to the queue, which is correct as a mechanism and silent as a policy. Whether partial payment settles anything, whether 4.90 vs 5.00 is a shortfall, and what a payer is told when their money lands and does not fit — those are undecided, and the queue will show them at volume the first spring the import runs.

    Why this is question 11 and not a footnote: it decides whether the module has one money path or two.

Resolved and no longer open, kept visible so the reasoning survives: activation on payment or on approval (on payment — D-040); whether the fee is per person or per household (per person, flat and ageless — D-037); and whether the household grouping survives at all (no — removed entirely, D-057); and, from round 6, whether the organization collects or records (collects, by bank API — D-075) and what payment methods exist (the enum is no longer a guess — D-075 again).

Count honestly, because the number moved in both directions. Of the eleven above, two are fully closed (4, 6) and one is half closed (3: the mechanics of a refund are settled, the authority to initiate one is not). But a new one arrived in the same round, because D-075 fixed how money moves and thereby exposed what it moves for — question 11. And D-057 did not close question 2: with no grouping, a per-family discount needs one designed again before it can be priced. Nine open questions, of which one is new and one got sharper by being answered.

The character of the list changed, and that is the real outcome. Until round 6 it held architectural questions — collect or record, which gateway, what statuses. It now holds only policy questions that require somebody in the organization to be asked: proration, discounts, insurance, waivers, invoices, accounting. This document no longer needs a rewrite; it needs answers.

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Data Model — Events
docs.text:
event, event_organizer, event_registration, event_question, event_answer.

Domain rationale: ../domain/07-events.md.

Nothing here is provisional. This module was designed against the authorization model rather than beside it, and every hook it uses — access_grant.scope_type = 'event', grant_scope_type, audiences, permission_level — was already in place and seeded. The tables below fill those hooks; they do not extend the model.

docs.title: 1. Why these five tables, and no event_series
docs.text:
Table What it is event The occasion. One owning unit, a date, a registration window, an optional capacity event_organizer Who is running it — an appointment on the event, not a grant (§5) event_registration One person's answer: attending, or not attending. Unanswered is the absence of a row event_question What this event asks registrants event_answer What one person said to one question

No recurrence. A weekly meeting is unit_participation, not an event (../domain/07-events.md §1). Adding event_series would mean every downstream table — registrations, capacity, presence, organizers, questions — needs a second possible home, and the feature that needed recurrence is already modelled.

No event_status column. Visibility is the permission model; cancellation is a fact (../domain/07-events.md §10).

docs.title: 2. event
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only public_id external identifier, required Unique. Generated when the event is created org_unit_id reference to org unit, required EXACTLY ONE owning unit, and it is never absent. A joint camp is one unit's event that another unit's children register for, via an audience grant — see ../domain/07-events.md §2. This is forced by D-049, not merely preferred: two owners would create an exception to "the root may not read a sub-unit's events" shaped exactly like a joint camp, with no principled place to stop title text, required description text, optional The committee's own notes — internal public_note text, optional Shown to registrants. Separate from description, which is internal: "bring a sleeping bag and a torch" vs. the committee's own notes location text, optional Free text: a camp site, an address, "the usual place" location_detail free-form jsonb, optional {lat, lon, meeting_point, …} when known starts_at instant in time, required An instant, not a date. A Thursday group meets at 5pm; a camp starts on Saturday morning. The instant carries a timezone, and the timezone is the organization's, recorded rather than assumed ends_at instant in time, required An instant, not a date, for the same reason all_day boolean, required Default false. Display only — an all-day camp still has instants underneath registration_opens_at instant in time, optional NULL = open as soon as the event is visible. The event is visible to whoever holds event.view, which for a fresh event is its organizers and nobody else (../domain/07-events.md §10), so NULL is a reasonable default and wrong for a jamboree whose sign-up should not open before the dates are fixed registration_closes_at instant in time, optional NULL = when the event starts. This is the "unlimited" case: registration stays open until the thing happens capacity integer, optional NULL = unlimited. Bed count, bus seats, fire-safety limit. Enforced as a WAITLIST threshold, not a block, and organizers may exceed it (../domain/07-events.md §8) waitlist_deadline instant in time, optional When an unpaid registration at a full event releases its place to the waitlist (§6). NULL = never releases. Only meaningful when the event has a fee AND a capacity; ignored otherwise. This is the ONE automatic transition in this module — see §6 for why it is accepted and what it costs fee_schedule_id reference to fee schedule, optional NULL = this event is free, which most are. Set = a fee applies; registering creates a fee_obligation (§6). The amount and currency live in fee_schedule, not here — events do not price themselves cancelled_at instant in time, optional Cancellation is a FACT, not a status, and this is the point where the "no status column" reasoning deliberately diverges: revoking grants would hide the cancellation from the registrants, who are exactly the people who must be told. A cancelled event stops accepting registrations and KEEPS every registration row — those rows are the record that the camp was planned and who was coming cancelled_by reference to person, optional Who cancelled. Set exactly when cancelled_at is set cancel_reason text, optional Free text, and it may be absent ("cancelled — see email") created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional updated_at timestamp, audit time, optional updated_by reference to person, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional Set on imported rows

Rules

  • ends_at is later than starts_at.
  • capacity is either absent or greater than zero.
  • When both registration_opens_at and registration_closes_at are set, the close is later than the open. When either one is absent nothing is required of the other — each is independently meaningful on its own.
  • cancelled_at and cancelled_by are set together or not at all. A cancellation has a who and a when, or neither. The reason is free text and may be absent ("cancelled — see email").
  • waitlist_deadline may be set only when both capacity and fee_schedule_id are set. A waitlist deadline is meaningless without a capacity to fill or a fee to pay, and stating this prevents a column that silently does nothing.
  • public_id is unique.

Indexes

  • Upcoming events by starts_at, and events by registration_closes_at — both restricted to rows that are not cancelled. Every "what is happening" and "what is still open" list excludes cancelled events, so the cancelled ones are simply not in the index.

docs.title: No status column, and why that is not an omission
docs.text:
Nothing is stored that can be derived. "Is this event over?" is ends_at in the past. "Is it cancelled?" is cancelled_at set. "Needs attention now" — the list an admin screen runs — is every event with cancelled_at absent and ends_at not yet past, ordered by starts_at.

completed is derived, never stored, so there is no state to keep consistent and no job to move rows between states. Draft is not a state either: a new event has no grants beyond its organizers, so nobody else can see it, and publishing is an access_grant, not an UPDATE. A status column and a permission system that both claim to answer "who may see this?" will eventually disagree, and the one that gets enforced is whoever wrote the last IF.

docs.title: Why fee_schedule_id and not an event_fee table
docs.text: The fee amount, currency and validity already live in fee_schedule (07-finance.md §2), which is temporal — so a 1998 camp's fee recomputes correctly from the 1998 schedule. An event_fee table would duplicate that and immediately drift. An event points at the schedule that prices it.

docs.title: 3. event_organizer
docs.text:
The absence of a valid_to is deliberate. This is a roster, not a period: you are on the list, or you are not. An organizer who drops out is removed (recorded in audit_log), because "was Jan an organizer of that camp?" must have one answer, not a set of intervals.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only event_id reference to event, required The event this person is on. Deleting the event removes its organizer rows — the one cascade in this design, and guard 2 in §8 is what makes it safe person_id reference to person, required organizer_role text, optional lead, assistant, cook, driver, medic, quartermaster — free text. NOT a controlled vocabulary: every organization labels these differently, and a closed list here would be a guess of the kind D-054 removed for unit types is_primary boolean, required Default false. The person the parents are told to call. At most one per event (§10 check 3) sort_order integer, required Default 0. Display order for the list. Cooks before drivers is a real preference and not something to derive note text, optional added_by reference to person, optional Who put them on the roster created_at timestamp, audit time

Rules

  • One row per person per event — the (event_id, person_id) pair is unique, over all rows.
  • At most one organizer of an event has is_primary set. The rule covers every row of the event; rows where the flag is not set are unrestricted, so an event may have any number of ordinary organizers and exactly one primary.
  • Removing an organizer is a removal of the row, not the ending of a period, and audit_log is where the history of it lives. There is nothing to overlap, so there is no no-overlap rule here.

Cascade on delete here, and nowhere else in this data model. It is justified because event_organizer is a roster of assignments on the event, not a business record: a deleted event has no organizers in the domain sense either. In practice nothing deletes an event — the deletion policy is temporal closure, and cancellation sets cancelled_at. The cascade exists so that a mistaken INSERT into a draft event can be cleaned up without leaving orphan rows, and it is the only cascade in the design. Deleting an event that has registrations is refused outright (§8, Guard 2), and the refusal belongs in the database rather than in the delete path: the reference from event_registration to event carries no cascade, so an import or a hand-written fix meets the same wall the screens do. A refusal only the screens knew about would delete the record of who was coming.

docs.title: Organizers are appointments, not grants
docs.text:
event_organizer is the domain answer to "who is running this camp?" — the labelled, ordered list that parents see. It is deliberately not an access_grant (../domain/07-events.md §5):

  • A grant has no room for organizer_role = 'cook'.
  • "Who is running this camp?" should not be answered by reading the permission table.
  • Revoking a grant to remove a cook would also revoke their ability to see the event at all, which is not what "they are no longer cooking" means.

Authority to act on the event does not come from this table. It comes from the owning unit's roles (via §7's rule), from an explicit access_grant, or from system.admin.

docs.title: 4. event_registration
docs.text:
One row per person per event. Two stored values; "unanswered" is the absence of a row.

Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only event_id reference to event, required person_id reference to person, required person_id, NOT membership_id — same reasoning as unit_participation (D-041, 03-membership.md §5). An event's roster must survive independently of how membership is recorded, and imported historical attendance has no membership row to point at. A 1998 camp roster is participation, and an inferred open-ended membership would make every one of those children a "current member" today through the gate (D-039, D-056) response enum: attending / not_attending, required TWO values. unanswered is written NOWHERE. It is the absence of a row, so "who has not replied yet?" is a subtraction, not a stored state (../domain/07-events.md §3). Returning someone to unanswered deletes the row, which audit_log records — the honest act, and the one that leaves least behind responded_at timestamp, required Default now. When the ANSWER was given, which may differ from when it was recorded. A phone call on Tuesday entered on Thursday has two dates and both matter source enum: self / staff / guardian / import, required Default self. How this person got here, and the audit answer to "how did they get in?". staff bypasses the contribute requirement deliberately (../domain/07-events.md §6): organizers may register anyone. guardian is acting-under-guardianship; the acting person is in access_log registered_by reference to person, optional NULL when source is self. Set otherwise: which organizer, or which guardian is_waitlisted boolean, required Default false waitlist_position integer, optional Order within the waitlist. Assigned on insert when the event is at capacity, and rewritten on promotion. See §5 is_confirmed boolean, required Default false. Registration is not the same as a held place. An event with NO fee confirms immediately on registration; an event WITH a fee confirms on payment (§6). This is the "payment confirms the place" rule, and it is the only place in this module where money changes a registration's meaning confirmed_at instant in time, optional Set exactly when is_confirmed is true was_present boolean, three-valued NULL = not yet marked — no register was taken. true = turned up. false = marked absent. THREE-VALUED ON PURPOSE: "we did not take a register" and "we took one and they were not there" are different facts, and only one is a safeguarding signal. For a camp this is the record of who was actually in the organization's care, and it cannot be reconstructed afterwards (§9) presence_marked_by reference to person, optional The person who took the register. Held by whoever has event.presence.mark, which is deliberately ONE LEVEL BELOW event.manage_participants (contribute, not manage) so the volunteer at the door is not also the person who can delete a child from the roster presence_marked_at instant in time, optional When the register was taken fee_obligation_id reference to fee obligation, optional Set when the event has a fee_schedule and this registration created an obligation. The reverse pointer from fee_obligation.event_registration_id also exists (§6) — both directions, because each is asked a different question: "what does this person owe for this camp?" and "what is this obligation for?" created_at timestamp, audit time updated_at timestamp, audit time, optional updated_by reference to person, optional import_batch_id reference to import batch, optional Set on imported rows

Rules

  • One row per person per event, full stop — the (event_id, person_id) pair is unique over all rows. This is what makes "unanswered = absence" work: there is exactly one place an answer could live.
  • A not_attending row has is_waitlisted false and is_confirmed false. A decline is not waitlisted and not confirmed; otherwise a "no" could hold a place on the waitlist, which is nonsense.
  • is_confirmed is true exactly when confirmed_at is set.
  • is_waitlisted is true exactly when waitlist_position is set.
  • Presence is marked all together or not at all: was_present, presence_marked_by and presence_marked_at are either all present or all absent, and was_present absent is the same condition as the other two absent. A partially-set trio is a bug, not a state.

Indexes

  • The set the capacity test counts — an event's registrations whose response is attending and which are not waitlisted. Capacity is compared against exactly this set (§5), and the other registrations of an event must not slow it down.
  • An event's waitlist in waitlist_position order, restricted to waitlisted rows.
  • An event's registrations by was_present, restricted to rows where presence has been marked at all.

docs.title: Why person_id, not membership_id
docs.text:
Same argument as unit_participation (03-membership.md §5), and it is stronger here. An imported 1998 camp roster names children who have no membership row to point at. With the corpus being large and number-bearing (D-056), linking to membership would make those rows unrepresentable — and, worse, an inferred open-ended membership created to satisfy the FK would make every one of those children a current member today through the gate.

The trade-off, stated: no database constraint can enforce "only members may register", and none is wanted — eligibility is capability (../domain/07-events.md §4), and capability is a grant, not a membership row.

docs.title: 5. Capacity and the waitlist
docs.text:
Capacity is a threshold, not a block. Registering for a full event succeeds and produces a waitlisted row.

Is this event at capacity? The question is asked of one event and answered only from the registrations it has: count its attending, non-waitlisted registrations and compare that count with its capacity. An event with no capacity is never full — with no capacity set there is nothing to reach, and the answer is no.

The placing rule runs before the row is written, once per row, on every insert, so that EVERY insert path obeys it — self-service, staff, guardian and import alike. Application-level placement would let one of the four paths forget, and the forgotten one would be the one that matters. The order of these steps is a rule: the decline branch settles all four flags and ends the rule, and the capacity test is counted before confirmation is decided, because confirmation is a property of the place the earlier steps gave the row.

  1. Read the event the registration names.
  2. A decline never occupies a place. If response is not attending, set is_waitlisted false and waitlist_position absent, set is_confirmed false and confirmed_at absent, and stop here — none of what follows applies to a "no".
  3. Waitlisting is a SELF-SERVICE outcome. Waitlist the row when all three of these hold: source is self; the event has a capacity; and the event's attending, non-waitlisted registrations already number at least that capacity. Then set is_waitlisted true and waitlist_position to one past the highest position already on that event's waitlist — 1 when the waitlist is empty. If any of the three fails, set is_waitlisted false and waitlist_position absent. A staff registration is admitted even past capacity: the organizer who knows there are two spare tents is not to be blocked by a number they cannot edit mid-camp (../domain/07-events.md §8). The overrun is permitted, attributed, and REPORTED (§10, check 5).
  4. Confirmation: immediate when there is no fee to wait for. If the event has no fee_schedule_id, set is_confirmed true and confirmed_at to now. Otherwise set is_confirmed false and confirmed_at absent — §6, payment confirms the place.
  5. Write the row carrying those flags.

The rule runs on insert only; a later edit of the row does not re-run it. Promotion and the release below write the same flags deliberately.

The source = 'self' disjunct is the whole of "organizers may register anyone", made mechanical. Removing it silently reverses the answer: every staff registration would be waitlisted behind self-service ones, and the leader adding a child on the day would be told the camp is full when they can see two spare beds.

docs.title: Promotion, which is a deliberate act
docs.text:
Promotion is not automatic — no trigger, no job. An organizer picks someone from the waitlist:

  1. Take the one registration this person holds at this event — the pair names exactly one row (§4).
  2. Clear the waitlist on it: is_waitlisted false, waitlist_position absent.
  3. Set is_confirmed and confirmed_at by exactly the test the placing rule uses: confirmed now when the event has no fee_schedule_id, unconfirmed with no confirmed_at when it has one.

The promotion deliberately bypasses the capacity test: the whole point of promoting is that a place has freed up, and re-testing would just fail again.

Promotion writes the same two flags the placing rule would have, so a promoted registration and an admitted one are indistinguishable afterwards — which is correct, because the difference between them is when, not what.

docs.title: When an unpaid registration releases its place
docs.text:
If waitlist_deadline is set, an unpaid registration at a full event releases its place to the waitlist at that moment. This is the one automatic transition in this module, and it is recorded as such. The release is scoped as narrowly as the rule can be: only at a full event, only with a fee configured, only past the deadline, only unpaid, and never a staff registration (which is admitted by hand and by a human who can see the roster).

  1. Take every registration that is attending, not already waitlisted, source self, and not confirmed.
  2. Keep only those whose event has a fee_schedule_id, has a waitlist_deadline, has that deadline already past, and is not cancelled.
  3. Move each one onto the waitlist: is_waitlisted true, waitlist_position one past the highest position already on that event's waitlist — 1 when the waitlist is empty.
  4. Take the place back: is_confirmed false, confirmed_at absent.

Why this is accepted despite the design's habit of avoiding automatic transitions. The design has spent real effort keeping state changes deliberate (D-023, D-040), and "payment confirms the place" reintroduces one. It is a deadline, not a sweep: it applies to a narrow conjunction, it is opt-in per event (waitlist_deadline is NULL by default, so most events never run it), and the state it produces is visible — the person is on the waitlist, not silently deleted. The alternative, no deadline at all, means a place is held forever by someone who never paid, which is worse.

docs.title: 6. Payments and confirmation
docs.text:
Registering creates a fee obligation; payment confirms the place.

Creating the obligation runs after the registration row is written, so that the registration has an id to be pointed at. The order is a rule: the obligation cannot be created before the registration it belongs to exists, and the registration's fee_obligation_id cannot be written before the obligation does.

  1. Read the event the registration is for.
  2. If the event has no fee_schedule_id, or the registration is not attending, stop — a free event owes nothing, and a place someone declined owes nothing.
  3. Read the fee schedule the event points at.
  4. Create one fee_obligation for this registration, carrying: person_id taken from the registration; event_registration_id set to the registration; the event's fee_schedule_id; the event's title as the description; the event's start and end as the obligation's period; the schedule's amount and currency; and a due date of the event's waitlist_deadline, falling back to the event's starts_at when it has none.
  5. Write the new obligation's id into the registration's fee_obligation_id.

The pointer that had to be restored. D-057 removed the household arm from the exactly-one rule over fee_obligation's target columns, leaving two of them (membership or membership request, never both). An event fee needs an arm back — and this time it is a real arm with data behind it, not the dormant hedge the household column was.

The arm lives in fee_obligation and is stated there in full (07-finance.md §2): exactly one of membership_id, membership_request_id and event_registration_id is set on every obligation. Still exactly one, not "at most three" — every obligation is for exactly one thing: a membership period, a membership request, or one person's place at one event. The per-person choice is deliberate, because the fee is flat and per person (D-037) and a family price would need the household grouping designed again first. Obligations carrying the event arm are indexed on event_registration_id, restricted to the rows where it is set.

docs.title: Confirming on payment
docs.text:
confirm_event_place(obligation) is called by the payment flow. It is not a rule on fee_obligation's status — the payment module owns that transition, and a rule there would make every fee, membership or event alike, confirm an event place.

  1. Take the obligation the call names.
  2. Follow its event_registration_id to the registration it pays for.
  3. Confirm that registration only when it is attending and not waitlisted — a waitlisted person stays waiting until promoted (§5), so paying does not by itself place them.
  4. Confirming means setting is_confirmed true and confirmed_at to now.

confirm_event_place is deliberately an operation the finance module calls, not a rule hanging off fee_obligation's status change. The argument is about ownership and does not depend on where the code lives: anything that fires because a fee became paid fires for membership fees and event fees alike, and "the fee is paid" means something different in each case: a membership activates (D-040), an event place confirms. Two transitions, two owners.

Free events confirm immediately — see the placing rule in §5. An event with no fee_schedule_id has nothing to wait for, and requiring "confirmation" for a free hike would be a state with no meaning.

docs.title: 7. event_question and event_answer
docs.text:
Fields — event_question

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only event_id reference to event, required The event that asks it. A question is defined per event, never shared (§7) label text, required Tent preference, Dietary requirements help_text text, optional position integer, required Default 0. Display order data_type enum: text / long_text / integer / decimal / bool / date / choice / multichoice, required choices list of text, optional For choice and multichoice only. An ordered list on the question rather than a child table: the options are a property of the question, they are ordered, and they are never referenced by anything else is_required boolean, required Default false. The person REGISTERING must answer. Not a gate on registration itself: a form that blocks sign-up is a form nobody completes, and the organizer would rather have the registration and chase the answer applies_to enum: attendee / organizer / all, required Default attendee. Who is asked. Organizers may be asked things attendees are not (T-shirt size for the leaders' shirts) and vice versa valid_from date, required Default today valid_to date, optional NULL = still asked. A question can be retired after people have answered it. Answers survive (an answer is never removed with its question), because "what did they say?" must outlive "do we still ask this?" created_at timestamp, audit time created_by reference to person, optional

Rules — event_question

  • choices is present exactly when data_type is choice or multichoice, and never otherwise. Stated as an equivalence rather than a one-way requirement so that a text question cannot carry a stray choices list that the UI might honour.
  • valid_to is either absent or later than valid_from.

Fields — event_answer

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id Internal only question_id reference to event question, required person_id reference to person, required Who ANSWERED — for a child, the child. The person who submitted on their behalf is in access_log and in registered_by, not here. Answers are about the person the question concerns value free-form jsonb, required Typed by question.data_type. One loose value rather than a column per type: the alternative is eight nullable columns only one of which is ever set, which is the shape 01-identity.md §6 rejected for person_contact answered_at timestamp, audit time Default now answered_by reference to person, optional

Rules — event_answer

  • One answer per question per person — the (question_id, person_id) pair is unique over all rows.
  • An answer is not removed when its question is retired: there is no delete rule from event_question to event_answer.

docs.title: Answers as rows, not JSONB on the registration
docs.text:
This is the choice that makes the feature worth having. The whole reason to collect "dietary requirements" is to be able to answer "who needs a gluten-free meal, and how many?" — and that is a question the data must answer directly: for one event and one question, take every answer given to it, group the answers by the value given, and count each group, largest group first.

With answers stored as a JSONB blob on the registration, that becomes JSON traversal, an index that does not help, and a report nobody writes. The cost is one row per answer — which is exactly the number of things the organization must act on.

docs.title: Reusable question libraries were considered and rejected
docs.text: A shared pool of question definitions — question_code, assigned to events — is structurally the requirement machinery removed in D-044. It earns its keep only when the same question must mean the same thing across events, and tent preference does not: what one camp asks and what another needs are allowed to differ. Per-event definitions keep them from having to agree, and avoid reviving a removed pattern for a benefit nobody asked for.

docs.title: Health facts, and the discipline this requires
docs.text:
An event form is how the people running an event find out what they need to know about the people who came. It used to be the only way. D-085 ended that, and the guidance below is still worth reading as a warning rather than a nicety — anything a form asks is read by whoever runs that event, and the number of such people is decided by whoever creates the event (D-061, ../domain/07-events.md §12).

This sentence's reason has now been rewritten twice, and the second rewriting killed the claim. It began as "the dependent.* namespace is unreachable by unit leaders"; D-074 deleted that namespace and the claim survived on a better reason — no event.* permission includes the medical record, and no wildcard is left to sweep it in (D-068). Both halves are now gone: there is no medical record (D-083), and the facts that would have been in one are attributes on the person, which a unit leader holding person.view over their own unit can read (09-attributes §4). A claim that had outlived two of its reasons should not be repaired a third time; it is stated as what is now true:

  • The form is no longer the ceiling on what an organizer may know. An organizer who is also a leader of the registrant's unit may already have read the allergy. Any document implying the contrary was quietly making a privacy promise the model does not keep.
  • What the form is for changed accordingly — it asks now, about this event, of a person who may not be in the system at all, and its answer carries a date. That is a genuine property the record does not have: a recorded attribute says what somebody believed, once, at no particular time. Whether the two should meet at all is AT-1, and the recommendation there is a confirmation pass rather than a silent prefill, precisely because a stale health fact that arrives looking authoritative is worse data than an asked question.
  • Nothing in the data model distinguishes a preference from a condition, and now nothing could: D-083 refused the category. "Vegetarian" and "coeliac" are both data_type = 'text' in event_answer.value, so the line is what an organizer types into label — form design guidance, not an enforced constraint:
Belongs on an event form Belongs on the person, as an attribute What the organizers need on the day, for this event Diagnoses, medication, allergies, conditions What a visitor who is not in the system must supply Anything already recorded, curable and audited on the record T-shirt size for a camp that is ordering shirts now Anything whose value outlives the event that asked

Asking a returning camper to restate a recorded allergy at every event is not a privacy measure; it is the same fact, fresher in one table and unmanaged in it. The honest reading of this section is that the event answer is where a health fact lands when the organization has not collected it properly — and the fix is the record plus a confirmation pass, not a cleverer form.

Open: the retention policy for answers. A dietary answer citing a medical condition is data of exactly the same class as everything else the organization holds about a person — D-083 settled that there is no specially-sensitive category, not that this data is insignificant — and there is no policy for how long answers survive their event. See EV-2, which notes that until it is answered the weakest-protected copy of a health fact is the freshest one.

docs.title: The unit-authority rule
docs.text:
The resolver matches scope exactly, so a unit_leader at ('org_unit', 7) does not satisfy a check at ('event', 42) — even when unit 7 owns event 42. This is the hinge of the module (../domain/07-events.md §6).

can_event(person, permission_code, event, at) is one permission check for events, used by the API in place of a bare can(). An event is an ARTIFACT of its owning unit, not a child of it, so a permission is satisfied at ('event', E) if it is satisfied at ('org_unit', E.org_unit_id) AND the event's owner is that same unit.

This is NOT inheritance downward. It does not reach the unit's SUB-units, and it does not grow when the hierarchy is restructured — the event's owner is one unit, fixed by D-049. Authority for a sub-unit's events still requires that sub-unit's own roles or an exposure, exactly as before.

The check has three steps, and the order is only the order of two independent questions:

  1. Ask can() whether the person holds the permission at scope ('event', the event's id), as of the given date.
  2. Ask can() the same question at scope ('org_unit', the event's owning unit), as of the same date.
  3. Either one being true is enough. If there is no such event, the answer is no.

can_event is a convenience wrapper, not a new channel. It calls can() twice on scopes that already resolve, and adds no authority of its own. If the organization later decides leaders should not automatically run every event their unit creates, deleting the second can() call is the whole change — and making organizers access_grant-based then needs no data migration, because nothing was written to access_grant to make this work.

docs.title: Guards
docs.text:
Guard 1 — the registration window. No registration row may be created for an event whose window does not admit it. The guard runs inside the transaction that inserts the row, on every insert path — and since there is nothing left to attach it to, that coverage is now a requirement on the paths rather than a property the database supplies for them. Steps 4 and 5 read the event's own dates and step 2 exempts a source value, so no constraint states this rule and no report would catch a violation the way a window violation should be caught: at the write. The order is a rule: "there is no such event" must be settled before anything reads the event's dates, and the staff carve-out must be answered before the checks it overrides.

  1. Read the event the registration names. If there is no such event, refuse the row — a registration cannot name an event that does not exist.
  2. If source is staff, admit the row and stop here. Staff may always register, including at a cancelled event (to record who had been coming) — they are acting deliberately and are attributed.
  3. Otherwise refuse the row if the event is cancelled (cancelled_at is set).
  4. Refuse it if registration_opens_at is set and has not yet arrived.
  5. Refuse it if the effective close has passed — registration_closes_at, or starts_at when registration_closes_at is absent. This is where "NULL = open until the event starts" is enforced.
  6. Admit the row.

Guard 2 — an event with registrations cannot be deleted. Deleting an event is refused as soon as the event has any registration row at all, and the refusal says what to do instead: cancel it (set cancelled_at) so the record of who was coming survives. Cancellation is the mechanism.

Guard 2 is what makes the cascade in §3 safe. Organizers cascade when an event is deleted — but an event that anyone registered for cannot be deleted at all. So the cascade can only ever fire on a draft with no registrations, which is the only case where losing the roster is harmless.

docs.title: Who has not replied yet?
docs.text:
"Unanswered" is a subtraction (../domain/07-events.md §3). The subtrahend is who could contribute — which, for an open event, is an audience.

The question asked of one camp is: every person who may register for it and has not answered. The audience is the eligible set, the registration table is the answered set, and the answer is the difference between them, listed by preferred name. What makes the question answerable at all:

  • The eligible set is evaluated, not stored: it is the people named by the event's access_grant rows through their audiences, assessed as of the day the question is asked, not as of the day the grant was written. A child who joined the pack last week is on this list; a child who has left is not.
  • Only grants on this event count, and only grants that are not revoked in level and have not been revoked themselves.
  • The answered set is one row per person at most (§4), so the subtraction cannot leave the same person on the list twice.
  • People who have been merged away are excluded, so a tombstone never turns up on a list somebody is being asked to chase.

This is the query that would be impossible if unanswered were a stored value, because the eligible set — an audience, evaluated as a rule — is what defines the question. Storing "unanswered" rows would mean enumerating an audience into rows, and re-enumerating whenever a child joins the pack.

docs.title: Who is actually coming?
docs.text:
Four numbers about one event, in one answer, all counted over that event's attending registrations: how many are not waitlisted (coming), how many are waitlisted (waiting), how many are unconfirmed and not waitlisted (holding a place without having paid), and the event's capacity. An event with no registrations still has to produce the row, with zeros.

The four numbers an organizer needs, in one row: coming, waiting, holding a place without having paid, and the limit. attending > capacity is the overrun, and it is visible here rather than prevented (§10 check 5).

docs.title: Who was actually there?
docs.text:
For one camp, the attending registrations listed with each person's preferred name, birth date and was_present, with the unmarked listed first — the unmarked sort ahead of both a mark and an absence recorded as false, because the unmarked are the work remaining. This is the camp roster as a safeguarding record, not a plan.

NULLS FIRST puts the unmarked at the top, which is the work remaining. Once every row is true or false, this is the answer to "who was in the organization's care at that camp" — and it is the reason was_present is three-valued rather than a boolean defaulting to false.

docs.title: 10. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify

  1. An event whose owning unit has closed. Counts events whose unit's status is closed while that unit's own period is still open; a non-zero result means either the event was miscategorised or the unit's closure was recorded without ending its future events.
  2. Overlapping events for the same unit. Counts pairs of events belonging to one unit, neither cancelled, whose start-to-end instants overlap. Not an error — a pack may run two things at once — but worth a glance, since it is often a duplicate entry.
  3. An event with no organizer. Counts events that are neither cancelled nor already begun and have no event_organizer row at all — an event nobody is running: either abandoned mid-setup, or a data-entry error. Not a rule on write, because an event is legitimately created before its organizers are named.
  4. A registration held by a person who has been merged away. Counts registrations whose person carries a merge pointer. The merge should have repointed them; a non-zero result catches the ones it missed.
  5. An event running over its stated capacity. Counts, for each non-cancelled event that has a capacity, its attending non-waitlisted registrations, and reports the events where that count exceeds the capacity. PERMITTED — organizers may exceed deliberately (../domain/07-events.md §8) — so this is a report, not an error. A pattern of overruns means the capacity numbers are wrong, not that the rule is.
  6. An unpaid registration holding a place past the waitlist deadline. Counts attending, non-waitlisted registrations on a non-cancelled event whose waitlist_deadline has passed and whose fee obligation stands at unpaid, partially_paid or overdue. It should be empty once the release in §5 has run — a non-empty result means the job is not running.
  7. An answer to a question the person was never registered for. Counts answers whose person has no registration for the event that owns the question. Either the registration was deleted, or the answer was written against the wrong person.

  8. Presence marked on a registration that declined. Counts not_attending registrations whose was_present is not absent. Contradictory: you cannot have been present at a thing you said you were not attending. Nothing above forbids the combination, so this is a written prohibition and a check rather than a guard — a prohibition nobody runs is a convention, not a guarantee.

  9. A registration outside its event's registration window. Counts registrations whose registered_at falls before the window opens or after it closes, excluding the ones an organizer recorded deliberately (registration_kind = 'organized', whose window is the event's own period). Guard 1 in §8 is supposed to make the first two shapes impossible, and there is no constraint behind that guard — a window spans two columns of two tables, so the check runs inside the writing transaction or nowhere (F-10 shape 3). A non-zero result is therefore evidence about the code, not the data: someone added a second path that places a registration.

  10. A fee-bearing event with registrations and no obligations. Counts non-cancelled events that require a fee and have at least one registration, where no fee_obligation exists for some of those registrations. The obligation is created by the code that places the registration (§6); there is no rule attached to the registration row that would create it, so a path that forgets produces a person with a confirmed place and no bill — invisible to every check here, because every row it left behind is individually correct. Money-versus-roster reconciliation (§6) is the same discovery arriving later and more expensively; this is the version worth running nightly.

Check 5 is the important one to read correctly. It will produce rows, and that is not a failure — exceeding capacity is a permitted, attributed act (../domain/07-events.md §8). What the report is for is the pattern: an event that overruns every year has a capacity number that is wrong, and the fix is to change the number rather than to start refusing people.

docs.title: 11. Open issues
docs.text:
Tracked in ../open-questions.md under G. Events.

  • ~~The age ceiling on an open event.~~ Settled: there is none (D-070). No min_age/max_age on event, no age branch anywhere in the registration path. If it is ever revisited the shape is a new built-in audience, not a column on the row.
  • ~~Whether event.manage_participants should split.~~ It did, into event.presence.mark at contribute (§4).
  • Retention of event_answer. Answers end with the event and there is no policy saying when (§7). This used to be argued from the answer being health data, which D-083 left without a referent: it is personal data, which makes the question ordinary rather than answered — and sharper, since the same sentence recorded as a person_attribute follows a different retention rule on purpose (EV-2).
  • Cancelled events and fees. Cancelling keeps the registrations. Whether it releases the obligations, refunds them, or neither is the finance module's decision (§6). That decision has since been taken for events (D-076): cancelling voids the outstanding requests and money that already arrived waits in the unmatched queue (07-finance.md §2b).
  • was_present as a safeguarding record. Whether presence needs its own retention or its own permission, given what it is (§9 of the domain doc).
  • Whether organizers should be access_grants after all. §8's can_event makes the unit's roles reach its events. If the organization would rather organizers be opt-in per event, that is one clause — and no data migration (§8).
  • Waitlist notification. Promotion is deliberate; telling the promoted person is not designed. It belongs to the communication module.

docs.title: Data Model — Personal Attributes
docs.text:
The layer every fact about a person lives in, once you subtract what they are called and counted as. Written because D-083 removed the category this file might otherwise have been built around — a privileged medical record — and D-084 put an organization-maintained vocabulary in its place.

Read domain/08-person-data.md first if the word "attribute" makes this look like a dumping ground. It is the opposite: a layer with a defined boundary, a curated vocabulary, and an explicit list of what it cannot do.

docs.title: 1. The sentence, and the boundary it draws
docs.text:
Everything the system knows about a person other than their name, their gender and their age is descriptive data of one class, held in fields, whose meaning the organization defines at runtime. Not files. Not a per-domain table each with its own permission codes. One kind of data, one kind of access, one vocabulary.

That sentence is a scope claim inherited almost verbatim from the answer that produced D-083, and it is deliberately wider than "health data". A drug dosage and a shoe size are the same kind of object: something the organization recorded about a person, which will be wrong in three years, which nobody can enumerate in advance.

The boundary is drawn by rules, not by sensitivity.

Stays structured, in its own table Becomes an attribute person_name history, gender, birth_date + birth_date_precision — 01-identity §2–3 Health: allergies, medication, conditions, instructions, checkups person_contact — purpose, primary flag, validity — 01-identity §6 Education, occupations, qualifications, languages person_identifier — per-scheme uniqueness — 01-identity §7 Insurance numbers, membership numbers of other bodies, measurements, clothing sizes account, account_credential — 01-identity §4–5 Dietary habits, transport preferences, notes, anything collected this season

The test for the left column: does a rule exist that this layer physically cannot hold? "Exactly one primary postal contact among the open rows", "a school id may repeat, a birth number may not", "one current name per person" — each is a constraint over a known set of columns. A key/value table has no known set of columns; that is its entire purpose. Folding those four tables in would have relocated working constraints into application code and been called uniformity, which is F-10 shape 3 built on purpose. Identity is closed because it was enumerated years ago and has not changed since. Description is open because nobody can enumerate it. That is the whole boundary, and it is worth restating in review whenever a new table tempts someone to put it in either column.

What is not here either, because it is not data about a person: relationships (04-relationships), belonging (03-membership), money (07-finance), event registrations and their answers (08-events), authority (05-authorization).

docs.title: 2. attribute_definition — the vocabulary
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id code text, required The stable handle. Stored as typed, compared normalized — see the rules below. label text, required What a human sees. description free text, optional What belongs in this field and what does not. Cheap to write, and the only defence against a code meaning four things to four people. value_type text, required One of: text, long_text, number, date, yes_no, one_of, date_year. Governs the input drawn and the warning given — not what may be saved (§4 of this file's rules, D-084). value_unit text, optional Display suffix — kg, cm. Rendering only. allow_multiple boolean, required, default false Whether more than one value may be current at once. Allergies: yes. Blood type: no. status text, required One of: proposed, live, retired. See the status rules. category text, optional Display grouping — health, contact-admin, program. Grouping only: it grants nothing and restricts nothing, and any sentence that says otherwise is reintroducing the sub-resource D-083 removed. sort_order integer, optional proposed_by, proposed_at person, timestamp Set when a value arrived for a code that did not exist. retired_at, retired_reason timestamp, free text Retiring is an administrative act and is explained. Standard columns 00-conventions §7.

Allowed values for one_of live in a small child table, attribute_option: definition, code, label, sort_order, status. It is a table rather than a comma-separated string because options are renamed, retired and re-ordered, and a retired option must keep meaning what it meant on the day it was chosen — a value stored against it is a historical fact.

Rules

  • Codes are unique in normalized form. Before comparison a code is trimmed, case-folded and has internal whitespace collapsed. Allergy, allergy and allergy are one code, and the second one is refused on write. This is the only anti-duplication rule the database can still enforce here, which is exactly why it is stated as a rule and not as a convention.
  • proposed is a real status with real behaviour. A value recorded against a code that does not exist creates a definition in proposed, owned by whoever proposed it. Proposed definitions appear nowhere in data entry, appear in the curation queue (§8 check 1), and their values are readable by anyone entitled to read the person — the person's data is not hidden from the organization because a label is waiting for approval. Curation promotes, merges, renames or discards it.
  • Retiring keeps the values. A retired code leaves data entry and stays readable, reportable and revivable. Deleting the label must never delete the fact underneath it: a code discovered to have been named badly is an administrative event, and if retiring it destroyed nine years of records it will never be retired, and the vocabulary accretes instead of being curated — the slow failure this whole table is arranged to avoid.
  • A definition with values may not be deleted, only retired (00-conventions §9 — references restrict, none cascade). A definition with no values ever recorded may be deleted, and that is the only delete this table offers.
  • Changing value_type does not rewrite values. Existing values are kept as they were written; the new type governs what is typed from then on. A type change is a display decision, and the history is not the display's to correct.
  • allow_multiple may go false → true freely, and true → false only with a report. Turning it off does not merge existing multiples; it leaves the database holding a shape the definition forbids, which §8 check 4 will then report forever. Ask first whether the multiples are real.

Permission. Creating, renaming, merging or retiring a definition needs attribute.define (permission catalog). Recording a value needs no new permission — see §4.

docs.title: 3. person_attribute — a value one person has
docs.text:
Fields

Field Kind Notes id surrogate id person_id reference to person, required attribute_definition_id reference to attribute_definition, required Points at the vocabulary, live or retired; never at nothing. A value with no code is a note, and notes are their own code. value text, required One column, always text. Not a jsonb, not parallel typed columns. See the note below. value_option_id reference to attribute_option, optional Set when the type is one_of; the value text is then a denormalisation kept for display, and the option reference is the truth. recorded_note free text, optional "the doctor said this may change in spring". Kept beside the value rather than inside it, so the value stays comparable. source text, optional self, guardian, staff, legacy_import. Standard columns created_at / created_by double as recorded at / recorded by.

There are no valid_from / valid_to columns, and that is a decision rather than an omission. A row here is the current belief, overwritten in place; the sequence of beliefs is in audit_log (D-085), which holds those values and is therefore the table §6 is about — this document's history is a permission mark away from being an empty list, and saying the two are connected is the most this section can honestly do about it. The corpus gives periods to things that are true over an interval — a membership, a contact address, an assignment — and a descriptive value is not that: it is a statement whose truth is asserted now about whatever it is about, with a timestamp on the assertion. Putting periods here would invite a UI that asks when an allergy began, which is a medical question the organization is not competent to record and has no rule that could use.

value is one text column, and there are no typed siblings. A value_number and a value_date beside it would let the database do something useful with a date — and would then make 2019, recorded as a year for a checkup, unsavable, which is the failure D-084 refuses: an empty field behind a validation error is a worse record than an imprecise one. The type belongs to the definition and to the form renderer; the storage stays uniform. What that costs is listed in §5 rather than discovered later.

Rules

  • A value may not be blank. Absence is the absence of a row (D-059); an empty string is a lie that looks like an answer.
  • At most one current value per (person, definition) unless the definition allows multiple. One row per pair, because there is no history — so the rule is a plain uniqueness rule except that whether it applies depends on a column in another table, which no constraint can express: F-10 shape 3. Check inside the writing transaction, and report the survivors (§8 check 4). A partial unique index would be the right tool for the single-valued definitions and the wrong tool for the rest; choosing per definition is how this rule becomes a report instead of a guarantee.
  • Overwriting is an update, not a delete-and-insert. The row keeps its created_at — that is when this fact first entered the system, which is a question someone asks — and the changed value with its author lands in the audit trail.
  • Values recorded against a proposed definition are hidden from forms and reports until curation, and are not hidden from anyone with read access to the person. The organization's data quality problem is not the family's confidentiality problem.

Indexes — on person_id (every read is per person), on attribute_definition_id (every report is per code), and the per-(person, definition) rule above.

docs.title: 4. Who may read, and who may write
docs.text:
Read: person.view, and nothing else. No attribute.* read permission exists, because there is nothing to gate that person.view does not already gate (D-083). The three channels behave normally:

  • A unit leader holding person.view scoped to their own unit reads their own members' descriptive data, including an allergy list.
  • A guardian at view or write reads the child's whole record; at none, none of it.
  • A person reads their own.

This makes person.view the widest read permission in the system, and the catalog marks it accordingly rather than leaving it at the level it had when the record was smaller than the person. Any future narrowing — "read everything except…" — is a decision entry about a second grant scope, not a new code with a suggestive name (E-7 is closed for exactly this reason).

Write: person.edit for values, attribute.define for the vocabulary. That split is the design: data entry is open to anyone who can already edit the person, because the alternative is the fact never getting recorded; the vocabulary is narrow, because the vocabulary is what makes the data queryable. An improvised need saves as a proposal, which is the one path out of the failure where a leader types a drug name into a notes field at 23:00 and it is never seen by a report again.

docs.title: 5. What this design cannot do
docs.text:
Stated here because an open key/value layer is repeatedly described as flexible by people who have not yet needed any of these, and because D-084 was taken with them in view rather than in the abstract.

Cannot Why What is done instead Constrain a value No constraint can reference the contents of a row chosen at runtime The definition's type drives a warning; a human may always save Type-check at the database Values are one text column ISO-format by convention, and §8 check 7 reports a type that is wrong for the whole definition Compare or aggregate safely 12 and 12 kg and twelve are three strings Report on the one_of codes; treat free text as a list to read, not a number Express the one-value rule as a constraint The rule reads another table (F-10 shape 3) Enforced in the writing transaction (§3), which is a guard and not a constraint; §8 check 4 reports what got past it. The two are not alternatives — one stops it, the other notices it did not Answer "what did we believe in 2019" from business data Rows hold the current belief only audit_log, which holds the values themselves (§6) and which D-081 records as the corpus's weakest control. This is the accepted risk, not a footnote: the history is real and nothing but an omitted line of code stands between it and being empty Restrict one field to some readers D-083 refused a privileged subset One scope over one record; a court-ordered exception is a decision entry, not a code Trust that a code means one thing Codes are typed by humans Normalized uniqueness, description on every definition, §8 check 2, and a named curator

docs.title: 6. Erasure, retirement, and the audit payload
docs.text:
Two opposite operations, and confusing them is the obvious mistake.

  • Retiring a code is administrative and keeps values. The label leaves service; the facts stay.
  • Redacting a person is legal and erases values. When a person is anonymised (00-conventions §8), every row in this table belonging to them is deleted. A redacted person with attribute values attached is a redaction that did not happen — §8 check 6, and the one check here that should alert rather than log.

The trail holds these values, and that is the load-bearing consequence of the whole module. An audit entry about a person_attribute carries the before and after images, as it does for a contact point or an assignment. Three things had to be true for that to be the right call, and it is worth reading them as a dependency rather than as reassurance:

  • D-083 says a diagnosis is not a different kind of fact from a shoe size, so a rule that stripped attribute values out of the payload while logging a change of address with its value would be a sensitive subset of the person record, reintroduced as a list of table names after it was deleted as a list of permission names.
  • D-085 overwrites values in place because the trail is their history, so a payload without values is not a conservative trail, it is no trail: the question in §5's table becomes unanswerable by design, and the reason overwrite was cheap enough to choose disappears with it.
  • Therefore the guard on audit_log carries person data now. An audit entry about a person is as sensitive as the person data it quotes, which is written as a requirement on audit.view in ../appendix/permission-catalog.md §8 and argued in 05-authorization §9 — where the case against copying data into a less-guarded place is, in this table, a description of the table itself. Whether that single guard is the right shape is not settled here: filtering history per entry, or splitting the permission into the trail's shape and its payloads, are both live options and both have costs (AT-4), the largest being that one of the three is already built, so declining to choose is a choice nobody has to sign.

What is left of the redactor is small, and says so. It scrubs the values that must never be logged at all — credentials, tokens, integration secrets — and it stopped carrying the personal-data case when the sensitive subset went: a key-name list cannot protect a table whose column names this organization invents at runtime, and allergy is not on it and never will be. 00-conventions §8 states that once for the whole schema, and 06-audit §2.2 keeps the withdrawn rule visible so nobody reinstates it by inference.

Erasure is the one thing here that is absolute. Erasing a person deletes their rows and removes their values from payloads already written, however lawfully (06-audit §4); a trail that keeps what the person asked to have forgotten is not a history, it is the thing they asked to be rid of, filed where it reads well.

docs.title: 7. The legacy import, which is where the vocabulary comes from
docs.text:
The old system's columns become codes, and this is the largest single event in the life of the attribute layer — most of the first two hundred definitions arrive here rather than from a deliberate act of design.

  • Every raw field name in a batch must map to a code, be mapped to discarded with a reason, or stop the batch. Silently dropping an unmapped column is how a decade of a fact the organization collected disappears on a Tuesday.
  • An unmapped column maps to a proposed code, named from the raw column, not to an existing code by similarity. A human merges near-duplicates afterwards; nothing guesses at import time, because an import-time merge is invisible and unreviewable.
  • The mapping is recorded on the batch, in import_batch.field_mapping, one entry per raw column (06-audit §3 explains why the grain is a column and not a staged row, which is the plausible wrong answer). The mapping is not the schema; changing it is an act of curation with an audit entry, not a migration.

docs.title: 8. Integrity checks
docs.text:
Invariants to verify

  1. Values recorded against a proposed definition, by age. The curation queue. Non-empty is normal; old is the finding: a proposal nobody has looked at for a quarter is a fact the organization is storing in a private language.
  2. Codes close enough to be the same thing — same normalized form after stripping punctuation and collapsing plural forms, or the same label. A list to read, not a failure, and the continuous cost of an open vocabulary.
  3. A live definition with no values ever recorded. Retirable. Worth knowing: a dead code in a picker is a small tax paid by everyone who opens the form.
  4. More than one current value for a definition that forbids multiples. The bypass of §3's cross-table rule — an import, a hand-fix, a path that skipped the check. Non-zero means the guard is missing, not that the data is odd.
  5. A value that is blank, whitespace, or longer than the type could have produced. A yes_no code with a three-sentence value is a definition being used as a note field, and the report is a conversation about which one it should have been.
  6. A redacted person with attribute rows, or with attribute values still present in audit_log. Should never be non-empty; this is the erasure guarantee and it alerts.
  7. A definition whose values contradict its declared type wholesale — a date code where nothing parses as a date. The type is advisory for one value and a signal for all of them: at that point the definition is wrong, not the data.

Check 1 and check 6 are the two that matter. One is the vocabulary rotting; the other is a person's data outliving their erasure. Everything else on this list is housekeeping.

docs.title: 9. Open issues
docs.text: Four, all registered in open-questions.md: whether event questions should bind to codes so a returning camper's allergy is prefilled rather than re-typed (AT-1), who holds attribute.define in the starting role set and how long a proposal may sit (AT-2), whether definition labels need translation (AT-3, inherited from the multi-language question in §H), and — the one this document cannot settle — whether one permission is enough to guard a trail that holds a child's values (AT-4), which is §6's weakest link stated as a question rather than as a design.

docs.title: Decision Log
docs.text:
Decisions taken, with the reasoning that produced them. Recorded so they are not re-litigated from scratch — and so that when a decision is reversed, the reason for the original choice is visible.

Status values: decided — settled, the data model reflects it (since D-072: the documents, not a schema file). proposed — recommended, awaiting your confirmation. assumption — taken by default, stated in italics in the docs, easily reversed. reversed — no longer in force; the entry is kept, marked, and the replacement is linked. Reversals are also listed together at the bottom.

Five SQL fences survive in this log, and only here. D-072 moved the schema out of the documentation, but it did not rewrite the entries that had been written in the schema — at D-035, D-041, D-060, D-066 and D-068. Each is a quotation of the shape a decision was made in, and each says below it where the requirement actually lives now. No later entry adds a fence: the rule for writing this log from here is D-081 — state the requirement, name the layer that owes it, and let an identifier be a name rather than an actor.

docs.title: D-001 — Person, account, and membership are three separate things
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your requirements) Date: initial design

Decision. person holds identity only. account holds login credentials and is optional. membership holds participation and is temporal. No member flags, no child/adult flag, no is_member on person.

Why. You described a person who was a member 1990–2010 and again from 2024. That is one person and two membership periods. Any design with person.is_member cannot express it, cannot answer "who was in Troop 12 in 1998?", and silently destroys 36 years of history the first time someone corrects a record.

Consequence. Membership questions are always date-qualified: ../data-model/03-membership.md provides is_current_member(), was_member_on(), current_member_category(), and membership_years().

docs.title: D-002 — Everything temporal is a period, never a boolean
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. valid_from / valid_to with valid_to IS NULL meaning "still true", and half-open [from, to) ranges. Overlap prevented by EXCLUDE USING gist constraints.

Why. Required by D-001, guardianship expiry, unit membership history, role terms, and grant expiry. Enforcing overlap in the database rather than in application code is essential: an import script, a manual SQL fix, or a future API will bypass application validation.

Consequence. Requires PostgreSQL with btree_gist. On MySQL, the guarantee weakens to triggers plus nightly checks — a materially weaker invariant to be recorded as an accepted risk if that platform is chosen.

docs.title: D-003 — Never hard-delete; merges leave tombstones
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. No deleted_at, no business-data DELETE, no ON DELETE CASCADE anywhere. Ended periods get valid_to. Merged people keep their row with merged_into_person_id. Erasure is redaction, not deletion.

Why. "Who attended this camp in 2003?" must resolve forever. A hard delete breaks the safeguarding record. Merges must be reversible because bad matches are inevitable.

Consequence. Every query must exclude merged and redacted rows — hence the v_person view and resolve_person() function, which exist so application code cannot forget.

docs.title: D-004 — No automatic merging, ever
docs.text:
Status: assumption ⚠ confirm or overrule

Decision. Every identity match, however strong, requires human confirmation. There is no confidence threshold above which the system merges on its own.

Why. A false-positive merge is a privacy incident: the survivor gains the absorbed person's permissions, and two people's records become one. A false negative is an inconvenience someone can fix. The asymmetry justifies the cost.

Reverse if: the volume of historical data makes manual review infeasible. If so, the high-confidence tier should be narrow (exact external identifier match only) and its application must be logged and alerted.

See: ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md

docs.title: D-005 — Permissions are grants, never derived from identity
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: initial design

Decision. Being a parent, a member, a leader, or a long-serving volunteer grants nothing. Every capability comes from an explicit, dated, revocable row.

You answered that both read and write access should be explicit for caretakers.

Why. The classic failure: a relationship ends (custody changes, a leader steps down) but access persists, because it was implied rather than granted. Explicit grants make access auditable and revocable.

Consequence. A guardianship row alone grants nothing; guardianship_permission rows do. A position_assignment alone grants nothing; role_assignment does.

docs.title: D-006 — Per-item permissions are capabilities on the item
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: initial design

Decision. You clarified that "per-item permission" means capability on that item — "person X may act on item Y" — not a participation record and not an eligibility gate. Implemented as access_grant with an ordered level (revoked < view < contribute < manage < admin).

Why. Isolates authorization from participation (D-005) and from eligibility, which will be a separate concept when events are specified.

Consequence. permission_level connects permission codes to the level they require, so one grant level serves many permissions without a hardcoded mapping.

docs.title: D-007 — Every resource has an admin level that subsumes narrower ones ⚠ REVERSED
docs.text:
Status: ~~decided~~ reversed by D-068 Date: initial design · reversed refinement round 5

Reversed. The per-resource <resource>.admin permissions and the resolver's prefix match are gone. The admin grant LEVEL (rank 40) is untouched — this decision conflated the two, and the collision is what made it hard to reverse cleanly. See D-068.

Decision. Per your instruction, every grantable resource exposes <resource>.admin, checked by prefix match, plus a single top-level system.admin.

Why. Without it, every new narrow permission requires updating every role that should already have implied it — and someone will miss one, producing a permission that silently is not granted. The prefix match makes new permissions automatically covered.

Consequence. The check is computed, not mapped. person.admin etc. are real permission rows so they appear in the role editor.

docs.title: D-008 — Organizations units are one self-referencing table with configurable types
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: initial design

Decision. One org_unit table with parent_unit_id self-reference and a configurable org_unit_type. Hierarchy via materialized path plus recursive CTE functions.

Why. You confirmed sub-units are core. Depth is a data question, not a schema question — a 40-year-old organization has changed its levels. One table means "everyone in this district" is one recursive query rather than a hand-written union.

Consequence. Nesting rules live in org_unit_type_rule plus a trigger. Units that closed remain queryable forever.

docs.title: D-009 — Unit membership links to person, not to membership
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. unit_membership.person_id → person.id, deliberately not membership_id.

Why. 1990s rosters have a unit and a year but no membership workflow. Linking to membership would make that data unrepresentable and lose the whole historical dataset.

Cost. Nothing enforces that a person with a unit membership holds an organization membership. Mitigated by application validation plus a nightly check (../data-model/03-membership.md, check 1).

docs.title: D-010 — Role assignments and access grants share a scope model and a resolver
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. role_assignment and access_grant are separate tables but share scope_type, the level model, and one can() function. Four authority channels (ownership, guardianship, item grants, roles), each dispatching from the permission's namespace, with an absolute deny check in front of them.

Amended (see D-031, D-032): the resolver's allow channels are now ordered by locality rather than by channel, and the deny channel is scope-independent.

Amended again by D-079, and this reaches the sentence above the amendment.
