"Each dispatching from the permission's namespace" was how the channels were found, and it is gone: dispatch is now subject ≠ actor for guardianship, and system. remains the only namespace with resolver-visible meaning. The four channels themselves are untouched — that part of this decision was durable for six rounds and is the part worth keeping. What the namespace rule turned out to be was a way of skipping the guardianship channel whenever the permission's name happened not to mark it as a guardian act, which is a thing a name cannot do. Note the shape of the failure for future amendments: the channel list was right and the routing over it was wrong, and every document that cited the routing copied the error.

Why. They are the same idea at two granularities — authority for a period, in a scope, granted by someone. A single resolver prevents the divergence that makes the weaker of two implementations an exploit. Separate tables because their lifetimes, granters, and revocation semantics genuinely differ.

docs.title: D-011 — scope_id on access_grant is polymorphic, with no foreign key
docs.text:
Status: assumption ⚠ a real fork — worth a deliberate decision

Decision. access_grant.scope_type + scope_id with no FK. Validated by grant_scope_type plus nightly orphan checks.

Why. Most of this system is unspecified (events, documents, and more). Polymorphism makes each new grantable type a config row rather than a schema migration.

Cost. No referential integrity. Mitigated by: grant_scope_type FK, application-level grant closure on item delete, nightly orphan detection, non-reused BIGINT ids.

Alternative. A grantable_item(id, item_type) supertable referenced by every grantable entity — full integrity, heavier design, migration per new type. Overrule this if you prefer integrity to flexibility.

docs.title: D-012 — Status strings compare by rank, never lexicographically
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. access_level is a lookup table with an integer rank. All level comparisons use rank.

Why. 'admin' < 'contribute' alphabetically. A string comparison silently inverts the levels and makes the most powerful level the least. It throws no error and passes most tests. This is the single most dangerous easy mistake in the design.

docs.title: D-013 — Explicit deny (revoked) is checked before everything
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. Resolver channel 0. A revoked grant overrides roles, item grants, and ownership. In the guardianship channel, is_granted = false overrides a granted dependent.admin.

Why. Without an explicit deny level there is no way to express "this person must not see this event" or "this guardian may not see medical records" when a broader grant would otherwise allow it. Court-ordered restrictions must not be overridable by a broader grant.

docs.title: D-014 — Roles do not inherit from other roles
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. No role-to-role inheritance. If unit_leader should have assistant_leader permissions, they are granted explicitly.

Why. Inheritance chains produce authorization answers nobody can predict by reading the configuration. Predictability matters more than configuration economy in an authorization system — the people who must reason about it are volunteers, not engineers.

Note: unit scope inheritance was a separate axis. It was reversed — see D-031. That reversal does not disturb this decision: role-to-role inheritance remains prohibited for the same reason it always was.

docs.title: D-015 — Authority inherits downward through the unit hierarchy ⚠ REVERSED
docs.text:
Status: reversed by D-031 Date: initial design

Decision (original). A role assigned at a unit covers that unit and all descendants. A district treasurer can act on troops within the district.

Why (original). Matches how organizations actually work — a district officer has district-wide responsibility.

Why it is reversed. Your rule: "The organization itself should not be able to itself decide permissions over the nested unit, it must come from the unit itself up. The only exception is the system admin." Downward inheritance makes every unit's authority decidable from above — a role written at the district level silently reaches into troops that never agreed to it. That is exactly the direction you excluded. The replacement is scope_exposure, where the unit grants coverage over itself.

Consequence, accepted. Organization-wide operational roles (national registrar, national treasurer) no longer work by assigning a role high in the tree. Tracked as the reworked C-1.

docs.title: D-016 — Renewal opens a new membership row, not an extended valid_to
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. Shape A. A renewal closes the prior membership and opens a new one, linked by renewed_from_membership_id.

Why. Extending valid_to destroys the ability to see that someone skipped a year and re-joined — the most commonly asked question about renewals — and makes retroactive corrections ambiguous. You asked for history preserved across decades.

Cost. More rows; queries must handle a chain. The self-reference makes the chain explicit rather than inferred.

docs.title: D-017 — Requests are separate from memberships
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. membership_request is its own table. A rejected request produces no membership row.

Why. A rejected request must not pollute member listings; a person may apply several times; review data has no meaning on a membership; submitting is self-service while reviewing is a staff capability.

docs.title: D-018 — membership_request records the subject and the submitter separately
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: initial design

Decision. person_id is the person who would become a member (the child). submitted_by_person_id is who submitted it (the parent).

Why. Collapsing them — the common shortcut — makes it impossible to answer "who applied for this child?" and falsely attributes the parent's action to the child. You confirmed caretakers act on behalf, which requires both parties to be recorded.

Consequence. The same pattern applies to payment.paid_by_person_id / payment.on_behalf_of and to access_log.on_behalf.

docs.title: D-019 — Household membership grants no access
docs.text:
Status: ⚠ PARTLY SUPERSEDED — the household tables are gone (D-057), so there is no household membership left to grant anything. The principle remains true and is the reason to keep this entry: shared address never implied access, the access never came from these tables, and it still does not. Date: initial design

Decision. household exists for billing and address grouping only. Being in a household grants no permission over any other member of it.

Why. A stepparent with no guardianship row has no access to the children's records. All access comes from guardianship + guardianship_permission. This is a safeguarding property, not an oversight.

docs.title: D-020 — Guardian permissions are scoped to the guardianship row
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: initial design

Decision. guardianship_permission.guardianship_id, not the (guardian, dependent) person pair.

Why. You answered that both read and write access must be explicit. Scoping to the pair would let a guardianship ending and a new one beginning (a renewed court order) silently retain all prior permissions. Scoping to the row forces a deliberate re-grant.

Cost. A re-granting step in a rare case. Accepted.

docs.title: D-021 — Health/medical access is separate from consent authority
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. dependent.medical.view and dependent.consent.give are distinct permissions.

Why. A parent who may consent to a camp is not necessarily a parent who may read a medical file, and vice versa. Court orders frequently restrict one without the other. Conflating them makes the common restriction inexpressible.

docs.title: D-022 — Lapsing and termination are different permissions
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. membership.lapse (administrative, non-payment) and membership.terminate (end for cause) are separate permissions, the latter held by very few.

Why. Conflating them means every volunteer who chases unpaid fees can expel a member. Termination in a youth organization is frequently a safeguarding decision.

docs.title: D-023 — Nothing is auto-lapsed or auto-terminated
docs.text:
Status: ⚠ partly superseded by D-040 and D-038 Date: initial design Superseded in part by: D-038 (age-out), D-040 (expiry), D-043 (background checks)

Decision (as originally written). The system produces worklists; humans act. Grace periods absorb late payments. Age-out is driven by membership_type.max_age but the transition is reviewed.

Why. Automatically removing a child's membership because a bank transfer was recorded late is a real harm. Automation should stop short of the consequence.

docs.title: What survives, and what does not
docs.text:
The principle survives and is still the design's default: for anything that is a judgement, the system produces a worklist and a human decides. Terminations for cause, safeguarding removals, and guardianship expiry at majority (D-024) all still work this way.

Two halves of the original text do not survive:

Original claim Now "Grace periods absorb late payments" The grace status is gone. There is a renewal window — dates, not a state (D-040). "Age-out is driven by membership_type.max_age" There is no max_age and no age-out. Membership is ageless (D-038).

The expiry is the one automatic transition. D-040 resolves the tension the original "why" names, and resolves it by removing the decision rather than the automation: the fee covers a fixed period, the period ends on a date everyone already knows, and nobody chooses anything. The late-bank-transfer case the original wording was protecting is absorbed by the window's backdating rule instead. The reversal is recorded in full at ../data-model/07-finance.md §4, including the one case the window cannot absorb.

docs.title: D-024 — Guardianship does not auto-expire at majority ⚠ REVERSED
docs.text:
Status: ~~assumption~~ reversed by D-069 Date: initial design · reversed refinement round 5

Reversed — but not in the direction you might expect. The alternative was not auto-expiry. D-024's sin was the review queue: still an automatic behaviour, still computing a majority date the system has no authority to assert. D-069 removes the queue and the date. The conclusion D-024 reached — do not silently strip access — is kept; the mechanism is withdrawn.

Decision. The system computes the candidate date and puts it on a review queue. Staff close the row.

Why. In many jurisdictions a parent's authority over health and school records does not end at 18, and thresholds vary. An automatic cutoff will silently strip legally valid access.

docs.title: D-025 — Audit log redacts sensitive values before insert
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. audit_trigger calls redact_audit_values() before writing. Free-text fields that may contain personal data are redacted.

Why. An audit log that stores the data it audits is a second copy of sensitive data with weaker access controls and longer retention. Redaction in a cleanup job is not sufficient — the job might not run.

docs.title: D-026 — Two audit trails
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. access_log (who accessed what, by what authority) and audit_log (field values before/after) are separate tables.

Why. Different retention needs, query patterns, and access permissions. Merging them produces a table too large to query and too sensitive to expose wholesale.

Consequence. access_log.authorization_channel + authorization_ref_id are what make it an audit trail rather than a log — they answer "by what authority?", which is the question asked in a dispute.

docs.title: D-027 — Legacy import is staged, reviewed, idempotent, and per-batch reversible
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: initial design

Decision. Six stages (staging → parse → match → review → apply → log). Dry-run mode. Deterministic source_row_hash for idempotency. Per-batch revert while no live data references the imported rows, refusing rather than partially applying.

Why. You confirmed historical records must be imported. Import errors into a four-decade dataset are expensive and often silent.

Consequence. Revert past the safe window is refused, not attempted — a "revert" that orphans live references is worse than an honest refusal.

docs.title: D-028 — Imported memberships never get a NULL valid_to
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. Imported rosters end at the end of the organizational year of the last roster the person appears in, marked data_confidence = 'low'.

Why. A NULL valid_to makes a 1998 member a current member in 2026 — inflating the member count and granting member privileges to people who left decades ago. This is the most dangerous possible default.

docs.title: D-029 — Finance design is provisional and will be rewritten
docs.text:
Status: assumption / open Date: initial design

Decision. ../data-model/07-finance.md exists only so that membership activation has a referent. Expect to rewrite it.

What is likely right regardless: payment_allocation as a many-to-many between payments and obligations (a parent paying for three children in one transfer is the common case, not an edge case), and fee_schedule with validity periods so historical amounts are reproducible.

See: the twelve open questions in that document.

docs.title: D-030 — Finer permissions will be added incrementally
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: initial design

Decision. The permission catalog in ../appendix/permission-catalog.md is a starting point. Adding a permission is a data change (one row plus permission_level rows), not a schema change.

Why. You asked for granularity and an admin fallback at every resource; the prefix-match rule (D-007) means new permissions are automatically covered by existing .admin grants, so granularity can be increased later without touching existing roles.

docs.title: D-031 — No downward inheritance of authority; scope_exposure is the only crossing
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: refinement round 2 Reverses: D-015

Decision. Authority is settled at the scope where it is granted and never inherited downward. A role assigned over a district does not cover the troops in it. The permission resolver performs no ancestor walk — unit_ancestors() must not appear in can(), grant_satisfies(), or can_act_for_dependent(), and integrity check 13 is a CI assertion that this stays true.

Authority crosses downward through exactly one mechanism: a scope_exposure row, written by the unit granting coverage over itself, naming a specific role_assignment — not a role — with its own validity period and withdrawal trail. The crossing is offered from below, never imposed from above.

Why. Your rule, stated twice: "The organization itself should not be able to itself decide permissions over the nested unit, it must come from the unit itself up. The only exception is the system admin." Downward inheritance violates it structurally, because a single row written anywhere above a unit would silently decide authority inside it.

The exception. The system_admin flag is checked before the resolver runs and is therefore outside this rule. It is scoped to the whole system, not to a unit, so it is not a counterexample to "authority originates at the unit" — but it is all-or-nothing and should be rare.

See: ../domain/06-authorization-model.md, ../data-model/05-authorization.md.

docs.title: D-032 — Deny is absolute; locality orders allows only
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: refinement round 2 Amends: D-013

Decision. Two separate rules that were previously conflated into "local overrides global":

  1. Deny is absolute and scope-independent. An explicit revoked at any scope wins over everything, including a more specific allow, the admin level, ownership, and guardianship. The deny check does not walk ancestors — a deny is matched at the organization scope or at the exact same scope, and that is sufficient to be absolute.
  2. Locality orders allows. Among allows, the most specific scope determines the level: item grant → unit grant (exact or exposed) → organization grant → role. First sufficient tier wins.

Why. "The local permission overrides the global one" is true for allows and dangerous for denies. Court-ordered restrictions and safeguarding suspensions must not be overridable by the accident of a grant being written closer to the item. Separating the two rules keeps the local-override intuition where it is correct and removes the one case where it is a safety failure.

See: ../domain/06-authorization-model.md, ../data-model/05-authorization.md.

docs.title: D-033 — Multiple people may occupy the same position
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: refinement round 2

Decision. Position occupancy is many-to-one by default. position.max_holders is NULL (unlimited, the default) or N ≥ 1 for a genuinely single-holder position (a chair). Overlap for the same person in the same position in the same unit is still prevented by an exclusion constraint; the holder limit is enforced by the check_position_holder_limit() trigger.

Why. Two co-leaders, three quartermasters, a shared secretary — the common case is multi-occupancy, so the schema must not make it a workaround. Keeping max_holders optional and defaulted to unlimited means the single-holder chair is the special case, not the rule.

Note. Position is not authority (D-005). Holding a position grants nothing by itself; is_leadership only suggests a role_assignment.

See: ../data-model/02-organization.md, ../domain/04-organization-structure.md.

docs.title: D-034 — The person record holds no deceased flag
docs.text:
Status: decided Date: refinement round 2

Decision. There is no deceased_at, no is_deceased, and no person-level death constraint anywhere in the model. Personhood ends when it ends; the organization does not record it.

Why. Your instruction: "Person does not need to hold the 'deceased' parameter, we do not log that." A death flag is also a data-protection liability (special-category data in some jurisdictions) and a merge hazard — it would need to survive person_merge conflicts that have no good resolution.

Consequence. "Deceased" now has exactly one encoding, and it is indirect: a membership that ended, a position_assignment that ended, a guardianship that ended. Historical records stay correct without it, because every participation is already a period (D-002).

docs.title: D-035 — One root unit; all sub-units nest arbitrarily beneath it
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3

Decision. There is exactly one top-level unit: the organization itself. Every other unit is a sub-unit of it, nested to arbitrary depth and in arbitrary combination — weekly meeting groups, smaller packs, sections, teams. The nesting is not a fixed ladder of national → region → district → group → troop.

Membership lives at the root. People register and pay at the organization, and the membership is theirs as a member of the organization. The sub-units do not hold memberships; they hold participation (D-041) and they are self-governing — their own events, their own local leadership, their own roster.

Why. Your answer: "The people are members of the main top-level unit. The smaller ones are totally arbitrary and can be arbitrarily nested… they all answer to the main unit, the people are mainly registered (and paid) under the top unit, but they can be also part of the smaller packs, that can have their own events, local leadership and so on."

Consequence. The single root was enforced structurally, not by convention — the statement of the moment, kept as it was decided:

-- Exactly one unit may exist at the root.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_org_unit_single_root ON org_unit ((true))
    WHERE parent_unit_id IS NULL;

The requirement now: at most one unit may have no parent, whatever emits the schema cannot emit it, and the migration owes it — 02-organization §3, via data-model/00 §6a.

This largely dissolves the organization-wide-role problem (C-1). That problem existed because "the organization" and "the units holding the data" were assumed to be different things. In this model they are the same: the root unit owns the person registry, the memberships and the fees, so a treasurer or registrar working at the root is not reaching into anything — that data is its own. What remains is a reporting question (may the root see what happens in the packs?), not a permission-inheritance one.

The no-downward-inheritance rule (D-031) still does real work in the other direction: the root cannot decide permissions inside a pack, and a pack that wants the root's help must expose its scope.

See: ../domain/04-organization-structure.md, ../data-model/02-organization.md.

docs.title: D-036 — Units cannot be reparented; a unit that moves is a new unit
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3 Resolves: C-2

Decision. org_unit.parent_unit_id is immutable. A unit never changes parent. If a troop genuinely transfers from one group to another, the old unit closes and a new unit is created under the new parent, the people are moved across, and the lineage is recorded in org_unit_relationship with a transferred_to relationship.

Why. Your answer, to the question of whether a unit may be reparented: "Not allowed at all — a unit that moves is a new unit."

Consequence — a large simplification. Because the parent never changes:

  • The materialized path/depth never needs a subtree cascade rewrite. The existing "reparenting is rare and dangerous; make it a single named procedure" warning disappears along with the danger.
  • Historical reports cannot silently change. "Who was in the 4th Troop in 2001?" keeps answering the same thing forever, because no unit's ancestry is ever edited.
  • The denormalized path stays trustworthy without versioning, which was the main reason retroactive reparenting was expensive.

Enforcement. A trigger rejects any change to parent_unit_id on an existing row. org_unit.transferred_to_unit_id (or the relationship row) records where the people went.

Amended after D-072. There is no trigger, and this is the one enforcement in this log that cannot be moved down a layer. parent_unit_id immutability is not expressible as a constraint — not because PostgreSQL lacks the feature an ORM fails to emit, but because no declarative constraint can talk about what a row used to be. So the rule now lives as a guard in the write path, and the record here has to be honest about what was lost on the way: This entry's original claim was that a trigger made reparenting unreachable from any client, including the legacy import. A write-path guard is reachable from exactly the clients the trigger was chosen to exclude. The compensations available are narrow and named in open question F-10, shape 4: a single named repository operation for hierarchy writes, and a test that attempts the update.

See: ../data-model/02-organization.md.

docs.title: D-037 — Exactly one membership type; the fee is flat and per person
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3 Supersedes: the child/adult/counselor/honorary/lifetime seed set

Decision. There is one membership: everyone who is a member is a member. The yearly fee is flat and per person — it does not vary by age, by household, or by whether the person is a child or an adult. Being a counselor or leader is a position (D-033), never a membership type.

Why. Your answers: "Only one for all, counselor is a position", and between one type with an age-varying fee, two types, or one flat fee, "One type, and the fee does not vary by age either."

The table is kept, with one seeded row. membership_type survives as a table rather than collapsing into a constant, because the document's own principle is that vocabularies are rows and not enums, and because a second type (an honorary or supporting membership) is a plausible future that would otherwise require a migration. The cost is an FK that currently always holds one value — an honest, small cost, recorded here rather than hidden.

Consequence. membership.membership_type_id becomes effectively constant, and the overlap exclusion constraint is no longer scoped by type — see D-041 and ../data-model/03-membership.md.

docs.title: D-038 — Membership is ageless
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3 Removes: membership_type.category, min_age, max_age, and the age-out workflow

Decision. Age has no bearing on membership. There is no age ceiling, no age floor, no automatic age-out, and no child/adult category on a membership. A person may be a member for life.

Why. Your answer: "No age boundary at all — anyone can be a member forever."

What survives. Age is still a fact about a person (person.birth_date) and it still matters where the law makes it matter:

  • Guardianship — a minor has a guardian, and consent is a guardian's act. This is a legal relationship, not a membership rule.
  • Safeguarding — a unit may declare whether minors take part in it.
  • Position eligibility — a scoutmaster may be required to be an adult.

What disappears is the machinery that made belonging conditional on age: the age-out worklist, max_age-driven completed transitions, the child→adult transition workflow, and the "is this person a child?" query.

Retired questions. D-3 (age-out timing), D-4 (child→adult transition) and D-5 (membership type vocabulary) are resolved by this decision and by D-037.

docs.title: D-039 — Member permissions require a current paid membership
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3 Resolves: A-2

Decision. The permission resolver does evaluate membership state. Authority held through a role is honoured only while the holder has a current membership, with exactly two carve-outs:

Channel / case Membership required? Roles with role.requires_membership = true Yes — no current membership, no access Roles with requires_membership = false (appointed counselors, local leaders) No — an adult volunteer keeps their leadership access with an unpaid fee Guardianship (dependent.*) No — guardianship comes from a legal relationship, not a membership Ownership (your own record) No — otherwise a lapse would lock a person out of the screen they renew on

Why. Your answer: "Yes — permissions conditioned on membership", and on how far the rule reaches: "Everything except guardianship and adult volunteers." The third option — locking an unpaid person out of even their own profile — was explicitly not chosen, which is why ownership joins guardianship as exempt.

The cost, stated plainly. This is a real coupling and it is worth naming rather than discovering later:

  • The cache must be invalidated on every membership transition, including the yearly expiry sweep, which is a bulk event touching everyone at once. The cache design must be built for this from the start, not retrofitted.
  • A lapse silently removes access. That is the intent, but "why can't I see this?" becomes a question whose answer is a date, not a decision someone made.
  • role.requires_membership changes meaning — from "reported, drives a worklist" to "enforced by the resolver". The "leaver with access" report remains useful, since it now detects roles that should have been closed rather than the mechanism doing the blocking.

See: ../domain/06-authorization-model.md, ../data-model/05-authorization.md.

docs.title: D-040 — The fee expires yearly; a date-tracked renewal window replaces a grace status
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3 Resolves: A-3, D-3 (grace modelling)

Decision. Membership activates on payment, and the fee is yearly, expiring at a fixed organizational date (typically January). When it expires:

  1. The membership lapses — the person is not a member and holds no member permissions from that date. There is no third "grace" status in the resolver.
  2. A renewal window — a fixed period such as three months, tracked as dates, not a status — follows the expiry. During it the person may renew without re-applying.
  3. A payment inside the window opens the new membership period at the expiry date, so the membership history shows continuous coverage with no gap and the person is not misclassified as a returning member.
  4. A payment after the window opens a new membership at the payment date, and the gap is real. It still does not require a new application.

The tension, named. You described the grace period as existing "for them to pay to stay members", and separately confirmed that during it they are "expired now, but they can rejoin without re-applying." Those pull in different directions on one point: whether the person is a member during the window.

This decision resolves it as: not a member during the window, but the record shows no gap once they pay. The alternative reading — genuinely continuing as a member through the window — would mean a lapse is not detectable until the window closes, and would put a third state into every permission check. If the organization would rather have the softer version, it is a change to membership.renewal_grace_days and the renewal rule, not a rewrite.

See: ../domain/05-membership-lifecycle.md.

docs.title: D-041 — Belonging to a sub-unit is a participation record, not a membership
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3

Decision. unit_membership is renamed unit_participation and reframed. A person holds exactly one membership (at the root unit, paid yearly — D-035) and zero or more participation rows, one per sub-unit they take part in.

Why. Your answer, to how the schema should record being "part of a smaller pack": "A participation record, separate from membership." The rename matters because the old name asserted something untrue — that belonging to a pack was a species of membership — and "three memberships, three statuses, three fee questions" is exactly the ambiguity the answer avoids.

Consequence — the overlap constraint simplifies. With one membership type (D-037), the exclusion constraint drops membership_type_id and becomes a person-level invariant — quoted as decided, in the form the constraint had at the time:

ALTER TABLE membership ADD CONSTRAINT ex_membership_no_overlap
    EXCLUDE USING gist (
        person_id WITH =,
        daterange(valid_from, valid_to, '[)') WITH &&
    )
    WHERE (status IN ('pending_payment','active','suspended'));

The requirement now: one person, one open membership, ever, where "open" means those three statuses — a no-overlap rule over a period, which is exactly the shape an ORM will not generate (open question F-10 shape 1); the temporal pattern is in 00-conventions §6 and the check that catches a bypass is 1b in 03-membership §7.

"Am I a paid-up member?" is now one row, one status, one date. That question was the reason the type was in the constraint.

A root participation row is created with the membership, so "everyone in unit X" is one uniform query whether X is the organization or a Thursday-evening pack.

See: ../data-model/03-membership.md.

docs.title: D-042 — Grants may target audiences, not only individuals
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3

Decision. A grant can name an audience instead of a person. Two kinds:

Kind Evaluated Examples Built-in audiences By a rule the resolver knows, not by a stored list everyone, all_members, the guardians of a given person, the participants of a given unit, the leaders of a given unit Named groups From a stored membership list someone administers "the summer camp kitchen crew"

access_grant therefore carries person_id or audience_id, never both.

Why. This came out of your answer about scope_exposure: "If the unit wants to expose something (a single event eg), they set the permissions to that event for 'everyone' or a group of people to expose it to them." The design had no way to express that — every grant named a person — which is a genuine gap your answer surfaced rather than a detail.

Built-in audiences are rules, not lists, and that is the important property: a new pack member automatically receives what the pack was granted, with no rows to maintain and no stale-group problem. Named groups are the escape hatch, and they carry that problem knowingly — nobody ever removes anyone from a group.

See: ../data-model/05-authorization.md.

docs.title: D-043 — No background checks are recorded in this system
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3 Resolves: A-4

Decision. The system records no background checks: no person_identifier scheme, no requires_background_check flag on membership types, positions or roles, no expiry report, no daily alert, and no person.background_check.* permissions.

Why. Your answer: "We do not have any background checks in place, at least not ones handled by the system."

What this removes. The whole person.background_check.* permission pair, the background_check requirement code, the background_check_officer seed role, the "leader with expired clearance" report, and one of the two reasons position.requires_adult_membership existed.

If that changes, the cleanest route is a requirement_code row plus an expires_at-bearing record — the machinery this decision removes was general enough to carry it. Recorded here so re-adding it is a deliberate act with a visible history rather than a surprise.

docs.title: D-044 — Nothing gates a membership request except identity and payment
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3

Decision. A membership request is accepted on identity and payment alone. The requirement_code and membership_request_requirement tables are removed — there is no blocking checklist, no evidence collection, and no waiver workflow.

Why. Your answer, asked what a request must contain to be accepted: "Just identity and the fee — nothing to verify." The option to keep the mechanism as empty infrastructure was offered and not taken.

What survives. Guardian consent for a minor's account is unaffected — that is a guardianship-layer fact (D-005), not a membership requirement, and its removal here does not weaken it.

docs.title: D-045 — The bulk scope-exposure tool is removed
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3

Decision. The bulk exposure tool is removed, along with the bulk:<batch> reason marker, the bulk branch in check_exposure_direction(), and integrity check 12 that listed bulk rows for review. Every scope_exposure row is written by the unit it covers.

Why. Two answers, in sequence. Asked whether the tool should exist, you said you did not know what it meant and described instead how you actually think about exposure — "they set the permissions to that event for 'everyone' or a group of people". Once audiences (D-042) were added to cover that case, the question was put again and your answer was: "Not needed if audiences are added."

Consequence — the rule is now absolute. There is no sanctioned bypass, no marker prefix, no exception to explain. scope.expose held at the covered unit is the only way a row is created, and it is enforced by the same predicate at three layers (domain/06 §2.5).

This is a genuine simplification, and it removes the design's most uncomfortable paragraph — the one arguing that the rule had to bend for scale.

docs.title: D-046 — Guardianship defaults depend on how the guardianship was created
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 3 Resolves: E-1

Decision. The default permission set granted when a guardianship is created depends on its source:

How it arose Default A parent self-registers their own child Full authority — dependent.admin Recorded manually by staff, or from a court order Set at creation — the person creating it chooses the set

Why. Your answer: "A parent self registering their own child gets full access, if it is created manually later, it can be set on creation."

Consequence. guardianship.source and guardianship_permission.grant_reason are what make the difference auditable — the same word ("guardian") now means two different default scopes depending on paperwork, and the record says which was chosen and why.

docs.title: D-047 — The fee expires on 1 January
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Resolves: A-4 (the date half)

Decision. The organizational membership year runs with the calendar: the fee for a year expires on 1 January. The yearly expiry sweep runs on that date, and the renewal campaign follows it.

Why. Your answer, from the three options offered: "1 January". It aligns the year with the calendar, so "a member this year" means what a reader expects, and the sweep, the campaign and the reports all land on a boundary nobody has to look up.

Consequence. membership_type.expiry_month / expiry_day carry it as data rather than as a constant, because a date written into code is a date the organization cannot move when it changes its mind. Every lapse date, the sweep, the renewal worklist and the cache invalidation derive from this one parameter; changing it re-dates every future period but leaves historical ones alone, which is the reason it is a parameter and not an expression computed into stored rows.

See: D-040, ../data-model/03-membership.md §1.

docs.title: D-048 — The renewal window is 60 days, and is a configuration parameter
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Resolves: A-4 (the window half)

Decision. The renewal window after the expiry date is 60 days. It is stored as a parameter (membership_type.renewal_grace_days), not compiled into the application.

Why. Your answer: "Make it 60 days, but it should not be hard to modify (even if it would be in the code)." The 60 is a starting value; the requirement is that it can be changed without a code change.

The design is already the parameter, deliberately. The window lives in the database, and in_renewal_window() reads it. So the second half of the answer is not a constraint to satisfy — it is a description of what is already built. The one thing that must not happen is a front-end or a scheduled job hardcoding 90 or 60; every reader goes through the column.

Consequence. Seat the sweep and the renewal campaign to read the window from the row, and the value can be tuned between years as the organization learns what actually gets paid.

See: D-040, ../data-model/03-membership.md §3.

docs.title: D-049 — The root may not read into its sub-units; scope_exposure is the only crossing
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Resolves: C-1

Decision. There is no reporting channel outside the permission model and none is built. A unit's own material — its events, its rosters, its local leadership — is visible to the root only when that unit writes a scope_exposure naming the assignment it is exposed to. Every crossing is a written, attributed act by the unit that owns the data.

Why. Your answer, from the three routes offered: "scope_exposure only". The no-downward-inheritance rule (D-031) is the organization's own constitutional principle — "the organization itself should not be able to itself decide permissions over the nested unit, it must come from the unit itself up." A reporting channel would be an exception to it that grows, because every subsequent question ("can the root see X?") has a plausible answer of "yes, for reporting". The rule is easier to keep when there is no side door to argue about.

The cost, named. The root must ask, per unit, per period, and nobody can make a pack expose its scope. For the questions the root genuinely needs to answer, this is less painful than it sounds — see the consequence below, which is the part that makes this decision affordable.

Consequence — most of C-1 dissolved when the root became the membership unit. The root owns the registry, the memberships and the fees (D-035), so a treasurer or registrar working at the root is not reaching into anyone else's data. These need no exposure at all:

Question Answered from Exposure needed How many members were there in 2019? membership — the root's own table No Who is currently a member? membership No What fees are outstanding? fee_obligation No Was this person a member on this date? membership No Who was in the 4th Pack in 1998? unit_participation, scoped to that unit Yes Which events did a pack run? the pack's own material Yes Who leads a pack? position_assignment, scoped to that unit Yes

The upper half is the organization's own records. The lower half is the unit's. This split is the whole of D-049: the root does not need to see into a unit to answer a question about membership, because membership is the root's.

One thing that now looks like a bug and is not. The registrar role (appendix/permission-catalog.md §11) holds unit_participation.view at organization scope. Under exact-match scoping that does not let the registrar read any sub-unit's roster — the role's scope is the root, and a sub-unit roster is a different scope. It reads the root participation rows, which is what the registrar actually needs (D-041, 03-membership.md §5.1). This will be misread as a mistake by someone who assumes a parent can see its children. It is not a mistake, and the catalog says so in place.

See: ../domain/06-authorization-model.md §2, ../data-model/05-authorization.md §5.

docs.title: D-050 — A renewal inside the window extends the existing root participation row
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Resolves: D-7

Decision. When a membership lapses on 1 January and the person pays inside the window, the new membership period is backdated to the expiry date (D-040) and the root-unit participation row is extended to cover the same span. It is not closed and reopened.

Mechanically, the sweep does not close the root row: it moves valid_to forward to 1 January, and the renewal clears it back to NULL (or sets the new period end), so the row tracks the membership across the boundary without ever being two rows.

Why. Your answer: "Extend the existing row." The alternative — close at the expiry date, open a new backdated row — is more literal about what happened, but it makes the renewal path diverge from the initial-creation path, and it produces two rows per person per year for the one row the schema most wants to be simple.

The honest cost, recorded rather than hidden. Extending erases the evidence that a lapse occurred: a person who lapsed and renewed looks, in unit_participation, exactly like a person who never lapsed. The gap exists only if you go and look at the membership rows. This is accepted deliberately, because:

  1. membership remains the authority on payment, and the lapse is fully visible there — the two rows disagree about nothing, they simply answer different questions.
  2. The participation table is a roster history ("who was in this unit when"), not a payment history. Erasing a gap in the roster is the correct thing to do: the child was in the pack across that period, and the question the table exists to answer has one answer, not two.

Consequence for the participation overlap constraint. ex_unit_participation_no_overlap (03-membership.md §5) is what makes the close-and-reopen alternative awkward, and extending avoids the constraint entirely. The integrity check that verifies the root row mirrors the membership (03-membership.md §7, check 1b) remains valid and unchanged: after a renewal the two agree, and during a lapse-only period — before any payment — the membership has ended while the root row has not yet been swept, which is why the sweep must run and must run before anything reads the roster for authority.

See: ../data-model/03-membership.md §5.1.

docs.title: D-051 — The membership gate is waived by a permission, not only by a role flag
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Resolves: D-6

Decision. A new permission, system.gate_exempt, waives the membership gate (D-039) for anyone who holds it. It is delivered the way every other permission is: by being placed in a role, which is then assigned to a person at the root or at a unit.

  • It is a system-namespace permission, so it can only arrive through a role_assignment — never through an access_grant. An item-level grant must not be able to lift the gate.
  • It is exempt from the gate itself. Holding it does not depend on membership, or it could not do its job.
  • It is scope-independent: a person who holds it anywhere is waived everywhere. This is what makes it "system-wide" — the gate is a property of the person's membership, so the waiver has to be too.

Why. Your answer: "Let's create a system-wide permission, that means that their permissions do not end if their membership lapses... The system.gate_exempt is one of the permissions that can be assigned to the permission groups."

This replaces the earlier framing, in which role.requires_membership was the only switch and the question was therefore which roles to exempt. It is a better fit for the model as it actually works: every organizational role is a permission group, a person may hold several at once (a leader may also hold a role carrying system_admin; a counselor may hold a role carrying event creation and person.view), and a role may be assigned at the root or at a unit. A flag on the role answers "is this role membership-dependent?"; a permission answers "is this person exempt?", which is the question the exemption actually is.

role.requires_membership stays. It is not superseded — the two compose, and they answer different questions:

Question Granularity Effect role.requires_membership = false Is this role membership-dependent? the role the role grants regardless of membership system.gate_exempt Is this person exempt? the person every gated role they hold is honoured

A role flag is the blunt form: it exempts everyone who holds that role, everywhere. The permission is the precise form: it exempts named people, and can be granted and revoked as an act of its own. The resolver honours a role if either applies.

Who holds it. system_admin — without it, the 1 January sweep lapses every membership including the administrator's, and the person who would repair the system loses the ability to use it on the day it breaks. That is a lockout, not a policy. Beyond system_admin, which roles carry it is settled in the role review (F-1) — the mechanism is fixed here, the membership of the list is data.

The evaluation must not go through can(). Reading the permission through the resolver would be circular: can() would have to evaluate the gate in order to learn whether the gate applies, and a lapsed holder of system.gate_exempt would be denied it by the very rule it exists to lift — an unbreakable lockout with no error message. The resolver therefore checks for the permission by direct lookup against live role assignments, outside its own gate condition. This is the one place the resolver reads the role tables without consulting itself, and it is deliberate.

Consequence. Integrity reports gain a row: who currently holds an exemption, and under which assignment. It is a small list of people who keep authority without paying, and it should be as visible as the system.admin holders already are.

See: ../data-model/05-authorization.md §3, ../data-model/05 §12, ../appendix/permission-catalog.md §11.

docs.title: D-052 — Roles are runtime data; the seed set is not a specification
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Resolves: the remainder of D-6, and the framing of F-1

Decision. Roles are created, edited, assigned and deleted by the organization at runtime — they are not a vocabulary the specification fixes. A person may hold several roles at once, at the root or at a unit, so a leader can hold a leadership role and a role carrying administrative permissions, and a counselor can hold a role carrying event creation and person.view.

Why. Your answer: "The roles should be create-able in the system, and it should be also possible to assign people, delete the roles and so on. So you don't really need to know which roles carry system.gate_exempt."

This is a correction to how the documentation was framing F-1. Three documents presented the role list as something awaiting approval, with a Waives gate column to be filled in. That was wrong: a role is a permission group, and which permissions an organization puts in a group is a configuration act, not a design decision. The seed set survives as a worked example of the shape; it is explicitly not a requirement list.

What this does not delegate. The shape stays fixed, and two properties of it are load-bearing precisely because a configuration screen must not be able to weaken them:

  1. system.gate_exempt is system-namespace, so it can only arrive through a role and never through an access_grant. An item grant cannot lift the membership gate.
  2. A role that has ever been assigned cannot be deleted, so the assignment history survives. Deleting system_admin would remove the only route to system.admin permanently.

Consequences, and what had to change in the schema.

Gap Fix is_system claimed "cannot be deleted" with nothing enforcing it A BEFORE DELETE trigger: refuses deletion of any role with assignments, and of any system role No permissions existed for role lifecycle role.create and role.delete added to the catalog, both 🔒🔒 Integrity check 16 Orphaned assignments

This decision was amended by D-053, which removed the retirement mechanism D-052 originally introduced. D-052 as first written gave role a valid_from/valid_to, added a role.retire permission, made the resolver check the role's period, replaced UNIQUE (code) with a partial index so retired codes could be reused, and added check 17 reporting roles expiring while still held. All of that is gone: a role is valid always. The correction came from the user in the same round, and the superseded reasoning is kept here rather than edited away, because the reason it looked right is instructive — retirement appears to be the elegant way to abolish a role in one act, and it is only when you ask what "a role that is not in force" means for an assignment made in 2019 that the problem shows.

The sharpest consequence, recorded because it is easy to miss. Editing a role's permissions takes effect immediately for every holder — no assignment touched, nobody notified. role.edit is a bulk privilege change wearing the clothes of a settings screen, and it is now marked as such. role.assign escalates one person; role.edit escalates everyone holding the role. Neither implies the other.

See: ../data-model/05-authorization.md §3, ../appendix/permission-catalog.md §11.

docs.title: D-053 — A role is valid always; only its assignment is temporal
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Amends: D-052

Decision. role has no valid_from / valid_to. A role is valid all the time, for as long as the row exists. The only period in the picture is role_assignment.valid_from / valid_to — who held it, and from when to when.

Why. Your answer: "The roles should be valid all the time, but their assignment to people shouldn't."

D-052 had just given role a period, on the reasoning that retiring a role is a neat way to abolish one in a single act. That was wrong, and the reason is worth recording because it is not obvious until you push on it: a role is a definition, and a definition does not come into and out of force. "What did unit_leader grant?" has one answer, and it is the same answer for every date. What varies is who held it, which is what role_assignment records.

The proposed retirement also creates a question with no good answer. If a role has a period and an assignment does not, then an assignment from 2019 rests on a role that is "not in force" — so was that person a leader in 2019? The honest answers are either "yes, and the role's period is irrelevant" (in which case the role's period never did anything) or "who knows" (in which case the design has damaged its own history). Making the role permanently valid avoids the question entirely.

What this removes. The whole retirement mechanism D-052 introduced:

Removed Replaced by role.valid_from, role.valid_to, ck_role_period, ix_role_current nothing — the columns are gone role.retire permission role.unassign, per assignment. A role nobody holds is unused, not retired The resolver's check on the role's period (channel 4) nothing. Channel 4 already checks the assignment's period, which was always the load-bearing one uq_role_code_current (partial unique, so retired codes could be reused) code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE — plain, because codes are never in competition Integrity check 17 (roles expiring while held) Reformulated as check 17 (unused roles) — a glance, not a warning

What this keeps from D-052. Roles are still runtime data: created, edited, assigned and — if never assigned — deleted. is_system still guard-rails deletion. role and role_permission are still audited, because role.edit still changes effective permissions for every holder at once. The BEFORE DELETE trigger stays.

The consequence worth carrying forward. Because a role never expires, the only thing that ends authority is the assignment ending. That puts the entire weight on role_assignment.valid_to, which is exactly where the design already wanted it — and it is why the open-ended assignment is called the classic access failure (data-model/05 §4). A role-based permission now has no expiry of its own; it is the assignment or nothing.

See: ../data-model/05-authorization.md §3, ../appendix/permission-catalog.md §7.

docs.title: D-054 — The sub-unit vocabulary is not seeded; the organization defines its own types
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Amends: D-008 in spirit; the self-referencing table is untouched

Decision. The unit-type seed data contains exactly one row: the root. No sub-unit types are seeded at all. org_unit_type is runtime data, like role (D-052): the organization creates the types it uses, renames them, and adds new ones as its structure changes.

Why. Your answer: "Seed only the root."

pack/group/team was a placeholder, and it was the last thing in the schema that was comfortably wrong — three invented words that would have read as a specification to anyone implementing the system. The deeper reason to remove rather than correct it: the organization's own vocabulary is not knowable at specification time, and guessing it badly is worse than not guessing. This is the same argument as D-052 applied to units. The retired national/region/district ladder (D-035) was a guess; so was its replacement.

Consequence: nesting is entirely permissive. org_unit_type_rule exists and is seeded with nothing, so any type may sit under any other — including under the root — until the organization states a rule. This was already true with the placeholder (data-model/02 §10); it is now true with no ambiguity about which types the permissiveness applies to. A new type is usable the moment it is created.

Consequence: the root type is special and must be seeded. The organization row stays, because exactly one unit must have parent_unit_id IS NULL (D-035) and that unit needs a type. It also carries the property that matters: allows_minors = false on the root type, since no minor belongs to "The Organization" as a unit — minors hold memberships and sub-unit participation.

What this means for every example in these docs. The words pack, troop, section and group still appear throughout the documentation as illustration — "a pack has its own roster" is how the prose explains a self-governing sub-unit. They are not types the system ships with. Read them as "some sub-unit type the organization has defined", the same way unit_leader in §11 of the permission catalog is a role the organization may not have.

What this removes. The three placeholder rows (pack, group, team) and the "PLACEHOLDER" note that graded them. Nothing else: no columns, no constraints, no checks. The change is confined to data-model/02 §10.

See: ../data-model/02-organization.md §10, ../domain/04-organization-structure.md §1–2.

docs.title: D-055 — The permission catalog is deliberately comprehensive and granular
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Amends: D-030

Decision. The permission catalog is large and granular on purpose, and it stays that way. It is a menu from which administrators assign people only what they actually need — not a checklist every deployment is expected to use in full. Adding a permission remains one row plus its permission_level rows (D-007), and further permissions will arrive with the modules not yet specified (events, documents, communication, reporting).

Why. Your answer, in full: "The permissions will be added by the additional modules I am yet to specify. It is good, that the list is large and granular so that the admins can assign people only the permissions they actually need."

This settles F-1, and it settles it in the opposite direction from the roles question. The two are not symmetrical and it is worth saying why, because the asymmetry looks like an inconsistency:

Roles Permissions What it is A grouping an organization invents A capability the code implements Who defines it The organization, at runtime The system, at build time Why Nobody can guess your vocabulary You cannot assign a power that is not expressible

A permission is not a preference. membership.terminate exists because the code has a terminate operation; an organization that never expels anyone simply never grants it. A role is the opposite: unit_leader is only meaningful because someone in this organization chose that word. So a comprehensive permission catalog costs nothing but rows, while a comprehensive role list would be a specification pretending to be data.

The sharp edge. Granularity is what makes least-privilege possible, so it is load-bearing rather than decorative — but .admin subsumption means a new permission is retroactively held by everyone with the namespace's .admin. Split a broad permission in two and an existing holder of the .admin gains both halves without an assignment being written. That is the intended behaviour (D-007), and it is also why role.edit is marked 🔒🔒: the catalog's granularity only helps if the grants are actually narrow.

What this does not settle. The catalog's contents remain open to revision as the unbuilt modules land — this decision fixes the disposition (comprehensive, granular, menu-like), not the exact 90 rows. permission.edit exists for later pruning, and appendix/permission-catalog.md §12 tracks what is still being decided.

See: ../appendix/permission-catalog.md, ../open-questions.md F-1.

docs.title: D-056 — The legacy import expects a large corpus with legacy member numbers
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4

Decision. The import is designed for a substantial historical corpus — thousands of records, not hundreds — and the old records carry a legacy member number. That number is imported into person_identifier with scheme = 'legacy' (data-model/01 §7).

Why. Your answer: "Large, with legacy member numbers."

This is the favourable case for D-004, and it materially changes what the import has to be:

If there were no numbers With legacy numbers Matching Name + birth date + address, probabilistic, review-heavy Exact key when the number is present; heuristics only for backfilling it Review burden Every match needs a human (D-004 assumed this) Only the unmatched remainder does Confidence "Probably the same person" "Same number, same person"

The consequence for the review design. D-004's "no automatic merging, ever" was costed on the assumption that review was the bottleneck and the corpus was small enough to review by hand. With thousands of rows,"review everything" is no longer feasible, and the honest position is that the number-bearing rows are the trustworthy set and the rest is a work queue. The number does the work the human would have done; the human handles the rows the number cannot resolve. This is a strengthening of D-004, not a weakening — the rule is unchanged, but the input is better, so the rule is cheaper to obey.

What must hold for this to work. The legacy number must be imported verbatim and never reissued. person_identifier is already the right home: it records a scheme and a value with a period, so a second numbering era can coexist with the first. The check that matters is that no legacy number is ever assigned to two people — worth an integrity check on the (scheme, value) uniqueness, which the table's index already provides.

The part that gets harder, not easier. Volume and numbers make identity resolution reliable, but they do nothing for the membership-vs-participation question raised by D-041. At this scale, a 1998 roster almost certainly records which unit someone attended and not whether their fee was paid, and the import must decide per row which of the two it becomes. The safe default — participation, unless there is payment evidence — matters more at thousands of rows than at hundreds, because the failure mode compounds: an inferred open-ended membership would make every 2003 roster member a current member today through the gate (D-039).

Not settled here: the exact volume, the format, and the year range — those are operational inputs the import batch will carry. B-1 stays open for the sample, but the shape of the answer is now known.

See: ../data-model/06-audit-and-import.md, ../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md, ../open-questions.md B-1.

docs.title: D-057 — household is removed
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 4 Supersedes: D-019 — the table it described is gone, but the principle it stated is not, and that is deliberate. Amends: D-037

Decision. The household and household_member tables are removed, along with fee_obligation.household_id, its CHECK arm, and ix_obligation_household. A person's address is a person_contact row of type postal — data-model/01 §6 — which already exists, already keeps history, and already carries a purpose ('billing') that the permission model can distinguish. Same-address matching for the legacy import becomes a query over person_contact, not a maintained table.

Why. Your answer: "Drop household entirely."

D-037 had already removed the load-bearing half: the fee is flat and per person, so there is no per-family price for a household to hold. What remained was two conveniences — "one invoice per household" and "which children lived at this address in 2003?" — and both are served by tables that must exist anyway:

  • The invoice. person_contact with purpose = 'billing' is where a billing address belongs. A household table was duplicating it under a different key, and the duplication had already gone stale: household.postal_address was documented as "denormalised from the billing contact's primary postal contact", which is a copy with no trigger keeping it true.
  • The 2003 address question. person_contact is temporal (valid_from / valid_to, "Addresses change; history is required"). So "who lived at this address in 2003?" is answered from the contacts table directly — and more honestly, because it asks about the address a person had, rather than requiring that someone first grouped those people into a household row that has itself since been renamed or split.

The one thing genuinely lost. A household is a group with a name and its own lifetime, and person_contact records addresses per person. Two people at one address are related by a query, not by a row — so there is nowhere to hang "the Novák family" as a first-class thing, and no valid_from for the grouping. Accepted, because no feature was using it: nothing set fee_obligation.household_id, and the display-name use (household.name) has no consumer in the design.

What this does not change. The safeguarding property D-019 was written to protect survives intact, and this is the point worth checking before deleting anything: being at the same address still grants no access. It never came from the household table in the first place — all access comes from guardianship + guardianship_permission (D-020). Removing a table that granted nothing cannot grant anything. The old D-019 entry stays in the log, marked superseded, because "why does living together not imply access?" is a question that will be asked again.

Also removed with it: integrity check 7 (households with no address and no billing contact), which has nothing left to check; the household bullet in data-model/04 §7; and D-9 in open-questions.md.

See: ../data-model/04-relationships.md, ../data-model/07-finance.md §2.

docs.title: D-058 — An event is a dated occasion owned by exactly one unit
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. event.org_unit_id is NOT NULL — exactly one owning unit. A weekly meeting group is not an event; it is unit_participation. Events are the things people register for: camps, trips, hikes, jamborees.

Why. Two answers, and the second is the structural one.

  • On ownership: "One owning unit." A joint camp between two packs is Pack A's event that Pack B's children register for. Pack B is a guest, and its access is written explicitly — an audience grant, a named person, at the level that fits. Nobody arbitrates "whose event is this?", and one unit remains the author of the record.
  • On recurrence: "No recurrence — meetings are participation." A Thursday group meeting forty times a year is already recorded as "this child takes part in this Thursday group." Forty event rows would say what one participation row says, with forty capacities, forty organizer rosters, and forty chances to be wrong.

The ownership rule is forced by D-049, not merely preferred by it. If an event could belong to two units, the root's inability to read a sub-unit's events would have an exception shaped exactly like a joint camp, with no principled place to stop. One owner keeps the rule total.

What this forecloses. There is no event_series, no RFC 5545 rule, no occurrence table, and no event_unit join table. Each would require every downstream table — registrations, capacity, presence, organizers, questions — to carry a second possible home.

Consequence worth stating. "Was Jan at the meeting on 14 March?" is not answerable from the events module. That is presence tracking for a standing group, which is a different feature. The boundary is deliberate; the confusion between the two is the thing to watch for.

See: ../domain/07-events.md §1–2, ../data-model/08-events.md §2.

docs.title: D-059 — "Unanswered" is the absence of a row; a registration stores two values
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. event_registration.response has two values — 'attending' and 'not_attending'. 'unanswered' is written nowhere. It is the absence of a registration row. "Who has not replied yet?" is a subtraction: (people who could contribute to this event) MINUS (people with a registration).

Why. Your answer: "Absent row — two stored values."

The framing that settled it was your own correction: registration is "positive with additional fields, or negative (or none)". "None" is not a third stored value — it is the lack of a record, and storing it would mean writing rows for people who have not acted.

Three reasons absence beats a stored value, and the third is decisive:

Absent row Stored 'unanswered' Rows written before anyone acts None One per person asked "Asked and silent" vs "never asked" Distinguishable — the eligible set is a query Indistinguishable without an invite table "Who has not replied?" A subtraction against an audience Requires enumerating the audience into rows

The third is the real argument. The eligible set is an audience — a rule the resolver evaluates (D-042) such as unit:7:participants or all_members. Enumerating it into 'unanswered' rows would mean re-enumerating every time a child joins the pack, and the stored rows would drift out of agreement with the rule that generated them.

Returning someone to unanswered removes the row (DELETE, recorded in audit_log). That is the honest act — it leaves the least behind, and "no row" then means the same thing whether the person never answered or their answer was withdrawn.

Consequence. unit_participation uses the same reasoning for the same reason, and this decision makes the pattern explicit: where a state is the absence of a fact, store the absence. Compare D-002 for the temporal case and D-053 for the definitional one.

See: ../data-model/08-events.md §4, ../domain/07-events.md §3.

docs.title: D-060 — Eligibility is capability; there is no separate rule engine
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5 Resolves: the deferral in D-006

Decision. Registration requires contribute capability on that event. Nothing else. There is no eligibility rule table, no age gate, no prerequisite system. event.register_self is already mapped to contribute in permission_level.

Why. Your answer: "I feel like the people with 'contribute' permissions (capabilities) on that item should be allowed to register."

This dissolves D-006's deferral rather than satisfying it. D-006 said "eligibility ... will be a separate concept when events are specified." Your answer says the separate concept was never needed: the capability ladder already is one.

view        may SEE the event
contribute  may REGISTER for it
manage      may ORGANIZE it
admin       may control it

Why audiences make this sufficient rather than merely simple. Registering 200 children individually is 200 grant rows — but opening an event to members is one, which the shape of the row made visible at the time:

INSERT INTO access_grant (scope_type, scope_id, audience_id, level)
VALUES ('event', :camp_id,
        (SELECT id FROM audience WHERE code = 'all_members'), 'contribute');

The requirement now, without the statement: an access_grant may address an audience instead of a person, so "everyone who is a current member may take part in this event" is one row rather than one per member — 05-authorization §8.

An age-gated camp is a camp opened to unit:<id>:participants for a unit whose participants are that age. This is the case audiences (D-042) were built for, and events are where the investment pays off.

What this does not do, stated plainly. It does not enforce an age ceiling on an open event. If a nine-year-old holds contribute on a camp for teenagers, they can register. The design decides eligibility by who may register, not by inspecting the person — the check is the grant. Whether that is sufficient is carried in ../open-questions.md rather than hidden.

Organizers are not bound by it. Anyone holding event.manage_participants may register anyone, and the registration records source = 'staff'. That is the permission's purpose: the leader who knows there is a spare bed is trusted, and the act is attributed.

See: ../domain/07-events.md §4, data-model/05 §7.

docs.title: D-061 — Event answers are read by that event's organizers
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. Answers to event_question are readable by the organizers of that event, with no additional permission. You confirmed the consequence explicitly: the event form is the route by which a camp leader learns a child has a nut allergy.

Why, and the part that must be recorded. This is only coherent — and only defensible — because the dependent.* namespace is unreachable by unit leaders. The permission catalog states it outright:

"Resolved only against guardianship_permission, never against roles. A unit leader does not get these by virtue of leading the unit — that is a safeguarding property."

So a camp leader cannot reach dependent.medical.* at all. Not by leading the pack, not by running the camp, not by being an organizer. There is no permission that changes it. Which means an allergy recorded on a camp form is the only way the people running the camp will know.

This is a widening, and it is recorded as one. Access to a child's health information moves from "few people, via a guardianship-scoped permission granted by the guardian" to "every organizer of any event the child registers for." That is a coherent position — the parent tells the people present, per event, and the medical file stays closed — but it is not an accident of where the gate was placed, and it must not be "fixed" later by tightening the wrong thing.

Two consequences that follow.

  1. Only preference-level detail belongs on a form. Nothing in the schema distinguishes "vegetarian" from "coeliac" — both are data_type = 'text' in event_answer.value. The discipline is in the form label, so it is guidance, not a constraint. A CHECK cannot tell them apart, and a keyword list would fail on the first unusual phrasing.
  2. Event answers are not a medical record. They are operational detail for one event, read by that event's organizers, and ending with the event. The two stores are not duplicates of each other and should not be merged or synchronised.

Open: the retention policy. A dietary answer citing a medical condition is health data with a retention obligation, and there is no policy yet.

See: ../data-model/08-events.md §7, ../domain/07-events.md §12, appendix/permission-catalog.md §9.

docs.title: D-062 — Organizers are appointed on the event, not granted
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. Events have an event_organizer roster, and it is the domain answer to "who is running this?" — labelled, ordered, attributed. It is not an access_grant, and it does not by itself confer authority to act on the event.

Why. Your answer: "Roster only; grants stay separate."

The tempting alternative, and why it fails. Write an access_grant at manage whenever an organizer is added, so "the organizers" is a query over grants and the two can never disagree. It fails on three counts:

Grant at manage event_organizer A cook's label No room for organizer_role = 'cook' organizer_role, free text Display order Not expressible sort_order, is_primary "Who is running this camp?" Read the permission table Read the roster Removing the cook Revokes their ability to see the event Removes them from the list

That last row is the practical one: "they are no longer cooking" does not mean "they may no longer see the camp."

event_organizer is the event-scoped analogue of position_assignment — an appointment on the thing being run. Like a position it may carry a label and an order; like a position it is not a permission bundle. organizer_role is free text, not a CHECK: every organization labels these differently, and a controlled vocabulary here would be a guess of the kind D-054 removed for unit types.

It has no valid_to, deliberately. A roster is not a period: you are on the list or you are not. An organizer who drops out is removed (audited), because "was Jan an organizer of that camp?" must have one answer, not a set of intervals.

How authority actually reaches an organizer is D-063 — the unit's roles reach its events.

See: ../data-model/08-events.md §3, ../domain/07-events.md §5.

docs.title: D-063 — An event is an ARTIFACT of its unit, not a child of it
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer, as a consequence you did not have to state) Date: refinement round 5 Amends: nothing. Extends: D-031

The problem. The resolver matches scope exactly. There is therefore no path from a unit_leader role held at ('org_unit', 7) to a check made at ('event', 42) — even when unit 7 owns event 42:

unit_leader ── holds role at ──► org_unit 7 (the pack)
                                     │
                                     │  ✗ NO PATH
                                     ▼
event 42 "Summer camp" ◄─ owned by ──┘    resolver checks scope exactly

The pack's leader — the person whose job is running the pack's camp — does not pass can(leader, 'event.view', 'event', 42). Nothing is broken; the answer is simply no. But the module cannot ship with that gap, because it would mean the leader must be granted every event their own unit creates.

Decision. A permission is satisfied at ('event', E) if it is satisfied at the event's owning unit, ('org_unit', E.org_unit_id), and that unit is the event's owner. One wrapper function, can_event(), calling can() twice.

Why this is not inheritance downward, and why that distinction is the whole point.

Inheritance (rejected, D-015/D-031) Artifact rule (chosen) What a leader gains Authority in the unit's sub-units too Authority over the unit's own events Blast radius Grows on every restructure Fixed — one owner, pinned by D-049 Reverses D-015, D-031 Nothing

An event is not a child of its unit; it is a thing the unit made. The unit's authority already covers the unit. Asking "may this person do this in Pack 7?" is asking the right question about the right scope — and it is a question the resolver already answers correctly.

Restructuring the hierarchy still changes nothing about who may do what. Adding a sub-unit still grants nobody anything. D-015 and D-031 stand untouched, and the rule is exactly as narrow as the case requires.

Why a wrapper function rather than a change inside can(). Putting this clause inside the resolver would make every permission check — on people, memberships, units, fees — evaluate an event-shaped rule. Keeping it in can_event() means the exception is visible, named, and confined to the module that needs it.

And it is a two-way door. can_event() calls can() twice and adds no authority of its own; nothing is written to access_grant to make it work. If the organization decides that leaders should not automatically run every event their unit creates, deleting the second can() call is the entire change, and it needs no data migration.

The root is unaffected. An organization-scoped registrar still cannot see a pack's camp — events are precisely the sub-unit records D-049 protects. The fix, if the root wants it, is one scope_exposure row naming one assignment.

See: ../domain/07-events.md §6, ../data-model/08-events.md §8.

docs.title: D-064 — There is no event status; visibility is the permission model
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 5

Decision. event has no status column. Draft is not a state: a new event has no grants beyond its organizers' own authority, so nobody else can see it, and publishing is an access_grant, not an UPDATE. completed is derived (ends_at < now()). Cancellation is a recorded fact — cancelled_at, cancelled_by, cancel_reason.

Why. Your answer, which is the right instinct: "Isn't the draft solved by not giving anyone else permissions, but the organizer?" It is, and it is better than a status enum for a reason worth stating:

A status column and a permission system that both claim to answer "who may see this?" will eventually disagree — and the one that gets enforced is whoever wrote the last IF.

With no status column there is nothing to disagree. The questions a draft flag would answer are all answered by grants:
