Two tables. attribute_definition is the vocabulary the organization maintains: a code, a label, a value type, whether several values may be open at once, and a status of live or retired. person_attribute is a value one person has: the definition it belongs to, the value, who recorded it and when. Nothing in the schema names a fact about a scout.

Why this is the shape and not the safer-looking one. The alternative — a column per fact — makes every collection habit a release. This organization's list of things it wants to know changes with the program: shoe sizes for a camp season, an insurance number for one country's requirement, a preferred contact language for one intake. A schema where that needs a migration produces the real failure instead of the apparent one: the field does not get added, and the information is collected on paper, photographed, and lost. D-083 removed the argument for a fixed set — a closed typed set is justified by needing to constrain the important fields, and the answer was that no field is more important than another.

Typing for rendering, not for law. A definition declares text, number, date, yes/no, one-of-a-list, or free text with a unit. The system uses it to draw the right input, to sort a list, and to warn — "that is not a date" — and it does not use it to refuse a save a human insists on. The reason the warning must not be a wall is that the value is not the system's to overrule: 2019 as a year for last_checkup is a truer record than an empty field behind a validation error, and the person typing it knows and the form does not. What this costs is stated plainly in 09-attributes §5: no database type checking, no constraint can reference a value, and no report may assume it understands a code.

Curation, because a vocabulary is the design. Anyone who may edit a person may record a value against an existing code. Creating a code needs attribute.define, which is a small permission held by few people. An improvised need at 23:00 is recorded as a proposal: the value is written into an uncatalogued code that is visible, unusable-by-default, and waiting for whoever curates the vocabulary to accept, rename, or merge it. The reason is the one failure this design is exposed to more than any other: an open vocabulary left open becomes allergy, Allergy, alergie and allergies (2), after which the layer still stores everything and answers nothing — which is the entirety of what the attribute table was built to do.

Two rules that keep a runtime vocabulary from decaying immediately:

  • Codes are normalized before comparison — trimmed, case-folded, whitespace-collapsed — and uniqueness is checked against the normalized form. This is not a nicety; it is the difference between four spellings surviving a week and four spellings surviving a decade, and it is a rule the database can still enforce.
  • Retiring a code never deletes values. A retired code disappears from data entry and remains readable, reportable, and revivable. Deleting the label must not delete the fact underneath it — a code discovered to have been badly named is an administrative event, and if it destroys nine years of records it will never be retired, and the vocabulary accretes instead of being curated. Redaction is the opposite case and the only eraser: when a person is anonymised (00-conventions §8), their values go.

See: data-model/09-attributes.md, D-085, open question F-10 for which of its rules the attribute layer can and cannot express.

docs.title: D-085 — The identity machinery stays structured; the boundary is rules, not sensitivity
docs.text:
Status: decided (from your answer) Date: refinement round 7 Follows: D-083, D-084

Your answer. Asked where the attribute layer starts, you chose keep the identity machinery structured — attributes take everything that has no table today, not the tables that exist.

The boundary, and it is a different boundary than "sensitive versus ordinary".

Stays structured Becomes attributes person_name history, gender, birth_date + birth_date_precision health and medical facts, education, occupations, languages, insurance, measurements, dietary habits, preferences, notes — everything with no table today person_contact — purpose, primary flag, validity period person_identifier — per-scheme uniqueness, decided by the scheme (D-080 item 1) account, account_credential

The test is whether a rule exists that the attribute layer physically cannot hold. "Exactly one primary postal contact among the open rows", "a school id may repeat but a birth number may not", "this person has one current name" — each is a constraint over a known set of columns, and a key/value table has no known set. Folding those tables in would not have simplified the model; it would have moved four working constraints into application code and called it uniformity, which is F-10 shape 3 manufactured on purpose. Descriptive data is open-ended because nobody can enumerate it; identity is closed because it was enumerated years ago and has not changed. That is the whole boundary.

Values are overwritten; audit_log is the history. Chosen over a history table, and worth noticing as a departure from the shape guardianship uses, where guardianship_permission keeps current value plus history. The difference is real and not inertia: a guardianship row is authority, and authority is asked "what was it on that date" as a routine part of answering whether an action was permitted — while a descriptive value is a description, and nobody queries the allergy list of 2019 except in an incident, which is exactly the case the audit trail exists for. The dependency is stated rather than glossed, and it has two halves. D-081 records that audit completeness is now a discipline rather than a guarantee, so choosing the trail as the only history buys simplicity with the one control the corpus admits is weakest — and the trail here is not a pointer into the record, it is the only copy of the values that ever existed, since the row itself holds one belief at a time. So the history exists if, and only if: (a) every write path writes its audit row, including the import, the sweep and the hand-fix, and (b) the trail is guarded as the copy of a child's whole record that this makes it (D-083 records why the values are logged rather than stripped, and what that demands of audit.view). If a safeguarding question is ever unanswerable because the trail was not written, or answerable by somebody who should not have been able to answer it, this is the decision that made that possible, and it should be reversed with those two sentences in front of the reader.

Who reads it: whoever the grants already say. A unit leader holding person.view over their own unit's members reads their descriptive data — no age branch, no special channel, no per-event grant, consistent with D-083's "not different in any way". This changes D-061's status without reversing it: the per-event answer form was designed as the only route by which an organizer learns a child has a nut allergy, because nothing else was readable. It is now the fallback for a fact the organization has not recorded, rather than the ceiling on what an organizer may know — and the discipline in 08-events §7 about what belongs on a form survives unchanged, because it was always about not re-collecting what the organization already holds.

Amends D-061. Its decision stands — answers are read by that event's organizers — but its premise that this is the only route to a health fact is superseded by this entry.

See: data-model/09-attributes.md, domain/08-person-data.md, data-model/01-identity.md.

docs.title: D-086 — A sensitivity mark grades what a grant exposes, not the table it reads
docs.text:
Status: decided — by the assistant, during round-7 propagation, not from an answer of yours. It follows mechanically from D-083, which is why it was taken rather than asked, but it changes two rows of a table you will read, so it is numbered and flagged rather than folded into prose. Reverse it if you read the marks differently. Date: refinement round 7 Follows: D-083, D-085

The problem the round produced. Two codes were found to be graded against their table's reputation rather than their payload's contents. audit.view sat at ⚠ while D-085 had just made its old_values/new_values the only surviving copy of a child's descriptive values — a log read by people who need not hold person.view, holding more than person.view shows. event.answer.view sat at ⚠ beside a note conceding that the answers under it "can be clinical".

Decision. The mark follows the content. audit.view, event.answer.view and person.view are all ⚠⚡, and the legend's top tier was reworded so it names whose data a grant exposes instead of naming a category of fields — "children's personal data, or the same about an adult where the code reads a whole person record". Wording matters here more than usual: the previous legend read "children's personal data or health data", which is a category D-083 deleted, and a legend that names a category invites somebody to write the code that separates it.

What a raise does and does not do. It changes no grant, no scope and no channel. An event's organizers still read that event's answers with no additional gate (D-061 stands); an auditor still reads the trail. A mark is the sentence a reviewer reads before ticking a box, and the reason it was worth two rows is the seed roles: auditor is now honestly described as a ⚠⚡ read over everything the system has ever believed about a child, which "just the logs" concealed, and event.answer.view arriving in a role handed to thirty volunteers is now visible at a glance.

Where this is enforced: nowhere. A sensitivity mark is a line in the catalog, reviewed by a human, and the check that a payload's contents match its code's mark does not exist and cannot be written against a runtime vocabulary — see AT-4, which asks whether one permission is the right shape for a trail that holds person data at all.

See: appendix/permission-catalog.md §8, data-model/09-attributes.md §6.

docs.title: Domain Overview
docs.text: What the organization is, who interacts with the system, and how the core lifecycles flow. Read ../glossary.md first — this document uses its terms strictly.

docs.title: 1. The organization
docs.text:
A youth organization (Scout-like: uniformed groups, trained adult leadership, camps and weekly meetings) with:

  • Child members — youth participants, typically organized into units.
  • Adult members — counselors/leaders who run units and hold positions.
  • Caretakers — parents and legal guardians of child members. They may or may not be members themselves.
  • Non-member supporters — people who interact with the organization (donors, volunteers, alumni) without holding a membership.

The organization has sub-units that nest and that have been reorganized repeatedly over four decades. Both facts are load-bearing and are handled in 04-organization-structure.md.

docs.title: 2. Actors
docs.text:
The system distinguishes actors by what they can do, not by what they are. The full treatment is in 02-actors.md; the summary:

Actor Has account? Has membership? Can do Anonymous visitor no no see public info, submit a registration or a membership request Registered person yes no maintain own profile, submit/renew a request, view own history Member (child) yes yes own profile, unit membership, event signups, own history Member (adult) yes yes as above, plus whatever their role assignments permit Caretaker yes maybe view/act on their dependents — only as explicitly granted Staff / registrar yes maybe organization-wide administrative permissions Historical record no yes (closed) nothing. Data only, never a login.

The last row matters: imported 1994 rosters create person rows with no account. They must never be blocked from import by a "users must have email addresses" rule.

docs.title: 3. The three lifecycles
docs.text: Almost everything in the system is one of three multi-step processes. They are separate because they succeed and fail independently: you can register without applying, apply without being accepted, be accepted without paying, and pay without ever joining a unit.

docs.title: 3.1 Account lifecycle
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                  │                                             │
 (none) ──register──> pending_verification ──verify──> active ──┴──> suspended
                                                            │              │
                                                            └──> closed <──┘

An account is about authentication only. It says "this person can log in". It says nothing about membership. A person can hold a verified, active account for years and never become a member — a parent who only ever manages their child is exactly this case.

docs.title: 3.2 Membership lifecycle
docs.text:
(none)
   │
   ├─ request submitted ──> under_review ──accept──> approved ──payment confirmed──> active member
   │                             │                                                    │
   │                             └──reject──> rejected                                 │
   │                                                                                   │
   │                                     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │                                     │                                             │
   │                                     ├──> lapsed (fee expired at the yearly date)  │
   │                                     ├──> terminated (cause, with reason)          │
   │                                     └──> suspended (temporary hold)               │
   │                                                                                   │
   │      ┌──────────────── renewal (no new application) ────────────────────────────┘
   │      │        inside the renewal window → the new period opens at the expiry date
   │      │        after it                  → the new period opens at the payment date
   │      ▼
   │   active member again
   │
   └──────────────────────── re-apply ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every transition creates or closes a row; nothing is overwritten. A person who was a member 1990–2010 and again from 2024 has two membership rows and the gap is visible as data, not inferred from a date.

Note the shape of the lapse. There is no completed state: it existed only for ageing out, and membership is ageless (D-038). And the lapse happens on a date, to everyone at once — the yearly expiry — which is why the renewal path matters more here than the word "grace" suggests (D-040).

Detailed in 05-membership-lifecycle.md.

docs.title: 3.3 Authorization lifecycle
docs.text:
(none) ──grant──> active ──expire/revoke──> inactive
                     │
                     └──delegate──> delegated grant (with end date, provenance recorded)

Every grant has a start, an end, a granter, and a reason. Nothing is permanent by default and nothing is revoked by deletion. Detailed in 06-authorization-model.md.

docs.title: 4. The relationships between people
docs.text:
Three distinct relationships, deliberately not merged:

Relationship Direction Example Grants access? Guardianship guardian → dependent parent → child No by itself — only the right_level (none / view / write) carried on the live guardianship row. Since D-074 that value is the whole authority; guardianship_permission keeps only its history. Membership member → the organization anyone → the root unit No. Participation participant → sub-unit child → Pack 12 No. Position held person → position in a sub-unit adult → scoutmaster of Pack 12 No. Only via role_assignment.

Membership and participation are two rows, not one (D-041). A person is a member of the organization and a participant in a pack — different facts with different lifetimes, which is why someone who stops attending on Thursdays is still a paid-up member, and someone who is paid up may take part in nothing.

The recurring theme: participation is not authority. A person can be deeply involved — a parent of three members, a 20-year veteran, a pack's founder — and still have no administrative access. Access comes only from an explicit grant. This separation is what makes the permission system auditable and what prevents the classic failure where a relationship ends (custody changes, a leader steps down) but access silently persists.

docs.title: The counselor-who-is-also-a-parent case
docs.text:
You named this case explicitly. It is not special:

  • One person row.
  • One open membership — member, like everyone else's.
  • A position_assignment making them a leader of their pack.
  • One unit_participation row for the pack they lead.
  • Two guardianship rows (to their own children).
  • Separate guardianship_permission rows for their parental capabilities.
  • role_assignment rows for their leadership authority.

Note there is no counselor membership type. Being a counselor is the position, not a kind of membership (D-037) — and this person's membership is identical to that of the child they lead, which is exactly the point.

Their leadership role grants authority over the unit's members. Their guardianship grants authority over their own children. These are different scopes and the system keeps them separate — critically, being a leader does not give them access to other people's children's records beyond what their leadership role explicitly permits.

This last point is a safety property, not a convenience. Child-protection rules generally require that a leader's access to minors' personal data be bounded by their function. Keeping role_assignment and guardianship_permission as separate tables makes that boundary enforceable and reportable.

docs.title: 5. Multiplicity, in both directions
docs.text:
You specified: one parent can manage multiple children; multiple children can be managed by the same parent. The model generalizes both:

  • One guardian → many dependents (many guardianship rows).
  • Many guardians → one dependent (both parents, stepparents, legal guardians — the schema makes no assumption that a child has exactly two, or exactly one).
  • A guardian's authority over each dependent is per-dependent, so a parent can hold full permissions for one child and only read access for another (a realistic custody arrangement).

The same person can also be a guardian of someone and a dependent of someone else — the relation is a general graph, not a two-level hierarchy. This costs nothing to allow and avoids a rewrite when a member turns 18 and becomes guardian to a sibling.

docs.title: 6. The four decades of history
docs.text:
This is the constraint that most shapes the schema, so it is worth stating plainly.

The system must answer, correctly and indefinitely:

  • "Who was in Pack 12 on 1 June 1998?"
  • "Was this person a member when they attended that camp in 2003?"
  • "This person registered in 2026 claiming they were a member in the 90s — is that true?"
  • "What was this unit called in 2001, and what is its successor unit today?"

Consequences, all of which the data model implements:

  1. Everything temporal is a period, never a boolean or a single date.
  2. Nothing is hard-deleted. Merges leave tombstones; units that closed keep their rows.
  3. Names change. Units get renamed and renumbered; people change names. Names live in child tables with validity periods, not as columns that get overwritten.
  4. Imported data is low-confidence. A 1994 roster has names and dates but no reliable unique key. Import therefore proposes identities and a human confirms them. See 03-identity-and-legacy.md.

docs.title: 7. What this design deliberately does not decide yet
docs.text:
These are referenced by the schema but not designed, pending your specification:

  • Events — the schema provides access_grant.scope_type = 'event' and leaves the event tables to you. See ../open-questions.md.
  • Fees and payments — a provisional shape exists in ../data-model/07-finance.md because membership activation depends on it. Expect to rewrite it.
  • Notifications, documents, reporting, API/UI. (Health records went off this list in round 7 — there is no health module, because D-083 found no category to build one around; the facts live in the personal-attribute layer, domain/08.)

docs.title: 8. Next
docs.text:
• Terminology → ../glossary.md
  • Accounts and registration → 02-actors.md
  • Historical data → 03-identity-and-legacy.md
  • Units → 04-organization-structure.md
  • Membership → 05-membership-lifecycle.md
  • Permissions → 06-authorization-model.md

docs.title: Actors, Accounts, and Self-Registration
docs.text: How a human being gets into the system, what an account is (and is not), and why registration is deliberately separate from membership.

docs.title: 1. The core separation
docs.text:
person ─────────── the human being. Exists even with no account and no membership.
     │
     ├── account ──── the ability to log in. Optional. Zero or more per person over time.
     │
     └── membership ─ the state of being a member. Optional. Zero or more periods.

These are three independent things. Any combination is legal:

State Example person, no account, no membership 1994 roster entry imported from paper. person, account, no membership A parent who registered to manage their child. person, account, membership An active member. person, no account, membership An adult member who never uses the system; staff manage them. person, account, lapsed membership Someone who let their membership lapse but still logs in.

The schema must not reject any of these. In particular there must be no requirement that a person has an email address, or that a member has an account — otherwise the historical import is impossible.

docs.title: 2. Who registers, and why
docs.text:
You said: "The people can register on their own to get access to the system, however they become member only if they request a membership, they get accepted and pay a yearly fee."

So registration produces an account, not a membership. The person is then a registered non-member — able to log in, maintain their profile, view their own history, and submit a membership request. This is the correct split, and it gives the system a clean place to hang capabilities that must work before membership exists:

  • A caretaker registering to manage a child before deciding whether to join themselves.
  • An adult applying to become a counselor, who needs to fill in an application first.
  • A returning member from the 90s reconnecting to their history.

docs.title: Registration paths
docs.text: Path Actor Result Self-registration adult, or a minor with guardian involvement person + account Registration on behalf caretaker registers a minor who has no account person (child) + guardianship Staff-created account registrar creates one for an adult who is not self-sufficient with computers person + account, flagged created_by_staff Legacy import no account created person only, record_origin = 'legacy_import' Self-registration claiming history adult registers and asserts a past membership person + account + identity_hypothesis

docs.title: Minor registration — the consent problem
docs.text: Assumption: a minor may not create an account unattended. The schema supports requiring a guardian's confirmation before a minor's account becomes usable, via account.guardian_consent_at. See ../open-questions.md for the age threshold and whether consent is required at all in your jurisdiction.

docs.title: 3. Account state machine
docs.text:
Status Meaning pending_verification Registered; email/phone not yet confirmed. Minimal capabilities. active Normal. suspended Temporarily blocked (security, disciplinary). Membership unaffected. closed Voluntarily or administratively closed. Retained for audit; login refused.

Two deliberate choices:

  • Suspending an account does not suspend a membership. They are separate lifecycles; a person can be an active member with a suspended account (they'd interact by phone).
  • Closing an account does not delete the person or their history. The account row is closed and retained. person and all membership rows are untouched.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
account holds authentication material. Two rules worth fixing now:

  1. The password hash lives in account_credential, not in account. This leaves room for multiple authentication methods (password, passkey, OAuth via a national Scout identity provider, staff-issued one-time links) without restructuring.
  2. Never share an account between a parent and a child. The temptation is real — "the parent will just log in as the kid" — but it destroys attributability. The correct mechanism is acting on behalf, which records who acted and as whom. An account shared between people makes every audit entry worthless, and in a youth organization the audit trail is the point.

docs.title: 4. Contact points and identifiers
docs.text:
A person's email, phone and address are rows, not columns. Each row carries its type, its purpose, its value, whether it is the primary one for that type and purpose, when it was verified, and the period it applied for.

Why not just person.email:

  • People have several emails (personal, school, work) and which one is primary changes.
  • A caretaker's contact details are often the effective contact for a child; the system needs both the child's own contact and the adult's.
  • Addresses change; you asked to preserve history. An address row with a validity period answers "where did this member live in 2003?" — a column cannot.
  • Changing an email must not lose the old one, because historical records may reference it.

Purpose is the field that makes this useful operationally: login, membership, emergency, billing, guardian_contact. A person can have one address for billing and another for emergency contact, and the permission system can treat them differently — emergency contacts are visible to a unit leader on a camp roster; billing details are not.

docs.title: External identifiers
docs.text:
One row per identifier held against a person: a scheme, a value, and when it was verified if it ever was. (scheme, value) is unique among the identifiers that are still current — a superseded number may be reused, a current one may not be shared.

For identifiers issued outside the system: a national Scout registration number, a government ID, an old membership card number from a previous system, a school ID. Keeping these separate from contact points means the legacy import has somewhere to put the old system's member numbers — which is precisely what makes reconnecting 1990–2010 members possible. See 03-identity-and-legacy.md.

docs.title: 5. Acting on behalf
docs.text:
Per your answer, both read and write access for a caretaker must be explicit. So:

  • A guardianship row establishes the relationship.
  • That row carries one right — none, view, or write. Being the parent implies nothing; a row at none grants literally nothing.

The right is one value, not a capability list (D-074). The dependent.* codes this document used to enumerate are deleted — eighteen of them across the catalog — and with them go the cases they existed for: a guardian who may register the child for events but may not read the medical record, or one who is "read-only, but not the medical file". Neither can be expressed — and the separation was declined, not merely left unbuilt (D-083): there is no medical record inside the person record to be excepted from, so a guardian at view reads the child's record whole. This is not a softening of the right. The three levels are unchanged, at the same ranks and with the same bluntness; what changed is that there is nothing left inside the record for a finer right to withhold. What survives is what made the list worth having — the right is explicit, dated, revocable and audited, one deliberate value per row rather than an inference from who someone is. write ranks at contribute and not at manage, so a guardian still cannot do organization-wide things and cannot reach a different dependent's records. A role that needs broad reach over its own side of the model still lists what it grants explicitly — there is no per-resource admin wildcard (D-068). History is kept: every change of the value is a new guardianship_permission row, and the value on the guardianship row is always the open one's.

How a check resolves. A check about a dependent is evaluated against the guardianship row for the (guardian, dependent) pair and the right level it holds, not against roles. This keeps the two authority channels distinct:

  • Roles answer "what may this person do in the organization?"
  • Guardianship answers "what may this person do regarding this child?"

A unit leader does not hold a guardian's right over unit members by virtue of leading the unit. If the organization genuinely needs leaders to see a camper's emergency contacts, that is granted through a role permission with a unit scope, resolved at the event, and audited — not through a fictional guardianship. That role-side code is person.view, and it has no narrower cousin to reach for if the grant turns out to feel too wide (08-person-data.md).

docs.title: Recording acts on behalf
docs.text:
Every operation performed on behalf of another person writes to access_log with both parties: actor_person_id is the parent, subject_person_id is the child, and on_behalf records that the actor acted for the subject rather than as themselves.

This is not optional bookkeeping. When a parent changes a child's address or registers them for a camp, the record must show that the parent did it, not the child. Without this, the audit trail falsely attributes the parent's actions to the child.

docs.title: 6. Effective contact for a minor
docs.text:
A recurring operational need: "who do we call about this child?" The answer is usually a guardian, but not always the same one, and not always the one with the most permissions.

Resolve it as three conditions on guardianship, applied in this order: the row's dependent is this child; the row is still open today, meaning valid_to is absent or later than today — a guardianship that has ended is not an answer, so the date is checked on the row rather than assumed; and is_primary_contact is set. The answer is the contact points of those guardians whose purpose is emergency.

is_primary_contact on guardianship is separate from the guardian's right level on purpose: a guardian with no system access at all can still be the emergency contact. Do not require login capability to be reachable in an emergency.

docs.title: 7. Open issues
docs.text:
• Minimum age to hold an account; whether guardian consent is legally required.
  • ~~Whether guardian permissions lapse automatically at majority, or by review.~~ Neither — no automatic transition and no review queue (D-069). What that left: whether the subject may end the guardianship themselves once adult. They may — the parties to a guardianship are principals on the row, and none of it routes through staff (D-073). Closed — see E-5.
  • Whether staff-created accounts are allowed for children, or only adults.
  • Whether a person may hold more than one active account at a time (recommend: no).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Identity Resolution and Legacy Data
docs.text:
How the system decides that two records describe the same human, and how four decades of paper and spreadsheet history gets brought in without corrupting live data.

This is the highest-risk area of the project. Get it wrong and either the history is unusable, or worse, two people's records get merged and you leak one member's data to another. The design below is deliberately conservative.

docs.title: 1. Why this is hard
docs.text:
A 1994 roster has: a name, maybe a birth date, an address, a unit, and a year. No email, no unique key, no way to log in. Meanwhile:

  • Names change (marriage, adoption, correction of a misspelling).
  • Names repeat. In a youth organization spanning decades, "Jan Novák" is many people.
  • Diacritics and transliterations vary across decades of manual entry (Novák / Novak).
  • Birth dates are often wrong by a digit, or recorded as year-only.
  • The same human appears in multiple rosters under slightly different spellings.

So: automatic matching will produce both false positives and false negatives. False positive (two people merged) is a privacy incident. False negative (one person split) is a data-quality annoyance. The design must therefore bias hard toward false negatives — never merge on a guess.

This document is about one half of a person. Everything it resolves is identity: the fields that make a row a particular human — names, birth date, the account, contact points, issued identifiers. Everything the organization records about that human beyond those is descriptive data, and it is deliberately absent from every table below: no descriptive value is a match signal, and none may become one. A clothing size or a dietary habit identifies nobody, and making matching depend on one would make the reliability of a person's history depend on what the organization happened to collect about them (08-person-data.md, D-085). The line between the two halves is drawn by what a machine may act on without a human, not by how delicate a fact feels; the test is stated in 08-person-data.md.

docs.title: 2. The three record classes
docs.text:
Every person row carries record_origin:

Origin Meaning Confidence Has account? self_registered A human created this by registering high yes staff_created A registrar entered this person high maybe legacy_import Imported from historical records low no

Legacy-imported people are provisional. They are fully queryable — "who was in Troop 12 in 1998" must work — but they are marked as unverified, they cannot be logged into, and they are the only rows eligible to be absorbed by a merge.

Rule: a merge always absorbs the lower-confidence row into the higher-confidence one. An import can never overwrite a self-registered person's data.

docs.title: 3. Identity hypotheses, not merges
docs.text:
The core mechanism. An identity hypothesis is a proposal that two person rows are the same human. It is a first-class table row, with a confidence score, evidence, a status, and a human decision.

The row holds the pair as person_a_id and person_b_id, stored in one order: person_a_id names the lower id, and the two are never the same person — a pair has one canonical spelling rather than two.

confidence is the matcher's score between 0 and 1; match_signals records which fields agreed and how strongly, which is what a reviewer reads to see why it was proposed. status is one of proposed, needs_review, confirmed, rejected, superseded. proposed_by says where the proposal came from — import_job, system, person or staff — and proposed_at when. reviewed_by, reviewed_at and review_note are the human part, and a hypothesis may not reach confirmed or rejected without a reviewed_at. At most one live hypothesis exists per pair — live means proposed, needs_review or confirmed.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
matcher proposes ──> proposed ──┬── staff confirms ──> confirmed ──> [merge executed]
                                  ├── staff rejects  ──> rejected (the pair becomes
                                  │                       proposable again — see §4)
                                  └── person asserts ──> needs_review → staff confirms/rejects

Two entry points:

  1. Import or background matching proposes hypotheses automatically at low confidence.
  2. A registering person asserts their own history — "I was a member 1990–2010" — which creates a hypothesis against the candidate rows, usually with proposed_by = 'person'.

A person's own assertion is evidence, not proof. It must still be reviewed, because claiming someone else's history is the obvious attack on an import-based system — and the prize is that person's data. Never auto-confirm a self-asserted link.

docs.title: 4. Match signals
docs.text:
The matcher scores candidate pairs on independent signals. Recorded in match_signals so a reviewer sees why the system proposed a match:

Signal Strength Notes Exact legacy member number decisive The corpus carries these (D-056). Same number, same person — matched, not scored. Exact birth date + exact normalised name strong Still not automatic — twins with similar names exist. Birth date within ±1 day or year-only match + name moderate Common with hand-written records. Name match after normalisation (diacritics, case, spacing) moderate Necessary but weak alone; "Jan Novák" is not unique. Same unit + overlapping membership period moderate Corroborating, not identifying. Same postal address at the same time moderate Strong if the address is distinctive. Read from person_contact history — there is no household table (D-057). Guardian name match weak Useful for minors in old records. Name-only fuzzy match weak — never sufficient alone

The decisive row changes the matcher's job. With a number on the record, the question is not "are these two the same person?" but "does this number already point somewhere?" — a lookup. The scored signals below are then for the rows the number cannot resolve: legacy records predating the numbering, records where the number is illegible, and people who were never issued one. At thousands of rows (D-056) this split is what makes D-004 affordable: the numbered rows are the trustworthy set and the rest is a work queue.

docs.title: Normalisation
docs.text:
Applied before comparison, and the normalised form is stored so matching is reproducible:

  • Unicode NFKD, strip diacritics, casefold, collapse whitespace.
  • Common nickname/legal-name equivalences (configurable per locale — Jan/Jano, Josef/Josip).
  • Typo distance (Levenshtein/Jaro-Winkler) above a threshold counts as a partial match, never a full one.

docs.title: Thresholds
docs.text:
• confidence < 0.60 — not surfaced. Stored only for diagnostics.
  • 0.60 ≤ confidence < 0.90 — proposed, queued for human review.
  • confidence ≥ 0.90 — still requires human confirmation, but flagged as high priority. There is no auto-merge threshold. A privacy incident from a bad merge is worse than any amount of manual review, and merges are irreversible in practice.

Assumption: you want no automatic merging at all, even for near-certain matches. If the volume of historical data makes that infeasible, an explicit opt-in auto-merge tier can be added — but it should be a deliberate decision, recorded in the decision log.

docs.title: 5. The merge operation
docs.text:
Merging is a soft merge: the absorbed row survives as a tombstone.

person (surviving, id=100)          person (absorbed, id=847, tombstoned)
        ▲                                     │
        │                                     ▼
        └────────── person_merge ────► merged_into_person_id = 100
                 (id, surviving_person_id, merged_person_id,
                  merged_at, merged_by, hypothesis_id, reason)

docs.title: What moves
docs.text: Table Action person_contact Reassigned to survivor. Conflicts (two is_primary of the same type) resolved by review, not by rule. person_identifier Reassigned. Duplicate scheme+value collapses to one. person_attribute Reassigned. Two current values for one code is a review item, never a choice made by rule — this table holds one value per person and code with no validity period to keep both, so unlike two past addresses a merge cannot leave the pair standing: the pair is raised as a field_conflict and a human decides, exactly as two is_primary contacts of one type are decided. Where the definition allows several values (allow_multiple), the two rows simply coexist and nothing is decided (../data-model/09-attributes.md §3). person_name Reassigned, keeping validity periods — this is how a maiden name survives. account Reassigned to survivor. If the survivor already has an account, the absorbed account is closed, not deleted. membership Reassigned. Overlapping periods flagged for review — with one type (D-037) and a person-level no-overlap rulet, an overlap here means a bad merge. unit_participation Reassigned, with the same overlap check. guardianship (as dependent) Reassigned. guardianship (as guardian) Reassigned. role_assignment, access_grant Reassigned. Union of permissions results — this is the security-critical step. person_merge Row inserted here. field_conflict Populated for anything that could not be resolved automatically.

docs.title: What does not happen
docs.text:
• Nothing is deleted. The absorbed person row keeps its id and gains merged_into_person_id. All historical foreign keys pointing at it still resolve, so "who was in Troop 12 in 1998" keeps working.
  • Overlapping memberships are never silently deduplicated. Two overlapping child memberships after a merge is suspicious — it may mean the merge was wrong. It becomes a review item.

docs.title: The security rule that must not be skipped
docs.text:
Merging unions the two people's permissions. If a bad merge is performed, the survivor gains the absorbed person's access. Therefore:

  1. A merge is always performed by a human with person.merge permission.
  2. The merged result's effective permissions are re-displayed for confirmation before the merge commits.
  3. Every merge is reversible via person_merge in the sense that the assignment can be moved back — but access_grant rows created during the merged period cannot be attributed. Hence rule 2.
  4. Merges invalidate cached permissions. See 06-authorization-model.md.

docs.title: 6. Reversing a merge
docs.text:
Support unmerge, because mistakes will happen. It is not symmetric — you cannot know which grants were exercised while merged — but you can restore the row split:

  1. Clear person.merged_into_person_id on the absorbed row. The tombstone comes off.
  2. Reassign rows created before merged_at back to the absorbed person.
  3. Flag rows created after merged_at for human review. Those are the ambiguous ones, and they are reviewed rather than split by a rule.
  4. Record the unmerge on the person_merge row, as reversed_at and reversed_by.

The access_grant rows are the specific hazard. Any grant created during the merged window might belong to either human. Flag every one of them; do not guess.

docs.title: 7. Legacy import pipeline
docs.text:
Staged, reviewed, idempotent. Never a direct write into live tables.

  source file(s)
       │
       ▼
  [1] staging_import          ── raw rows, verbatim, with the source file + line ref
       │
       ▼
  [2] staging_import_row      ── parsed: normalised name, parsed birth date,
       │                          detected unit, parse warnings
       ▼
  [3] matching                ── for each row, find candidate person rows and score them
       │
       ▼
  [4] review queue            ── human confirms: link to existing | create new | discard
       │
       ▼
  [5] apply                   ── writes person / membership / unit_participation
       │
       ▼
  [6] import_log              ── what was applied, by whom, when; reversal instructions

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Idempotent. Re-running the same import must not duplicate people. Each staged row carries a deterministic source_row_hash; re-import matches on it.
  • Reversible per batch. import_log records every row created or modified in a batch, so a bad batch can be rolled back without touching other data.
  • Never overwrites self-registered data. If a legacy row matches a self_registered person, the import may add historical memberships but never alters names, contacts, identifiers, or descriptive values the person maintains themselves.
  • Preserves provenance. Every imported row records import_batch_id and source_reference (file + line), so any value can be traced back to the paper it came from. When someone disputes a historical record, you can show them where it came from.
  • Records uncertainty rather than guessing. A row that cannot be parsed cleanly goes to the review queue with the raw value intact — it does not get a best-effort guess written as if it were fact.

docs.title: Raw columns become codes
docs.text:
The pipeline was drawn when a legacy column could only ever be a name, a date or a unit. Old rosters also carry columns about the person — a remarks column, a "medical" column, a list of shirt sizes — and each of those arrives at step [5] as a value against a code, not as a blob beside the record. Two consequences for staging, where the rest of the rules for this live (../data-model/09-attributes.md §7):

  • A raw column that maps to no code stops the batch, unless someone maps it or marks it discarded with a reason. An unmapped column is a decade of something the organization used to collect vanishing quietly, which is the class of failure the rest of this document exists to prevent on the identity side.
  • A column nobody recognises becomes a proposed code named from the column, never a guess at an existing code: an import-time merge is invisible and unreviewable, and the review queue above is for people, not for vocabulary. The column→code mapping is recorded once per batch, and changing it is curation with an audit entry rather than a migration.

docs.title: Historical memberships from imports
docs.text:
An imported roster row typically yields:

  • a person with record_origin = 'legacy_import'
  • a membership with valid_from = roster year start, valid_to = roster year end (or null if it was the last known roster and the member's status is unknown)
  • a unit_participation row linking them to the historical unit
  • data_confidence = 'low' on all of the above

What a 1998 roster actually tells you is participation, not membership. This is the one place the membership/participation split (D-041) really bites on legacy data, and it is worth being deliberate about rather than generating both rows by reflex:

The old record says It becomes Confidence "was in Pack 12 in 1998" unit_participation, 1998-01-01 → 1998-12-31 Reasonable — the roster is decent evidence of this "was a member in 1998" (a membership list, or a fee ledger) membership Good — a payment record is strong evidence "was in Pack 12 in 1998" with no fee evidence unit_participation and a membership marked data_confidence = 'low' Weak — this is an inference, and the discussion below applies

The temptation is to generate a membership for every roster row, because that is what the old data model implied. Do it, but mark it as inferred, because is_current_member() and the permission gate (D-039) both read membership, and an inferred membership from 1998 is harmless while an inferred membership row that runs to valid_to IS NULL would make someone a member today. The no-overlap rule makes this concrete, whatever ends up enforcing it: a person-level "one open membership" rule means the import must not leave an open membership for someone whose only evidence is a roster.

End dates are often unknown. For an imported member last seen in a 2003 roster, the membership should end at a defensible date — not left open, which would falsely make them a current member, and not guessed. Convention: end at the end of the school/organizational year of the last roster they appear in, marked as inferred. The participation row can be bounded the same way. Document the rule you choose; it will be questioned.

docs.title: 8. The returning-member case
docs.text:
The scenario you described — member 1990–2010, returns 2024 — should be the smooth path, because it is a common and important one (returning alumni become adult leaders and donors).

Flow:

  1. Person registers in 2024, self-asserting past membership.
  2. The system matches them against legacy rows and proposes hypotheses.
  3. A registrar reviews and confirms.
  4. The person's two memberships (1990–2010, 2024–present) now sit under one person row.
  5. Their profile shows their full history; the gap is explicit data.
  6. Any seniority or "years of service" calculation reads across both.

Steps 2–3 can be streamlined when the match is strong (exact old membership number), but the confirmation step remains, for the reason in §3.

docs.title: Self-service without weakening the guarantee
docs.text: Rather than auto-linking, give the person a claim flow: they assert a past membership, staff confirm. Record the assertion on the hypothesis row, so that if the claim later proves false, you can see it was self-asserted rather than discovered.

docs.title: 9. Open issues
docs.text:
• Volume and formats of historical data — determines whether manual review of every match is feasible, or whether a high-confidence tier is needed.
  • Whether the old system issued member numbers (would make §4's strongest signal available).
  • How much of an old roster becomes a membership and how much becomes participation (§7). This got harder when the two were split apart (D-041): the import must decide per record class, and an inferred membership running to today would make a 2003 roster member a current member under the permission gate.
  • Retention periods for members who request erasure — the shape is settled (redact the person, keep the financial and membership skeleton), but the durations need legal input. See ../open-questions.md.
  • Whether twins/siblings with similar names and the same birth date need a documented disambiguation procedure (recommend: yes, and never merge them automatically).

Resolved and no longer open, kept visible so the reasoning survives: the erasure mechanism (redact the person, keep the financial and membership skeleton) — only the retention durations remain open.

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Organization Structure
docs.text: Units, their types, their nesting, and — the part that is usually skipped — how to keep all of that true across four decades of reorganization.

docs.title: 1. One root, arbitrary sub-units
docs.text:
There is exactly one top-level unit: the organization itself. Everything else is a sub-unit nested beneath it, to arbitrary depth and in arbitrary combination — weekly meeting groups, smaller packs, sections, teams.

                    THE ORGANIZATION              ← the single root. depth 0.
                    ┌──────┴──────┬────────┐
                 Pack A        Pack B    Pack C      ← created by the organization
                ┌───┴───┐
          Thursday grp  Saturday grp                 ← created by the pack
              ┌───┴───┐
           Older  Younger                             ← arbitrary depth

This is not a ladder of levels. There is no fixed national → region → district → group → troop sequence, no required intermediate level, and no type that must appear at a particular depth. A sub-unit may contain sub-units to any depth, and the arrangement is the organization's business rather than the schema's.

docs.title: Membership lives at the root; participation lives in the sub-units
docs.text:
The distinction that makes this work:

Where it lives What it means Membership The root unit "This person is a member of the organization." Paid yearly. Participation Any sub-unit "This person takes part in this weekly group."

People register and pay at the organization, and their membership is theirs as a member of the organization — not a membership of a pack. The packs they attend are recorded separately, as participation (§5), because belonging to a Thursday-evening group and being a paid-up member of the organization are different facts with different lifetimes. See data-model/03-membership.md.

docs.title: Sub-units are self-governing
docs.text: A pack has its own events, its own local leadership, and its own roster. It is not an administrative subdivision of the root; it is a thing that runs itself and answers to the root. That is why authority originates at the unit and why the root cannot decide permissions inside a pack.

docs.title: Why one table, not pack/group/troop tables
docs.text:
• Depth is a data question, not a schema question. The organization invents and retires grouping arrangements; each one must be a row, not a migration.
  • "Who is in this pack and everything under it?" becomes one recursive query rather than a hand-written union across tables.
  • Units get renamed and renumbered constantly. A pack table would need rename history alongside; here a rename is one row in org_unit_name.

A unit row carries its unit_type_id — the organization type for the root, and otherwise whatever type the organization has defined; a parent_unit_id, absent only for the single root and immutable thereafter (§3); a short human code such as T12; the current display name; the period the unit existed, as valid_from and valid_to; and a status of proposed, active, merged or closed.

The single root is enforced structurally, not by convention: among all unit rows, at most one may have no parent. The rule counts every row rather than only the open ones, so a root that has closed does not make room for a second one.

docs.title: Why types are rows, not an enum
docs.text:
The unit vocabulary in a long-lived organization changes — a type that existed in 1995 may be gone, and a new one may be needed in 2027. An enum requires a deployment to change; an org_unit_type row does not.

This goes further than it used to: no sub-unit types are seeded at all (D-054). org_unit_type is runtime data, like role (D-052) — the seed carries the root type and nothing else, and the organization creates the types it uses. Earlier revisions seeded pack/group/team, and before that a national/region/district ladder; both were invented words that read as a specification. The words below are still used throughout these docs as illustration — "a pack may only sit directly under the root" is an example of a rule, not a type the system ships with.

A type row is a code and a name, plus allows_minors, is_leaf — may it contain sub-units — an optional max_depth ceiling, and a sort_order.

allows_minors is a safeguarding flag, not a membership rule: it lets the system validate that a unit which does not supervise minors never has any placed in it, without hardcoding which type codes those are. Membership itself is ageless — see ../decisions/decision-log.md.

docs.title: 2. Nesting rules
docs.text:
Because sub-units nest arbitrarily, the rules are permissive by default and express only the genuine constraints the organization wants to state. Most organizations need very few.

A rule pairs two types and answers one question about them: may a unit of parent_type_id contain a unit of child_type_id. max_children is an optional cap on how many it may contain. is_required asks the separate question — must a unit of the child type have a parent of the parent type at all.

A type with no rules at all is unconstrained. That is the default and it is deliberate: the organization is free to invent a new kind of group and nest it wherever it likes without asking the schema's permission first. Rules exist to constrain where the organization has decided it wants constraint — a pack may only sit directly under the root, say.

This is a table rather than a check constraint because nesting rules change over decades and because a constraint buried in code is invisible to the people configuring the organization.

Do not enforce nesting in the application layer only. A check clause cannot express it — the rule reads two tables and a history — and since D-072 the trigger that used to carry it is gone from these documents too, so the obligation has to be placed deliberately rather than assumed from a schema. Put it in a constraint or a check inside the writing transaction, at the migration layer, and expose the rules in an admin UI. If it is only validated by the form, a data import will violate it — which is not a hypothetical here: the legacy corpus is precisely a data import, arriving before the admin UI exists. See ../data-model/00-conventions.md §6a for which layer survives which kind of writer.

docs.title: 3. Unit names and renumbering — the history problem
docs.text:
A unit called "4th Pack" in 1998 may be "Pack 12" today, or may have been split into two, or merged into another. The system must answer both:

  • "What was this unit called in 2001?"
  • "Is this the same unit as the one in the 1998 roster?"

docs.title: Names are temporal rows
docs.text:
One row per name a unit has gone by: the name and code it carried, the period it carried them for, and a change_reason of rename, renumber, reorganisation or correction.

org_unit.name is a denormalised convenience holding the current name. The history lives here. Queries about the past read this table; they must never read org_unit.name.

docs.title: Renumbering is a rename, not a new unit
docs.text: When "4th Pack" becomes "Pack 12" and the participants stay, that is one unit with two name rows. Creating a new unit would orphan all the history and make "who was in Pack 12 in 1998?" answerable only by luck.

docs.title: Splits and mergers
docs.text:
These do create or close units:

The record of one names the source_unit_id and the target_unit_id, the relationship from one to the other — split_from, merged_into, successor_of or renamed_to — the effective_date, and a note.

A participation history must survive a split: when Pack 12 splits into Pack 12 and Pack 31, people who moved to 31 get a new unit_participation row starting at the split date, and their old row closes at the same date. No rows are rewritten. The org_unit_relationship row records that 31 came from 12, so a historical query can follow the lineage if asked.

Design rule: never rewrite a unit_participation to point at a different unit. Close it and open a new one. Rewriting destroys the answer to "where was this child in 2003?"

docs.title: A unit never changes parent
docs.text:
parent_unit_id is immutable. If a group genuinely transfers from one pack to another, the old unit closes and a new unit is created under the new parent, the people are moved across, and the lineage is recorded as an org_unit_relationship.

This is a significant simplification rather than a limitation:

  • The materialized path never needs a subtree cascade rewrite, so the dangerous operation disappears along with its danger.
  • Historical reports cannot silently change. "Who was in the 4th Pack in 2001?" keeps answering the same thing forever, because no unit's ancestry is ever edited.
  • Retroactive reparenting — the hard case — becomes unrepresentable rather than difficult.
  • scope_exposure rows cannot shift meaning under their authors. A reparent would move a unit in or out of a parent's reach, silently re-scoping rows nobody edited. It cannot happen, so it cannot be forgotten.

No write may change parent_unit_id on a row that already has one. Until D-072 this was a trigger; nothing in the docs carries it now, and unlike most such rules no report catches the violation either, because the damage is not a bad row, it is a set of previously-correct rows whose meaning moved. So this one needs a positive guard in the write path — reject the update, do not warn about it — and a test that attempts the update. See data-model/02-organization.md.

docs.title: 4. Positions
docs.text:
A position is a defined slot in a unit. A position assignment is a person filling it for a period. This split is what lets the system say "Pack 12 has no scoutmaster right now" and "this position has been vacant since March" — both operationally important, and neither expressible if positions only exist when filled.

A position is defined against a unit_type_id and carries a code — scoutmaster, assistant_leader, treasurer, quartermaster are the ordinary ones — a title, a max_holders, and requires_membership: must the holder be a current member.

An assignment joins three things and dates them: the position, the org_unit it is filled in, the person filling it, and the period. It also carries is_primary, because some people hold several positions; an appointment_reference to the appointment letter or record; and an ended_reason.

docs.title: Multiple people share one position
docs.text:
Several people may occupy the same position at the same time, and that is the default. A pack with three assistant leaders, two quartermasters, or a rotating team of instructors is ordinary, not exceptional.

position.max_holders is how a single-holder position is expressed — 1 for a scoutmaster, NULL (unlimited) for everything else. Two consequences worth being explicit about:

  • Multiple occupancy is the default, not an exception. max_holders is nullable, so a newly invented position accepts several holders without anyone declaring it. Single occupancy is the case that has to be stated.
  • The limit belongs to the position, not the hierarchy. A parent unit cannot declare that a nested unit has one scoutmaster. What positions a unit defines, and how many holders each admits, is that unit's own business — the same principle as authority over a unit originating at the unit.

The limit is enforced below the application — a constraint or a check inside the writing transaction — rather than in the form, because the limit lives on a different table and because max_holders > 1 cannot be expressed as a unique index. The reason this cannot wait for the ORM to work it out is the second clause: there is no declarative shape for "at most N open rows", so a generated schema silently has no limit at all, and the failure is invisible until two people hold the one chair. See ../data-model/02-organization.md.

A person may hold the same position in the same unit across separate periods — left in 2020, returned in 2024 — and both periods remain as distinct rows. Overlapping assignments of the same person to the same position are prevented; sequential ones are the point.

docs.title: Positions are not permissions
docs.text:
Holding the scoutmaster position does not by itself grant any system capability. The position is an organizational fact; authority comes from role_assignment. Keeping them separate means:

  • The organization's structure can be recorded completely, including for historical periods, without implying that a 1998 scoutmaster has system access today.
  • A vacant position and an unfilled role are different reports.
  • Changing what a scoutmaster can do in the system is a permission change, not a restructuring of the organization's records.

In practice a workflow will offer "appoint as scoutmaster" as one action that creates both a position_assignment and the corresponding scoped role_assignment. That is convenience; the schema stays separate.

docs.title: Eligibility
docs.text:
requires_membership handles the common rule that a leader must be a current member. Enforcing it as a database constraint is not possible (it depends on temporal membership state), so it is an application rule plus a periodic consistency report. Do not attempt to enforce it with a foreign key.

Note this is reported for positions but enforced for roles: the permission resolver itself checks membership state for roles that require it — see D-039 and §6.

docs.title: 5. Participation (unit_participation)
docs.text:
A sub-unit's roster is participation, not membership. These are different facts:

Membership Participation Of what The organization (the root unit) One sub-unit How many Exactly one at a time Zero or more, simultaneously Costs money Yes — the yearly fee No Ends when The fee is unpaid The person stops attending

A person may take part in a Thursday group, a weekend pack and a summer team at once, while holding a single membership. Moving between groups is one row edit and costs no membership.

A participation row is a person, an org_unit, and a period, with a join_reason_code and a leave_reason_code, an is_primary marking which group to show first, and a role_in_unit that is a display convenience and not an authorization fact — nothing in the permission model reads it.

A participation row is created for the root unit when the membership is created, so "everyone in unit X" is one uniform query whether X is the organization or a Thursday-evening pack. The schema detail is in data-model/03-membership.md.

docs.title: 6. Historical units
docs.text:
Units that closed must remain queryable. org_unit.status = 'closed' with valid_to set. They are excluded from pickers by default and included in historical reports always.

Two things to get right:

  1. A closed unit is not deleted. Historical unit_participation rows reference it, and "who was in the 4th Pack?" must work forever.
  2. Reopening reuses the row if it is genuinely the same unit, or creates a new one if the organization considers it a fresh start. This is an organizational judgement, not a technical one — record which was chosen and why on the unit, so the answer is not re-litigated every time someone asks about the 80s unit with the same number.

A unit that changes parent is a new unit (§3), so parent_unit_id is immutable and the historical answer to "where did this unit sit?" never changes retroactively.

docs.title: 7. Units and permissions
docs.text:
Units are a scope for authority. The same role assignment mechanism handles both organization-wide and unit-scoped authority:

An assignment names a person and a role, the scope it applies in, and the period. The scope is a scope_type of organization or org_unit, with scope_id absent for the former and a unit for the latter — the two always agree, and there is no third shape.

So "treasurer of the organization" and "treasurer of Pack 12" are the same table and the same role — differing only in scope_type/scope_id.

Authority does not flow down the hierarchy. This is the rule that most shapes the permission system, and it is stated in full in 06-authorization-model.md. In brief:

  • A role assignment at a unit covers that unit only.
  • A parent unit — including the organization itself — cannot decide permissions inside a nested unit.
  • But not everything is a nested unit's business. The person registry, the memberships and the fees belong to the root (D-035), so an organization-scoped role acting on them is working at its own scope. What a sub-unit owns is its own events, its own rosters, its own local leadership.
  • Authority crosses a unit boundary downward only where the unit itself has written an explicit scope_exposure row granting a specific role assignment coverage over it.
  • system_admin is the sole exception.

A permission check therefore matches the scope exactly, plus any explicit exposures. There is no ancestor walk in permission resolution. unit_ancestors() exists in the schema for reporting and for the exposure-direction check, but it must never appear in a permission path — see data-model/02-organization.md.

docs.title: Unit-scoped access grants
docs.text:
Beyond roles, a unit can be the target of an item-scoped grant: an access_grant whose scope type is org_unit, whose scope id is that unit, and whose level says how much.

This is how you grant someone authority over a unit's data without giving them an organization-wide role — a temporary administrator for one pack, for instance. Note the grant is written against the unit, and creating it requires access_grant.create held at that unit. A parent unit cannot create it.

The grantee may also be a set of people, rather than one person (D-042): access_grant.person_id and access_grant.audience_id are mutually exclusive. "Expose this event to everyone" or "to this pack's leaders" is one row with an audience — a rule the resolver evaluates against current state — rather than one row per person. This is what replaced the bulk scope-exposure tool (D-045), and it is why that tool had no remaining job.

docs.title: 8. Open issues
docs.text:
• The actual unit type vocabulary and nesting rules. Because nesting is permissive by default and one root is mandatory, this is now a much smaller question: which types exist, and which of the few genuine constraints does the organization want stated as rules.
  • Whether the root unit may see what happens in its sub-units without those sub-units exposing their scope — a reporting/audit question, not a permission-inheritance one. D-035 argues the root already owns the registry and the fees, so this is narrower than it first appears.
  • Whether is_leadership should automatically create a role_assignment, or only suggest it.

Resolved and no longer open, kept here so the reasoning is visible: the organizational structure itself (§1), retroactive reparenting (now prohibited — §3), unit types containing children (§1), and whether a person may belong to several units at once (yes, by participation — §5).

All tracked in ../open-questions.md.

docs.title: Membership Lifecycle
docs.text: Register → request → accept → pay → member. Plus the parts that are usually forgotten: gaps, returns, multiple periods, and renewal.

docs.title: 1. The flow you described
docs.text:
"The people can register on their own to get access to the system, however they become member only if they request a membership, they get accepted and pay a yearly fee."

Four distinct stages, each a separate record, because each can independently fail, stall, or be reversed:

Stage Record Can be reversed? What it means 1. Register person + account account can be closed "This person can log in." 2. Request membership_request yes — reject/withdraw "This person applied." 3. Accept membership_request.status = 'approved' yes — revoke before activation "The organization said yes." 4. Pay fee_obligation + payment refund "The obligation is met." 5. Activate membership opened yes — lapse/terminate "This person is a member."

Why stage 5 is separate from stage 3. Approval and activation are distinct because payment sits between them. A person can be approved and never pay; the organization needs to see that state ("approved, awaiting payment") to chase it, and it must not appear as a member.

Decided: membership activates on payment (D-040). membership opens at stage 5, and pending_payment is a real membership status so that "approved, awaiting payment" is a visible worklist rather than an invisible backlog.

docs.title: 2. Membership request
docs.text:
A request records the person it is for, the membership type asked for, and the unit the applicant would like — optional, because the organization may assign the unit at approval instead. status is one of draft, submitted, under_review, approved, rejected, withdrawn, expired, and submitted_at says when it went in. The review is carried on the same row: who took it up, when they decided, and on a rejection a rejection_reason_code with a free-text rejection_note beside it. When an approval produces a membership, membership_id is set to it.

An approved request points at the membership it produced; the link is not optional once the approval exists.

docs.title: Why a request is not a membership with a status
docs.text:
Tempting to collapse them, but:

  • A request can be rejected, producing no membership at all. A membership row with status rejected would pollute every "list members" query forever.
  • A person may submit several requests over time (rejected in 2024, approved in 2025). One table for both would need a request-version column and every query would need to filter it.
  • Requests carry review data (who reviewed, why, what was checked) that has no meaning on a membership.
  • Requests have different permissions: submitting is self-service; reviewing is a staff capability.

docs.title: There are no request requirements
docs.text:
Removed entirely (D-044). A request is accepted on identity and payment alone: no blocking checklist, no evidence collection, no waiver workflow, no requirement_code and no membership_request_requirement table.

Your answer, asked what a request must contain to be accepted: "Just identity and the fee — nothing to verify." The option to keep the mechanism as empty infrastructure for later was offered and not taken, which is the right call — a checklist that is always empty is a checklist nobody maintains, and it would have implied a gate that does not exist.

What this does not weaken. Two things that look like requirements are unaffected, because neither was a membership requirement to begin with:

  • Guardian consent for a minor's account is a fact about the guardianship relation, held in guardianship_permission, not a box ticked during an application (data-model/04).
  • Position eligibility — a scoutmaster must be an adult — is a property of the position (data-model/02 §7.1), not of membership. Membership is ageless (D-038).

And background checks do not exist in this system at all (D-043). If the organization introduces them, the home is a dated record with an expiry, and it belongs at the position-eligibility layer rather than the membership gate — a lapsed check is a reason someone may not hold a role, not a reason they stop being a member.

docs.title: 3. Membership
docs.text: A membership row belongs to one person and one membership type, and carries a status of pending_payment, active, lapsed, terminated, completed or suspended — always chosen deliberately, never defaulted. The period is valid_from and valid_to, and an absent valid_to means the period is still open: it is the current membership, not a row someone forgot to close. joined_via_request_id records the request it came out of, termination_reason_code the reason it was ended, data_confidence is high, medium or low — legacy imports are low — and import_batch_id is set on imported rows and on nothing else.

docs.title: Overlap rules — the invariant that matters
docs.text:
A person must not hold two open memberships at the same time, and the rule is enforced by the database rather than by application code. Its precise statement is in data-model/03-membership.md §3; what it says, in words:

  • Two membership periods of one person may not cover the same date while either of them is pending_payment, active or suspended. Those three statuses are the whole of the rule's reach — a lapsed row, a terminated one and a completed one are outside it, which is why an ending period and a later beginning one sit beside each other without complaint.
  • Periods are half-open, so a membership ending on 30 June and another opening on 30 June do not collide.

The constraint used to be scoped to membership_type_id, because a person might legitimately be an honorary and an adult member at once. With one membership type (D-037) that escape hatch is gone, and the constraint becomes the clean person-level invariant: one person, one open membership, ever. The type column was what made "am I a paid-up member?" a hard question; now it is one row, one status, one date (D-041).

Assumption: btree_gist is available (PostgreSQL), because a temporal overlap is the one rule that can only be refused during the write that would create it. If the target database cannot express exclusion constraints, the fallback is a check inside the writing transaction plus the nightly consistency report — one of the strongest guarantees in the model degrading into the weakest class (data-model/00 §6a, open question F-10 shape 1): an application-level count is wrong exactly when two writers run at once, which is when an overlap is actually created, and the report finds it a day later in a form nobody can attribute. So it is not merely "weaker" and must be recorded as an accepted risk, chosen deliberately, rather than discovered in a migration tool's limitations.

docs.title: There is one membership type, and membership is ageless
docs.text:
A type row is a code and a name, four calendar values, and a sort_order. The calendar values start at twelve months' duration, expiry_month 1 and expiry_day 1 — the fee expires on 1 January (D-047) — and renewal_grace_days 60, which is the renewal window and not a status (D-048).

Seeded with exactly one row, member (D-037). Everything the old type carried — category, min_age, max_age, requires_background_check, requires_guardian_consent, fee_schedule_id — is gone, and what is left is the two parameters a period needs: how long it lasts, and how long after it the person may renew without re-applying. The fee itself is not a property of the type at all: it is a flat per-person amount that lives on fee_schedule and is snapshotted onto each obligation, so "what did we charge in 1998?" is answered from the obligation, not the type.

Membership is ageless (D-038). No age floor, no age ceiling, no age-out, no child→adult transition. Age survives as a fact about a person (person.birth_date) and matters where the law makes it matter: guardianship, safeguarding, and position eligibility (§7 was the age-transition section — there is no longer a §7). Being a counselor or a leader is a position, never a membership type.

docs.title: 4. Multiple memberships over a lifetime
docs.text:
This is your 1990–2010 / 2024–present case. It is not an edge case; it is the normal shape of a long-lived organization's data.

person 100 — Jan Novák
  ├── membership #1   member   1990-09-01 → 2010-06-30   terminated  (left)
  │     └── unit_participation   Pack 12  1990-09-01 → 1998-06-30
  │     └── unit_participation   Pack 31  1998-09-01 → 2010-06-30
  ├── (gap 2010 → 2024 — 14 years, no membership rows)
  └── membership #2   member   2024-10-01 → NULL          active
        └── unit_participation   Group 5  2024-10-01 → NULL
        └── position_assignment  scoutmaster, Group 5  2025-01-01 → NULL

Note what the two membership rows now share: the same type. They differ only in their period and their end reason. In the original framing this person was a child member and then an adult member; in this one they were a member, twice, and were a child and then an adult the whole time. The second framing is the true one, and it is why the memorable case still works: the person never changed, and neither did the type — only the period did.

Everything the system needs follows from this:

  • "Is this person a member?" → is there a membership with valid_to IS NULL (or covering today) and status = 'active'?
  • "How long have they been a member?" → sum of membership period lengths, not today − first join date. The gap must not count.
  • "How old were they when they joined?" → membership #2.valid_from − person.birth_date.
  • "Are they an adult?" → is_minor(person_id), computed from person.birth_date. In 2005 the same query said yes. The membership row is identical either way; only the person's birth date and today's date moved.

Never store is_member, member_since, member_type, or is_child on person. Every one of those is derivable, and every one of them will be wrong the moment history is corrected or a person returns.

docs.title: 5. Transitions and who can perform them
docs.text:
From To Trigger Permission required — draft person starts an application own draft submitted person submits membership.request.create (own, or the guardianship channel at write for a guardian — D-074) submitted under_review reviewer picks it up membership.request.review under_review approved reviewer approves membership.request.approve under_review rejected reviewer rejects membership.request.approve any withdrawn applicant withdraws own, or guardian with permission approved membership pending_payment approval processed system pending_payment active payment confirmed system (or fee.record for manual) active lapsed fee unpaid past the organization's expiry date membership.lapse or the yearly sweep active terminated disciplinary / cause membership.terminate — separate, more restricted permission active suspended temporary hold membership.suspend
