1. Only preference-level detail belongs on a form. A dietary preference ("vegetarian", "no pork") is an operational note for the cook. A condition ("coeliac", "nut allergy") is medical data, and nothing in the schema distinguishes them — the difference is what the organizer types into a label. So the discipline is in the form design, not the constraint: data-model/08 §7 states it, and it is guidance, not enforcement.

2. This is the route by which a leader learns a child has a nut allergy, and that is a deliberate widening. A guardian's reach over a child is one value on the guardianship row — none, view or write — read by a channel of its own, entered only when the act is about someone other than the actor and never answered by a role or a grant (D-074, D-079; appendix/permission-catalog.md §9). The namespace that used to spell this out is deleted, the safeguarding property it carried is not:

"A unit leader does not get these by virtue of leading the unit — that is a safeguarding property."

Corrected in round 7, because this sentence was doing work it could no longer do. It used to read "so a camp leader cannot reach a child's medical record at all" — and after D-083 there is no medical record to be unreachable, so the sentence is not merely out of date, it describes a guarantee the model never had once the category disappeared. What is actually true, in the two forms that matter:

  • No role gets it by leading. The starting role set gives a unit_leader their unit's roster, positions and events — and no read over a person's data (permission-catalog §11). That is the safeguarding property, exactly as before: leadership is not guardianship, and the guardianship channel answers only for the person its row names.
  • It is now one grant away, deliberately. Whoever holds person.view over a child's unit reads the whole record, allergy list included. Nothing in the resolver will stop that and nothing should — but a document that promised it was impossible would have been trusted, and a promise the model does not make is worse than none.

**The widening in the next paragraph is therefore unchanged in substance and better stated: the protection is a decision about a role, revisitable by whoever administers roles, not a wall."

Which means: under the starting roles, an allergy recorded on a camp form is the only way the people running the camp will know. That is a coherent and defensible configuration — the parent tells the people present, per event, and nobody outside the family holds the fact — but it is a widening from "few people, via a guardianship-scoped permission" to "every organizer of any event the child registers for", and it is recorded as such in D-061, with the reasoning, so that nobody later "fixes" the apparent duplication between the two stores by tightening this one.

Event answers are not the person's record. They are operational detail for one event, read by that event's organizers, and they end with the event — while the same fact, recorded on the person, is audited, curable and erased with them. D-083 made those two copies the same class of data, which is what turns the retention question below into a real one, and AT-1 into the alternative: collect the fact once, confirm it at the door. See §11 for the retention question, which is open.

docs.title: 13. Open issues
docs.text:
Moved to ../open-questions.md under G. Events, where they are tracked with the rest. The ones this module raises:

  • ~~The age ceiling on an open event~~ — settled: accepted as a risk, the grant is the rule, and closing it later would mean a new audience rather than a column (§4, D-070).
  • Event answer retention (§12). Answers end with the event — but a dietary answer naming a condition is data of exactly the same class as what the person record holds, held under weaker rules and fresher. No policy yet; see EV-2.
  • Cancelled events and fees (§10–11). Cancelling keeps the registrations; whether it releases the obligations, refunds them, or neither is the finance module's call.
  • Presence for minors and the safeguarding record (§9). was_present is the "who was in our care" record. Whether it needs its own retention or its own permission is unresolved.
  • Whether organizers should be an access_grant after all (§5–6). The rule in §6 makes the unit's roles reach its events; if the organization would rather organizers be opt-in per event, that is one clause to change.

docs.title: Domain — Personal Data
docs.text:
What the system knows about a person, why it is all one kind of thing, and what that choice costs. The tables are in ../data-model/09-attributes.md; the reasoning is D-083, D-084 and D-085.

This module began as "design the health records module". It ended as this, because the first question — what is a health record here — turned out to have a much larger answer than the one the question was expecting.

docs.title: 1. One class of data, and no privileged corner
docs.text:
Asked how to protect medical data, the answer given was that everything about a person apart from their name, their gender and their age is medical data, stored in fields rather than files — and that medical data is not different in any way.

Read as a scoping decision it removes the category the module was supposed to be about. There is no special shelf inside the person record, no code list whose names begin with something clinical, no access path that exists only for the sensitive part. A drug dosage, a preferred contact language and a shoe size are the same kind of fact: something the organization wrote down about somebody, which will be out of date in three years, which nobody could have enumerated when the schema was designed.

The consequence is uncomfortable and intended: the permission that reads a person's record now reads everything in it. A volunteer with that permission sees the allergy list and the insurance number and the note about who in the family the child actually lives with. That is not an accident of implementation, it is what "not different in any way" means, and it is why the catalog marks reading a person as one of the serious permissions in the system rather than an ordinary one.

docs.title: The three exceptions, and why they are exceptions
docs.text:
Name, gender and age stay structured, in the identity model (../domain/03-identity-and-legacy.md). Not because they are less sensitive — a name is the most persistent piece of data here — but because they answer a different question. They are what a person is called and counted as; everything else is what the organization happens to have noticed. The three are also the only descriptive facts that have been stable across every system this organization has used, which is the practical test for whether something earns a column.

The boundary between "identity machinery" and "descriptive data" is drawn by a harsher test than sensitivity, and it is worth stating plainly because it is the test a reviewer will want to argue with: a fact keeps its own table when there is a rule about it that an open layer cannot express. "Exactly one primary postal contact", "a school id may repeat but a birth number may not", "one current name" — those rules need a known set of columns, and an open layer's whole value is that it has none.

docs.title: 2. The vocabulary is the system
docs.text:
If the organization decides at runtime what it collects, then the list of things it collects is the part of the design that matters. The tables are trivial; the vocabulary is not.

An open vocabulary left open decays the same way every open vocabulary does. Within months there will be allergy, Allergy, alergie, and allergies (2), each with some of the values, and after that the layer still stores everything and answers nothing — which is the single thing an attribute layer exists to avoid. Three defences, none clever:

  • Codes are compared in normalized form, so the obvious duplicates are refused rather than filed.
  • Recording a value is open; naming a thing is not. Anyone who can edit a person can write down what the doctor said tonight. Creating a code — deciding that this is now a thing the organization knows about people — takes a permission and a person who reads what they are given.
  • An improvised need becomes a proposal, not a workaround. The failure this is aimed at is specific and familiar: at 23:00 on a Friday, there is no field for "carries an adrenaline auto-injector", so the leader types it into a notes box, and it is never read by anyone again. A proposal is visible, queued and curable; a notes box is neither.

Curation is a job, and the documents say so rather than assuming it happens. An unwatched proposal queue is the same information loss arriving slowly instead of all at once (../data-model/09-attributes.md §8).

docs.title: 3. Who needs to know what
docs.text:
Who What they need What the design gives them A unit leader The allergies and instructions for the children in their unit, tonight, without asking permission Whatever the organization has granted them, and nothing more. The starting role set gives a leader their unit's roster and events but not a read over the child's record — that is a deliberate choice about a role, not a wall in the model, and granting person.view on the unit hands over the entire record including the allergy list. See the paragraph below the table A guardian Everything about their child, or nothing, depending on what the organization decided The guardian right level — none, view, write — over the whole record (D-074) The person themselves Their own data Their own record, which is not a special case in the resolver — "about you" is already a channel An event organizer What matters on the day, for the people who registered The registration, and the event form that asks. Where the organization already recorded a fact, AT-1 asks whether the form should prefill from it rather than re-asking every camper every season A first aider at a camp The short list: what is this child allergic to, what do they take, what should we do The values are fields, so a list can be produced. This is the argument for fields over documents, and it is the reason "files" was rejected in the answer that started this module

The leader row carries the sharpest edge in this module, and it should be read twice. Before round 7 the corpus asserted that a leader cannot reach a child's medical information — which was argued from a namespace that no longer exists, then from the absence of an event.* code, and is now simply not a property of the model: there is no privileged subset to be kept away from anybody. What remains is the same decision wearing its honest clothes — the starting roles do not give leadership a read over the record, because leadership is not guardianship — plus the fact that the organization may hand it over deliberately, in one grant, and see exactly what that exposes. That is a better position than a guarantee nobody could have configured away, and a worse one than the documents used to claim (permission-catalog §11 note 3).

The last row is the one that justifies the whole shape. A scanned form in a drawer is a legally tidy answer and a useless one at 23:00 in a tent; the fact has to be something a screen can show somebody who is not thinking clearly.

docs.title: 4. What was refused, and what it cost
docs.text:
The granular medical file, refused on the merits. Every previous design of this system carried a way to restrict one person's access to the medical part of a child's record while leaving the rest. Its justification was always a story about a court order. That story was put to you directly and declined: a guardian's rights are what the guardian's permission says; medical data is not different (E-7, closed).

What is genuinely lost. A system that cannot say "everything except the diagnoses" cannot express an arrangement a court might actually order. It will instead express it as a guardian who either has the record or does not, and somebody will have to explain the difference to a parent. The trade made is that the current model fails visibly — one decision, in one place, audited — while the granular model fails quietly, because a list of eighteen ticks nobody read is not a safeguard, it is a receipt. If the case ever arrives in reality, the route back is one new grant scope over a defined set of data, argued once as a decision, and not a fresh namespace of suggestive permission names.

The per-field type wall, refused deliberately. A field declared as a date warns when someone types 2019, and lets them save it. The wall is the wrong tool precisely in the cases that matter most to health data, where the true value is imprecise and the imprecise answer is better than no answer: probably allergic to wasp stings, mother thinks it was only once is a fact worth keeping, and a validation error would discard it in favor of an empty field.

The narrow one: no history on the row. Values are overwritten and the audit trail holds the sequence — holds the values themselves, not a note that something changed, since a trail that will not say what changed cannot serve as a history and the trade below would be a lie. Elsewhere the model keeps history in business tables when the question "what was it on that date?" is routine — guardianship is the standing example. Here it is not routine; it is what someone asks during an incident. So the history of a child's allergy list lives in the one control these documents elsewhere admit is now discipline rather than guarantee (D-081), and it lives there in two dependencies, not one: somebody has to write the audit row, on every path including the ones nobody thinks of, and somebody has to keep the trail guarded as the copy of the whole person record that it is. That is a real risk, accepted in the open rather than discovered later, and D-085 is the entry to reverse if it ever bites.

docs.title: 5. Forgetting
docs.text:
Two operations that look alike and must not be confused.

  • Retiring a thing the organization collects keeps what was collected. The label leaves the form; the values stay readable and reportable, and the label can come back. Deleting a name must not delete nine years of facts, or nobody will ever retire a badly-named thing and the list will only ever grow.
  • Erasing a person deletes what was collected, everywhere, including in the trail's payloads. The organization keeps that it held a record and that it was removed — and not what the record said.

Between them sits the rule that changed twice in one round, and the second change is the one to keep.

The audit trail carries these values, in the clear, because it is the only place they have a history. What changed is not what the trail holds but who may read it: an entry about a person is as sensitive as the person data it quotes, so the permission that opens the trail sits with the serious permissions rather than among the administrative ones (permission-catalog §8). The trail used to scrub a list of sensitive field names, which made sense while there was a sensitive subset and became incoherent the moment there was not — a list of names is only as good as somebody having predicted the name of every field that would matter, and this organization invents those names at runtime. An interim draft of these documents responded by refusing to log descriptive values at all, and that was withdrawn: it put medical-shaped fields in a stricter class than a change of address, which is the privileged corner this module exists to have deleted, and it left the history empty, which is the thing D-085 was chosen for. The protection is the guard. It is one line in one table of one appendix, and the documents say so where they describe it (../data-model/09-attributes.md §6).

What erasure does is absolute in a way the guard is not. It deletes the values and reaches into the trail to delete them again from copies written years earlier, lawfully, when nobody was asking questions about them.
